Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

• ••Introduction••
	• The text is a translation of Francis Turretin's "Institutes of Elenctic Theology"
	• The translation was done by George Musgrave Giger and edited by James T. Dennison, Jr.
	• The book is a comprehensive work on Reformed theology, covering various topics and doctrines
• ••Turretin's Life and Work••
	• Francis Turretin was a Swiss Reformed theologian born in 1623
	• He wrote "Institutes of Elenctic Theology" in three volumes, published between 1680 and 1685
	• The book is considered a classic in Reformed theology and has been widely influential
• ••Theology and Its Divisions••
	• Turretin discusses the nature and scope of theology, including its divisions and branches
	• He argues that theology is a rational and systematic study of God and divine things
	• Turretin rejects the idea that natural theology is sufficient for salvation
• ••The Object of Theology••
	• Turretin affirms that God and divine things are the primary objects of theology
	• He argues that theology is concerned with the knowledge of God and His attributes
	• Turretin rejects the idea that human reason is the sole principle and rule for theology
• ••The Genus of Theology••
	• Turretin discusses the genus of theology, including its theoretical and practical aspects
	• He argues that theology is both theoretical (concerned with knowledge) and practical (concerned with action)
	• Turretin rejects the idea that human reason has no use in matters of faith
• ••The Use of Consequences••
	• Turretin argues that the doctrines of faith and practice can be proved by consequences drawn from Scripture
	• He rejects the idea that theology can only be proved by the express word of God
	• Turretin affirms the use of philosophy in theology
• ••Fundamental Articles and Errors••
	• Turretin discusses the distinction between fundamental and non-fundamental theological topics
	• He argues that some topics are essential to the Christian faith, while others are not
	• Turretin rejects the idea that errors in theology can be tolerated or ignored
• ••The Holy Scriptures••
	• Turretin discusses the nature and authority of the Holy Scriptures
	• He argues that the Scriptures are truly authentic and divine
	• Turretin affirms the necessity of Scripture for salvation and the Christian life
• ••The Word of God••
	• Turretin discusses the nature and necessity of verbal revelation
	• He argues that a verbal revelation was necessary for the salvation of humanity
	• Turretin rejects the idea that the word of God can be committed to writing without divine command
• ••The Authority of the Holy Scriptures••
	• Turretin affirms the authority and divine inspiration of the Holy Scriptures
	• He argues that the Scriptures are the ultimate authority for Christian doctrine and practice
	• Turretin rejects the idea that the authority of the Scriptures can be questioned or doubted

Here are the 21 points with sub-bullets:

••I. Real Contradictions in Scripture••

• Do real contradictions occur in Scripture?
	• We deny
• Are there any inexplicable passages which cannot be explained and made to harmonize?
	• We deny

••II. Divine Authority of Scripture••

• From what source does the divine authority of the Scriptures become known to us?
	• We deny dependence on the testimony of the church
• Does it depend on the testimony of the church either as to itself or as to us?
	• We deny

••III. The Canon••

• Has any canonical book perished?
	• We deny
• Are the books of the Old Testament still a part of the canon of faith and rule of practice in the church of the New Testament?
	• We affirm against the Anabaptists

••IV. Apocryphal Books••

• Ought Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Ecclesiasticus, the two first books of the Maccabees, Baruch, the additions to Esther and Daniel to be numbered among the canonical books?
	• We deny against the papists

••V. Purity of the Sources••

• Have the original texts of the Old and New Testaments come down to us pure and uncorrupted?
	• We affirm against the papists

••VI. Authentic Version••

• Are the Hebrew version of the Old Testament and the Greek of the New Testament the only authentic versions?
	• We affirm against the papists
• Is the present Hebrew text in things as well as words so authentic and inspired that all extant versions are to be referred to it as a rule and, wherever they vary, to be corrected by it?
	• We affirm
• May we desert the reading it supplies, if judged less appropriate, and correct it either by a comparison of ancient translators or by suitable judgment and conjecture and follow another more suitable reading?
	• We deny

••VII. Versions••

• Are versions necessary, and what ought to be their use and authority in the church?
	• (No sub-bullet)

••VIII. The Septuagint••

• Is the Septuagint version of the Old Testament authentic?
	• We deny

••IX. The Vulgate••

• Is the Vulgate authentic?
	• We deny against the papists

••X. Perfection of the Scriptures••

• Do the Scriptures so perfectly contain all things necessary to salvation that there is no need of unwritten traditions after it?
	• We affirm against the papists

••XI. Perspicuity of the Scriptures••

• Are the Scriptures so perspicuous in things necessary to salvation that they can be understood by believers without the external help of oral tradition or ecclesiastical authority?
	• We affirm against the papists

••XII. Reading of the Scriptures••

• Can the Scriptures be profitably read by any believer, and ought he to read them without permission?
	• We affirm against the papists

••XIII. Sense of the Scriptures••

• Whether the Scriptures have a fourfold sense: literal, allegorical, anagogical, and tropological?
	• We deny against the papists

••XIV. Supreme Judge of Controversies••

• Whether the Scriptures (or God speaking in them) are the supreme and infallible judge of controversies and the interpreter of the Scriptures?
	• We affirm
• Or whether the church or the Roman pontiff is?
	• We deny against the papists

••XV. Authority of the Fathers••

• Are the writings of the fathers the rule of truth in doctrines of faith and in the interpretation of the Scriptures?
	• We deny against the papists

••XVI. The One and Triune God••

• Can the existence of God be irrefutably demonstrated against atheists?
	• We affirm
• Are there any atheists properly so called?
	• We deny

••XVII. Unity of God••

• Is God one?
	• We affirm against the heathen and Tritheists

••XVIII. Name of God••

• Is his name so peculiar to God alone as to be incommunicable to creatures?
	• We affirm against the Socinians

••XIX. Divine Attributes••

• Can the divine attributes be really distinguished from the divine essence?
	• We deny against the Socinians

••XX. Distinction of Attributes••

• Is the distinction of attributes into communicable and incommunicable a good one?
	• We affirm

••XXI. Simplicity of God••

• (No sub-bullet)

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

• ••The Nature of God••
	• Is God most simple and free from all composition? (affirmed)
	• Is God infinite in essence? (affirmed)
	• Is God immense and omnipresent as to essence? (affirmed)
• ••The Eternity of God••
	• Does the eternity of God exclude succession according to priority and posteriority? (affirmed)
• ••The Immutability of God••
	• Is God immutable both in essence and will? (affirmed)
• ••The Knowledge of God••
	• Do all things fall under the knowledge of God, both singulars and future contingencies? (affirmed)
• ••The Will of God••
	• Does God will some things necessarily and others freely? (affirmed)
	• Can the will of God be properly distinguished into different types (e.g. will of decree, will of precept)? (affirmed)
• ••The Justice of God••
	• Is vindictive justice natural to God? (affirmed)
• ••The Goodness, Love, Grace, and Mercy of God••
	• How do these attributes differ from each other? (not specified)
• ••The Power of God••
	• What is the omnipotence of God, and does it extend to things that imply a contradiction? (denied)
• ••The Holy Trinity••
	• Is the mystery of the Trinity a fundamental article of faith? (affirmed)
	• In the one divine essence are there three distinct persons: the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit? (affirmed)
• ••Predestination••
	• Ought predestination to be publicly taught and preached? (affirmed)
	• Is the fixed and immovable end of life determined by the decree of God? (affirmed)

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

• ••Predestination of Angels••
	• The predestination of angels is affirmed
	• The predestination of men is denied
• ••Object of Predestination••
	• The object of predestination is not man as creatable or capable of falling, but rather as created and fallen
	• The object of predestination is not man's potential, but rather his actual state
• ••Cause of Election••
	• Christ is not the cause and foundation of election
	• Election is not made from the foresight of faith or works, but from the grace of God alone
• ••Certainty of Election••
	• The election of certain men to salvation is constant and immutable
	• The believer can be certain of their own election with an infallible and faith-based certainty
• ••Reprobation••
	• The decree of reprobation is absolute and depends on the good pleasure of God alone
	• Sin is not the proper cause of reprobation
• ••Will of God••
	• The will of God is not to save persevering believers and condemn the unbelieving
	• The will of God is not a conditional will or universal purpose of pitying the whole human race
• ••Order of Divine Decrees••
	• There is no order to be admitted in the divine decrees
	• The divine decrees are not subject to a temporal or causal relationship
• ••Creation••
	• The ability to create is not communicable to any creature
	• The world was not created from eternity or could have been
• ••Creation of Man••
	• Man was created in a state of original righteousness
	• Original righteousness is natural, not supernatural
• ••Immortality of the Soul••
	• The soul is immortal in virtue of its intrinsic construction
	• The soul is not mortal in nature and condition
• ••Origin of the Soul••
	• Souls are created by God, not propagated
	• Souls are not generated from parents, but created by God

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••Is Providence Occupied Only in Conversation and Sustentation?••
	• The authors deny this, affirming that Providence is also involved in the government of things.
	• They argue that God acts and concurs with things through a particular, specific, and immediate concourse.

â€¢ ••The Concourse of God••
	• The authors affirm that God concurs with second causes through a particular and simultaneous concourse.
	• They also affirm that God's concourse is not limited to simultaneous action, but also involves a previous concourse.

â€¢ ••Reconciling God's Concourse with Human Liberty••
	• The authors acknowledge the challenge of reconciling God's concourse with human liberty and contingency.
	• They do not provide a clear solution to this problem.

â€¢ ••The Providence of God in Evil••
	• The authors deny that sins fall under Providence, and argue that God is not the author of sin.
	• They also deny that their doctrine implies that God is the author of sin.

â€¢ ••The Use and Abuse of the Doctrine of Providence••
	• The authors acknowledge that the doctrine of Providence can be used and abused.
	• They do not provide further guidance on how to avoid abuse.

â€¢ ••Angels••
	• The authors affirm that angels are spiritual and incorporeal substances.
	• They also affirm that angels have knowledge, will, and power.

â€¢ ••The Ministry of Angels••
	• The authors deny that a particular angel is assigned as a perpetual guardian to each believer.
	• They also deny that angels are our intercessors with God or worthy of worship.

â€¢ ••The State of Man Before the Fall••
	• The authors affirm that Adam had the power to believe in Christ.
	• They also affirm that Adam had the promise of eternal and heavenly life.

â€¢ ••The Covenant of Nature••
	• The authors affirm that God made a covenant with Adam, which was a natural covenant.
	• They also affirm that this covenant was not a covenant of works.

â€¢ ••Sin in General and in Particular••
	• The authors affirm that the formal reason of sin consists in illegality (anomia).
	• They also deny that the hekousion (voluntary) is of the essence of sin.

	• The doctrine of original sin is affirmed
	• Original sin is propagated to us by generation

	• The nature of free will in a state of sin is debated
	• The papists, Socinians, and Remonstrants are opposed on this issue
• ••Virtues of the Heathen••
	• The virtues of the heathen are considered
	• The papists are opposed on this issue

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••Translation Approach••
	• The translation is literal and faithful to the original
	• The translator, Giger, adhered strictly to Turretin's style
	• The translation preserves the scholastic style, including awkward phrasing and bulky subordinate clauses

â€¢ ••Scholastic Latin Terms••
	• Readers can refer to Richard A. Muller's Dictionary of Latin and Greek Theological Terms for aid in understanding Turretin's technical vocabulary
	• The "Glossary" compiled by Richard McKeon is also a useful resource

â€¢ ••Editorial Work••
	• The editor has attempted to preserve the fidelity of Giger's translation while improving readability
	• Sentences have been shortened, parentheses added, and archaic phrases revised

â€¢ ••Text Editions••
	• The translation is based on the 1847 Edinburgh/New York edition
	• This edition is a reprint of the 1688-90 version with corrections in a few Scripture citations

â€¢ ••Text Variations••
	• The 1679-85 version was reprinted in 1680-86 and 1682-88
	• The 1696 reprint included the encomium of Melchoir Leydekker and the ode of Adrian Reeland

â€¢ ••Scripture Quotations••
	• All Scripture quotations have been checked and corrected where necessary
	• Scripture quotations are based on the King James Version

â€¢ ••Bibliographical Data••
	• The editor has attempted to provide full bibliographical data for Turretin's citations
	• This includes references to classical authors, early church fathers, and other sources

â€¢ ••Turretin's Style••
	• Turretin frequently cites Scripture passages by chapter only
	• The editor has attempted to provide the appropriate verses of the chapter from the context of Turretin's remarks

â€¢ ••Readability••
	• The editor has attempted to improve readability while remaining faithful to Giger's English and Turretin's Latin

â€¢ ••Subjectivity••
	• Some of the editorial work is subjective, based on the editor's judgment of readability
	• The editor has attempted to remain faithful to the spirit of Giger's English and Turretin's Latin

• ••Verification of Quotations••
	• The author has verified over 1,000 quotations from other authors in Turretin's work.
	• Online bibliographical databases, indexes, and concordances were used for verification.
	• The author cooperated with numerous libraries to examine Turretin's citations.
• ••Citation Process••
	• Citations were incorporated into the body of the text, not relegated to footnotes.
	• Corrections of Turretin's citations are indicated by an •.
	• Typesetting mistakes may have contributed to errors in Turretin's citations.
• ••Dictionary of Personalities••
	• A dictionary catalogue of personalities was created, containing over 1,000 individuals.
	• The dictionary includes first name, last name, alternate names, dates of birth and death, and references to a dictionary or encyclopedia.
• ••Citation Identification••
	• The author has identified over 96 of Turretin's citations.
	• About 4 of citations remain unidentified (indicated by a •).
	• In some cases, the author was unable to identify the work Turretin is citing.
• ••Citation Entry••
	• Citations were entered in a way that accurately locates Turretin's quotation.
	• Sometimes, additional information about book, chapter, and section was provided.
• ••Greek and Hebrew Words••
	• Greek and Hebrew words and phrases were transliterated according to a table in the front of the volume.
	• Turretin used only unpointed Hebrew expressions, which the author has followed.
• ••Abbreviations••
	• Abbreviations for series, frequently cited works, books of the Bible, etc. will be found in the table of abbreviations.

	• The publication of the Institutio will take three volumes.

• ••Turretin's Dedication••
	• Turretin dedicates his work to the noble men of the Senate of Geneva.
	• He praises the city of Geneva for its many blessings, including its religion and liberty.
• ••Geneva's Blessings••
	• Turretin notes that Geneva is a small city, but one that has received many gifts from God.
	• He highlights the city's two greatest glories: its religion and its liberty.
• ••Geneva's Unique Status••
	• Turretin compares Geneva to other cities, noting that it is a "Goshen" where the sun of righteousness shines.
	• He contrasts Geneva with the "Egypt" of the world, which is shrouded in darkness and error.
• ••Turretin's Praise••
	• Turretin praises Geneva for its unique status as a city where the divine dayspring is adored.
	• He notes that Christ is the sun and shield of the city, providing protection and blessing.
• ••Argument for Celebrating Providence••
	• Turretin argues that Geneva's blessings provide a just argument for celebrating the providence of God.
	• He notes that the city's glories are a testament to God's amazing work in its midst.
• ••Conclusion••
	• The author concludes by expressing gratitude to those who have helped with the project.
	• He also expresses praise for the city of Geneva and its many blessings.

â€¢ ••The Legacy of Geneva's Pious Ancestors••

â€¢ ••The Importance of Preserving Religion••
	• The author believes that preserving religion is just as important as preserving liberty
	• The author sees religion as the "ark of the covenant" and the "indubitable pledge of God's presence"

â€¢ ••The Threats to the Reformation••
	• The author mentions various groups and individuals who have attempted to undermine the Reformation
	• These include sworn foes of the Reformation, perfidious Simonists, and others

â€¢ ••The Anabaptists••
	• The Anabaptists made a disturbance in the year 1536, shortly after the start of the Reformation
	• They were a fanatical rabble who threatened the holy discipline of morals

â€¢ ••Peter Caroli••
	• Peter Caroli was a Sophist who used deceitful arts to undermine the Reformation
	• He was a master of changeable and iniquitous calamities

â€¢ ••Sebastian Castellio••
	• Sebastian Castellio was a leader of modern semi-Pelagians who corrupted orthodox doctrine
	• He mixed together errors from Samosatenianism and Manichaeism

â€¢ ••Jerome Bolsec••
	• Jerome Bolsec attempted to corrupt the doctrine of predestination and saving grace with Pelagian poison
	• He did this in the year 1551

â€¢ ••Michael Servetus••
	• Michael Servetus was a monster of wickedness who blasphemed against the holy Trinity
	• He was thrown into prison and suffered a just punishment in 1553

â€¢ ••Other Enemies of the Reformation••
	• Satan continued to renew the strife and excite new enemies of the Reformation
	• These included Valentine Gentilis, Paul Alciatus, and others who joined forces with Servetus

â€¢ ••The Authority of Predecessors••
	• The author praises the predecessors of the current rulers for their defense of the Reformation
	• They were "strenuous and hearty defenders of the cause of piety"

	• Rather, it is whether first principles (adequate and proper to true religion) are held among all men

â€¢ ••The role of natural theology••
	• Natural theology is useful to men in various ways, including:

		- As a bond of external discipline among men
		- As a subjective condition for the admission of the light of grace
		- As an incitement to search for a more illustrious revelation
	• However, the question is whether natural theology is sufficient for salvation

â€¢ ••The insufficiency of natural theology••
	• The reasons for this include:
		- There can be no saving religion without Christ and faith in him
		- Christ is revealed nowhere except in the gospel
		- Faith comes by hearing the word, not by natural reason

â€¢ ••The Christian religion as the only ordinary way of salvation••
	• The Christian religion is the only ordinary way of salvation, but God can extraordinarily grant salvation to those who live in a holy manner according to the law of nature

â€¢ ••The Remonstrants' views on the Gentiles••
	• Some Remonstrants, like Arminius, admit that Gentiles and others can be saved through a right use of the light of nature

â€¢ ••The papists' views on salvation••
	• Some papists, like Abulensis and Durandus, hold that salvation is possible without knowledge of Christ

â€¢ ••The orthodox view on the Gentiles••
	• The orthodox view is that the Gentiles are without excuse for not knowing God, but they are not saved through natural theology

â€¢ ••The design of God in revelation••
	• The design of God in revelation is not to save those to whom it is made, but to reveal the true religion and prepare men for salvation through faith in Christ

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Introduction to the Question••

• The question is whether human reason can judge contradictions in matters of faith.
• The controversy is with the Lutherans, particularly the Ubiquitarians.

••II. The Origin of the Question••

• The Lutherans argue that the judgment of contradiction in faith does not belong to reason, but to Scripture.
• They cite various theologians, including Lucas Osiander and Balthasar Mentzer.

••III. The Nature of Reason••

• Reason is not the corrupted reason of fallen humanity, but the restored and enlightened reason of the Holy Spirit.
• Reason is not the foundation of faith, but an instrument of knowledge.

••IV. The Use of Reason in Theology••

• Reason is used in theological controversies, but not as a mixture of philosophy and theology.
• The principles of reason are not peculiar to philosophy, but can be found in natural theology.

••V. The Middle Term in Theological Arguments••

• The middle term in theological arguments is not drawn from philosophy, but from Scripture.
• The principles of reason are used to prove articles of faith, but are not formal principles of philosophy.

••VI. The Rule of Consequence••

• The rule of consequence is the rule of just consequence impressed upon the rational creature by God.
• This rule is not the rule of truth itself, but the rule by which we can know and discern what follows from a truth.

••VII. The Judgment of Contradiction••

• The question is not whether reason can reach into the mysteries of faith, but whether it can judge contradictions.
• The judgment of contradiction is a matter of discretion, bound and limited by the word of God.

••VIII. The Limitations of Reason••

• Reason is limited by the word of God and must always be proved by it.
• The judgment of discretion is sufficient for our own conviction, even if it does not produce conviction in others.

••IX. The Importance of Scripture••

• Scripture is the foundation of faith and the rule of truth.
• The principles of reason are given in Scripture and are used to prove articles of faith.

••X. The Conclusion••

• Human reason can judge contradictions in matters of faith, but only within the limits of Scripture and the rule of consequence.

	• Examples: Bereans (Acts 17:11), Corinthians (1 Corinthians 10:15)

	• Goal: perfection of the man of God in knowledge of truth and conviction of gainsayers (Timothy 3:16, Titus 1:9)

	• Knowledge of affirmation and negation, and the doctrine of contradiction, belong to reason

	• But must be considered as divine, proceeding from the light and influence of the Holy Spirit

	• But can judge the power of God from the word (Matthew 19:26, 2 Timothy 1:12, Psalm 115:3)

	• But unenlightened reason can lead to danger when judging from corrupt principles

	• But can be heard when it is obedient and judges from the word

••VI. Types of Contradictions••

• Reason can judge not only direct and formal contradictions
	• But also indirect and implied contradictions (deduced by necessary consequence)
• Examples: the blood of Christ cleanses us from all sin, therefore there is no purgatory; Christ ascended into heaven, therefore he is not everywhere

••VII. The Necessity of Knowing Truth••

• It is not necessary to know distinctly the things themselves and their essence to ascertain a contradiction
	• Sufficient if the truth of conclusions is known from which a judgment of contradiction can be formed

••VIII. The Importance of Using Reason Correctly••

• Although many things may seem contradictory to a number of persons which are not really so
	• It does not follow that something of the kind ought to appear so which is not, to men rightly using reason and thought

••IX. The Distinction between Sound and Renewed Reason••

• It is one thing to speak of sound and renewed reason in the abstract
	• Quite a different thing to speak of it in practice, in the context of the Church and the gospel

â€¢ ••Reasons for using consequences••: There are many things that establish the use of consequences in things of faith.
	• The design of Scripture, the nature of man, the wisdom of God, and the practice of heretics all support the use of consequences.

â€¢ ••The nature of man••: Man is a rational creature capable of reasoning and searching the Scriptures.
	• He is not satisfied with just the words, but seeks to penetrate to the sense and meaning of Scripture.

â€¢ ••The wisdom of God••: God is infinitely wise and foreseeing, and spoke in such a way that what can be lawfully gathered from his words should be considered as his word.
	• This implies that consequences can be drawn from Scripture.

â€¢ ••The practice of heretics••: Heretics often deny the use of consequences to defend their errors.
	• The Arians, for example, denied the homoousion because it was not explicitly stated in Scripture.

â€¢ ••The example of Christ and the apostles••: Christ and the apostles often used consequences to prove their points.
	• Christ proved the resurrection of the dead from the formula of the covenant, and the apostles proved that Jesus was the true Messiah.

â€¢ ••The authority of Christ and the apostles••: While the authority of Christ and the apostles is infallible, their consequences are not necessarily infallible in themselves.
	• The force of their consequences comes from their authority as speakers, not from the consequences themselves.

••I. Philosophy and Theology••

• Theology and philosophy have distinct principles and limits
	• Theology deals with divine and supernatural things
	• Philosophy deals with natural and human things

••II. Critique of Philosophy in Theology••

• Introducing philosophical concepts into theology can lead to errors
	• New distinctions and phrases can obscure theological truths
	• Philosophy should not be allowed to "thrust its pruning hook" into theology

••III. Distinction between Philosophy and Theology••

• Philosophy does not deny theological mysteries, but rather keeps its own bounds
	• The physician does not meddle with geometry, nor the lawyer with natural science
	• Philosophy should not be used to judge supernatural and divine things

••IV. Paul's Critique of Philosophy••

• Paul condemns vain and false philosophy, not true philosophy in itself
	• He criticizes the philosophers of his time for corrupting the gospel
	• He warns against the "worship of angels" and "enticing words" that deceive

••V. True Philosophy vs. False Philosophy••

• True philosophy is not condemned by Paul, but rather its abuse
	• He criticizes philosophers who become vain in their imaginations
	• He disputes with Stoics and Epicureans, but not with philosophy itself

••VI. God as Author of Philosophy and Reason••

• God is the author of philosophy and natural reason, but not of their interpretations
	• Philosophy is a natural enlightenment, while Scripture is a gracious revelation
	• God's authorship of philosophy does not imply His authorship of human interpretations

••VII. The Fathers' Critique of Philosophy••

• Some early Church Fathers spoke severely of philosophy
	• Tertullian calls philosophers the "patriarchs of heretics"
	• They warn against the dangers of philosophical error and deception

••VIII. Philosophy's Limits••

• Philosophy should not be used to judge supernatural and divine things
	• Its limits should be kept distinct from theology and other sciences

••IX. The Abuse of Philosophy••

• False philosophers use philosophy to lead people away from the truth
	• They introduce new and erroneous doctrines, such as the worship of angels
	• They use deceitful words and sophisms to recommend human traditions

••X. Conclusion••

• True philosophy is not condemned by Paul, but rather its abuse and misuse
	• The Church should be cautious of philosophical error and deception, but not reject true philosophy.

â€¢ ••Cainan's inclusion in Luke 3:36 is disputed••
	• The inclusion of Cainan in the genealogy of Jesus is not found in the Septuagint version of the Bible.
	• This is attributed to the carelessness of copyists or a desire to make Luke's gospel consistent with the Septuagint.

â€¢ ••Evidence against Cainan's inclusion••
	• Moses and the books of Chronicles do not mention Cainan in their genealogical records.
	• Chaldean paraphrases omit Cainan in the book of Genesis and Chronicles.
	• Josephus, Berosus, and Africanus do not mention Cainan.

â€¢ ••Impact on sacred chronology••
	• If Cainan is included, the chronology of Moses would be disturbed.
	• Abraham would not be the tenth from Noah, but the eleventh.

â€¢ ••Lack of evidence in manuscripts••
	• The Codices do not contain Cainan.

	• Ussher saw the book of Luke written in Greek-Latin on ancient vellum and did not find Cainan.

â€¢ ••Scaliger's affirmation••
	• Scaliger affirms that Cainan is lacking in the most ancient copies of Luke.

â€¢ ••Authenticity of Luke's gospel••
	• Even if the passage is a mistake, the authenticity of Luke's gospel is not called into question.

â€¢ ••Hebrew custom••

â€¢ ••Types of fathers••

â€¢ ••Christ's fatherlessness••

â€¢ ••Correction regarding Abraham's purchase••

	• The error can be easily corrected from the Hebrew text.
	• Scripture should be explained by Scripture.

â€¢ ••Importance of correcting errors in Scripture••
	• Errors in Scripture can be easily corrected from other passages.
	• The authenticity of Scripture is not compromised by correcting errors.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••Stephen's reference to the purchase of a field••
	• Stephen refers to the purchase of a field by Jacob, not Abraham
	• The field was bought from the children of Hamor, Shechem's father, for 100 lambs (Gen. 33:19)

â€¢ ••Abraham's involvement••
	• Some may object that Stephen says Abraham bought the field, not Jacob
	• However, Abraham can be understood as a genitive or patronymic, referring to Jacob or his descendants

â€¢ ••Patronymic usage••
	• In the Bible, the names of fathers are often used to refer to their descendants
	• Examples include David referring to Rehoboam, Rehoboam referring to Abijah, and David referring to Christ

â€¢ ••Beza's interpretation••
	• Beza suggests that the name Abraham is a gloss, added by a scribe

â€¢ ••Joseph's burial••
	• Moses mentions Joseph alone because he was a prophet and foresaw the deliverance of Israel
	• Joseph's bones were carried to Canaan, and he provided for this by an oath (Gen. 50:25)

â€¢ ••Enallage and synecdoche••
	• Stephen could have spoken in the plural by an enallage of number or a synecdoche of the whole
	• This would allow him to refer to the Israelites as a whole, rather than just Joseph

â€¢ ••Other patriarchs' burials••

	• The Jews held all the patriarchs in equal regard and reverence, and had similar hopes and faith

â€¢ ••Jerome's testimony••
	• Jerome relates that he saw the sepulchers of the twelve patriarchs in Shechem
	• This testimony is considered more reliable than that of Josephus, who says the patriarchs were buried at Hebron

â€¢ ••Propriety of the text••
	• The text can be understood with propriety, even without the father of Shechem being mentioned
	• Examples of this include Luke 24:10 and Herodotus' use of the word "father"

	• Moses says the field was bought for 100 lambs, while Luke says it was bought for a sum of money

â€¢ ••Restricting universal terms••

	• Similarly, "all things are lawful for me" (1 Cor. 10:23) refers to things that are lawful and indifferent.

â€¢ ••Christ's prohibition on swearing (continued)••

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Papist View of Scripture Authority••

• The papists claim that Scripture is authentic and divine, but only relatively so, i.e., only because of the church's testimony.
• They distinguish between "absolute" and "relative" authority, with the church's testimony being the formal reason for believing Scripture's authenticity.

••II. Critique of Papist View••

• This distinction is used to deceive and avoid the odium of their impious doctrine.
• Authority should not be considered absolutely, but relatively, and therefore Scripture cannot be authentic in itself without being so as to us.

••III. Papist Opinion on Scripture's Authority••

• Others have confessed that Scripture's authority as to itself is suspended upon the church's testimony.
• This is evident in their other controversies, where they deny Scripture's perfection, perspicuity, or purity.

••IV. Statement of the Question••

• The question is not whether the Bible is authentic and divine, but whence it is known to us as such.
• Papists suspend Scripture's authority upon the church's testimony, while we maintain that it is believed to be divine on account of itself.

••V. Foundation of Faith••

• The question concerns the argument or principal motive used by the Spirit to persuade us of Scripture's truth.
• It is not about the foundation or efficient cause of faith, which belongs to another question concerning free will.

••VI. Threefold Cause••

• A threefold cause can be granted for the manifestation of Scripture's truth:
	• The direct argument of the church's testimony (papist view)
	• The rational argument from Scripture's marks (our view)
	• The Holy Spirit's application of Scripture to us (acknowledged by both sides)

••VII. Papist Motive••

• Papists maintain that the principal motive for believing Scripture's authenticity is the church's voice.
• We, on the other hand, believe that Scripture is primarily and principally believed to be divine on account of itself.

••VIII. Church's Testimony••

• The church's testimony has its own weight, but it is not the primary reason for believing Scripture's authenticity.
• We will see later that the church's testimony is not the only argument for Scripture's truth.

••IX. Scripture's Marks••

• Scripture's marks, such as its perfection, perspicuity, and purity, are the rational arguments for its authenticity.
• These marks are the direct evidence of Scripture's divine inspiration.

••X. Conclusion••

• The question concerns the argument or principal motive used by the Spirit to persuade us of Scripture's truth.
• We maintain that Scripture is believed to be divine on account of itself, while papists suspend its authority upon the church's testimony.

••I. The Old Testament and the New Testament••

• The Old Testament and New Testament are not two separate covenants, but rather two modes of revelation:
	• The Old Testament is prophetic, shadowy, and typical, promising a Messiah to come.

• The apostles are called "ministers of the spirit and not of the letter" (2 Cor. 3:5, 6):
	• This refers to the legal economy of the Old Testament, not the books themselves.
	• The New Testament is more effective than the Old Testament because it works by the Spirit.

••III. The Continuity of the Old Testament••

• The Old Testament is not antiquated as to its substance or internal form:
	• It is only the mode of administration and external observances that have changed.
	• The New Testament does not replace the Old Testament, but rather builds upon it.

• The life of the Old Testament ceremonies and the law is distinct from the books of the law and prophets:
	• The Old Testament ceremonies and law are related to the life of the people, not the books themselves.
	• Christians have the express image of the things, not just a shadow.

••V. Christ's Relationship to the Law••

• Christ does not dispute against Moses and the real precepts of the law:
	• He acts as the interpreter and vindicator of the law, rejecting corruptions and glosses.
	• He restores the law to its purity and genuine sense.

••VI. The Perfection of the New Testament••

• The New Testament is perfect intensively as to the substance of saving doctrine:
	• However, it is not perfect extensively as to the whole extent of divine revelation.
	• The New Testament speaks only of Christ already come, not of him about to come.

••VII. The Use of the Old Testament••

• The perfection of the New Testament does not exclude the use of the Old Testament:
	• The Old Testament testifies to its dependence on the New Testament.
	• The reiterated testimony of many witnesses concerning the same thing is stronger and confirms our faith.

••VIII. What Was Given by Christ••

• That which was in no way given by Christ does not pertain to Christians:
	• However, the law given by Moses was also given by Christ, as the Lord.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Introduction••

• The question of the purity of the original texts of the Old and New Testaments is a matter of debate between Protestants and Catholics.
• The question is not whether the original texts are perfect, but whether they have been corrupted to the point of being unreliable.

••II. Definition of Original Texts••

• The original texts refer to the apographs, or copies, of the autographs written by the authors under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit.
• The autographs themselves no longer exist.

••III. The Question at Hand••

• The question is not whether some errors have crept into the manuscripts, but whether the original texts have been so corrupted that they can no longer be trusted.
• The papists affirm that the original texts have been corrupted, while Protestants deny it.

••IV. Variance of Opinion among Catholics••

• Not all Catholics agree on the issue of the purity of the original texts.
• Some, known as "Hebraizers", have recognized the purity of the sources and defended it.
• Others, such as Stapleton and Lindanus, have vehemently urged the corruption of the sources.

••V. Arguments for the Purity of the Original Texts••

• The providence of God ensures that the original texts have not been corrupted.
• The Christian church has always labored to preserve the manuscripts with great zeal.

••VI. Argument 1: Providence of God••

• God could not permit the corruption of the original texts, which were written by inspiration for the salvation of men.
• To assert that God has permitted the corruption of the original texts would be derogatory to God's promise to be present with the church.

••VII. Argument 2: Fidelity of the Christian Church••

• The Christian church has always labored to preserve the manuscripts with great zeal.
• It is not credible that the church would either corrupt the original texts themselves or suffer them to be corrupted.

••VIII. Implications of Corruption••

• If the original texts have been corrupted, it would be impossible to establish a reliable canon of faith.
• The doctrine of salvation would be uncertain and unreliable.

••IX. Conclusion••

• The providence of God and the fidelity of the Christian church prove that the original texts have not been corrupted.

••X. Final Argument••

• The fact that new revelations are not to be expected after the Scriptures have recorded God's entire will concerning the doctrine of salvation makes it impossible for God to have permitted the corruption of the original texts.

••I. Papist View of the Septuagint••

• The papists believe the Septuagint is divinely inspired and authoritative
	• They consider the translators to be prophets who received special help from the Holy Spirit

••II. Papist View of the Translators••

• The papists believe the translators were prophets who received direct inspiration from the Holy Spirit
	• They argue that the translators were not just interpreters, but prophets who were guided by the Holy Spirit

••III. Reformed View of the Septuagint••

• The Reformed view is that the Septuagint is not divinely inspired, but rather a human translation
	• They argue that the translators were not prophets, but rather interpreters who used human study and labor to create the translation

••IV. Authority of the Septuagint••

• The Reformed view is that the Septuagint has human authority, not divine authority
	• They argue that the translation was created by human effort, not by prophets or men who were God-breathed

••V. Reasons for the Reformed View••

• The Septuagint was created by human study and labor, not by divine inspiration
	• The translators consulted with each other and compared notes, which is not characteristic of prophetic writing
• The Septuagint has many variations and discrepancies with the original sources
	• This suggests that the translation was not created under the direct inspiration of the Holy Spirit

••VI. Additional Reasons••

• The Septuagint was not created by prophets, but by interpreters who were not guided by the Holy Spirit
	• The translators did not have the same level of inspiration as the original authors of the Bible
• The Septuagint has many false interpretations and discrepancies, which suggests that it was not created under divine inspiration

••VII. Historical Significance of the Septuagint••

• The Septuagint was the authorized version of the Greek and Latin churches for 600 years
	• It was widely used and respected in the early Christian church

••VIII. Use of the Septuagint in the Early Church••

• The apostles and evangelists used the Septuagint in their writings and quotes from the Old Testament
	• The Septuagint was widely used in the early Christian church, but this does not necessarily mean it was divinely inspired

••IX. Conclusion••

• The Reformed view is that the Septuagint is not an authentic or authoritative version of the Bible
	• They argue that it was created by human effort, not by divine inspiration

••X. Implications of the Reformed View••

• The Reformed view has significant implications for the authority and interpretation of the Bible
	• It suggests that the Bible should be interpreted in its original languages, rather than relying on a human translation.

	• This implies that the Vulgate's authenticity is not absolute, but rather conditional on its agreement with the sources.

••I. The Obscurity of Scriptures••

	• The practical knowledge of the Scriptures is peculiar to believers alone (1 Cor 2:14, 15; 2 Cor 4:3).

••II. The Mode of Delivery••

• The papists' reasons for the obscurity of the Scriptures from the mode of delivery cannot be proven.
	• The Scriptures are not so obscure that they cannot be ascertained by proper study.
	• The things contained in obscure passages are either not essential to salvation or are elsewhere clearly explained.

••III. Comparative Obscurity••

• The Scriptures are not absolutely obscure, but rather comparatively obscure in relation to a particular state.
	• The Old Testament Scriptures are obscure compared to the New Testament, but this does not destroy their perspicuity.
	• The Scriptures are sufficient for the state and age of the Old Testament church.

	• The papists' opinion is based on Rule IV, which interdicts the Bible in the vulgar tongue.

	• The papists consider the prohibition of the Scriptures as a universal law until it is repealed.

	• Believers ought to read the Scriptures without waiting for permission from a bishop or priest.
	• The Scriptures are a perfect rule of faith and practice.

• The question is not whether the reading of the Scriptures is absolutely necessary.
	• The question is whether believers may freely read the Scriptures without permission.

• The papists' prohibition of the Scriptures has consequences for the people.

••X. The Reformed Response••

• The Reformed response is to affirm the right of believers to read the Scriptures freely.
	• Believers ought to read the Scriptures without waiting for permission from a bishop or priest.

â€¢ ••Papists' view of Scripture••

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Unity of Sense in Scriptures••

• The Scriptures have only one sense, evident from:
	• The unity of truth (truth is one and simple)
	• The unity of form (there is only one essential form of any one thing)
	• The perspicuity of the Scriptures (they cannot allow various foreign and diverse senses)

••II. Question of Multiple Senses••

• The question is not whether there is only one conception in the sense of the Scriptures
• The question is whether there may be many diverse and non-subordinated senses of the same passage

••III. Sources of Explanation••

• Distinguish the sense of the Scriptures from their application
• The sense is one, whether simple or composite, proper or figurative
• The application can be diverse, including instruction, reproof, correction, etc.

••IV. Allegory and Anagogy••

• Allegory and anagogy are not diverse senses, but applications of one literal sense
• Allegory refers to instruction, anagogy refers to instruction, and tropology refers to correction

••V. Innate vs. Invented Allegory••

• Allegory can be either innate (intended by the Holy Spirit) or invented by men
• Innate allegory is contained in the compound sense as a part of it

••VI. Intellect of God••

• Although God's intellect is infinite, it does not follow that the sense of the Scriptures is manifold
• The signification of expressions is measured by God's certain and determinate intention, not by his copiousness

••VII. Book Written Within and Without••

• The book written within and on the back side, within and without (Ezk. 2:10; Rev. 5:1) does not mean a twofold sense of one and the same Scripture
• It refers to the multitude of things written everywhere

••VIII. Difficulty of Passages••

• Difficulty of passages does not imply a manifold intention of God
• It implies some ambiguity in the words or weakness of our intellect

••IX. Significations of Words••

• Words can have various significations in the abstract, but on the hypothesis of a passage, they are referred to only one of these significations by the Holy Spirit
• These significations are to be ascertained by a consideration of the context and analogy of faith

••X. Literal Sense••

• The literal sense is the primary sense of the Scriptures
• It is the sense intended by the Holy Spirit, and all other senses are derived from it

••I. Definition of Atheism••

• Atheism is not the total extinction of natural knowledge, but rather a suppression of the knowledge of God.
	• Impious men try to persuade themselves that there is no God and fear no divine vengeance.
	• This is not a complete rejection of deity, but rather a lack of knowledge of the true God.

••II. Gentiles as Atheists••

• Gentiles are called atheists because they lack knowledge of the true God.
	• This does not mean they recognize no deity at all, but rather that they do not know the true God.
	• Polytheists are also atheists because they do not know the true God.

••III. Ancient Conceptions of Atheism••

• In ancient times, atheists were not necessarily enemies of every deity, but rather despisers of idols and false gods.
	• Socrates was accused of being an atheist, but this was because he rejected false gods, not because he rejected the concept of deity altogether.

••IV. Types of Atheism••

• There are two types of atheism: one that is temporary and due to negligence or criminality, and one that is permanent and due to a lack of knowledge of God.
	• The former can occur, but the latter cannot.

••V. Examples of Atheists••

• Famous atheists like Julius Caesar and Vaninus may have externally denied the existence of God, but their internal persuasion is unknown.
	• Their morals suggest that they may have had internal conflicts and tortures of conscience.

••VI. The Nature of Man••

• No one knows what is in man, except the spirit of man which is in him.
	• However, it is certain that no one can completely cast out the sense of deity from their heart.
	• This is a self-evident principle based on the constitution of man.

••VII. The Unity of God••

• The question of whether God is one can be reduced to three principal opinions: anarchy, polyarchy, and monarchy.
	• Christians affirm that God is one in the sense of monarchy.

••VIII. The Meaning of "One"••

• The word "one" can be used in two senses: affirmatively only or exclusively.
	• In the former sense, it means undivided in itself and divisible by others.
	• In the latter sense, it means exclusive and indivisible.

••IX. The Implications of God's Unity••

• If God is one, then He must be indivisible and exclusive.
	• This has implications for our understanding of God's nature and attributes.

••X. The Christian Affirmation••

• Christians affirm that God is one in the sense of monarchy.
	• This is in contrast to the heathen and Tritheists, who hold different opinions about God's nature.

â€¢ ••The Nature of God's Attributes••
	• God's attributes are imperfect conceptions of his essence
	• They represent God's nature, but not in its totality
	• We divide God's nature into various attributes due to our finite understanding

â€¢ ••Abstraction and Precision••
	• God's attributes are presented to us through precise abstraction
	• This involves thinking of one attribute without thinking of another
	• Exclusive or privative precision is not used to define God's attributes

â€¢ ••The Question of Distinction••
	• The question of whether God's attributes are really distinct from his essence is debated
	• The Socinians argue that they are really distinct, while the orthodox argue that they are virtually and eminently distinct

â€¢ ••Real and Virtual Distinction••
	• Real distinction implies that things are diverse in essence
	• Virtual distinction implies that things are diverse in operation or effect, but not in essence

â€¢ ••The Nature of God's Simplicity••
	• God is most simple and perfect, which means that he cannot have real distinctions
	• Real distinctions imply that things are diverse in essence, which is opposed to God's simplicity

â€¢ ••The Consequences of Real Distinction••
	• If God's attributes really differed from his essence, he would not be most perfect
	• He would also be mutable, as he would have passive potency within himself

â€¢ ••The Evidence for Virtual Distinction••
	• The diversity of conceptions of God's attributes implies virtual distinction
	• This is because we can form distinct formal conceptions of God's perfections

â€¢ ••The Relationship Between Attributes and Essence••
	• God's attributes are virtually distinct from his essence
	• This means that they are not really distinct, but rather distinct in operation or effect

â€¢ ••The Implications of Virtual Distinction••
	• Virtual distinction implies that God's attributes are not really separate from his essence
	• This means that they are not independent entities, but rather aspects of his single, simple essence

â€¢ ••The Conclusion••
	• God's attributes are virtually distinct from his essence and from one another
	• This is because they are aspects of his single, simple essence, and not really separate entities.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Distinction of Attributes••

• The attributes of God are essentially and intrinsically one, but may be distinguished:
	• Intellectually (in our understanding) due to diverse formal conceptions
	• Objectively and effectively due to various external objects and effects

••II. Sources of Explanation••

• Our formal conceptions of God's essence and properties may be diverse, but cannot be called false
• There are objective conceptions that are virtually and eminently distinct, yet indivisible in God

••III. Mutual Predication••

• Attributes may be mutually predicated of each other in an identical sense, but not in a formal sense
• This is because they are formally distinguished in our conceptions and by their objects

••IV. Conceiving God's Nature••

• He who conceives God's nature as actually and really diverse conceives what is false
• He who conceives God's nature as one in itself, but more than one virtually and extrinsically, conceives imperfectly and inadequately

••V. Absolute and Relative Attributes••

• The divine attributes may be regarded either absolutely and subjectively in themselves or relatively as to their effects towards creatures
• Punitive justice and sparing mercy are opposed in the latter sense, but not in the former

••VI. Properties of God••

• The properties of God are many on the part of the object and end, but not on the part of the subject or principle, which is one and perfectly simple

••VII. Priority and Posteriority••

• Priority and posteriority as to absolute and real being imply a real difference, but not where there is only priority and posteriority as to known and intelligible being

••VIII. Definition of God's Nature••

• The definition of God's nature in itself differs from our conceptions of that nature
• Our conceptions of God's nature are rather of our understanding than of the thing itself

••IX. Distinction of Attributes••

• The distinction of attributes into communicable and incommunicable is a good one
• This distinction is based on the twofold nature of communication: essential and formal, and by resemblance and analogy

••X. Communicable and Incommunicable Attributes••

• All the properties of God are equally incommunicable, but may be communicated by resemblance and analogy
• This distinction is not equally received by all, and requires further explanation

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••I. Communicable and Incommunicable Attributes••
	• Communicable attributes are those that can be found in creatures, such as goodness, justice, and wisdom.
	• Incommunicable attributes are those that are strictly proper to God and cannot be found in creatures, such as infinity and eternity.

â€¢ ••II. Types of Communicable Attributes••
	• Affirmative attributes are attributed to God by way of eminence or causality.
	• Negative attributes remove from God whatever is imperfect in creatures.

â€¢ ••III. Analogy of Attributes••
	• Communicable attributes are predicated of God and creatures analogically, by analogy of similitude and attribution.
	• Analogy of similitude is when things are called by the same name due to a certain similarity between them.
	• Analogy of attribution is when one name is attributed to more than one thing, with one being the primary and principal instance.

â€¢ ••IV. Predication of Attributes••
	• Communicable attributes are not predicated of God and creatures univocally or equivocally.
	• They are predicated analogically, with God being the primary and principal instance.

â€¢ ••V. Participation in the Divine Nature••
	• Believers are said to be partakers of the divine nature analogically, not univocally.
	• This is due to the benefit of regeneration, which impresses upon them the marks of holiness and righteousness.

â€¢ ••VI. Distinction of Attributes••
	• The distinction of attributes into communicable and incommunicable argues no inequality of the divine properties.
	• All divine properties are equally essential to God.

â€¢ ••VII. Communication of Divine Properties••
	• The distinction of attributes cannot favor the error of those who maintain that the divine properties were communicated to the human nature of Christ.
	• Communication in the concrete (person) differs from communication in the abstract (nature).

â€¢ ••VIII. Simplicity of God••
	• The Socinians deny that simplicity can be attributed to God according to the Scriptures.
	• The author affirms that God is most simple and free from all composition.

â€¢ ••IX. Implications of Simplicity••
	• Simplicity implies that God is free from all composition and complexity.
	• This is a key aspect of God's nature and attributes.

â€¢ ••X. Conclusion••
	• The distinction of attributes into communicable and incommunicable is a key aspect of understanding God's nature and attributes.
	• This distinction argues for the simplicity and freedom of God from all composition.

â€¢ ••Simple and Composition••
	• "Simple" has two senses: absolute and comparative.
	• Absolute simplicity excludes composition in all kinds of being, while comparative simplicity excludes composition only with respect to some things.

â€¢ ••God's Simplicity••
	• God's simplicity is considered a physical attribute, not a moral one.
	• It means that God is free from all composition and division, and incapable of composition and divisibility.

â€¢ ••Proof of God's Simplicity••
	• God's simplicity is proved from:
		- His independence (God is not composed by another)
		- His unity (God is absolutely one and cannot be divided)
		- His perfection (composition implies imperfection)
		- His activity (God is a pure act with no passive admixture)

â€¢ ••Removal of Composition••
	• God's simplicity is demonstrated by the removal of all types of composition:
		- Physical (matter and form)
		- Quantitative (parts)
		- Subject and accident
		- Logical (genus and difference)
		- Metaphysical (act and power)
		- Essence and existence

â€¢ ••Essence and Existence••
	• In created things, essence and existence are distinct.
	• In God, essence and existence are not distinct, and existence is necessary.

â€¢ ••God's Nature••
	• God's nature is conceived as a being by essence (existing in virtue of its own essence).
	• God's essence is such that he always exists.

â€¢ ••Philosophical Implications••
	• Philosophers describe God as a being by essence, which exists in virtue of its own essence.
	• God's nature is such that he cannot be conceived as not existing.

â€¢ ••Implications for Understanding God••
	• Understanding God's simplicity is essential to clarifying the mystery of the Trinity.
	• God's simplicity has implications for our understanding of his nature and attributes.

â€¢ ••Orthodox Teaching••
	• The orthodox have consistently taught that God's essence is perfectly simple and free from all composition.

	• God's omnipresence is not to be understood as a physical presence in space
	• It is not to be understood as a multiplication or extension of God's essence
	• It is rather a simple and incomprehensible infinity of the divine essence

â€¢ ••The Rabbis' Understanding••
	• The rabbis call God "place" (mqvm) to indicate that he is not contained in place, but contains all things in himself
	• This understanding is echoed by Theophilus, who says that God is the place of all things, and is place to himself

â€¢ ••The Socinians' View••
	• The Socinians, with Vorstius, argue that God is contained in heaven, but deny that he is omnipresent in essence
	• They argue that God's presence is only as to virtue and operation, not as to essence

â€¢ ••The Orthodox View••
	• The orthodox believe and confess the immensity and omnipresence of God, not only as to virtue and operation, but primarily as to essence
	• They believe that God's omnipresence is not to be understood in terms of physical contact or extension

â€¢ ••The Mode of God's Omnipresence••
	• The orthodox believe that the mode of God's omnipresence should not be curiously inquired into or rashly defined
	• They believe that it is sufficient to know that God's omnipresence does not consist in the multiplication of the divine essence or the extension of a corporeal mass

â€¢ ••Scriptural Evidence••
	• Scripture ascribes omnipresence to God, as seen in Ps. 139:7-10 and Is. 66:1
	• These passages indicate that God is present everywhere, and that he cannot be contained in temples made with hands

â€¢ ••God's Presence in All Things••
	• God's presence is not limited to a particular place or location
	• He is present in all things, and is not contained in any place

â€¢ ••The Magnitude of God's Substance••
	• The magnitude of God's substance is so great that it completely fills the universe
	• This is why God cannot be included in temples made with hands, as seen in Is. 66:1

â€¢ ••The Incomprehensibility of God's Omnipresence••
	• God's omnipresence is a simple and incomprehensible infinity of the divine essence
	• It is beyond human comprehension, and should not be rashly defined or inquired into.

Here are the 14 points with sub-bullets:

••I. God's Immutability••

• God's existence is not changed by creation
	• God's essence remains the same
	• God's relation to the creature is new, but not God himself

••II. God's Immutability in Creation••

• God was not changed by creation
	• God's will to create was always efficacious
	• The act of creation is transient, not immanent

••III. God's Immutability in Incarnation••

• The Word (Logos) was made flesh, not by conversion, but by assumption
	• The Word's hypostasis (person) remained unchanged

••IV. God's Will and Immutability••

• God can will the change of things without prejudice to his immutability
	• God decreed the creation and preservation of the world
	• God decreed the destruction of the world with a flood

••V. God's Knowledge and Immutability••

• God's knowledge does not change with the thing known
	• God knew the change would take place and decreed it
	• God's knowledge is not affected by the thing known

••VI. Indifference and Mutability••

• Indifference is not the same as mutability
	• The cause of indifference is liberty, not mutability
	• God's will can be indifferent before the decree, but not after

••VII. Power and Immutability••

• The power to vary God's own acts is not the principle of mutability
	• A perfect will does not vary, but an imperfect will may
	• God's power is not the cause of mutability

••VIII. Decrees and Immutability••

• It is one thing to inquire whether God might have determined himself to other objects
	• Another thing to ask whether God could rescind a decree
	• We deny that God can rescind a decree, but assert that he might have determined himself to other objects

••IX. Repentance and Immutability••

• Repentance is attributed to God after the manner of men, but must be understood after the manner of God
	• Not with respect to God's counsel, but to the event
	• Not in reference to God's will, but to the thing willed

••X. Unfulfilled Promises and Threatenings••

• Unfulfilled promises and threatenings do not argue a change of will
	• They were conditional, not absolute
	• The condition must be understood as tacit and implied

••XI. Predictions and Immutability••

• Predictions of death or destruction do not imply a change of will
	• They are declarations of what would happen unless God interposed

••XII. Necessity of Immutability••

• The necessity of immutability does not imply Stoic fate
	• It is an extrinsic necessity, from the hypothesis of the divine will
	• It does not interfere with the liberty and contingency of things

••XIII. Conclusion••

• The immutability of God is a necessary attribute
	• It is not a limitation on God's power or will
	• It is a fundamental aspect of God's nature

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••The Nature of Possibility and Impossibility••
	• Possibility and impossibility can be relative to different things or perspectives.
	• Something can be possible with respect to potency or the second cause, but impossible with respect to God's decree and foreknowledge.

â€¢ ••Temporal Identity and Power••
	• Temporal identity of power refers to the ability to do or not do something at a particular time.
	• Contingency applies to this concept, not to the power of temporal identity.

â€¢ ••Contradictions and Possibility••
	• A contradiction arises when a thing is about to happen and not about to happen at the same time.
	• However, a thing can be about to happen and still be possible not to happen.

â€¢ ••Futurition and Possibility••
	• Futurition refers to the truth of a thing happening, while possibility refers to the truth of a thing being able to happen.
	• These two concepts are not mutually exclusive and can be true at the same time.

â€¢ ••Infallibility and Contingency••
	• The infallibility of an event does not take away its contingency.
	• Things can happen necessarily as an event, but contingently as to the mode of production.

â€¢ ••Necessity and Contingency••
	• Necessary things have an intrinsic necessity due to their causes and nature.
	• Contingent things, on the other hand, have an extrinsic necessity due to the event, but are still contingent in nature.

â€¢ ••Freedom of the Will••
	• The freedom of the will is not overthrown by a hypothetical necessity or the infallibility of the event.
	• Men's actions can be free and spontaneous, yet still necessary with respect to God's decree and foreknowledge.

â€¢ ••God's Foreknowledge and Decree••
	• God's infallible foreknowledge implies the infallibility of futurition and the necessity of consequence.
	• However, it does not imply coaction or violence, nor does it take away from the will its intrinsic liberty.

â€¢ ••God's Role in Sin••
	• God's foreknowledge of sins does not imply that he is the cause of them.
	• God foreknows sins as certainly about to be, but does not effect them as sins.

â€¢ ••God's Decree and Execution••
	• God's decree and foreknowledge do not subject men to an intrinsic necessity.
	• Therefore, God is not guilty in his foreknowledge and decree, just as he is not guilty in the execution of his will.

	• God's statement "Now I know that thou fearest God" refers to the knowledge He gave to others, not His own knowledge

â€¢ ••God's Knowledge of Sodom••
	• God's statement "I will go down and see whether the cry of Sodom is true" does not imply ignorance
	• He already knew the nature and degree of Sodom's impiety
	• This statement is made to emphasize God's role as a good and exact Judge

â€¢ ••God's Expectations••
	• God's statement "I expected grapes from the vineyard" does not imply ignorance
	• He charged the people to be studious of good works
	• He expected fruit from them, just as a husbandman expects fruit from a properly cultivated vineyard

â€¢ ••God's Knowledge of Future Contingents••
	• God conceives future contingent things as certainly future
	• He knows them relatively to His decree as necessarily about to take place
	• He knows them relatively to their cause as indeterminate and contingently future

â€¢ ••Middle Knowledge••
	• The question of whether there is a middle knowledge in God between the natural and free
	• The author denies this, against the Jesuits, Socinians, and Remonstrants

â€¢ ••The Two Old Middle Knowledges••
	• The knowledge of God is one and simple intrinsically, but can be considered in different ways extrinsically
	• It is commonly distinguished into the knowledge of simple intelligence (or natural and indefinite) and the knowledge of vision (or free and definite)

â€¢ ••Knowledge of Simple Intelligence••
	• The knowledge of things merely possible
	• It is called indefinite because nothing is determined concerning them by God
	• It is founded on the omnipotence of God

â€¢ ••Knowledge of Vision••
	• The knowledge of future things
	• It is called definite because future things are determined by the sure will of God
	• It depends on God's will and decree

â€¢ ••Differences between Natural and Free Knowledge••
	• In object: natural knowledge is occupied with possible things, while free knowledge is about future things
	• In foundation: natural knowledge is founded on God's omnipotence, while free knowledge depends on His will and decree
	• In order: natural knowledge precedes the decree, while free knowledge follows it

Here are 10 bullets and sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Introduction to Middle Knowledge••

• The Jesuits, Fonseca, Lessius, and Molina, introduced a third type of divine knowledge, called "middle knowledge"
• This knowledge is situated between natural and free knowledge

••II. Definition of Middle Knowledge••

• Middle knowledge is the foreknowledge of God about future conditional events
• These events depend on the liberty of the creature, not on God's free decree
• Middle knowledge is distinct from natural knowledge (which deals with possible things) and free knowledge (which deals with future things)

••III. Purpose of Middle Knowledge••

• The Jesuits introduced middle knowledge to defend the semi-Pelagian heresy of foreseen faith and good works in election
• They wanted to support the idea of free will to counter the Dominicans' arguments

••IV. Adoption by Other Groups••

• The Socinians and Remonstrants adopted middle knowledge to preserve free will
• They defended it in their writings, such as Arminius' "Certain Articles" and Vorstius' "Tractatus theologicus"

••V. Statement of the Question••

• The question is not whether God knows future contingencies, but whether they belong to a distinct type of middle knowledge
• The authors deny that middle knowledge is a distinct type of knowledge

••VI. Scope of the Question••

• The question concerns contingent conditional future things, not necessary conditional future things
• Contingent conditional future things can be and not be, depending on the condition

••VII. Nature of Middle Knowledge••

• The question is whether contingent conditional future things can be certainly and determinately known antecedently to God's decree
• The authors deny that middle knowledge is a distinct type of knowledge that can provide such certainty

••VIII. Critique of Middle Knowledge••

• The Dominicans fiercely criticized middle knowledge as most false
• The Jansenists of today agree with the Dominicans' critique

••IX. Implications of Middle Knowledge••

• If middle knowledge is accepted, it would imply that God's decree is not the sole cause of future events
• It would also imply that free will is not entirely free, but is influenced by God's foreknowledge

••X. Conclusion••

• The authors deny that middle knowledge is a distinct type of knowledge that can provide certainty about contingent conditional future things.

Here are 12 bullets and sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. The Question of God's Knowledge••

• The question is whether God has a special decree concerning the certain futurition of things
	• The Jesuits, Socinians, and Remonstrants affirm this, while the orthodox deny it

••II. The Nature of God's Knowledge••

• There are three types of knowledge: natural, free, and middle
	• Natural knowledge is of things possible
	• Free knowledge is of things future and decreed by God
	• Middle knowledge is of conditional future things

••III. The Impossibility of Middle Knowledge••

• Reasons against middle knowledge:
	• (1) Natural and free knowledge already cover all knowable things
	• (2) Conditional future things are not true apart from the divine will
	• (3) The created will is subject to divine providence and cannot be independent
	• (4) Uncertainty cannot be ascribed to God

••IV. Natural Knowledge••

• Natural knowledge is of things possible
• It does not cover conditional future things

••V. Free Knowledge••

• Free knowledge is of things future and decreed by God
• It covers conditional future things that are certain to happen

••VI. The Created Will••

• The created will is subject to divine providence
• Its acts depend on the divine decree

••VII. The Nature of Conditional Future Things••

• Conditional future things are not true apart from the divine will
• They depend on the determination of the divine will

••VIII. The Impossibility of Middle Knowledge (continued)••

• (1) Natural and free knowledge already cover all knowable things
• (2) Conditional future things are not true apart from the divine will
• (3) The created will is subject to divine providence and cannot be independent
• (4) Uncertainty cannot be ascribed to God

••IX. The Dependence of the Created Will••

• The created will depends on the divine decree
• Its acts are not independent and indeterminate

••X. The Certainty of God's Knowledge••

• God's knowledge is certain and not uncertain
• Middle knowledge, being occupied with an uncertain object, cannot be certain

â€¢ ••Problem of God's Knowledge••
	• God's knowledge of future events is uncertain
	• God's knowledge cannot be based on the nature of things themselves, as they are free acts in a created will
	• God's knowledge cannot be based on the infinity of divine knowledge, as it would change the nature of things

â€¢ ••Two Possible Solutions••
	• Solution 1: God's knowledge makes the event certain
		- But then how can the will be free?
		- Where is the indifference of the will?
	• Solution 2: God's knowledge foresees the event as certain
		- But how can the foresight of an uncertain and indifferent thing be itself certain?

â€¢ ••Eternal Existence of Things••

	• They can only have intentional being from eternity, by reason of the decree in which they obtain their futurition

â€¢ ••Necessity of the Event••
	• The certain necessity of the event cannot be founded on the contingent connection of ends
	• It cannot be founded on the knowledge that recognizes but does not make the thing

	• God's knowledge is only conjectural if it is based on a contingent cause
	• A determinate act cannot flow from an indifferent cause
	• A necessary conclusion cannot flow from a contingent antecedent

â€¢ ••Middle Knowledge••

â€¢ ••God's Dependence on the Creature••

	• On the supposition of middle knowledge, a reason for predestination can be assigned out of God's purpose and good pleasure

â€¢ ••The Cause of Existence vs. Futurition••

â€¢ ••The Will of God••
	• The will of God is directed towards the good.
	• The object of God's will is twofold: himself (as the infinite good) and created things (as finite goods).

â€¢ ••Necessity in God's Will••
	• Necessity is twofold: absolute and hypothetical.
	• Absolute necessity refers to God's nature, which cannot be otherwise (e.g., God is good).
	• Hypothetical necessity refers to what necessarily follows from a given condition (e.g., if God predestinated Jacob, Jacob must be saved).

â€¢ ••Free Will in God••
	• Free will can refer to spontaneity or indifference.
	• When asking if God wills some things freely, we're referring to the liberty of indifference (whether God could have willed otherwise).

â€¢ ••Types of Things Willed••
	• There are two kinds of things willed: principal (ultimate ends) and secondary (means to those ends).
	• The will is carried necessarily to principal things, but freely to secondary things.

â€¢ ••God's Will for Himself••
	• God wills himself necessarily, both hypothetically and absolutely.
	• This is because he is the ultimate end and highest good, which he cannot but will and love.

â€¢ ••God's Will for Created Things••
	• God wills created things freely, by decree.

â€¢ ••Hypothetical Necessity in God's Will••
	• Even if God wills created things freely, the decree being posited, he cannot not will them.

â€¢ ••Absolute Necessity in God's Will••
	• God's will is absolute in the sense that he cannot deny himself or his own glory.

â€¢ ••God's Will and His Nature••
	• God's will is inextricably linked to his nature, which is good and just.

â€¢ ••Distinction between decretive and preceptive will••

Here are 12 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Distinction of Will••

• The will of God is distributed into two types:
	• Decretive will (eudokian)
	• Preceptive will (euarestian)

••II. Decretive Will (Eudokian)••

• Refers to God's decree or volition to do or permit something
• Can be designated by the phrase "it seemed good in thy sight" (Mt. 11:26)
• Example: God's good pleasure (eudokian) in predestinating us (Eph. 1:5)

••III. Preceptive Will (Euarestian)••

• Refers to God's will to propose to the creature his duty as a thing pleasing to him
• Can be designated by the phrase "good and acceptable" (Rom. 12:2)
• Example: God's will to which we ought to conform (Rom. 12:2)

••IV. Relationship between Eudokian and Euarestian••

• Not mutually exclusive, but rather complementary
• Eudokian refers to God's decree, while euarestian refers to God's approval

••V. Acceptability to God••

• Whatever God has decreed to be done is truly grateful to him
• God's will is not to perform what would not please him

••VI. Designation of Will••

• Eudokian designates the will by which God decrees to do or permit something
• Euarestian designates the will by which God proposes to the creature his duty as a thing pleasing to him

••VII. Interchangeability of Terms••

• Eudokian and euarestian can be used interchangeably in certain contexts
• Example: "In whom I am well pleased" (Mt. 3:17) can be referred to either eudokian or euarestian

••VIII. Complacency••

• Euarestian implies the mere complacency by which God approves something as just and holy
• Does not properly include any decree or volition in God

••IX. Approbation vs. Volition••

• Approbation is not forthwith God's volition
• Example: Approving a thing does not immediately mean willing it

••X. Promises of Salvation••

• The promises of giving salvation to believers belong to the euarestian will
• Does not connote any condition, decree, or volition concerning the giving of salvation

••XI. Nature of God••

• The euarestian will implies the agreement of the thing with the nature of God
• God cannot but love what is agreeable to his holiness

••XII. Conclusion••

• The distinction between eudokian and euarestian is important for understanding God's will and nature.
