Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••Distinction of the divine will••
	• The distinction of the divine will into antecedent and consequent is proposed by some, but rejected by others.
	• This distinction is often attributed to John of Damascus and later adopted by the Scholastics.

â€¢ ••Antecedent and consequent will••
	• The antecedent will is said to be the will of God that precedes human action.
	• The consequent will is said to be the will of God that follows human action.

â€¢ ••Variations of the distinction••
	• Some theologians retain the distinction, but in a different sense from the Neopelagians.
	• They distinguish between the antecedent will as related to precepts and promises, and the consequent will as related to decrees.

â€¢ ••Rejection of the distinction••
	• Our men reject the distinction in the sense of the Scholastics and Neopelagians.
	• They reject the idea that the antecedent will is the purpose of God concerning the salvation of all men universally.

â€¢ ••Arminian interpretation••
	• The Arminians interpret the antecedent will as the will of God that precedes human action.
	• They interpret the consequent will as the will of God that follows human action.

â€¢ ••Consequences of the distinction••
	• The distinction is injurious to God, as it attributes to him contrary wills.
	• It implies that God wills the salvation of some, but not all, which is contradictory.

â€¢ ••Examples of the distinction••
	• The Arminians use examples to illustrate the distinction, such as God willing to establish the kingdom of Saul, but later willing to hurl him from his kingdom.

â€¢ ••Inconsistencies in the distinction••
	• The distinction implies that God wills something to be done, but does not will it to be done.
	• It implies that God wills the salvation of some, but not all, which is contradictory.

â€¢ ••Implications for human freedom••
	• The distinction implies that human freedom is not absolute, as God's will is prior to human action.
	• It implies that human decisions are not entirely up to us, but are influenced by God's prior will.

â€¢ ••Rejection of the Arminian interpretation••
	• Our men reject the Arminian interpretation of the antecedent and consequent will.
	• They reject the idea that God's will is prior to human action, and that human decisions are influenced by God's prior will.

â€¢ ••Critique of the Antecedent Will••

â€¢ ••The Will of God is the Primary Rule of Justice••
	• The question of whether the will of God is the primary rule of justice is a matter of debate among theologians.

	• The affirmative opinion holds that all moral good and evil depend on the free will of God.

â€¢ ••The Will of God as the Primary Rule of Justice••
	• The will of God can be called the primary rule of justice either intrinsically (with respect to God) or extrinsically (with respect to all things out of God).
	• In the extrinsic sense, the will of God is regulated by his justice, while in the intrinsic sense, the justice in us is regulated by nothing else than his will.

	• The law of God can be either natural and indispensable (founded on his nature and holiness) or free and positive (depending only on his will).

â€¢ ••The Will of God as the First Rule of Justice••
	• The will of God is the first rule of justice extrinsically and in reference to us.
	• This is because the fountain of justice ought to be sought nowhere else than in the will of God, which is most perfectly just in itself.

â€¢ ••The Will of God as a Rule of Justice••
	• Theologians say that the will of God is the supreme rule of justice.
	• Whatever God wills is therefore just and good because he wills it.

â€¢ ••The Limitations of the Will of God••

	• It is a rule in things that have only a free and positive goodness, but not in things that have essential goodness.

â€¢ ••The Nature of Essential Goodness••
	• Essential goodness is found in moral acts that are good and just per se and in their own nature.

â€¢ ••The Reasons for Essential Goodness••
	• There is granted in God natural justice and holiness antecedent to his free will.

	• God's goodness is the source of all his gifts
	• It is exhibited in the highest manner through the diversity of gifts
	• It is a demonstration of the inexhaustible fountain of divine goodness

â€¢ ••Love of God••
	• Love flows from God's goodness and communicates himself to creatures
	• There are threefold distinctions in the divine love:
		- Love of the creature (philoktisia)
		- Love of man (philoanthropia)
		- Love of the elect (eklektophilia)

â€¢ ••Degrees of love••
	• Love is unequal because some effects of love are greater than others
	• Regard is had to the good that God wills to anyone
	• Love is threefold: benevolence, beneficence, and complacency

â€¢ ••Threefold love of God••
	• First, love of benevolence: God wills good to the creature from eternity
	• Second, love of beneficence: God does good to the creature in time
	• Third, love of complacency: God delights in the creature on account of the rays of his image seen in them

â€¢ ••Effects of love••
	• By the love of benevolence, God elects us
	• By the love of beneficence, God redeems and sanctifies us
	• By the love of complacency, God gratuitously rewards us as holy and just

â€¢ ••Commendations of God's love••
	• The majesty of the lover
	• The poverty and unworthiness of the loved
	• The worth of him in whom we are loved
	• The multitude and excellence of the gifts that flow out from that love

â€¢ ••The loved one••
	• God loves us who are in the highest preeminence and happiness
	• Men are beloved, not only as empty and weak creatures, but as sinners and guilty rebels
	• They are beloved in Christ, the delight of God's heavenly Father

â€¢ ••The effects of God's love••
	• The effects of God's love are greater than the effects of human love
	• God's love is a demonstration of his goodness and wisdom

â€¢ ••Scriptural references••
	• John 3:16 refers to the love of benevolence
	• Ephesians 5:25 and Revelation 1:5 refer to the love of beneficence
	• Isaiah 62:3 and Hebrews 11:6 refer to the love of complacency

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Love and Grace••

• Love is a fundamental aspect of God's nature
	• It is both numerous and valuable
	• It is the foundation for salvation and the gift of God himself

••II. Types of Grace••

• Grace can be taken either affectively or effectively
	• Affectively: with respect to God's internal act
	• Effectively: with regard to the effects it produces in creatures

••III. Affective Grace••

• Affective grace denotes the favor and benevolence of God
	• It is the favor by which God loved and elected us to life from eternity
	• It is the favor by which God regards us as gracious and accepted in the Son of his love

••IV. Effective Grace••

• Effective grace indicates all the gifts of the Holy Spirit gratuitously given to us by God
	• Ordinary gifts: faith, hope, and love for each one's salvation
	• Extraordinary and miraculous gifts: for the common edification of the church

••V. Types of Effective Grace••

• Gifts gratuitously given (gratiae gratis datae)
• Gifts making acceptable (gratiae gratum facientis)
	• Note: this distinction is false, as all gifts are gratuitously given and cannot make us acceptable to God

••VI. Grace Making Acceptable••

• This implies the benevolence of God towards us
	• By which he makes us acceptable in Christ, not from our merit but by his gratuitous love

••VII. Distribution of Grace••

• Grace is distributed into decretive and executive
	• Decretive: the eternal purpose of God concerning the electing of us
	• Executive: the universal dispensation of that wonderful mystery in redemption and calling

••VIII. Mercy••

• Mercy is to be attributed to the benevolence of God
	• Which is the same as the favor and benevolence of God

••IX. Relationship between Mercy and Grace••

• Mercy is a part of the broader concept of grace
	• It is the same as the favor and benevolence of God

••X. Conclusion••

• Grace is a fundamental aspect of God's nature and character
	• It is the foundation for salvation and the gift of God himself

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••Mercy is a divine attribute••
	• Attends upon the grace of God
	• Relieves human misery without anguish or perturbation

â€¢ ••Mercy springs from God's goodness alone••
	• Not from external causes like blood ties or friendship
	• Requires misery in the object, but only as a condition, not a cause

â€¢ ••Mercy is freely exercised••
	• Can exert or not exert itself without injury to anyone
	• Hence, "he hath mercy on whom he will have mercy" (Rom. 9:18)

â€¢ ••Mercy is twofold: general and special••
	• General mercy: God succors all creatures in misery (Ps. 104:27)
	• Special mercy: God has compassion on his elect, saving them through Christ

â€¢ ••General mercy is temporal and secular••
	• Concerned with the good of this life
	• Special mercy is saving and eternal, blessing believers with salvation and eternal life

â€¢ ••The magnitude of God's mercy is immense••
	• From the principle of pitying (God's good pleasure)
	• From the objects of mercy (men who deserve nothing)
	• From the mode and effects (pardoning sins, removing misery, bestowing eternal good)
	• From the duration (eternal)

â€¢ ••Mercy is opposed to divine justice and severity••
	• "To rejoice against judgment" (Jam. 2:13)
	• "For where sin abounded, grace did much more abound" (Rom. 5:20)

â€¢ ••Mercy is also opposed to the multitude of miseries and temptations••
	• God frees us from all great miseries and temptations (Ps. 103:8; Eph. 2:4, 5)

â€¢ ••Mercy is not a refuge for the impious and unrepentant••
	• Only the penitent and pious receive mercy
	• The impious and unrepentant are "vessels of wrath fitted to destruction" (Rom. 9:22)

â€¢ ••The power of God extends to all things, including contradictions••
	• The text does not explicitly discuss the power of God, but the question is raised in the next section

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••I. Definition of Power••
	• Power is the divine essence itself productive outwardly
	• It indicates the force and faculty of acting, not the right and authority to do anything

â€¢ ••II. Passive Power in God••
	• Passive power implies the principle of suffering from another, which is not granted to God
	• It would imply imperfection and change, which are not attributes of God

â€¢ ••III. Actual and Ordinate Power••
	• Actual power refers to God's ability to do what he wills, irresistibly and in the time and manner he chooses
	• Ordinate power refers to God's ability to do what is consistent with his perfect nature

â€¢ ••IV. Absolute Power••
	• Absolute power refers to God's ability to do more than he actually does, without contradiction or imperfection
	• It is distinct from actual power, which refers to what God actually does

â€¢ ••V. Rejection of Absolute Power••
	• Some theologians, like Calvin, reject absolute power as a profane and detestable invention
	• However, Calvin does not deny that God can do more things than he actually does by his actual power

â€¢ ••VI. Object of God's Power••
	• The object of God's power is the possible, i.e., whatever is not repugnant to be done
	• The impossible falls under the omnipotence of God not from a defect in his power, but from a defect in the possibility of the thing

â€¢ ••VII. Impossible and Possible••
	• Impossible and possible are used in three ways: supernaturally, naturally, and morally
	• Supernatural impossibility refers to what cannot be made even by the divine power (e.g., a sensitive stone)

â€¢ ••VIII. Supernatural Possibility••
	• Supernatural possibility refers to what can take place at least divinely (e.g., a miracle)

â€¢ ••IX. Natural and Moral Impossibility••
	• Natural impossibility refers to what cannot be done by natural means (e.g., a square circle)
	• Moral impossibility refers to what is contrary to moral law (e.g., lying)

â€¢ ••X. Conclusion••
	• The concept of power is complex and multifaceted, involving actual, ordinate, and absolute power
	• Understanding the different senses of "possible" and "impossible" is essential to grasping the nature of God's power.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••Definition of the Impossible••
	• The naturally impossible is what cannot be done by the powers of nature and second causes.
	• The morally impossible is what cannot be done according to the laws of holiness.
	• The supernaturally impossible is what cannot be done by supernatural power.

â€¢ ••Types of Impossibility••
	• Impossible by nature: repugnant to the nature of a thing with respect to all causes.
	• Impossible with respect to second causes: surpasses the usual and customary course of nature.

â€¢ ••God's Power••
	• God can do the naturally impossible, but not what is said to be such either morally or supernaturally.
	• God cannot do what is repugnant to his nature or involves a defect or imperfection.

â€¢ ••Omnipotence••
	• God's power is not diminished by what he cannot do.
	• God is omnipotent because he cannot do certain things, such as die or be deceived.

â€¢ ••Object of God's Power••
	• It is not all that can be conceived or imagined.
	• It is not only what God wills, but also what can be done and what God can do.

â€¢ ••Contradictories••
	• A contradictory is logically impossible and includes contradictory predicates.
	• A repugnance may be immediate and explicit or mediate and implicit.

â€¢ ••Immediate and Mediate Repugnance••
	• Immediate repugnance: explicitly contradictory terms (e.g. a deed undone).
	• Mediate repugnance: virtually and implicitly contradictory terms (e.g. God corporeal and mortal).

â€¢ ••Principle of Indubitable Truth••
	• It is impossible for the same thing to be and not to be at the same time.

â€¢ ••Contradictories and God's Power••
	• Contradictories do not fall under God's power because they involve a repugnance.

â€¢ ••Conclusion••
	• The impossible is what cannot be done by God's power, either because it is repugnant to the thing or because it involves a defect or imperfection.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••God's Power is Not Extended to Contradictions••
	• God cannot perform impossibilities
	• Contradictions are impossible because they are incompossible
	• A contradiction is a non-entity and cannot be done by God

â€¢ ••The Proper Object of Divine Power••
	• The proper object of divine power is that which is not repugnant
	• When God is said to be omnipotent, "all things" refers only to entities, not impossible or contradictory things

â€¢ ••God's Power is Not Limited by Infinity••
	• God's power is not limited by its infinity
	• The power of every agent must be estimated from its proper object

â€¢ ••God Can Do Things Above Human Reason••
	• God can do things that are above human reason
	• However, this does not mean God can do things contrary to reason

â€¢ ••God Cannot Do Things Contrary to Reason••
	• God cannot do things that imply a contradiction
	• Our right reason may fail to understand divine truth, but it contains nothing contrary to that truth

â€¢ ••Two Types of Statements About God's Power••
	• One type: God can do more than we can understand and conceive
	• Another type: God can do things that imply a contradiction (which is denied)

â€¢ ••God's Power and the Nature of Contradiction••
	• To do contraries is one thing, to do contradictories is another
	• God can do the former, but not the latter

â€¢ ••God's Power and the Nature of Time••
	• God could have made the past not to be the past in a divided sense
	• However, in the compound sense, God cannot make what is past to be not past

â€¢ ••Denying God's Omnipotence••
	• Asserting that God cannot do certain things does not deny his omnipotence
	• We understand this only of things implying a contradiction and arguing some fault or imperfection in the first cause

â€¢ ••The Nature of Contradiction and God's Power••
	• We reckon things to be contradictory when we deny that God can do them
	• Examples of contradictions include accidents subsisting without subjects and any being existing without a subject

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••God's Power and Ability••
	• God's power is not limited by the possibility of doing contradictories.
	• God's ability to do something does not imply that it is possible in itself.

â€¢ ••John's Statement••
	• John's statement in Mt. 3:9 does not prove that God can do contradictories.
	• It only rebukes the vainglory of the Jews and declares that God can miraculously raise up a new people from stones.

â€¢ ••Interpretation of "Stones"••
	• The locution "stones" can be understood figuratively or literally.
	• Figuratively, it refers to foreign nations that worshipped stones and are compared to them in Scripture.
	• Literally, it means that God can raise up spiritual children from stones.

â€¢ ••God's Power and Nature••
	• God's power is infinite with respect to essence and mode of operation.
	• God's power is not limited by the fact that all his works are finite.

â€¢ ••God's Power and Operation••
	• God exercises his infinite power either mediately (through second causes) or immediately (without other causes).
	• In the former sense, God exerts his power in a finite degree, while in the latter sense, he exerts it in an infinite manner.

â€¢ ••Impossibility and God's Power••
	• The impossibility of a thing arises more on the part of the thing than on the part of God.
	• Nothing is impossible on the part of the thing that is not also impossible on the part of God.

â€¢ ••God's Power and Creation••
	• If God could make an infinite in actual extension and number, it would be such that God could not add to it.
	• This is absurd, and to suppose any creature to be infinite in act or extension or number is a contradiction.

â€¢ ••God's Deception••
	• The proposition that God can deceive if he will is not necessarily true.
	• God neither will nor can deceive, and his power is not limited by the possibility of doing so.

â€¢ ••God's Power and Perfection••
	• God's power is the highest power and perfection.
	• God's power is not limited by the fact that he cannot communicate his virtue to a creature in an infinite degree.

â€¢ ••God's Power and Agency••
	• God's power is not limited by the fact that he operates through second causes.
	• God's power is infinite and can operate in an infinite manner when he acts immediately.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••God cannot deceive••
	• Deceiving someone is equivalent to lying or speaking falsely
	• If God can deceive, he can also lie, which is opposed to his nature
	• Deceiving would imply that God can sin, which is also opposed to his nature

â€¢ ••God's nature is immutable••
	• God's nature is characterized by goodness, holiness, and justice
	• He cannot do what is evil, unjust, or impure, even if he willed it
	• His will and power are derived from his nature

â€¢ ••God cannot do what he cannot will••
	• God's will deduces power into act
	• Whatever God can do, he can also will to be done
	• This is not absurd, as it is consistent with God's simplicity and truth

â€¢ ••God cannot deceive if he wills••
	• Deceiving would involve a contradiction to God's nature
	• God cannot perform contradictions
	• If God can deceive, he could obligate us to believe a lie with divine faith

â€¢ ••Faith in Scripture would be wavering••
	• If God can deceive, our faith in Scripture would always be uncertain
	• We could not persuade an atheist that God did not deceive
	• The atheist could argue that God's words are unreliable

â€¢ ••God's power and will are not separate••
	• God's power extends to more things than his will in the exercised act
	• However, his will is not more widely extended than his power in the signified act
	• Both his power and will are derived from his nature

â€¢ ••God's decree and permission are different••
	• God can decree the commission of an error by a creature and permit a creature to be deceived
	• However, he cannot immediately deceive anyone himself, as this involves the relation of sin

â€¢ ••God's will is not limited by his decree••
	• Although God's decree may limit what he can will, it does not limit what he can do
	• God can do anything if he wills, as long as it does not involve a repugnancy to his nature

â€¢ ••God's goodness and justice limit his will••
	• God cannot will to do what is evil, unjust, or impure
	• This limitation is derived from his goodness and justice, not from his decree

â€¢ ••God's nature is the basis for his actions••
	• God's actions are derived from his nature, which is characterized by goodness, holiness, and justice
	• His will and power are consistent with his nature, and he cannot do what is contrary to it.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••The Dominion of God••
	• The dominion of God is a fundamental concept in understanding God's nature and role in the universe.
	• It is a topic of inquiry in the context of God's sovereignty and right to do as he pleases.

â€¢ ••The Foundation of God's Dominion••
	• God's dominion is founded on two principles:
		- Preeminence and eminence of nature (God's superiority and perfection)
		- Amplitude and excellence of beneficence (God's kindness and blessings to his creatures)

â€¢ ••Types of Dominion••
	• There are two types of dominion:
		- Natural dominion (based on God's power and nature)
		- Economical dominion (based on Christ's role as Mediator and God-man)

â€¢ ••Natural Dominion••
	• Natural dominion is:
		- Essential to God's nature
		- Based on the decree of providence
		- Universal, embracing all creatures
		- Eternal and immutable

â€¢ ••Economical Dominion••
	• Economical dominion is:
		- Based on the decree of predestination
		- Especially terminated on the church
		- Characterized by saving benefits peculiar to the elect
		- Exercised by Christ as Mediator and God-man

â€¢ ••Key Differences between Natural and Economical Dominion••
	• Principle and origin: natural dominion is based on God's power, while economical dominion is based on Christ's role
	• Foundation: natural dominion is based on the decree of providence, while economical dominion is based on the decree of predestination
	• Objects: natural dominion is universal, while economical dominion is especially terminated on the church
	• Effects: natural dominion has common effects on all creatures, while economical dominion has saving benefits peculiar to the elect
	• Administration: natural dominion is exercised by God together with the Father and Holy Spirit, while economical dominion is exercised by Christ as Mediator and God-man
	• Duration: natural dominion is eternal and immutable, while economical dominion will have an end, at least as to mode.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••God's Dominion••
	• Universal and absolute
	• Unlimited and not accountable to anyone
	• God's will is not subject to human judgment or censure

â€¢ ••Absolute and Ordinate Right••
	• Distinction between God's absolute right and ordinate right
	• Absolute right is God's sovereignty over all creatures
	• Ordinate right is the order of reason and justice revealed in the law and gospel

â€¢ ••Foundation of Absolute Right••
	• Based on God's excellence and preeminence over all creatures
	• Based on the dependence of all creatures on God

â€¢ ••Ordinate Right••
	• Based on the covenant entered into with the creature
	• Revealed in the law and gospel
	• Has place in the ordinary dispensation of God towards men

â€¢ ••Predestination••
	• Proof of both absolute and ordinate right
	• God's election and reprobation are based on his sovereign will
	• God's mercy and hardening are revealed in predestination

â€¢ ••Absolute Right in Predestination••
	• God's election and reprobation are based on his good pleasure
	• God's sovereignty is revealed in predestination

â€¢ ••Ordinate Right in Predestination••
	• God's election and reprobation are based on his promise and covenant
	• God rewards faith and works graciously

â€¢ ••Relationship between Absolute and Ordinate Right••
	• Absolute right is not contrary to the law, but above and beyond it
	• Ordinate right is subordinate to absolute right

â€¢ ••Justice and the Law••
	• The law is not the sole rule of justice
	• God's nature and will are also part of the rule of justice

â€¢ ••Autocratic Right••
	• God's sovereignty is not limited by human notions of justice
	• God's autocratic right is not repugnant to justice, but subordinates it

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. God's Absolute Right••

• God's absolute right is not based on justice, but on his free will and pleasure.
	• This right is not limited by human understanding or definition.
	• It is not to be curiously searched into or rashly defined.

••II. Limitations of Human Understanding••

• Humans are not capable of fully understanding God's absolute right.
	• We are insignificant compared to God and should not dispute his authority.
	• We should dismiss curious and useless questions about God's majesty.

••III. Importance of God's Right••

• God's right is supreme and absolute, and he can do with his own what he pleases.
	• It is always holy and agreeable to God's perfect nature.
	• God's right is not opposed to his wisdom, goodness, and holiness.

••IV. Scriptural References••

• When Scripture speaks of God's absolute right, it refers to what he can do, not what he actually does.
	• This is to stop the mouths of those who jeer at God's liberty.

••V. Natural and Free Right••

• God's right can be divided into natural and free right.
	• Natural right is founded on God's nature and is eternal and indispensable.
	• Free right depends on God's pleasure and will and is positive and dispensable.

••VI. Natural Right••

• Natural right includes:
	• God cannot deny himself and give his glory to another.
	• The rational creature must obey and be under the law of God.
	• God must govern the world and prescribe holy and just commands.

••VII. Free Right••

• Free right includes:
	• The permissions of sin.
	• The bestowal of distinguishing grace.
	• The institution of the symbolic and ceremonial law.

••VIII. The Holy Trinity••

• The absolute consideration of God leads to the relative consideration of the persons of the Trinity.
	• The mystery of the Trinity is incomprehensible to reason and example.

••IX. Understanding the Trinity••

• The words "essence," "substance," "subsistence," "person," and "Trinity" must be understood in the context of divine revelation.
	• The church should properly use these words to describe the Trinity.

••X. Essence••

• The word "essence" or "nature" (ousias) refers to the whatness (quidditatem) of a thing.
	• It is used in Scripture to describe God's nature and attributes.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••Substance••
	• Attributed to God by the fathers
	• Not from standing under accidents, but from subsisting through and from himself
	• Some fathers use "substance" to mean "nature" or "essence", while others use it to mean "three substances in the deity"

â€¢ ••Subsistence••
	• Marked by the word "subsistence" (hyparxis in Greek)
	• A mode of subsisting or personality
	• Distinguished from "to exist", which means a thing actually is without its causes

â€¢ ••Types of Subsistence••
	• ••Constitutive subsistence••: constitutes a substance in the being of a substance
		- Explained by independence from the subject
		- Belongs to all substances, incomplete as well as complete
	• ••Suppositum subsistence••: constitutes a suppositum (a singular substance)
		- Explained by incommunication or incommunicability
		- If intellectual, it is called a person

â€¢ ••Humanity of Christ••
	• Has constitutive subsistence by which it is constituted in the being of a substance
	• Not a human suppositum, but united with and adjoined to the word to constitute the God-man

â€¢ ••Hypostasis••
	• Designates subsistence
	• Can be taken either generically and wisely for the very substance of a thing
	• Or strictly for the subsistence of a thing and a suppositum

â€¢ ••Distinctions between Essence and Hypostasis••
	• Some fathers made no distinction between essence and hypostasis
	• The Synod of Sardica declared it heretical to assert three hypostases, but orthodox to assert only one

â€¢ ••Athanasius and Jerome••
	• Athanasius wrote that hypostasis means substance and nothing else
	• Jerome would not suffer the mention of three hypostases, lest three divine essences and three Gods might be implied

â€¢ ••Council of Alexandria••
	• Determined that one essence could be held, yet three hypostases
	• Reconciled the apparently contradictory passages of the fathers

â€¢ ••Reconciliation••
	• Easily made between the apparently contradictory passages of the fathers
	• Depends on understanding the different uses of "substance" and "hypostasis"

â€¢ ••Implications••
	• The distinction between constitutive and suppositum subsistence has implications for understanding the nature of the Trinity and the person of Christ

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••Definition of Person••
	• The word "person" is used to denote an intellectual suppositum
	• It is not derived from the stage, where actors wear masks, but rather from the concept of a subject with a form

â€¢ ••Person vs. Hypostasis••
	• The Greeks use "hypostasis" to denote subsistence, while the Latins use "persona"
	• The opinion of the Greeks is now the common opinion received by all

â€¢ ••Scriptural Evidence••
	• Scripture uses the word "subsistence" to describe the relationship between the Father and the Son (Heb. 1:3)
	• The Son is called the "express image" of the subsistence of the Father

â€¢ ••Personality and Subject••
	• The word "person" is properly concrete and marks the subject with the form from which it is denominated
	• It can also be taken abstractly, which can lead to a twofold definition of a divine person

â€¢ ••Abstract and Concrete Definitions••
	• The abstract definition of a divine person is a subsistence in the essence of God by which it is distinguished by an incomunicable property
	• The concrete definition of a divine person is the individual that subsists, is living, intelligent, and not sustained by another

â€¢ ••Perfection and Subsistence••
	• The abstract definition expresses more fully the perfection of the divine persons
	• The concrete definition more clearly sets forth the truth of their subsistence

â€¢ ••The Word "Trinity"••
	• The word "Trinity" is proper to this mystery and is found in Scripture in the concrete (1 Jn. 5:7)
	• There was no necessity for the papists to derive it from tradition to betray the cause of faith to heretics

â€¢ ••Scriptural Evidence for the Trinity••
	• Scripture uses the word "Trinity" in the concrete to describe the relationship between the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit
	• The Trinity is a mystery that is revealed in Scripture and is not derived from tradition

â€¢ ••Definition of the Trinity••
	• The Trinity is a mystery that is properly concrete and marks the subject with the form from which it is denominated
	• It can also be taken abstractly, which can lead to a twofold definition of the Trinity

â€¢ ••Perfection and Subsistence of the Trinity••
	• The abstract definition of the Trinity expresses more fully the perfection of the divine persons
	• The concrete definition of the Trinity more clearly sets forth the truth of their subsistence

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••The Trinity can be deduced from Scripture••
	• Bellarmine confessed that the Trinity can be evident from Scripture
	• The Greek word "Trias" may seem to imply only the number three, but was consecrated by ecclesiastical custom to denote the Trinity

â€¢ ••The word "Trinity" is used instead of "triplicity"••
	• "Trinity" implies a single essence, while "triplicity" implies a multiplication of essence
	• God is said to be triune (trinus), not triple, because there are three persons but only one numerical essence

â€¢ ••The controversy over "homoousion"••
	• The word "homoousion" was introduced to counter the Arian heresy
	• The Arians accused the orthodox of introducing a recent invention, but Athanasius demonstrated that the word was used before the Arian heresy

â€¢ ••The Arians attempted to destroy the force of "homoousion"••
	• The Arians added a letter to the word to create "homoiousion", implying a similar but not the same essence
	• The Council of Ariminum/Rimini (A.D. 359) used the word "homoiousion" instead of "homoousion"

â€¢ ••Athanasius detected the subterfuge••
	• Athanasius taught that there was not a similar, but the same essence in the Father and Son
	• The orthodox resisted the Arian attempt to destroy the force of "homoousion"

••I. The Plurality of Persons in the Unity of Essence••

	• This is in contrast to God's frequent use of the singular verb in other passages.
	• The use of "our image" instead of "my image" implies a common nature among the persons.

••II. Objections to the Plurality of Persons••

• Objection 1: God speaks in the plural for the sake of honor, like kings and princes.
	• However, this is unusual for the first person to speak of himself in the plural.
	• No examples can be found in Scripture where God speaks in the plural for the sake of honor.
• Objection 2: If God spoke in the plural for the sake of honor, he would always do so.
	• However, God does not consistently use the plural verb in other passages.
• Objection 3: This enallage would be useless and dangerous, as it would lead to a false understanding of a plurality of persons.

••III. The Address to Angels••

• Objection: The passages in question address angels, not God.
	• However, this cannot be the case in the three passages mentioned:
		- Genesis 1:26: Angels did not assist in the creation of man, and man was not formed in their image.
		- Genesis 3:22: Those addressed are equal to God and their likeness is aimed at according to the promise of the serpent.
		- Genesis 11:7: The work of confusing tongues pertains to God alone, and Jehovah alone is said to descend, see, and confound.

••IV. The Spirit of God••

• The passage in Genesis 1:2 mentions "the Spirit of God" moving upon the face of the waters.
	• This cannot be understood as the air or wind, as neither had been created.
	• No distinction of things had been made, and no angel had been created.
	• The use of the plural verb "let us make" in Genesis 1:26 is consistent with the use of the singular verb in Genesis 1:2.

••V. Conclusion••

• The use of the plural verb in Genesis 1:26, combined with the address to angels in the three passages, suggests a plurality of persons in the unity of essence.
	• This is a fundamental doctrine of the Christian faith, and is supported by Scripture.

â€¢ ••No Composition in God••

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Introduction to the Distinction of Persons••

• The distinction of persons in the Trinity is based on their order and relationships.
• The text argues that the distinction is not a mere negation, but a positive concept.

••II. Distinction of Persons within Themselves••

• The distinction of persons is observed in two ways:
	• Within themselves (intus)
	• In their operations (foris)
• The order of the persons is:
	1. Father (first person, from no one)
	2. Son (second person, from the Father)
	3. Holy Spirit (third person, from the Father and the Son)

••III. Preeminence of the Father••

• The Father has a certain preeminence over the Son and Holy Spirit:
	• In subsisting (existing), the Father precedes the Son and Holy Spirit
	• In working (operating), the Father operates from himself, while the Son operates from the Father

••IV. Personal Properties••

• Each person has unique personal properties:
	• Father: agennÄ“sia (self-begotten, unbegotten)
	• Son: gennÄ“sis (begotten from the Father)
	• Holy Spirit: ekporÄ“sis (from the Father and the Son by spiration)

••V. Explanation of Personal Properties••

• The personal properties are not common to all persons, but singular to each:
	• They agree with the persons as persons and constitute their incommunicability
	• They are not absolute entities, but modifications and characters of the essence

••VI. Relations between Persons••

• The persons are distinguished by relations:
	• Relations are not predicamental (accidental), but transcendental
	• Each person has a peculiar subsistence and property, and a peculiar relation

••VII. Nature of Relations••

• Relations are real on the part of the foundation (the internal operations):
	• They are not absolute entities, but only modifications and characters of the essence
	• They are not real beings (realia), but only declarative of the persons a posteriori

••VIII. Paternity and Other Relations••

• Paternity (and other relations) are declarative of the persons a posteriori:
	• They are regarded in their external and respective being
	• They are not constitutive of the persons, but only declarative of their relationships

••IX. Implications of the Distinction of Persons••

• The distinction of persons has implications for our understanding of the Trinity:
	• It emphasizes the unique relationships and properties of each person
	• It highlights the preeminence of the Father and the Son's dependence on the Father

••X. Conclusion••

• The distinction of persons in the Trinity is a complex and nuanced concept:
	• It requires careful consideration of the relationships and properties of each person
	• It has significant implications for our understanding of the nature of God.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. The Nature of Divine Generation••

• The concept of divine generation is distinct from physical and finite generation
	• Physical generation involves change, imperfection, and priority of nature or time
	• Divine generation is incomprehensible and ineffable
• The Scholastics' attempts to explain divine generation are futile
	• It is not only incomprehensible but also inexpressible
	• Athanasius and Hilary argue that it is not fitting to seek to understand the mode of divine generation

••II. Similitudes and Analogies••

• Similitudes and analogies are used to illustrate the mystery of divine generation
	• Examples include the mind understanding itself and the sun emitting rays
	• These analogies can serve to illustrate the mystery, but not fully determine its mode
• Scripture alludes to these similitudes when describing the Son of God
	• As Logos, Wisdom, image of God, and brightness of the Father's glory

••III. The Importance of Sobriety••

• We must be wise and sober in our understanding of divine generation
	• Content with the fact that the Scriptures reveal, rather than anxiously seeking to define or understand its mode
	• Leave the mode of divine generation to God, who alone perfectly knows himself

••IV. The Deity of the Holy Spirit••

• The question of the Holy Spirit's deity is distinct from the question of his eternity
	• The anti-Trinitarians do not deny the Holy Spirit's eternity, but his personality
• The personality of the Holy Spirit must be demonstrated against the anti-Trinitarians

••V. The Holy Spirit's Personality••

• The question concerns the Holy Spirit regarded hypostatically and designating one of the persons singularly
• The question is not whether the Holy Spirit is a thing or a creature or some virtue of God
	• But rather whether he is a divine person, distinct from the Father and the Son

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. The Holy Spirit is a divine person••

• The Holy Spirit is not disputed as a divine attribute, but rather the question is whether he is a divine person.
• The Holy Spirit is affirmed as a divine person.

••II. Reasons for affirming the Holy Spirit as a divine person••

• Various personal actions are attributed to the Holy Spirit, such as:
	• Teaching (Jn. 14:26)
	• Testifying (Jn. 15:26, Rom. 8:16)
	• Revealing future things (1 Tim. 4:1)
	• Searching the deep things of God (1 Cor. 2:10)
	• Creating (Gen. 1:2)
	• Making pregnant a barren virgin (Lk. 1:35)
	• Exercising operations of every kind and conferring gifts (1 Cor. 12:11)

••III. Objections to the Holy Spirit being a divine person••

• Personal properties are often ascribed to things, but this does not mean they are not persons.
• Examples include:
	• Sin deceiving and killing (Rom. 7:11)
	• The law speaking (Rom. 3:19)
	• Charity believing and hoping (1 Cor. 13:7)
	• The blood of Abel crying out (Gen. 4:10)

••IV. Refuting the objection of personification••

• Personification (prosopopoeia) is not applicable to the Holy Spirit because:
	• The subject of a prosopopoeia is usually a corporeal thing lacking life and sense.
	• Scripture does not explain the Holy Spirit as a figurative or personified entity.
	• The expressions concerning the Holy Spirit are not transferable to inanimate things.

••V. Refuting the objection of allegory••

• The opinion of the adversaries can easily be transformed into allegories, but:
	• Scripture does not speak of the Holy Spirit figuratively in one place and then explain it elsewhere.
	• The expressions concerning the Holy Spirit are not transferable to virtues or other things.

••VI. The Holy Spirit as a distinct person••

• The Holy Spirit is set forth as distinct from the Father and the Son.
• He is also set forth as another one and sent from both (Jn. 15:26, 16:7).
• The name "Paraclete" ascribed to him implies a personal office in Christ.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. The Filioque Controversy••

• The Greeks and Latins disagreed on the procession of the Holy Spirit
	• Greeks: Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father only
	• Latins: Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son

••II. The Council of Florence••

• The Council of Florence (1439) determined that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son
• The Eastern churches still disagreed with this decision

••III. Scriptural Support for the Filioque••

• The Holy Spirit is sent from the Son as well as from the Father (Jn 16:7)
• The Holy Spirit is called the Spirit of the Son as well as the Father (Gal 4:6)
• Whatever the Spirit has, he has from the Son no less than from the Father (Jn 16:13-15)

••IV. The Son's Role in the Procession••

• The Son breathes the Holy Spirit on his disciples in time (Jn 20:22)
• Therefore, the Son must have breathed the Holy Spirit from eternity

••V. The Father and Son's Role in the Procession••

• The Father and Son breathe the Holy Spirit not as two diverse principles, but as two self-existent persons concurring in the procession
• The breathing power is the same in both the Father and the Son

••VI. The Holy Spirit's Proceeding••

• Although the Holy Spirit may be said to proceed from the Father, it is not denied that he proceeds from the Son
• The mission of the Holy Spirit is ascribed to the Son, and whatever the Father has, the Son is said to have equally

••VII. The Mode of Subsisting••

• Since breathing virtue is numerically one in the Father and the Son, it is not good to say that the Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son
• However, it is not improper to say that the Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son in terms of the order and mode of procession

••VIII. The Omission of Filioque in Primitive Creeds••

• The expression filioque was omitted in certain primitive creeds because there was no controversy about the procession of the Holy Spirit at that time
• However, it was prudently added later to correct rising errors

••IX. The Nature of God's Decrees••

• God's decrees are internal acts of God that are discussed in relation to his essence, attributes, and persons
• The inquiry is whether God's decrees are in God and how they are in him

••X. The Existence of God's Decrees••

• Scripture testifies to the existence of God's decrees (e.g. pronoia, prothesis, horismene, boule, eudokia)
• The decrees are in God, and their existence is a matter of theological inquiry

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••The Decree of God••
	• The decree is attributed to God's will and omniscience

â€¢ ••Types of Divine Acts••
	• ••Immanent and Intrinsic Acts••: personal acts within God's nature (e.g. to beget, to spirit)

	• ••Efficient Cause••: God's decree is the reason why future things are future

	• Ideas are properly called decrees

â€¢ ••The Nature of God's Decrees••
	• Decrees are not accidents, but essential to God's nature

â€¢ ••Idea of God and Man••
	• Idea is ascribed to God and man in different ways
	• In man, idea is impressed and then expressed in things
	• In God, idea is only expressed, not impressed, as it comes from within

â€¢ ••God's Knowledge••

	• No similitude seems possible between God and creatures

	• The decree is distinguished into three things:

		- The tendency outside himself, without internal addition or change
		- The object itself or the things decreed, which have a reason of the end

â€¢ ••Necessity and Freedom••
	• The decree is necessary in the first mode (as a principle)
	• The decree is free in the latter mode (as a relation)

â€¢ ••Dependence on Another••
	• What is dependent on another as a cause is not God
	• What depends on another as a principle (like the decree) is posterior in the signification

â€¢ ••God's Essence and Will••
	• God's essence and will are not changed by the decree
	• The decree is an expression of God's internal constitution

â€¢ ••God's Liberty••
	• God's liberty is free only in the exercised act, not in the signified act
	• God's liberty is free as to the respect and relation outside himself, but not as to the absolute existence within

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. God's Nature and Decrees••

• God's decrees are not separate from His nature, but are an expression of it.
	• God's essence determines itself to act in a particular way.
	• God does not act through something superadded to His nature.

••II. The Nature of God's Decrees••

• God's decrees are necessary intrinsically, but free extrinsically.
	• This does not imply a real distinction in God, but rather a relation outside of Himself.
	• The decrees are not many intrinsically, but are identified in the infinite being of God.

••III. The Eternality of God's Decrees••

• The Socinians deny the eternity of God's decrees.
	• They argue that some decrees were made before the creation of the world, while others were made at different times after creation.

••IV. Orthodox View of Eternality••

• The orthodox view affirms that all God's decrees are absolutely eternal.
	• Reasons for this view include:
		- Scripture ascribes eternity to God's decrees (e.g. Mt. 25:34, Eph. 1:4, 2 Tim. 1:9, 1 Pet. 1:20)
		- The adverb "before" in Scripture does not imply a temporal act
		- The fixing of some decrees does not exclude, but includes and supposes the others analogically

••V. Implications of Eternality••

• If God's decrees were made only in time, He would take counsel as if He were uncertain.
	• This would imply a limitation in God's knowledge and power.
• The eternity of God's decrees is necessary for His omniscience and sovereignty.

••VI. Scripture's Teaching on Eternality••

• Scripture extends the concept of eternity to all God's decrees, not just certain ones.
	• This is seen in passages such as Acts 15:18, where James asserts that "known unto God are all his works from eternity".

••VII. The Relationship Between Foreknowledge and Decrees••

• If God's foreknowledge is eternal, it is necessary that the decree upon which it is founded should also be eternal.
	• This is because God's foreknowledge is based on the decree, which determines the future.

••VIII. The Implications of Temporal Decrees••

• If God's decrees were made only in time, it would imply a limitation in His power and knowledge.
	• This would undermine the doctrine of God's sovereignty and omniscience.

••IX. The Orthodox View of God's Decrees••

• The orthodox view affirms that God's decrees are not many intrinsically, but are identified in the infinite being of God.
	• This view is based on the doctrine of God's simplicity and the nature of His decrees.

••X. Conclusion••

• The eternity of God's decrees is a fundamental aspect of the orthodox view of God's nature and sovereignty.
	• This view is based on Scripture and is necessary for a proper understanding of God's power, knowledge, and sovereignty.

Here are 12 concise bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

• ••I. God's Decrees are Eternal••
	• Agree with God's infinite wisdom and perfection
	• Not susceptible to new decrees or changes
• ••II. Distinction between Absolute and Restricted Eternity••
	• Scripture speaks of eternity in the same way
	• Eternity is indivisible and simultaneous, not successive
• ••III. Sources of Explanation••
	• Priority and posteriority of decrees are relative to human conception
	• Priority and posteriority refer to things decreed, not the decrees themselves
• ••IV. What is Not Eternal••
	• Something is not eternal if it has a prior in the order of time and duration
	• God is prior to his decrees in the order of nature, not time
• ••V. Cause and Effect••
	• A cause is not always prior to its effect in the order of time
	• Effects can be simultaneous with their causes
• ••VI. God's Decrees and Time••
	• God's decrees are not changed or made only in time
	• Changes in God's dispensation towards men are accommodated to human understanding
• ••VII. Eternal Decrees and Creatures••
	• Creatures are not eternal, but God decreed their existence from eternity
	• Creatures are said to have been only as to being as known and intentional
• ••VIII. Eternal Decrees and Execution••
	• The decree itself does not cease after execution
	• The thing decreed ceases to be in a state of becoming, but the decree remains true
• ••IX. Diverse Decrees••
	• Decrees can be diverse with respect to the things decreed
	• There are no opposed decrees with respect to the same objects
• ••X. God's Decrees and Human Understanding••
	• God's decrees are not opposed to human understanding
	• Human understanding is accommodated to God's ways, not the other way around

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

• ••God's Decrees are Eternal and Consistent••
	• God's decrees are from one God and should be considered as the effects of one and the same decree.
	• God's will is consistent with itself, like a physician using diverse remedies for a sick man.
• ••God's Liberty in Decreeing••
	• The eternity of God's decrees does not take away his liberty in decreeing.
	• God's nature was indifferent to decreeing this or that thing, unlike the necessary connection between the Father and the Son.
• ••Conditional Decrees••
	• The question concerns whether God's decrees are absolute or conditional a priori and antecedently.
	• The Socinians and others assert that God's decrees are conditional, while the author denies this.
• ••Reasons for Denying Conditional Decrees••
	• Every decree of God is eternal, so it cannot depend on a condition that takes place only in time.
	• God's decrees depend on his good pleasure, not on any condition outside of God.
	• Every decree of God is immutable, unlike a conditional decree which is mutable.
	• It is repugnant to God's wisdom and power to make decrees that depend on an impossible condition.
• ••Absurdity of Conditional Decrees••
	• It is absurd for the Creator to depend on the creature, God on man, and the will of God on the things themselves.
	• This would imply that God's will is subject to change based on human decisions.
• ••God's Decrees are Absolute••
	• God's decrees are absolute, depending on his good pleasure alone.
	• This is in contrast to conditional decrees, which depend on a condition outside of God.
• ••No Distinction between Absolute and Conditional Decrees••
	• The distinction between absolute and conditional decrees is not a valid one.
	• The Socinians and others who contend for the idol of free will are mistaken in their understanding of God's decrees.
• ••God's Decrees are Not Suspended on a Condition••
	• God's decrees are not suspended on a condition containing power and of uncertain event outside of God.
	• This would imply that God's will is subject to change based on human decisions.
• ••God's Decrees are Not Mutable••
	• Every decree of God is immutable, unlike a conditional decree which is mutable.
	• This is because every condition is mutable, especially if not decreed by God.
• ••God's Wisdom and Power••
	• It is repugnant to God's wisdom and power to make decrees that depend on an impossible condition.
	• God's decrees are not subject to change based on human decisions or external conditions.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••God's Decrees are Absolute••
	• There is no middle knowledge (scientia media) that can predict future conditional things.
	• Therefore, there is no conditional decree that can be placed under it as a foundation.

â€¢ ••Conditional Decrees are Inconsistent with God's Nature••
	• Conditional decrees imply that God was either ignorant of the event or that the event was not in God's power.
	• This is derogatory to God's wisdom, power, and constancy.

â€¢ ••French Synods Rejected Conditional Decrees••
	• The French Synods repeatedly proscribed conditional decrees as ineffective and deceitful.
	• They saw them as contrary to God's wisdom, power, and constancy.

â€¢ ••Sources of Explanation••
	• Faith and perseverance are related to salvation, but they do not hold the relation of powerful conditions to God's eternal decree.
	• God decreed salvation to individuals, and also decreed faith and perseverance to them as necessary means.

â€¢ ••Conditional vs. Absolute Decrees••
	• It is one thing for the thing decreed to be conditional; another for the decree itself.
	• The former can be granted, but not the latter.

â€¢ ••Conditions and Volition••
	• An antecedent cause or condition of the thing willed can be granted, but not immediately of the volition itself.
	• Faith and repentance are not the condition or cause of the act of willing in God.

â€¢ ••Conditional Promises and Threats••
	• Conditional promises and threatenings do not favor conditional decrees.
	• They pertain to the preceptive will and are appendages to the divine commands.

â€¢ ••Decrees and Futurition••
	• Conditional promises and threats show only the necessary connection of the condition with the thing conditioned.
	• They involve no futurition of the thing.

â€¢ ••Hypothetical Promises and Threats••
	• Every hypothetical promise or threat ought to be referred to some decree upon which it depends.
	• This decree should be absolute, not conditional.

â€¢ ••Connection vs. Futurition••
	• The gospel proposition to save sinners if they believe is founded upon an absolute decree.
	• This decree concerns the connection between faith and salvation, not the futurition of the thing itself.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••God's Decrees are Absolute••
	• God's decrees are not conditional, but rather absolute and certain.
	• They are not based on human actions or decisions.

â€¢ ••Faith and Salvation••

â€¢ ••The Absurdity of Conditional Decrees••

â€¢ ••The Nature of God's Decrees••

â€¢ ••God's Unchanging Decrees••

â€¢ ••God's Sovereignty••
	• God's decrees are not changed by human prayers or actions.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••The Promise to the Israelites••
	• The promise to the Israelites was made by God to introduce them into the land of Canaan.
	• The promise was conditional on their obedience, which ceased, and thus the promise and contract also ceased.
	• The promise did not refer to each individual in the generation, but rather to those in the following generation.

â€¢ ••Conditional Decrees••
	• A conditional decree implies that the decree is suspended on a condition.
	• However, the decree concerning the salvation or condemnation of men is not conditional, but rather will be fulfilled according to God's good pleasure.
	• The decree is not suspended on the condition of human actions, but rather is fulfilled infallibly.

â€¢ ••Hypothetical Will••
	• The hypothetical will is equivalent to a conditional decree.

â€¢ ••Conditional Will••

â€¢ ••The Question of Necessity••
	• The question of necessity is agitated between the author and the Pelagians and semi-Pelagians.
	• The author affirms that the decree necessitates future things.

â€¢ ••Types of Necessity••
	• Necessity can be viewed in two ways: in God or in the things themselves.
	• In God, there are two types of necessity: absolute and hypothetical.
	• In things themselves, there are three types of necessity: physical and internal, of coaction, and hypothetical.

â€¢ ••Necessity in God••
	• Absolute necessity in God is based on his immutable nature.
	• Hypothetical necessity in God is based on his immutable will.
	• This last type of necessity is twofold: one of immutability from the immutable decree, and another of infallibility from his infallible foreknowledge.

â€¢ ••Necessity in Things Themselves••
	• Physical and internal necessity in things themselves is based on second causes.
	• Necessity of coaction in things themselves is based on an external principle acting violently.
	• Hypothetical necessity in things themselves is based on the ordination of God whose will cannot be changed nor his foreknowledge be deceived.

â€¢ ••The Question of Necessity in the Decree••
	• The question of necessity does not concern absolute and physical necessity with respect to second causes in themselves.
	• The question does not concern the necessity of coaction because the decree brings no violence to second causes.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Introduction••

• The question concerns hypothetical and consequential necessity with respect to the certainty of an event and its futurition from the decree.
• The authors assert that the decree implies the necessity of the event.

••II. Reasons for Necessity••

• ••Reason 1: Eternal and Unchangeable Counsel••
	• God's counsel is eternal and unchangeable.
	• Therefore, things decreed by God must take place in the appointed time.
• ••Reason 2: Scripture Predicts Necessity••
	• Scripture predicts that certain events must happen (e.g., Mt. 18:7, Mt. 26:54).
	• These predictions imply a necessity that arises from the decree.
• ••Reason 3: Examples of Necessity••
	• Even casual and fortuitous things are said to happen necessarily (e.g., Ex. 21:12-13, Prov. 16:33).

••III. Foreseen Events••

• ••Foreseen Events are Necessary••
	• All things are foreseen by an infallible foreknowledge (Acts 15:18, Heb. 4:13).
	• Therefore, they must necessarily happen infallibly.

••IV. Sources of Explanation••

• ••Physical Necessity vs. Hypothetical Necessity••
	• Physical necessity takes away liberty and contingency.
	• Hypothetical necessity, however, does not take away contingency.

••V. Necessity and Immutability••

• ••Necessity and Immutability of the Decree••
	• The decree's necessity and immutability take away contingency with respect to the first cause.
	• However, this does not take away contingency with respect to second causes.

••VI. Contingency and Necessity••

• ••Contingency and Necessity in Different Respects••
	• The effect may be called both necessary and contingent at the same time.
	• This is because the decree determines the mode of futurition, but not the nature of things.

••VII. Liberty and Contingency••

• ••Liberty and Contingency in Relation to the First Cause••
	• All things are said to be necessary in relation to the first cause.
	• However, taken according to themselves, certain things can be free, contingent, and fortuitous.

••VIII. Necessity of the Decree••

• ••Necessity of the Decree and Creaturely Liberty••
	• The necessity of the decree takes away the liberty of independence and irresponsibility.
	• However, it does not take away the liberty of spontaneity and self-determination.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Necessity and Freedom••

• The necessity of the event is only hypothetical, ensuring the certainty of the event without taking away the nature and properties of second causes.
	• This means that Adam sinned necessarily with respect to the decree and the futurition of the thing, but freely with respect to his will and mode.
• The necessity of the decree does not detract from the wisdom and justice of God.
	• God's wisdom and justice are not compromised by the necessity of the decree, as it does not hinder men from acting freely or God from apportioning rewards and punishments.

••II. God's Decree and Sin••

• Although all things are said to be necessary from the decree, God cannot be reckoned the author of sin.
	• The decree is not the physical or ethical cause of sin, but rather permissive and directive.
• Sinners cannot be excused because of the necessity of the decree.
	• The necessity of the decree does not take away their liberty and choice in acting, nor hinder them from exercising their acts most freely.

••III. Guilt and Responsibility••

• Those who follow out the decree of God are not to be considered as obeying it.
	• The decree is not the rule of our actions, but the law of God.
• Those who sin against the preceptive will by violating the law laid down for them are not to be esteemed less guilty.
	• Examples include Herod and Pontius Pilate, who did not escape incurring the guilt of a terrible crime by their crucifixion of Christ.

••IV. The End of Life••

• The fixed and immovable end of the life of each man with all its circumstances is determined by the decree of God.
	• This means that a person cannot die in another moment of time or by another kind of death than that in which they do die.
• The Socinians and Remonstrants deny that the term of life is so fixed and determined by the providence of God.
	• They argue that the term of life can be either protracted or shortened, but this is denied by the author.

••V. Statement of the Question••

• The question of whether the term of life is fixed and determined by the providence of God is pressed upon us by the Socinians and Remonstrants.
	• This question was discussed by John van Beverwyck in his Epistolica Questio de Vitae Termine (1636).
• The term of life may be common and general (such as is assigned to the human race) or special (such as is given to the duration of this or that individual).

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Introduction••

• The question is not about whether humans are appointed to die by God's decree
• The question concerns the special term (termino speciale) of life, whether a unique and immovable moment of birth and death is fixed by God for each one

••II. Movable vs. Immovable Term••

• The term of life can be movable or immovable in different senses
	• Movable with respect to second causes (physical germ of life)
	• Immovable with respect to the first cause (divine or divine foreknowledge)
• The question is whether the hyperphysical term is immovable

••III. Distinction of Thomas Aquinas••

• Fate as in second causes is movable, but as from divine foreknowledge is immovable
• Not by an absolute but by a conditional necessity

••IV. Fixing the Term of Life••

• Fixing the term of life is either absolute antecedently or consequently
• The question concerns the absolute fixing antecedently, not the use of second causes and means
• The question is whether the term of life is fixed and immovable, not with respect to second causes, but the first (God's eternal decree)

••V. Orthodox View••

• The orthodox hold that the term of life is fixed and immovable
• The Remonstrants and Lutherans following the Socinians hold that it is indefinite and movable

••VI. Proof from Job 14:5••

• The reasons for the orthodox view include:
	• From Job 14:5, where Job addresses God and says that his days are determined
	• The number of his months are with God, and he has appointed his bounds that he cannot pass

••VII. Objections••

• Objections to the orthodox view include:
	• The expression is conditional on account of the particle 'm
	• Job speaks of the common term prefixed to human life, not the special and peculiar term

••VIII. Conditional vs. Absolute Necessity••

• The orthodox view holds that the term of life is fixed and immovable, not by an absolute but by a conditional necessity

••IX. Implications••

• If the term of life is fixed and immovable, it means that God has decreed the length of each person's life
• This has implications for the use of second causes and means, such as medicine and vice

••X. Conclusion••

• The question of whether the term of life is fixed and immovable is a matter of theological debate
• The orthodox view holds that it is fixed and immovable, while the Remonstrants and Lutherans following the Socinians hold that it is indefinite and movable.

	• The answer is no, because man creatable is a non-entity

â€¢ ••Reasons Why Man Creatable is Not the Object of Predestination••
	• A non-entity cannot be the object of predestination
	• The salvation and destruction intended by predestination are ends introduced into a subject that already exists

â€¢ ••Creation and Predestination••
	• The object of creation (or the decree of creation) was a non-entity
	• This does not necessarily mean that the object of predestination was also a non-entity

â€¢ ••The Nature of the Object of Predestination••
	• The object of predestination is a person with a certain quality or condition
	• The question is whether the fall was a condition or quality prerequisite in the object of predestination

â€¢ ••The Implications of the Answer••
	• If man creatable was not the object of predestination, then God's predestination was not based on the fall
	• This has implications for our understanding of God's sovereignty and human responsibility.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••The Object of Predestination••
	• The object of predestination is not man as creatable, but man as created and fallen.
	• This is because predestination concerns the production of the thing, not its object from predestination.

â€¢ ••Man as Creatable vs. Man as Fallen••
	• The decree concerning the creation of man should have for its object man creatable.
	• The decree concerning the salvation or damnation of man should regard man as fallen.

â€¢ ••The Nature of Predestination••
	• Predestination regards man as fallen, not as creatable or apt to fall.
	• This is because redemption or destruction was destined for man, not his potential for creation.

â€¢ ••The Object of Predestination: All or Some?••
	• Either all creatable men were the object of predestination or only some of them.
	• If only some, then they were not indefinitely foreknown, but definitely as about to be.

â€¢ ••The Absurdity of Limited Predestination••
	• If only some creatable men were predestined, then no reason can be given why the others were not.
	• This leads to absurdity, as it implies that God's decree was based on chance rather than purpose.

â€¢ ••The Importance of Creation in Predestination••
	• To find a discrimination between those who could be presented to God predestinating or not, we must descend to the decree of creation.
	• We must suppose them as really to be created and not only as creatable.

â€¢ ••The Nature of God's Attributes••
	• God's attributes of mercy and justice suppose an object clothed with certain qualities.
	• It is repugnant to the nature of these attributes to suppose that their effects can be destined to creatures neither miserable nor guilty.

â€¢ ••The Means of Predestination••
	• If predestination regards man as creatable or apt to fall, then the creation and fall were the means of predestination.
	• This is absurd, as the creation and fall have no necessary connection with election or reprobation.

â€¢ ••The Order of Providence and Predestination••
	• The creation and fall belong to the natural order and dispensation of providence.
	• Salvation and damnation belong to the supernatural order of predestination.

â€¢ ••The Absurdity of Means in Predestination••
	• If the creation and fall were means of predestination, then God entered into the counsel of saving and destroying man before he had decreed anything about his futurition and fall.
	• This is absurd, as it implies that God's decree was based on chance rather than purpose.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. The distinction between conditions and means••

• Conditions are necessary for something to happen, but are not the means by which it happens
	• Example: disease is a condition for healing, but not the means by which healing occurs

••II. Misrepresentation of the doctrine of predestination••

• Some people misrepresent the doctrine of predestination as if God reprobates men before they are sinners
	• This would imply that God creates people to damn them, which is not the case

••III. The importance of considering man as fallen••

• When considering predestination, it is safer and more true to consider man as fallen and in a corrupt state
	• This is supported by Scripture, which says that we are chosen out of the world, not as creatable or capable of falling, but as fallen and in the corrupt mass

••IV. The relationship between election and calling••

• The object of election is the same as the object of calling
	• This means that God elected man as a sinner because he is called as such

••V. The election of men in Christ••

• The election of men is made in Christ, which means that it regards man as fallen
	• This is because people cannot be elected in Christ except as to be redeemed and sanctified by him

••VI. The meaning of "chosen in Christ"••

• To be "chosen in Christ" means to be chosen as a sinner and miserable, not just as a person chosen by Christ
	• This is supported by the parallel passage in 2 Timothy 1:9, which says that grace was given us in Christ before the world began

••VII. The aspect of Christ in the election••

• The aspect of Christ in the election is as Redeemer, not just as God
	• This is confirmed by the whole order of things in the chapter, which treats of Christ under that aspect

••VIII. The object of predestination••

• The object of predestination is the mass of which Paul speaks in Romans 9:21, which is a corrupt mass
	• This mass is the source of both vessels of mercy and vessels of wrath

••IX. The nature of the corrupt mass••

• The corrupt mass is the source of both sin and misery
	• This is supported by the examples of Isaac and Ishmael, Jacob and Esau, who are proposed as examples of gratuitous election or just condemnation

••X. The implications of the doctrine of predestination••

• The doctrine of predestination implies that God elected man as a sinner because he is called as such
	• This means that the object of election must necessarily be man as fallen.

â€¢ ••Subordination of things••
	• The subordination of things is not absolute, but rather limited to things that are naturally subordinate.
	• This subordination does not apply to the creation, fall, and redemption of man.

	• The means to achieve different ends must be different.

â€¢ ••Dispensations and subordination••
	• A leap is made from the natural order of providence to the supernatural order of predestination.

â€¢ ••Coordination, not subordination••
	• God's decrees are not subordinated to each other, but rather coordinated.

â€¢ ••Objective subordination••
	• Subordination is to be understood objectively, not subjectively.

â€¢ ••God's decree and the wicked••

â€¢ ••The Adversarial View on Election••

â€¢ ••The Tenth Question: The Cause of Election••
	• The tenth question concerns the cause of election: is Christ the cause and foundation of election?

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Statement of the Question••

• The question is not about whether Christ is the means of executing the decree of election, but rather whether he is the impulsive and meritorious cause of the decree itself.
	• The adversaries want to affirm that Christ is the cause of the decree, while the orthodox deny this.

••II. Clarification of the Question••

• The question is not about Christ's role in the salvation of individuals, but rather about his role in the decree of election itself.
	• The question is whether Christ is the foundation of election a priori, or whether the decree of election is independent of an impulsive cause and antecedent conditions.

••III. Distinction between the Effect and the Act of Willing••

• The question is not about whether Christ is the cause of the effect of salvation, but rather about whether he is the cause of the act of willing that leads to salvation.
	• The orthodox deny that Christ is the foundation of election a priori, while the adversaries affirm it.

••IV. Historical Background••

• The Arminians and some Lutherans have built their opinions on the idea that Christ is the meritorious cause of election.
	• They argue that Christ's merits are the cause of predetermination, and that God's election is based on Christ's foreseen merits.

••V. Orthodox Position••

• The orthodox argue that election is based on God's mere good pleasure, and not on any cause outside of God.
	• They cite Scripture, such as Exodus 33:19, to support their position.

••VI. Rejection of the Adversaries' View••

• The orthodox reject the idea that Christ is the foundation of election a priori.
	• They argue that this view would lead to universalism and the destruction of God's absolute election.

••VII. Agreement with Some Divines••

• Some of the orthodox agree with the Arminians and Lutherans that Christ is the meritorious cause of election, but only in the sense that he is the means of executing the decree.
	• However, they reject the idea that Christ's merits are the cause of the decree itself.

••VIII. Rejection of Universalism••

• The orthodox reject the idea that God's election is based on general love or philanthrÅpia.
	• They argue that this view would lead to universalism and the destruction of God's absolute election.

••IX. Scriptural Support••

• The orthodox argue that Scripture supports their position, citing passages such as Exodus 33:19 and Romans 9:15.
	• They argue that these passages show that election is based on God's mere good pleasure, and not on any cause outside of God.

••X. Conclusion••

• The orthodox conclude that Christ is not the foundation of election, but rather the means of executing the decree.
	• They argue that this view is supported by Scripture and is necessary to preserve God's absolute election.

â€¢ ••Election and Predestination••
	• The question of whether election is made from the foresight of faith or works, or from the grace of God alone
	• The controversy surrounding this question is the core of the Pelagian controversy

	• The question is not about the absolute decree of election, but about whether it is influenced by motives and preceding conditions
	• The question is not about whether God has reasons for his decree, but whether these reasons are in man outside of God

	• The question is not about whether faith is a condition or cause of salvation, but whether it is a condition or cause of the decree itself in God
	• The question returns to whether the mere grace and good pleasure of God is the cause of election, without being suspended upon the foresight of faith or works

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Predestination to Glory and Life••

• Predestination to glory and life is of faith as the condition foreseen by God in the elect.
	• This means that faith is the condition that God foresees in the elect, not the cause of election.

••II. Capellus' Opinion••

• Capellus says that the will of God concerning the glorification of man is founded upon the condition of faith and repentance.
	• However, God himself works in us to fulfill this condition.

••III. Rejection of the Opinion••

• This opinion is rejected as too crude and dangerous because it differs from the traditional view of a purely gratuitous election.
	• The traditional view is that election to glory as well as to grace is entirely gratuitous.

••IV. The Traditional View••

• The traditional view is that election to glory as well as to grace is entirely gratuitous.
	• No cause, condition, or reason existed in man upon which God chose this rather than another one.
	• Election depended solely on God's good pleasure (eudokia).

••V. Election is Not from Foreseen Faith••

• Election is not from foreseen faith.
	• Faith and obedience are the fruit and effect of election, not the cause or previous condition.

••VI. Arguments for the Traditional View••

• The arguments for the traditional view are:
	• Faith and obedience are the fruit and effect of election.
	• The same thing cannot be at once the cause and effect.
	• Faith and obedience are the result of election, not the cause.

••VII. Scripture Supports the Traditional View••

• Scripture supports the traditional view:
	• "Whom he predestinated, them he also called" (Rom. 8:30).
	• "He hath chosen us, that we should be holy" (Eph. 1:4).
	• "As many as were ordained to eternal life, believed" (Acts 13:48).

••VIII. Augustine's View••

• Augustine says that calling is the means by which the elect become elect, not the other way around.
	• If the elect were chosen because they believed, they would have deserved to be elected.

••IX. Objections to the Traditional View••

• Objections to the traditional view are:
	• Romans 8:30 does not mean calling to faith, but to suffering.
	• The answer is that no other calling can be meant than to faith and obedience.

••X. Conclusion••

• The traditional view is that election to glory as well as to grace is entirely gratuitous.
	• No cause, condition, or reason existed in man upon which God chose this rather than another one.
