Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Papists' Opinion••

• The Papists' opinion on election is based on the Council of Trent's decree
	• Denies that anyone can know with certainty that they have obtained God's grace
	• Denies that those who have been justified can determine with certainty that they have been justified
	• Pronounces a curse on those who say that the justified are bound to believe they are predestined

••II. Papists' Interpretation••

• Most Papists, especially the Jesuits, interpret the decree to mean that believers can hope for their future happiness, but cannot be certain
	• They believe that certainty can be obtained through conjectures and probable signs, but not through faith

••III. Arminians' Opinion••

• The Arminians deny that there is a sense of election in this life, except a conditional one
	• They believe that believers can know that they will remain in God's grace and obtain eternal life if they persevere in faith
	• They believe that this certainty is conditional and only of the present, not the future

••IV. Statement of the Question••

• The question is not whether election is perceptible to us a priori, but rather a posteriori
	• Election is perceptible through observing the fruits of election in ourselves and ascending from the effects to the cause
	• This is done through a practical syllogism, where the major is read in the word and the minor is read in the heart

••V. Ordinary and Common Manner••

• The question concerns the ordinary and common manner of knowing election, not an extraordinary revelation
	• This is done through the energy and full conviction of faith
	• It concerns the certainty of faith, not a probable and conjectural certainty

••VI. Certainty of Faith••

• The question concerns the certainty of one's own election, not the certainty of another's election
	• This certainty is not the same as the certainty of every kind, which excludes all fear of the contrary

••VII. Conditional Certainty••

• The Arminians believe in a conditional certainty, where believers can know that they will remain in God's grace and obtain eternal life if they persevere in faith
	• This certainty is not absolute, but rather dependent on perseverance

••VIII. Doubt and Fear••

• The Arminians believe that doubt and fear are necessary for believers, as they prevent them from luxuriating in a false sense of security
	• They believe that believers should doubt their election until the moment of death, when it will be complete

••IX. Ordinary Revelation••

• The question concerns the ordinary and common manner of knowing election, not an extraordinary revelation
	• This is done through the word of God and the conviction of faith

••X. Practical Syllogism••

• The question is answered through a practical syllogism, where the major is read in the word and the minor is read in the heart
	• This syllogism is: "Whoever truly believes and repents is elected; now I believe, therefore I am elected."

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Reprobation and Sin••

• God's abandonment of man and denial of grace is not the accidental cause of sin.
	• Sin follows voluntarily from the denial of grace, unlike darkness following the non-illumination of the sun.

••II. Causality of Sin••

• God's denial of grace does not attribute causality to sin.
	• God denies grace justly and is not bound to give it to anyone.
	• The capability of sinning comes from man himself, not from God's denial.

••III. Positive Act of Reprobation••

• The positive act of reprobation speaks to a destination to damnation and hardening.
	• This includes two things: destination to damnation and destination to intermediate judgments.

••IV. Reprobation and Damnation••

• Reprobation is more extensive than damnation.
	• Reprobation includes a decree of not having mercy, not giving Christ as Mediator, and not calling effectively.

••V. Twofold Relation of God••

• God has a twofold relation in reprobation: as Lord and as Judge.
	• As Lord, God exercises a negative act (preterition) in denying grace to some.
	• As Judge, God exercises a positive act (pre damnation) in sentencing the guilty to punishment.

••VI. Positive Act of Reprobation••

• The positive act of reprobation is a decree to visit with deserved punishment.
	• This includes destination to damnation and hardening.

••VII. Reprobation and Election••

• Reprobation is considered either absolutely or comparatively.
	• Absolutely, it can be asked why God reprobated or elected one person.
	• Comparatively, it can be asked why God elected one person rather than another and reprobated one person rather than another.

••VIII. Absolute Decree of Reprobation••

• The question of the absolute decree of reprobation is not whether it is absolute from the final cause.
	• The question is whether it is absolute from the formal cause (the will of God).

••IX. Reprobation and Justice••

• Reprobation demonstrates the majesty and glory of God.
	• It restrains the audacity of the reprobate, who cannot justly ex postulate with God.

••X. Reprobation and Election••

• Reprobation is considered in the same way as election.
	• Both are considered absolutely or comparatively, with respect to one or many.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Arminian View of Reprobation••

• The Arminians believe that reprobation is based on foreseen unbelief.
	• They argue that God's decree of reprobation is made according to the consideration of antecedent unbelief and final perseverance.
	• They hold that the object of reprobation is man as a finally unbelieving and impenitent individual.

••II. Calvinist View of Reprobation••

• Calvinists deny that foreseen sin or unbelief is the cause of reprobation.
	• They argue that no other quality or condition is presupposed in the reprobate than that which is found in the elect and is common to the whole corrupt mass.
	• They believe that the sole good pleasure of God makes the difference between the elect and reprobate.

••III. Absolute Decree of Reprobation••

• Calvinists argue that the decree of reprobation is absolute.
	• They believe that it is not based on any quality or condition in the individual, but solely on the good pleasure of God.
	• They argue that this is consistent with the biblical teaching that God's will is the cause of hardening (Rom. 9:18).

••IV. Reasons for the Absolute Decree••

• Calvinists argue that reprobation is made from good pleasure, not from foreseen unbelief.
	• They point to the example of the twins in Romans 9:11, who were elected and reprobated before they had done anything good or bad.
	• They argue that the power of God over his creatures is infinite, and that he can reprobate one and elect another.

••V. Comparison with the Potter and the Clay••

• Calvinists argue that the power of God over men is greater than the power of the potter over the clay.
	• They point out that the potter's power is finite and limited, while God's power is infinite.
	• They argue that man is the creature of God, but the mass is not the creature of the potter.

••VI. Response to the Exception••

• Calvinists argue that it does not avail to make the exception that the decree precedes all conditions performed, but not foreknown.
	• They point out that the words of Paul preclude this retreat (Rom. 9:14).
	• They argue that the purpose of God according to election is the only reason for the difference between the elect and reprobate.

••VII. Objection to the Purpose of God••

• Calvinists argue that the purpose of God according to election is not based on faith or unbelief.
	• They point out that Paul objects to himself in Romans 9:14, and argues that there might seem to be injustice with God if only the purpose of God makes the difference between equals.

••VIII. Conclusion••

• Calvinists conclude that the absolute decree of reprobation is proved.
	• They argue that it is based solely on the good pleasure of God, and not on any quality or condition in the individual.

••IX. Implications of the Absolute Decree••

• Calvinists argue that the absolute decree of reprobation has implications for our understanding of God's sovereignty and justice.
	• They believe that it is consistent with the biblical teaching that God's will is the cause of hardening.

••X. Response to Objections••

• Calvinists respond to objections that the absolute decree of reprobation is unjust or arbitrary.
	• They argue that it is based solely on the good pleasure of God, and that it is consistent with the biblical teaching that God's will is the cause of hardening.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Introduction to the Problem••

• The order of the decrees of God is a matter of debate among theologians.
• Different opinions exist on how to arrange the decrees.

••II. Supralapsarian Opinion••

• ••Order of Decrees••: The supralapsarian opinion proposes the following order:
	• 1. The decree of predestination
	• 2. The decree of creation
	• 3. The decree of permission of the fall
	• 4. The decree of sending Christ for salvation
• ••Critique••: This order is criticized for being harsh and less suitable.

••III. Critique of Supralapsarian Opinion••

• ••Harshness••: The first act of God's will towards some creatures is an act of hatred.
• ••Inconsistency••: God imparts love from a principle of hatred.
• ••Misconception••: God exercises mercy and justice towards non-existent creatures.
• ••Gratuitous Assertion••: The creation and fall are means of election and reprobation.

••IV. Arminian Opinion••

• ••Order of Decrees••: The Arminian opinion proposes the following order:
	• 1. The decree to constitute Christ as Mediator and Savior
	• 2. The decree to receive penitents and believers into favor
	• 3. The decree to leave impenitent and unbelieving in sin and damnation
	• 4. The decree to send Christ for salvation
• ••Pelagian Doctrines••: The Arminian opinion is criticized for introducing Pelagian doctrines.

••V. Critique of Arminian Opinion••

• ••Dangerous Extreme••: The Arminian opinion is considered a more dangerous extreme than the supralapsarian opinion.
• ••Introduction of Pelagian Doctrines••: The Arminian opinion is criticized for introducing Pelagian doctrines under the pretext of a new order.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

• ••The Remonstrants' view of God's decrees••
	• They believe God decreed four things: the means for repentance and faith, the ordination of faith and perseverance, the means to achieve faith, and the ordination of salvation or damnation for particular individuals.
	• These decrees are seen as subordinate to each other, with the first three being general and the last being particular.
• ••The connection between the decrees••
	• The connection between the decrees is contingent and eventual, not necessary.
	• It is possible that Christ's mediation and the law of faith could be given, but no one would believe and be saved, resulting in the whole being damned.
• ••The Remonstrants' opinion on the order of the decrees••
	• They presented their view in the Synodical Acts (1620).
	• This view is seen as a departure from the traditional Calvinist view of God's decrees.
• ••The implications of the Remonstrants' view••
	• It corrupts the doctrine of gratuitous predestination and delivers it over to the mind of the Pelagians.
	• It makes election and reprobation acts of justice, rather than acts of God's good pleasure.
	• It implies that God only foresees faith, but does not produce it.
	• It suggests that the difference between men is due to nature and free will, rather than grace and the Holy Spirit.
• ••The biblical critique of the Remonstrants' view••
	• The view is contrary to Scripture, which attributes the cause of the difference between men to grace alone (1 Cor 4:7; Eph 2:8).
	• It is also contrary to the idea that faith is the gift of God (Eph 2:8).
	• It implies that God cannot elect to faith without also electing to salvation (Ps 65:4; Acts 13:48; Rom 8:30).
	• It does not make a clear distinction between those to be saved and those to be damned.

••I. Creation and Omnipotence••

• The mode of production of a creature requires infinite power, which is a characteristic of omnipotence.
	• This is because creation brings a creature forth from nothing.
	• Omnipotence is required to accomplish this instantaneous act.

••II. Creature's Dependence on a Subject••

• Every creature acts in dependence upon a subject.
	• However, there is no preexisting subject since creation makes and posits its subject.
	• The creature does not suppose the subject, but rather creates it.

••III. Cause and Effect••

• Every cause (principal and instrumental) should reach the work itself.
	• However, no creature can be so elevated as to be capable of a work of infinite power.
	• This is because creation is an instantaneous act and has no subject upon which its labor can be exercised.

••IV. Miracles and Creation••

• Although creatures may concur in the working of miracles, they cannot concur equally in creating.
	• In miracles, a subject is always supplied for the instrument to be occupied.
	• In creation, no subject is supplied, and therefore no instrumental cause can be granted.

••V. God's Role in Creation••

• God created all things by a word, not after the manner of an instrument and ministerial cause.
	• The Word is the eternal Son of God, who is the same in essence with the Father.
	• The Holy Spirit is also a part of the total cause of creation.

••VI. Causality and Energy••

• The same nature belongs to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
	• Therefore, the same causality and energetic force is shared among them.
	• The order of acting is preserved among them.

••VII. Communication of Creative Power••

• God is not able to communicate creative power to the creature.
	• This does not argue impotency in God, but rather from its perfection.
	• Such a communication is absurd, both on the part of God and the creature.

••VIII. Recreation and Creation••

• It requires the same power to create and recreate.
	• Infinite power is required for creation, and no less is demanded for recreation.
	• Conversion is often expressed under the name of creation and the exceeding great power of God.

••IX. Ministry of Men in Recreation••

• If God effects recreation by the ministry of men and the preaching of the word, this is not done by them as the physical cause.
	• Rather, it is done by them as the moral cause.
	• The Holy Spirit by his efficacy alone can perform the work.

••X. Question Concerning the Eternity of the World••

• The question has two parts: actual eternity and possibility.
	• The first part concerns whether the world was really from eternity.
	• The second part concerns whether at least it could have been.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Objection to Emanation••

• The objection from the emanation of the sun's rays, which are coeval with the sun
	• The relation of things acting by emanation differs from that of those acting by transmutation (natural from free agents)
	• The effects can be coeval with the cause, but not in the case of transmutation

••II. Repugnance of Creation••

• Creation is out of nothing, carrying with it newness of being
	• A thing must be conceived not to have been before it could be produced
	• Therefore, it cannot have been eternal
• The phrase "ex nihilo" denotes a nothing of terminus, implying that the creating was not and afterwards began to be

••III. Impossibility of Creature's Eternity••

• Eternity is repugnant to what has a successive and finite duration and being
	• Every creature as such has a successive and finite being and duration
• If the creature is eternal, it would have existed either in the eternity of God or in its own
	• If in its own, there would be two eternals, two infinites, and the duration of God and the creature would be equal
	• If in the eternity of God, the existence of creatures would be the existence of God

••IV. Formal Relation of Creature to God••

• The creature depends essentially upon God and has a beginning of existence
	• What depends upon another must be after it and so cannot be eternal
	• "When you maintain that a thing has a beginning of its being, you deny it by that very fact to be eternal," as Lactantius says

••V. Eternal Agent and Coeternal Object••

• An eternal agent requires a coeternal object
	• God is not an eternal agent in this sense because he began to act out of himself only in time
• God was from eternity a sufficient cause actually, but not in action (in actu)

••VI. God's Sufficiency and Action••

• God was from eternity a sufficient cause actually because he always existed and always willed to create the world
	• But he was not from eternity in action (in actu) because he did not will to create from eternity, but only in time

••VII. God's Change and Potency••

• Agents who act by volition alone differ from those in whom laborious efforts are required besides the volition
	• The latter pass from potency to act, from volition to the effecting
• God did not change from potency to act and from leisure to work when he created the world

••VIII. God's Practical Volition••

• God produced the world by his practical volition, which is a mere volition
	• This is different from agents who require laborious efforts besides the volition

••IX. Change in the World••

• A certain change was made in the world, which passed from non-existence to existence
	• But not in God, who remained in himself the same

••X. Conclusion••

• The objections to the emanation of the creature's eternity are based on the repugnance of creation and the impossibility of the creature's eternity
	• The formal relation of the creature to God and the nature of God's sufficiency and action also support this conclusion

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Clouds and Water••

• Clouds are formed from water evaporated by heat and congealed by cold air.
	• This is confirmed by the nature of clouds and the writings of Pliny.
• Moses describes the waters as twofold: above and below.
	• The clouds, which are waters, cannot be those below, so they must be referred to those above.

••II. Supercelestial Waters••

• The Lutherans and some Scholastics have invented the concept of "supercelstial waters".
	• This is done to make the ascension of Christ and believers into heaven more difficult.
• These waters are of no use, as they cannot cool the heat of the heavens or compress the heavens.
	• They also cannot reach the heavenly orbs, which are firmly established by God.

••III. Location of Clouds••

• Clouds are not above the ethereal heaven, but above the aerial heaven.
	• This is because the clouds are attracted to the sun in constituted nature.
• God can raise the clouds up extraordinarily without the sun in nature.
	• This means that the clouds can be above a part of the expanse, rather than the whole expanse.

••IV. The Flood••

• The "windows of heaven" in Genesis 7:11 denote copious showers from dense clouds.
	• This is a metaphorical description of the flood that overwhelmed the former world.

••V. The Works of the Third Day••

• The works of the third day include the collection of the lower waters.
	• This collection is into certain beds, separating them from the land.
• The land is freed from the waters, making it a fit residence for animals and men.
	• The collected waters are stored in the sea, with tubes for perennially gushing fountains and great rivers.

••VI. Translation of vy'mr••

• The opinion that the work of the third day belongs to the second day is not readily admitted.
	• This is because there is no reason to translate vy'mr as "now he had said" in v. 9.
• The verb vy'mr is always translated as "and he said" in other places in the chapter.
	• This suggests that the work of the third day is distinct from the second day.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. The Image of God••

• The image of God is a concept that refers to the relationship between God and humanity.
	• It can be understood as the archetype or the things themselves in God.
	• It can also refer to the ectype or the similitude itself, which is in man and the relation to God himself.

••II. What the Image of God Does Not Consist Of••

• The image of God does not consist in a participation of the divine essence.
	• This means that the nature of man is not a shadow of the divine and a part of the divine breath.
	• Only the Son of God is the image of the invisible God in this sense.
• The image of God does not consist in a figure of the body or external bearing.
	• This means that the image of God is not something that can be seen in the physical body.
	• The body may reflect some aspects of the image of God, but it is not the primary seat of the image.

••III. What the Image of God Consists Of••

• The image of God consists in gifts bestowed upon man by creation.
	• These gifts are both essential and accidental, internal and external.
	• They place man in a degree of nature, perfection, and authority that is unique among visible creatures.
• The image of God consists in three things:
	• (a) Nature: the spiritual and immortal nature of man.
	• (b) Rectitude of nature: the right relationship between man and God.
	• (c) The happy state founded upon both: the state of being that results from the relationship between man and God.

••IV. The Seat of the Divine Image••

• The proper seat of the divine image is the soul, not the body.
	• The body may reflect some aspects of the image of God, but it is not the primary seat of the image.
	• The soul is the seat of the image because it is the source of man's power over the rest of creatures and his ability to contemplate and know God.

• Dominion is the power given to man by God to be the chief over all lower creatures.
• Dominion is mentioned in Genesis 1:26 as a part of the creation of man in the image of God.
• Dominion is common to both man and woman, but man has it peculiarly as the head of the household.
• Dominion was broken and diminished by the fall, but was confirmed to Noah after the flood.

••III. Immortality••

• Immortality is not only of the soul itself, but also of the whole subsisting substance (i.e. the body).
• Immortality is conditional, meaning that man would not die if he had not sinned.
• The absolute immortality of the saints is a separate question.

••IV. Original Righteousness••

• The question of whether original righteousness is natural or supernatural is a matter of controversy.
• The Romanists argue that it is supernatural, while the author argues that it is natural.
• The author will treat the nature of the state of integrity, the truth of original sin, and the condition of free will in a separate question.

••V. Definitions of Natural and Supernatural••

• Natural is used in four ways:
	• Originally and subjectively, meaning drawn from nature and concreated with it.
	• Constitutively and consecutively, meaning constituting the nature of a thing or following from its principles.
	• Perfectively, meaning agreeing with the nature and adorning and perfecting it.
	• Transitively, meaning propagated with the nature.
• Supernatural is not defined in this text, but is implied to be something that is not natural in the sense of being drawn from nature.

••I. Introduction••

	• Immortality of the soul (concerned with happiness)

••III. Proximate vs. Remote Mortality••

• The question is whether Adam was mortal by a proximate power (necessarily dying) or remotely mortal (having a remote power of death).

• The reasons for Adam's immortality are:
	• (1) Man was made in the image of God, which contains holiness and immortality.
	• (2) If Adam was righteous, he ought to have been immortal due to the necessary connection between righteousness and life.

••V. Connection between Righteousness and Life••

• There is a necessary connection between righteousness and life:
	• (a) From the order of God, who has joined righteousness and life in the law.
	• (b) From the nature of the thing itself, which demands that homogeneous things (moral good and physical good) should not be separated.

••VI. God's Love and Goodness••

• God's love and goodness imply that he would wish his creatures to be happy and immortal:
	• God cannot but love himself and his creatures.
	• God wishes his creatures well and does them good.

• Adam's sin contracted the death threatened as the punishment of sin:
	• This is the reason why Adam died.

••VIII. Christ's Example••

• Christ's example is used to illustrate the separation of righteousness and life:
	• Although Christ was righteous, he died.

••IX. Dispensational Separation••

• The separation of righteousness and life is not perpetual:
	• It can occur for a time and by dispensation.

••X. Conclusion••

• The question of Adam's immortality is complex and involves different types of immortality and the connection between righteousness and life.

â€¢ ••The Origin of the Soul••
	• The question of whether souls are created by God or propagated is a topic of debate among theologians and philosophers.
	• The two main opinions are creationism and propagationism.

â€¢ ••Creationism••
	• The majority of orthodox theologians and philosophers believe in creationism.
	• This view holds that souls are created immediately by God and infused into the body.
	• The soul of Adam is cited as an example of creation, as God breathed life into him (Genesis 2:7).

â€¢ ••Propagationism••
	• This view is held by some Lutherans and is associated with Tertullian.
	• Propagationists believe that souls are propagated from the semen of the parents or from the soul of the father.
	• There are different sub-views within propagationism, including:
		- Souls are propagated from the semen of the parents.
		- Souls are propagated from the soul of the father by an inscrutable and unknown process.
		- Souls are propagated by a spiritual and incorporeal seed.

â€¢ ••Arguments for Creationism••
	• The law of creation: the origin of our souls should be the same as that of Adam's soul.
	• Scripture: the Bible teaches that God created Adam's soul (Genesis 2:7).
	• Reason: the soul is immaterial and simple, and cannot be produced by any other source than God.

â€¢ ••Objections to Propagationism••
	• If souls are propagated from the semen of the parents, they would be corporeal and subject to corruption.
	• The process of propagation is unknown and inscrutable.

â€¢ ••Augustine's View••
	• Augustine suspends his judgment on the question of the origin of the soul.
	• He testifies that he still does not know what to believe on this matter.

â€¢ ••Tertullian's View••
	• Tertullian was a proponent of propagationism and wrote a treatise on the soul.
	• His view was followed by the Luciferians and some Latin theologians.

â€¢ ••The Lutherans' View••
	• The Lutherans generally hold to propagationism.
	• Some Lutherans believe that souls are propagated by the soul of the father in a spiritual manner, like light kindling light.

â€¢ ••The Common Opinion••
	• The most common opinion among propagationists is that souls are propagated by the soul of the father in a spiritual manner.

â€¢ ••The Creation of Souls••
	• The creation of souls is proven by the law of creation, Scripture, and reason.
	• The soul of Adam is cited as an example of creation, and the origin of our souls should be the same as his.

••III. Implications of Soul Propagation••

• If souls are propagated, the parents of the body and soul should be the same.
• However, the Bible distinguishes between the fathers of the flesh and the Father of spirits.
• The flesh refers to the body, not the old man or inborn corruption.

••IV. Meaning of "Spirit"••

• The word "spirit" refers to the non-corporeal part of man, opposed to the body.
• It does not refer to spiritual gifts or the Holy Spirit.

••V. Antithesis between Fathers of the Flesh and Father of Spirits••

• The antithesis between the two would not stand if God were called the Father of spirits immediately.

• However, the concourse of man in the production of the spirit is not excluded either.

••VII. Arguments from Reason••

• The soul is propagated by generation, either from both parents or from one only.
• However, neither of these options can be said to be true.
• If the whole soul is propagated, the parents will be without it and be deprived of life.
• If a part of the soul is propagated, it will be divisible and consequently material and mortal.

••VIII. Difficulties with Modes of Propagation••

• All modes of propagation are pressed by serious difficulties.
• They cannot be admitted without overthrowing the spirituality of the rational soul.

••IX. Impossibility of Soul Propagation••

• The soul cannot be propagated from the power of seed, as this would imply a material and divisible origin.
• The effect cannot be more noble than its cause, and corporeal and elementary things cannot produce a spiritual and rational thing.

••X. Conclusion••

• The Bible teaches that God is the Father of spirits, distinct from the fathers of the flesh.
• The origin of the spirit is different from the origin of the body, and the soul is not propagated by generation.

	• The soul is created to be joined to the body, and the body is created to be the instrument of the soul.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. The Federal Promise and Immortality••

• The federal promise made to the patriarchs implies that God is the God of the living, not the dead.
	• This means that the souls of the patriarchs are immortal.
	• It also implies that their bodies will be raised from the dead.

••II. Foundations for the Reasoning••

• The covenant between God and man demands the existence of those with whom the covenant was made.
	• This is necessary for the relation between God and men to exist.
	• It also allows for the communication of benefits to men.
• The covenant is eternal, remaining even after death.
	• God is still called the God of the patriarchs even after their death.
• The covenant was made with the whole man, not just the soul.
	• This implies that the patriarchs, as whole men, will exist after death and forever.

••III. Implications of the Covenant••

• The patriarchs, as God's covenant partners, ought to live forever.
	• This is because God is their God by an eternal covenant.
• The resurrection of the body is implied by the covenant.
	• The whole man, including the body, will enjoy the life of God.

••IV. Immortality of Nature••

• The immortality of believers is extended to the immortality of nature.
	• This is because the one necessarily supposes the other.
• The souls of the wicked will not perish, but will be visited with punishments.

••V. Different Exit of Body and Soul••

• Passages that describe a different exit of the body and soul imply that the soul subsists after the destruction of the body.
	• This is because the soul returns to God, its extrinsic and efficient principle.
	• The body returns to the dust, its material and intrinsic principle.

••VI. Biblical Passages••

• Ecclesiastes 12:7 implies that the soul subsists after the destruction of the body.
	• The body returns to the dust, while the spirit returns to God.
• Psalm 146:4 also implies that the soul subsists after the destruction of the body.
	• The breath of man goes out, while he returns to his earth.

••VII. Christ's Teaching••

• Christ teaches that the soul cannot be destroyed with the body.
	• He distinguishes between men, who can kill the body, and God, who can destroy both body and soul in hell.
• Christ's teaching implies that the soul subsists after the destruction of the body.

••VIII. Eternal Life and Punishment••

• Passages that promise eternal life to believers or threaten the wicked with eternal punishment imply that the soul subsists after the destruction of the body.
• Passages that treat of the last judgment and eternal judgment also imply that the soul subsists after the destruction of the body.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••1. The Nature of Providence••
• The concept of providence is closely tied to the idea of God's approval and love.
• God strengthens, examines, and exercises those whom he approves and loves.
• Those who have never experienced adversity are more burdened by it than those who have.

••2. The Distribution of Good and Evil••
• The distribution of good and evil is a demonstration of God's wise providence.
• This distribution is a wonder that Christians should not doubt.
• The Gentiles themselves have derived an argument in favor of providence from this distribution.

••3. The Question of Fate••
• The question of whether God's providence is rightly called "fate" is necessary to clarify the use of the word among Christians.
• The doctrine of providence must be freed from calumnies and opposition from Romanists and others.

••4. The Derivation of the Word "Fate"••
• The word "fate" is derived from the Latin "fando," meaning "speaking" or "utterance."
• The concept of fate is also known as "eimarmenÄ“" in Greek, meaning "appointed" or "determined."
• The Stoic philosophers used the word to signify providence, which was later borrowed by Christians.

••5. Types of Fate••
• There are four types of fate:
	• Physical fate: the order and series of natural causes defined to their effects.
	• Mathematical fate: the necessity of things and events arising from the position of the heavens and stars.
	• Stoical fate: the necessity of all things and events.
	• Christian fate: the providence of God.

••6. Physical Fate••
• Physical fate is the order and series of natural causes defined to their effects.
• Its principle is nature or the power of acting, which God imparted to things in creation.
• The effects are all those events that depend on natural causes.

••7. Mathematical Fate••
• Mathematical fate is the necessity of things and events arising from the position of the heavens and stars.
• It is also known as "astral" fate, and is associated with the Chaldeans and astrologers.
• This type of fate is said to impel the wills of men to their acts.

••8. Stoical Fate••
• Stoical fate is the necessity of all things and events.
• It is associated with the Stoic philosophers, who used the word to signify providence.
• This type of fate is often opposed to the Christian doctrine of providence.

••9. Christian Fate••
• Christian fate is the providence of God.
• It is the concept of God's wise and loving guidance of the world.
• This type of fate is distinct from the other three types, which are often associated with pagan or Stoic ideas.

••10. The Use of the Word "Fate"••
• The word "fate" is used in many ways by authors, leading to a fourfold classification of fate.
• The use of the word "fate" among Christians must be clarified to avoid confusion and opposition.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••Three types of fate••
	• Jewish and Pharisaical fate
	• Stoical fate
	• Other types of fate (not specified)

â€¢ ••Jewish and Pharisaical fate••
	• Ascribed to fate whatever happens
	• Believed in astrological fate ("all things depend upon planets")
	• Limited by Josephus, who said Pharisees attribute some, not all things to fate

â€¢ ••Stoical fate••
	• Defined by Chrysippus as a natural order and connection of all things
	• Defined by Cicero as the order and series of causes
	• Subjected God himself to fate, according to Seneca

â€¢ ••Stoical fate: two possible interpretations••
	• Some believe Stoics held that all causes were natural and defined, taking away human liberty and contingency
	• Others believe Stoics only asserted the immutability of divine decrees, without taking away human liberty or contingency

â€¢ ••Augustine's interpretation of Stoical fate••
	• Believed Stoics called fate the connection and series of all causes
	• Believed Stoics ascribed fate to the supreme will and power of God
	• Believed Stoics did not take away human liberty or contingency

â€¢ ••Difference between Stoical fate and Christian view••
	• Stoics subject God to necessity, while Christians subject necessity to God
	• Stoics believe in a natural and eternal series of causes, while Christians believe in a difference between natural and free causes

â€¢ ••Stoical fate: a misunderstanding••
	• Many people impute a different fate to the Stoics, imposing a fatal and ineluctable necessity on all things
	• This is not the genuine opinion of the Stoics, according to Augustine

â€¢ ••Christian view of fate••
	• Places necessity in God himself and his eternal decree
	• Believes in a difference between natural and free causes

â€¢ ••Stoical fate: not to be disturbed••
	• If the genuine opinion of the Stoics is as Augustine describes, they are not to be disturbed
	• They approach the truth, but are still separated from the Christian view

â€¢ ••Conclusion••
	• The Stoical fate is a complex and multifaceted concept
	• Christians must be careful not to misunderstand the Stoics and their views on fate.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

• ••Christian Fate••
	• The fourth fate is the series and order of causes depending on divine providence.
	• It produces its own effects and is considered a temporal series of causes.
	• It is distinguished from providence by reason of the subject (God vs. second causes), order (fate depends on providence), and object (all things lie under providence, but not under fate).
• ••Definition of Fate••
	• Boethius defines fate as "an immovable disposition inherent in movable things, by which divine providence weaves together each in its own orders".
• ••Use of the Word "Fate"••
	• The word "fate" may be used in a sound sense, but it is contaminated by heathenism and superstition.
	• Calvin advises against using the word in the Christian school.
	• The word "providence" is safer to use because it is handed down in Scripture.
• ••Augustine's Opinion••
	• Augustine believed that if someone calls the power and will of God "fate", they should hold the opinion but correct the language.
• ••Object of Providence••
	• The question is whether all things, great and small, contingent and free, natural and necessary, come under providence.
	• The authors affirm that providence encompasses all things.
• ••Narrow Limits of Providence••
	• Some people restrict providence to heavenly things only, leaving room for chance and fortune in the sublunary world.
	• Others extend providence to the sublunary world, but only to natural and necessary things.
	• Some Scholastics hold that providence only applies to great things, excluding the mean and minute.
• ••Thomas Aquinas' View••
	• Thomas Aquinas asserts that providence applies to all things, great and small, and that it is not limited to heavenly things.
• ••Providence and Fate••
	• Providence is the divine decree itself, while fate is the disposition of all causes to their own effects.
	• Fate depends on providence and is a temporal series of causes.
• ••Calvin's Advice••
	• Calvin advises against using the word "fate" in the Christian school because it is contaminated by heathenism and superstition.
• ••Scriptural Basis••
	• The word "providence" is handed down in Scripture, while the word "fate" does not appear in Scripture.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••God's Providence is Universal••
	• God's providence extends to all things, without exception
	• This includes both heavenly and sublunary things, great and small

â€¢ ••Reasons for Universal Providence••
	• God created all things, so he must also take care of them
	• It would be unbecoming for God to create something and then abandon it

â€¢ ••Conclusion••

	• This is established by Scripture and is a fundamental aspect of God's nature.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Introduction to Providence••

• God's providence is described as consisting of two acts:
	• Conservation: God conserves all creatures in their own state
	• Government: God governs universals and singulars, directing them to ends foreappointed by him

••II. The Question of Providence••

• The question is not whether God's providence is concerned with the conservation of things, but rather:
	• Whether the whole relation of providence consists in conservation and the power of second causes to act
	• Or whether it also consists in government by which God himself acts and efficaciously concurs with his creatures

••III. Durandus' Opinion••

• Durandus and some Romanists place providence and the concourse of God only in:
	• Conserving the strength of creatures and permitting them to act at pleasure
	• Not involving God in the actual exciting of actions

••IV. The Jesuits' Opinion••

• The Jesuits confess that God's providence does not consist only in conservation, but also in the influx and concourse of God
• However, they maintain that the concourse of God is:
	• General and indifferent, determined by second causes
	• Not antecedent and previously moving, but rather the second cause determines itself before the first cause acts

••V. The Thomists' Opinion••

• The Thomists and Dominicans determine that God's providence involves:
	• Physical predetermination: all second causes are predetermined to acting by God
	• God acting immediately on the will, determining it to will or not will this in particular, not only in good but also in evil actions

••VI. The Controversy••

• The controversy between the Thomists and Jesuits revolves around the nature of God's concourse with his creatures
• The Thomists argue that God's providence involves a more direct and efficacious concourse, while the Jesuits argue that it is more general and indifferent

••VII. The Role of Second Causes••

• The Jesuits argue that second causes determine themselves before the first cause acts
• The Thomists argue that God predetermines the actions of second causes

••VIII. The Nature of God's Concourse••

• The Jesuits argue that God's concourse is not antecedent and previously moving, but rather the second cause determines itself before the first cause acts
• The Thomists argue that God's concourse is immediate and efficacious, determining the will of creatures

••IX. The Purpose of God's Providence••

• The Jesuits argue that God's providence is to vindicate God from the causality of sin and to establish the liberty and indifference of the human will
• The Thomists argue that God's providence is to direct creatures to their proper ends and to bring about good

••X. Conclusion••

• The controversy between the Thomists and Jesuits revolves around the nature of God's concourse with his creatures and the role of second causes in God's providence.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. God's Providence••

• God's providence is not limited to conservation, but also includes a particular and immediate concourse.
	• This means God actively works with secondary causes to achieve his ends.

••II. Scripture's Teaching••

• Scripture attributes God's actions to himself, even when secondary causes are involved.
	• Examples: God sending Joseph into Egypt, turning the king's heart, and using the wicked as instruments.
	• This implies God's effective concurrence with secondary causes.

••III. Conservation vs. Concourse••

• Conservation refers to God's preservation of faculties, while concourse refers to his effective working with secondary causes.
	• The two are not mutually exclusive, but concourse is a more active and specific involvement.

••IV. Instrumental Analogy••

• The relationship between God and secondary causes is like that between an artificer and his instruments.
	• Instruments may have the faculty to operate, but they require the artificer's concurrence to do so.

••V. Dependence on God••

• As creatures depend on God for their being, they also depend on him for their actions.
	• This dependence is not limited to conservation, but also includes God's effective concurrence.

••VI. Passages on God's Work••

• Passages like "we live and move and have our being in God" (Acts 17:28) imply God's effective concurrence.
	• Other passages, such as Philippians 2:13 and 1 Corinthians 12:6, also suggest God's active work in believers.

••VII. God as Lord of the World••

• As the Lord of the world, God regulates and rules over all that exists and is done in it.
	• This requires a more active and specific involvement than mere conservation or general concourse.

••VIII. Regulation and Order••

• God's regulation of the world involves a destined order that includes both the setting of ends and the ordination of means.
	• This order is not possible through mere conservation or general concourse.

••IX. Mode of Being and Working••

• The mode of working follows the mode of being, so creatures should have themselves in working as they do in being.
	• This implies that God's providence should involve effective concurrence, not just conservation.

••X. Conclusion••

• The orthodox approach to God's providence emphasizes a particular and immediate concourse, not just conservation.
	• This approach is supported by Scripture and the nature of God's relationship with the world.

â€¢ ••Physical vs. Moral Concourse••
	• The text discusses physical concourse, not moral concourse
	• Physical concourse refers to the interaction between a cause and its effect

â€¢ ••Mediate and Immediate Concourse••
	• A cause can act either immediately or mediately
	• Immediate concourse occurs when no other substance is interposed between the cause and effect
	• Mediate concourse occurs when another substance is interposed between the cause and effect

â€¢ ••Immediate Concourse••
	• God acts immediately by an immediation of virtue (his own power) and subsisting substance (his own essence)
	• God uses second causes as means, but still acts immediately

â€¢ ••Concourse by Way of Principle and Action••
	• Concourse can occur by way of principle (God conserving the power of the second act) or by way of action (God being the proximate principle of the operation)
	• The text focuses on concourse by way of action

â€¢ ••Previous and Simultaneous Concourse••
	• Previous concourse is the action of God that excites and moves creatures to action
	• Simultaneous concourse is the action of God that produces the action of the creature as to its being or substance

â€¢ ••Types of Previous Concourse••
	• Previous concourse can be predetermining (God determining the outcome of the creature's action)
	• Previous concourse can also be exciting (God exciting the creature to action)

â€¢ ••Types of Simultaneous Concourse••
	• Simultaneous concourse can be concomitant (God flowing together with creatures into their actions and effects)
	• Simultaneous concourse can also be continued previous concourse (God's action continuing from the previous concourse)

â€¢ ••God's Action in Concourse••
	• God's action in concourse is not a separate action from the creature's action
	• God's action is the very same as the creature's action, but with a different intention (tending to the same end)

â€¢ ••Cooperation of God••
	• The cooperation of God is the same as the very action of the creature
	• God's cooperation is not a separate action, but an integral part of the creature's action

â€¢ ••Focus of the Text••
	• The text focuses on physical concourse, specifically concourse by way of action
	• The text does not discuss moral concourse or concourse by way of principle.

	• Weighty reasons support the opinion that previous concourse is true and safer.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

• ••Limitations of the Axiom••
	• The axiom "action and effect belong rather to the principal than the instrumental cause" has limitations.
	• It holds good in homogeneous causes, but not in heterogeneous causes.
• ••Homogeneous Causes••
	• The axiom holds good when both causes are positive or privative, physical or moral.
	• Example: the word of God sanctifies us, and the Holy Spirit is the principal cause.
• ••Heterogeneous Causes••
	• The axiom does not hold good when one cause is positive and physical, and the other is privative and moral.
	• Example: the sword is not the culpable cause of homicide, and neither is the man wielding it.
• ••Types of Instruments••
	• The axiom holds good in proper, pure, and irrational instruments that borrow from the principal agent.
	• Example: a sword is a pure instrument, and the man wielding it is the principal cause.
• ••Mixed Instruments••
	• The axiom does not hold good in metaphorical and mixed instruments that have something of their own mixed.
	• Example: a horse struck by a spur is not a pure instrument, but has its own cause of lameness.
• ••Rational and Mixed Instruments••
	• Sinners are not proper and pure instruments, but rational, metaphorical, and mixed.
	• Their wickedness is the proper and adequate cause of sin.
• ••Moral Action••
	• The axiom holds good when the action of the principal cause is morally the same as the action of the instrumental cause.
	• Example: the disciple of Pelagius has a poor opinion of grace, and so does Pelagius himself.
• ••Material and Physical Action••
	• The axiom does not hold good when the action is the same materially and physically, but not morally.
	• Example: the same physical action can be just or unjust according to the diversity of agents.
• ••Principal and Instrumental Cause••
	• The principal cause is positive, physical, and irresponsible, while the instrumental cause is privative and moral.
	• Example: God is the principal cause, and men are the instrumental cause of sin.
• ••Specification of the Act••
	• The specification of the act as to moral being arises from the diverse moral circumstances, not from the substance of the real physical act.

		- In causes by themselves, which produce the effect.
		- In causes subordinated essentially and by necessity of nature.

	• Calvin asserts that God's sovereignty extends to the permission and ordination of sin

	• Calvin's views are opposed to the Pelagian and Scholastic views of bare and idle permission

â€¢ ••The Dispensation of God••
	• Calvin's view of the dispensation of God is not the efficiency of crimes, but the permission of them
	• This permission is not idle, but rather the governing of crimes and directing them to certain objects and ends

â€¢ ••The Causality of Sin••
	• Calvin's view of the causality of sin is not the infusion of wickedness, but the direction of enemies to certain objects by God
	• This direction is for the execution of God's just judgments, as seen in examples from Scripture

â€¢ ••The Secret Will of God••
	• Calvin's view of the secret will of God is not the complacency of God in sins or an impulse to sins as such
	• Rather, it is the motion of God's will in three ways: physical, judicial, and directive

â€¢ ••Calvin's View of the Devil••
	• Calvin's view of the devil is that he and all the wicked conceive, attempt, and commit no evil deed except as God has permitted
	• This view is not a justification of sin, but rather a statement of the Scriptural truth that God permits evil deeds to occur

â€¢ ••Scriptural Basis••
	• Calvin's views are based on Scripture, and he quotes Scripture to support his arguments
	• Calvin's views are not novel or innovative, but rather a restatement of traditional Christian doctrine

â€¢ ••Calvin's Intent••
	• Calvin's intent is to oppose the will of God to the figment of bare and idle permission
	• Calvin's views are meant to teach that sin and evil deeds occur by the certain counsel and providence of God.

â€¢ ••Calvin's View of God's Providence••
	• Calvin argues that God's providence restrains the devil and the wicked from harming the faithful.
	• This restraint is not a result of God's permission, but rather his immutable counsel.

â€¢ ••Coaction vs. Necessity••
	• Calvin's view is not one of coaction, where God forces the devil and the wicked to act against their will.
	• Instead, it is a necessity of infallibility, where God's providence ensures that the devil and the wicked will not succeed in their evil plans.

â€¢ ••The Devil and the Wicked as Instruments••

	• Calvin argues that God works in the minds of the wicked, but not in a way that implies theomartesianism (the idea that God is the author of evil).

	• Calvin responds to critics who accuse him of introducing theomartesianism.

	• The Bible mentions the prince of demons and eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels (Mt. 25:41)

••II. Augustine's Opinion••

	• He believes in the existence of seats, dominions, principalities, and powers in the heavenly arrangements
	• However, he does not know what they are or what the differences between them are
	• He condemns those who try to define the angelic hierarchy too precisely

••III. The Romanist and Scholastic View••

• The Romanists and Scholastics have developed a more detailed understanding of the angelic hierarchy
	• They attribute this understanding to Dionysius the Areopagite
	• Dionysius divides the angels into three classes or hierarchies: highest, middle, and lowest
	• Each class has three subclasses, resulting in a total of nine classes and many thousands of angels

••IV. The Angelic Hierarchy According to Dionysius••

• Dionysius describes the angelic hierarchy as follows:
	• The highest class includes cherubim, seraphim, and thrones
		- Cherubim excel in the light of knowledge and illuminate others with wisdom
		- Seraphim burn with divine love and enkindle others
		- Thrones contemplate God's judicial glory and equity and rule over others in judgment
	• The second class includes dominions, principalities, and powers
		- Dominions regulate the duties of angels
		- Principalities preside over peoples and provinces
		- Powers restrain the power of devils
	• The third class includes virtues, archangels, and angels
		- Virtues work miracles
		- Archangels conduct embassages in important affairs
		- Angels conduct lesser affairs

••V. The Angelic Hierarchy According to Dionysius (continued)••

• Dionysius believes that the angels should be distinguished by reason of knowledge
	• The angels of the first class behold God and perceive the reasons of things
	• The second rank knows universal causes according to God
	• The third rank ascertains the causes of things as they are gathered from proximate causes

••VI. The Angelic Hierarchy in Other Traditions••

• The Jews also distribute the angels into various classes, constituting ten hierarchies
	• The highest are below the throne of majesty
	• The lowest live with men and sometimes converse with them
• The Jews hold that the superior angels are denoted by "chief princes" (Dan. 10:13) and those who "stand in the presence of the Lord" (Ps. 138:1)

	• The first liberty of will was to be able not to sin (posse non peccare)
	• The last will be much greater, not to be able to sin (non posse peccare)

â€¢ ••The First and Last Immortality••
	• The first immortality was the power of not dying
	• The last will be much greater, the incapability of dying

â€¢ ••The Power of Perseverance••
	• The first was the power of perseverance, the power to not desert the good
	• The last will be the happiness of perseverance, the want of power to desert the good

â€¢ ••The Question of Adam's Power to Believe in Christ••
	• This question lies between us and the Arminians
	• The Arminians argue that Adam never had the power to believe in Christ, and therefore could not have lost it by sin

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••Adam's Ability to Believe in Christ••
	• Arminius and Corvinus argue that Adam had the potential to believe in Christ before the fall.
	• They claim that Adam's power to believe in Christ was not dependent on his actual faith, but rather on his potential faith.

â€¢ ••The Question at Hand••
	• The question is not whether Adam actually believed in Christ, but whether he had the potential to believe in Christ if it had been revealed to him.
	• The orthodox view is that Adam did not actually believe in Christ as the Redeemer because Christ had not been revealed to him.

â€¢ ••Adam's Power to Believe••
	• Adam received the power to believe every word of God.
	• This power is evident from the perfection of Adam's nature, which is bound to render faith and obedience to God.

â€¢ ••The Nature of Faith••
	• Faith in Christ is a part of the general notion of faith.
	• Adam's power to believe every word of God implies that he also had the power to believe the word of the gospel.

â€¢ ••The Gospel Covenant••
	• Corvinus argues that the gospel covenant was not absolutely credible to upright man without a contradiction.
	• However, the text responds that the gospel could be credible with respect to the future time if God had revealed it to Adam.

â€¢ ••The Power to Love and Obey••
	• Before the fall, Adam had the power to love God and obey him in all things.
	• This power implies that Adam also had the power to believe God when he spoke.

â€¢ ••The Exception of Force••
	• The text argues that the power to believe God differs from the power to believe Christ because the word of the law and the gospel are opposed in their total genus.
	• However, this difference does not arise from a defect of power, but rather from the revelation of the object.

â€¢ ••The State of Integrity••
	• Adam's state of integrity did not prevent him from having the power to believe the gospel.
	• The text argues that the gospel was not credible in the state of integrity only because it was not revealed to Adam.

â€¢ ••The Revelation of the Object••
	• The text argues that the power to believe is not dependent on the revelation of the object.
	• Rather, the revelation of the object is what makes faith possible.

â€¢ ••The Implications of Adam's Power••
	• If Adam had the power to believe in Christ, this would imply that he had the potential to be redeemed.
	• This would also imply that the fall was not a necessary part of God's plan, but rather a consequence of Adam's free choice.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. The Law and Gospel••

• The law and gospel are both the word of God and the object of our faith and obedience.
	• They are equally authoritative and deserving of our trust.

	• This is because the law and gospel are both expressions of God's will.

• The upright angels knew the promised Redeemer and rejoiced in him.
	• This knowledge was revealed to them by God.
• Man in his state of integrity could also have known the future Redeemer.
	• This is because there is the same reason for both the angels and man to know the Redeemer.

	• Both are repugnant to the state of integrity, but could have been received by man in innocence.

	• Therefore, he could also have had faith in Christ if he had been predicted to him.

	• It occupied itself with many things, even if it couldn't exercise itself about a certain object (the Redeemer).

	• It's only called vain and idle when it can and should act, but doesn't.

••V. Faith in the Remission of Sins••

• Upright Adam couldn't believe in the remission of present sins.
	• But he could have believed that there would be remission if God revealed it to him.

	• But it's possible to believe that one will fall and need the grace of God and faith in Christ.

••VI. The Law and the Gospel••

• Faith in Christ is not prescribed specifically in the law.
	• But it's contained in it generically and implicitly.
• The law commands us to believe every word of God and all his promises.
	• Therefore, no one could obey the law who was not prepared to believe the word of the gospel.

••VII. The Loss of Power••

• Adam had no need of new powers for rising from the fall.
	• Unless he lost that power by the fall.
• Adam lost all his power with original righteousness by sinning.
	• Therefore, he couldn't rise by his own strength after the fall.

••VIII. The Covenant of Nature••

• A covenant among men is a mutual agreement about the mutual bestowal of goods and offices.
	• But this definition may not apply to God's covenant with Adam.

••IX. The Nature of the Covenant••

• The covenant of nature may be different from a human covenant.
	• It may be a unilateral agreement or a different kind of agreement altogether.

••X. The Implications of the Covenant••

• The covenant of nature may have implications for our understanding of God's relationship with Adam.
	• It may shed light on the nature of sin and the need for redemption.

â€¢ ••Conditions of a Covenant••
	• The parties must be equal or in a certain order
	• Each party must have control over the goods or duties they offer
	• Each party must be independent and not bound to perform duties without agreement

â€¢ ••Limitations of a Covenant with God••

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Introduction••

• The text discusses the promise of eternal life in relation to Adam and the covenant with God
• Two main views are presented:
	• View 1: The promise of eternal life was not given to Adam, but rather a promise of earthly happiness
	• View 2: The promise of eternal life was given to Adam, and it was a heavenly and eternal life

••II. View 1: The Promise was not of Eternal Life••

• This view is held by Socinus and Volkelius
• They argue that the promise of eternal life was not given to Adam, but rather a promise of earthly happiness
• They refer to the blessings of the New Testament as the source of eternal life

••III. View 2: The Promise was of Eternal Life••

• This view is held by the orthodox
• They argue that the promise given to Adam was not only of a happy life in paradise, but also of a heavenly and eternal life
• They contend that Adam was to be carried to heaven after a life of perfect obedience and perseverance

••IV. Reasons for View 2••

• The law of works promised heavenly and eternal life, therefore the law prescribed to Adam also promised this
• The law is the same in substance in both cases
• Examples from Scripture include Leviticus 18:5, Matthew 19:16-17, and Romans 7:10

••V. Christ's Role in Acquiring Eternal Life••

• Christ acquired eternal and celestial life by fulfilling the righteousness of the law
• This could not have been done unless the law had promised heavenly life to the obedient
• Christ's death and resurrection restored the life that Adam lost, and this life is now available to us through Christ

••VI. The Threatening of Death••

• The threatening of death in Scripture implies that Adam would have attained eternal life if he had persevered in obedience
• Christ is called the tree of life, implying that he restored the life that Adam lost

••VII. Conclusion••

• The question is not whether Adam had the privilege of immortality in his upright state, but whether the promise of eternal life was given to him
• The orthodox view is that the promise was given to Adam, and it was a heavenly and eternal life.

••I. The Garden of Eden••

• The Garden of Eden was a paradise that was perpetually green and never shed its leaves.
• According to Pliny, it was a place of great beauty and wonder.

••II. The New Paradise••

• The new paradise is prepared for believers by God through Christ.
• It is a place in heaven, filled with mystical and divine trees bearing healthy fruits.
• It is watered by the perennial stream of living water and rivers of pleasure.
• In this place, sin and death are forever banished, and Satan can never return.

••III. The Nature of Sin••

• Sin is a deflection from the design or purpose of God.
• It is a wandering from the end proposed to us in creation and in the law of God.
• The Greek word "hamartia" means "a not reaching" or "missing a mark".
• Sin is also called "anomia" or "discrepancy from the law".

••IV. The Definition of Sin••

• Sin can be viewed in two aspects: concrete and material, or abstract and formal.
• In the concrete sense, sin is a desire, word, or deed contrary to the law of God.
• In the abstract sense, sin is nothing other than anomia or discrepancy from the law.
• The law of God is the standard by which sin is measured.

••V. The Law of God••

• The law of God is the only lawgiver who can save and destroy.
• It is the law that is impressed upon the consciences of men and is committed to writing in the Word of God.
• Human laws and customs are not the standard by which sin is measured.

••VI. The Etymology of Sin••

• The word "peccatum" comes from the Hebrew word "cht'h", which means "deflection" or "wandering".
• It is also derived from the Greek word "hamartia", which means "a not reaching" or "missing a mark".
• Other etymologies of the word "sin" include "rebel" and "to act irrationally like beasts".

••VII. Sin in General••

• Sin is a true deflection and wandering from the end proposed to us in creation and in the law of God.
• It is a lack of the legal rectitude that ought to be in us.

••VIII. Sin in Particular••

• Sin can be viewed in two aspects: original and actual sin.
• Original sin refers to the fall of angels and Adam, while actual sin refers to the sins committed by individuals.

••IX. The Consequences of Sin••

• Sin leads to wickedness and misery.
• It is a deflection from the design or purpose of God.
• It is a wandering from the end proposed to us in creation and in the law of God.

••X. The Nature of Sinners••

• Sinners are compared to dogs, swine, vipers, lions, and animals of like kind.
• They are said to be irrational and act like beasts.
• They are also said to be "rakes" or indulgers in lust.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Guilt and Sin••

• Guilt is a consequence of sin, but not the same as sin itself
	• Guilt is the obligation to punishment arising from sin
	• Sin is the nature of the offense against God

••II. Illegality and Condemnation••

• Illegality (anomia) is the nature of sin
• Condemnation (krima) is the consequence of sin, which follows illegality
	• Condemnation is a necessary consequence of sin, but not the same as sin itself

••III. Guilt and the Law••

• Guilt follows sin, partly from the natural right of God to punish sin
• Guilt also follows sin from the sanction of the divine law, which threatens punishment for sin

••IV. Separation of Guilt from Sin••

• Guilt can be separated from sin through the substitution of a surety (Christ)
	• This separation is not through nature or law, but through grace from the gospel

••V. Papist Distinction between Guilt of Culpability and Guilt of Punishment••

• Papists distinguish between guilt of culpability (reatus culpae) and guilt of punishment (reatus poenae)
	• Guilt of culpability is the guilt of being unworthy of God's grace and worthy of condemnation
	• Guilt of punishment is the guilt of being subject to condemnation and punishment
• This distinction is empty, as culpability and punishment are related and guilt is the obligation to punishment arising from culpability

••VI. Papist View of Mortal and Venial Sin••

• Papists divide sin into mortal and venial
	• Mortal sin is a sin that turns man entirely away from God and deserves eternal punishment
	• Venial sin is a sin that does not wholly turn away from God, but hinders progress to God and can be easily expiated

••VII. Punishment of Believers••

• Some punishments are still visited upon believers after the remission of culpability
	• These punishments are medicinal and castigatory, for the correction of the believer
	• They do not imply that there remains any guilt of punishment

••VIII. Question of Venial Sin••

• The question is whether any venial sin can be granted
	• The papists affirm that venial sin can be granted, but this is denied by the author

••IX. Papist Design in Dividing Sin into Mortal and Venial••

• The papist design in dividing sin into mortal and venial is to curry favor for the perfection of righteousness, supererogatory works, the merit of works, and purgatory
	• This design is not obscure, and is confirmed by the Council of Trent

••X. Conclusion••

• The author denies that any venial sin can be granted, and argues that all sins are mortal in their own nature.

â€¢ ••The National Synod's decree••
	• The Synod met at Charenton in 1644 and sanctioned the doctrine of imputation
	• The decree condemned the view that restricts original sin to hereditary corruption, excluding the imputation of Adam's first sin

â€¢ ••Placaeus' attempt to escape the Synod's decree••
	• He distinguished between immediate and mediate imputation
	• He argued that the immediate imputation is not the same as the mediate imputation, which follows the hereditary corruption

â€¢ ••Placaeus' view on imputation••
	• He argued that the sin of Adam is imputed to us through the hereditary corruption
	• He maintained that we share in Adam's sin and habitually consent to it through this corruption

â€¢ ••The Synod's decree and Placaeus' view••
	• The Synod's decree condemned the view that restricts original sin to hereditary corruption
	• Placaeus' view on imputation was opposed to the Synod's decree, but he attempted to escape its force by distinguishing between immediate and mediate imputation

â€¢ ••The distinction between immediate and mediate imputation••
	• Placaeus argued that the immediate imputation is not the same as the mediate imputation
	• However, this distinction was seen as a way to raise a smoke and retain the name of imputation while ignoring its meaning

â€¢ ••The consequence of Placaeus' view••
	• If the sin of Adam is imputed to us only through the hereditary corruption, then there is no proper imputation of Adam's sin
	• This view was seen as a way to avoid the Synod's decree while still retaining the name of imputation

â€¢ ••The controversy over imputation••
	• The controversy over imputation was a major issue in the Remonstrant controversy
	• The Synod's decree and Placaeus' view on imputation were central to this controversy.

â€¢ ••Understanding Imputation••
	• Imputation refers to the act of attributing someone else's sin or righteousness to us
	• It's a complex concept that requires careful consideration of the relationship between the one committing the sin and the one to whom it's imputed

â€¢ ••The Question at Hand••
	• The Synod is discussing whether the sin of Adam is imputed to all his descendants
	• This question is distinct from the sin of Adam itself, and from the concept of original sin inherent in humanity

â€¢ ••The Nature of Adam's Sin••
	• The Synod is focusing on the first actual sin committed by Adam, which violated the primordial law and broke the covenant with God
	• This sin is distinct from the habitual sin that Adam may have had within himself

â€¢ ••The Scope of Imputation••
	• The question of imputation does not concern all of Adam's descendants, but only those who descend from him in the ordinary way of generation
	• This excludes Christ, who was conceived in an extraordinary and supernatural way

â€¢ ••Types of Imputation••
	• Imputation can be either of something foreign to us or properly ours
	• The Synod is discussing the latter kind of imputation, where something is attributed to us that is not our own

â€¢ ••The Basis of Imputation••
	• Imputation requires a peculiar connection between the one committing the sin and the one to whom it's imputed
	• This connection can be natural, moral/political, or voluntary

â€¢ ••The Threefold Union••
	• The threefold union refers to the relationships between:
		- A father and his children (natural)
		- A king and his subjects (moral/political)
		- Friends or a guilty person and their substitute (voluntary)

â€¢ ••Imputation in the Context of Christ and Us••
	• The Synod notes that the imputation of our sins to Christ and his righteousness to us is a key aspect of the Christian faith
	• This imputation is based on the natural and moral/political unions between Christ and humanity

â€¢ ••The Conditions of Imputation••
	• Imputation requires a connection between the one committing the sin and the one to whom it's imputed
	• This connection can be established through natural, moral/political, or voluntary relationships

â€¢ ••The Purpose of Imputation••
	• Imputation serves to attribute the sin or righteousness of one person to another, often with the goal of punishment or justification
	• The Synod is seeking to understand the nature and basis of imputation in the context of Adam's sin and its impact on humanity.

	• Calvin approved of the doctrine of imputation in his writings.

	• Calvin's formula of the confession of faith stated that all humans are born infected with original sin.
	• This was due to Adam's rebellion against God, which rendered him liable to all miseries.

	• Calvin believed that humans are born under the curse of God and condemned due to Adam's sin.
	• He also believed that humans are heirs of eternal condemnation due to Adam's rebellion.

	• He argued that this is a just consequence of Adam's rebellion against God.

	• Calvin believed that human nature is corrupt due to Adam's sin.
	• He argued that humans are born infected with original sin and are under the curse of God.

	• Beza and others distinguished between guilt and corruption, stating that they cannot be separated but should be understood separately
	• Guilt refers to the imputation of Adam's sin, while corruption refers to the punishment that follows

â€¢ ••Synod of Dort••
	• The Synod of Dort, a group of theologians, agreed with Calvin and Beza's opinion
	• They stated that God decreed to call a certain number of people from Adam's seed, who were guilty and corrupt due to Adam's fall

â€¢ ••Peter Martyr's Opinion••
	• Peter Martyr agreed with Calvin and Beza's opinion
	• He stated that original corruption is the punishment of Adam's sin and that it is inflicted upon us as a result of Adam's fall

â€¢ ••Imputation of Adam's Sin••
	• Peter Martyr and others believed that Adam's sin is imputed to humanity, making us guilty and corrupt
	• They stated that this imputation is the basis for our original sin and corruption

â€¢ ••Chamier's Opinion••
	• Chamier agreed with Calvin, Beza, and Peter Martyr's opinion
	• He stated that we cannot be made inherently unrighteous by one man (Adam) unless the unrighteousness of Adam is imputed to us

â€¢ ••Imputation and Constitution••
	• Chamier believed that our righteousness or unrighteousness is constituted by the imputation of Adam's sin and Christ's obedience
	• He stated that we are made unrighteous by Adam's sin and righteous by Christ's obedience, but only through imputation

â€¢ ••Genevan Church's Opinion••
	• The Genevan Church, as represented by Calvin, Beza, and others, held to this opinion
	• They believed that humanity's guilt and corruption are a result of Adam's sin and are imputed to us

â€¢ ••Biblical Support••

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Imputation of Sin••

• The sin of Adam is imputed to his posterity due to his personal disobedience.
	• This is a key doctrine in understanding the nature of sin and its consequences.
• The obedience of Christ is also imputed to believers, who are considered to be in Christ by grace.
	• This is a key aspect of the doctrine of justification.

••II. Orthodox Agreement••

• The doctrine of imputed sin is not unique to one theologian, but is shared by many orthodox theologians.
	• Examples include Amyrald, Mestrezat, and Testard.
• These theologians argue that another's sin can be imputed to those connected to the author of the sin.
	• This is based on the idea that the punishment of the first man's sin should be extended to his posterity.

••III. Consequences of Sin••

• The punishment of the first man's sin should be extended to his posterity.
	• This includes suffering the numerous miseries that follow from sin.
• The condemnation of sin is not an inherent quality, but rather an obligation to punishment or a declaration of that obligation.
	• This is how the apostle understands the doctrine of justification.

••IV. Imputation of Righteousness••

• The righteousness by which we are justified in Christ is not an inherent quality, but rather the right to obtain absolution or the absolution itself.
	• This is a key aspect of the doctrine of justification.

••V. The Role of Adam••

• Adam is considered the head of his posterity, and his sin is imputed to them.
	• This is based on the idea that the justice of God could not impute sin to us unless we were in Adam.
• The corruption of Adam has descended to us really and inheres in us.
	• However, the imputation of his disobedience precedes and corruption is derived to us by generation.

••VI. The Covenant••

• The first man was the root of the human race, both naturally and economically.
	• He owed either happiness or misery, the latter by sinning and the former by persevering in divine rectitude.
• God entered into covenant with Adam, not as with a private man, but as the head and surety of the whole race.

••VII. Original Sin••

• Original sin is a doctrine of the highest importance to the surer perception of the misery of man and the necessity and efficacy of saving grace.
	• It is deservedly placed among the primary doctrines of the Christian religion.
• Original sin is sometimes used more broadly to embrace imputed and inherent sin.
	• It is taken to be resolvable into two parts by some theologians.

	• This is true despite her being "highly favored" and chosen by God.

••VI. Propagation of Sin••

• The propagation of sin is not an accident that passes from subject to subject.
	• The immediate subject of sin is human nature, not the person.
	• Human nature is vitiated by the actual transgression of the person.

••VII. Mode of Propagation••

• The mode of propagation of sin is obscure and difficult to explain.
	• However, the propagation itself is not to be denied.
	• The mode of propagation will be discussed in a special question.

••VIII. Nature of Original Sin••

• There are two extremes to be avoided about the nature of original sin.
	• One extreme is that original sin is placed in the corruption of the very substance of the soul.
	• The other extreme is that original sin is merely a privation or a lack.

••IX. Original Sin as a Positive Quality••

• Original sin is not merely a privation or a lack, but a certain positive quality.
	• This is a matter of debate and will be discussed further.

••X. Conclusion••

• The nature of original sin is complex and difficult to understand.
	• It is not a blessing of nature, but a blessing of grace.
	• It is a positive quality that affects human nature and is propagated through generations.

	• (2) In the creation of the rational soul with the want of original righteousness
	• (3) In the constitution of the whole compound by the union of the soul with the body

	• The theory that the soul is vitiated by the body is not satisfactory without further explanation

	• Understanding sin propagation is crucial for understanding the nature of sin and human corruption

â€¢ ••Augustine's response••
	• Augustine's response to Julian's argument is that sin can enter through a wide open gate (Rom 5:12)
	• This response highlights the importance of understanding the nature of sin and human corruption.

â€¢ ••Creation of the Soul••

â€¢ ••Types of Souls••
	• A soul is considered "pure" if it has the habit of holiness
	• A soul is considered "impure" if it has the habit of unrighteousness
	• A soul is considered "not pure" if it has no good or bad habits, but is simply created with natural faculties

â€¢ ••God's Role in Sin••
	• God cannot be considered the author of sin, even if souls are created without original righteousness

	• Souls can be considered guilty in Adam, even if they were not present in him as to origin of essence
