â€¢ ••The Union of Soul and Body••
	• The union of soul and body is the third degree of propagation
	• This union makes sin formal and consummate, not just privative (by a want of righteousness)

â€¢ ••Corruption of the Soul••
	• The soul can be corrupted by the body due to the great sympathy between the two
	• The morals of the soul follow the temperament of the body

â€¢ ••Scriptural Evidence••
	• Scripture testifies to the corruption of the soul by the body (e.g. Luke 21:34, Wisdom 9:15)
	• The soul is weighed down by the corrupt body

â€¢ ••The Nature of Corruption••
	• The corruption of the soul is not just a matter of its operations being affected by the body
	• It is a habitual corruption that exists from birth

â€¢ ••The Role of the Body••
	• The body is not just a passive recipient of the soul's operations
	• It actively affects the soul and contributes to its corruption

â€¢ ••Original Sin in Infants••
	• Original sin would not exist in the soul of infants if it were only a matter of the soul's operations being affected by the body
	• However, the habitual corruption of the soul is present from birth, even in infants.

â€¢ ••The Nature of Sin••

â€¢ ••Actual Sin••

â€¢ ••The Causes of Actual Sin••

â€¢ ••The Consequences of Actual Sin••
	• Actual sin has consequences, such as punishment and separation from God

â€¢ ••Definition of Sin••

â€¢ ••Examples of Sin of Depravity••

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. The Nature of Sin••

• The act of sin is distinct from the person who sins, and can be yielded to due to weakness.
	• This can occur with or without struggling.
	• The sinner serves sin in various ways, including through delight and continuation of the sinful act.

••II. The Kingdom of Sin••

• The kingdom of sin can be either absolute and total, or partial and comparative.
	• The former belongs to the unregenerate, while the latter can belong to believers who fall into grievous sins.
	• Examples of believers who fell into grievous sins include David and Solomon.

••III. Pardonable and Unpardonable Sins••

• Sins can be either pardonable or unpardonable.
	• Pardonable sins can be remitted by God's grace.
	• Unpardonable sins, such as the sin against the Holy Spirit, cannot be pardoned by justice.

••IV. The Sin Against the Holy Spirit••

• The question is what constitutes the formal reason of the sin against the Holy Spirit.
	• The sin is not simply final impenitency, as all reprobates die in it.
	• It is also not made up of six species, such as presumption, desperation, and resistance to recognized truth.

••V. The Nature of the Sin Against the Holy Spirit••

• The sin against the Holy Spirit is not committed against the person of the Holy Spirit, but rather against his operation.
	• The Holy Spirit's operation is distinct from his person, and is related to his office and work.

••VI. Why the Sin Against the Holy Spirit is Unpardonable••

• The sin against the Holy Spirit is unpardonable because it is a rejection of God's work and operation.
	• This sin is a rejection of the Holy Spirit's role in illuminating and convicting the sinner.

••VII. The Formal Reason of the Sin Against the Holy Spirit••

• The formal reason of the sin against the Holy Spirit is not yet clear.
	• Theologians have offered various opinions on the matter, but no consensus has been reached.

••VIII. The Distinction from Other Sins••

• The sin against the Holy Spirit is distinct from other sins, such as mortal and venial sins.
	• The distinction between mortal and venial sins has been discussed previously.

••IX. The Implications of the Sin Against the Holy Spirit••

• The sin against the Holy Spirit has significant implications for the sinner's relationship with God.
	• This sin is a rejection of God's work and operation, and can lead to eternal separation from God.

••X. The Importance of Understanding the Sin Against the Holy Spirit••

• Understanding the sin against the Holy Spirit is crucial for theologians and believers alike.
	• This sin is a serious offense against God, and requires careful consideration and reflection.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••Establishing the question••
	• The question is whether original sin is properly a sin or a punishment of an antecedent sin.
	• The Jesuits, Socinians, and Remonstrants of the day deny the imputation of the first sin.

â€¢ ••Defining sin and punishment••
	• The question is not whether sin is formally a punishment, but whether it can be considered a punishment materially and specifically.
	• Our opponents deny that sin can be punishment, while the orthodox affirm it.

â€¢ ••Three ways sin can be punishment••
	• Sin can be punishment with respect to itself.
	• Sin can be punishment with respect to the antecedent sin in the one who is punished.
	• Sin can be punishment with respect to another's sin.

â€¢ ••Sin as punishment of itself••
	• Sin is its own punishment, as virtue is its own reward.
	• Sin is an accident that disagrees with the subject and is hurtful, causing separation from God and depriving the creature of holiness.

â€¢ ••Sin as punishment of preceding sin••
	• The idolatry of the heathen is punished by the abominable lusts to which they are delivered (Rom. 1:24-27).
	• The sin of David is punished by the incest of Absalom.

â€¢ ••Scriptural proof••
	• Scripture establishes that sin is the punishment of sin (2 S. 12:11, 12).
	• The incest of Absalom is put forward as a punishment of David sent by God.

â€¢ ••Objection and response••
	• It cannot be objected that there was nothing penal in the case of David, only a bare permission.
	• We respond that the punishment of David should be a public disgrace and loss inflicted upon him before the sun and all Israel.

â€¢ ••Proportion between sin and punishment••
	• The proportion between sin and punishment is established by the law of retaliation (lex talionis).
	• The punishment of David is a just proportion to his sin, as he is punished openly before the sun and Israel.

â€¢ ••Scriptural proof from Romans••
	• Scripture also establishes that sin is the punishment of sin (Rom. 1:24-26).
	• God punishes the idolatry of the heathen by delivering them to abominable lusts.

â€¢ ••Conclusion••
	• Sin is rightly called the punishment of sin, as established by Scripture and reason.

••I. The Subject of Free Will••

• The subject of free will is not just the intellect or the will, but both faculties conjointly.
	• The intellect is involved in decision-making (proairÄ“sis), while the will is involved in freedom.
	• The two faculties are connected in a way that they cannot be separated from each other.

••II. The Relationship Between Intellect and Will••

• The intellect and will are mutually connected by a strict necessity.
	• They are not separate faculties, but rather different aspects of the same faculty of the soul.
	• The intellect judges and understands, while the will loves or hates what is judged to be good.

••III. The Nature of Free Will••

• Free will is a mixed faculty or a union of intellect and will.
	• It is not just one or the other, but both faculties working together.
	• The decision of the intellect is terminated in the will, while the liberty of the will has its roots in the intellect.

••IV. The Distinction Between Intellect and Will••

• The distinction between intellect and will is not intrinsic, but rather extrinsic with regard to objects.
	• The same faculty of the soul judges and understands, and then loves or hates what is judged to be good.
	• What is affirmation and negation in the intellect is desire and avoidance in the will.

••V. The Essence of the Soul••

• Besides the essence, there are only three things in the soul: faculty, habit, and act.
	• The "decisions" of the mind are not an act or a habit, but rather a faculty that can be separated from man.

••VI. The Nature of Necessity••

• Not every necessity is repugnant to freedom of will.
	• Only a certain kind of necessity is incompatible with liberty.
	• The orthodox truth maintains that one kind of necessity is incompatible with liberty, while another kind cordially unites with it.

••VII. The Distinction Between Liberty and Necessity••

• Liberty is variously distinguished.
	• Some make liberty threefold: from necessity, from sin, and from misery.
	• The first kind of liberty is of nature, while the second is of grace.

••VIII. The Error of Pelagians••

• The Pelagians assert that every necessity is opposed to the freedom of the will.
	• This is a capital error that leads to an erroneous doctrine about the essence of liberty.
	• The Pelagians design to take away the will of man from the necessity of divine determination and government.

••IX. The Orthodox Truth••

• The orthodox truth maintains that not every necessity is at variance with liberty.
	• One kind of necessity is incompatible with liberty, while another kind cordially unites with it.

••X. The Importance of Understanding Free Will••

• Understanding the nature of free will is crucial for understanding the relationship between intellect and will.
	• It is also important for understanding the distinction between liberty and necessity.

	• The sinner is impotent to restore himself to spiritual life.
	• This impotence is similar to that of a dead man, who cannot bring himself back to life.

â€¢ ••Differences between a Dead Man and a Sinner••
	• There are various differences between a dead man and a sinner.
	• However, the simile of spiritual death is precise in the point that the sinner is destitute of the life of grace.

â€¢ ••Remaining Spiritual Life••
	• The sinner may have some remaining spiritual life that allows him to know God and worship him in some measure.
	• However, this remaining life is not sufficient to overcome the servitude of sin.

â€¢ ••Objections to Spiritual Death••
	• The adversaries object that the similitude of spiritual death is not precise.
	• However, the Holy Spirit's intention is to convey the idea that the sinner is destitute of the life of grace.

â€¢ ••Implications of Spiritual Death••
	• The implications of spiritual death are that the sinner is unable to know anything true or do anything good.
	• This is similar to the state of a dead man, who cannot bring himself back to life.

â€¢ ••The Similitude of the Stony Heart••

â€¢ ••The difference between believers and unbelievers••

â€¢ ••The inequality of grace••

â€¢ ••The Papists' Argument••
	• The papists use the example of the heathen who strove after virtue to argue that strength for good survives to the free will in a state of sin.

	• The Calvinists deny that the heathen's actions can be called properly and univocally good works.

â€¢ ••The Inability of the Unrenewed Man••

â€¢ ••Conditions of a Good Work••
	• A good work requires three things:

		- The work must be done to the glory of God (1 Cor. 10:31)

â€¢ ••The Defects of the Heathen's Virtues••
	• The heathen's virtues were defective in all three particulars:
		- They lacked faith or a clean heart
		- They had no internal and spiritual obedience

â€¢ ••The Athenians' Worship••

â€¢ ••The Apostle's Accommodation••
	• The apostle Paul tempered his rebuke with praise when speaking to the Athenians
	• He did not simply call them "too superstitious," but rather "as too superstitious" to avoid seeming too harsh

â€¢ ••The Vanity of the Heathen's Worship••

	• They claim that the apostle's words "ye ignorantly worship" (Acts 17:23) prove the vanity of their worship

â€¢ ••The Papists' Denial of the Question••

â€¢ ••The Calvinist's Response to the Papists••
	• The Calvinists argue that the papists' denial of the question is irrelevant to the issue at hand
	• They claim that the papists' argument is based on a flawed understanding of the heathen's virtues and the nature of good works.

â€¢ ••Augustine's Opinion••
	• Augustine believed that true virtue exists only in those who are righteous, and righteousness comes only through faith.
	• He argued that the Pelagians, who believed in human ability to achieve righteousness, were mistaken.

â€¢ ••The Nature of Virtue••
	• According to Augustine, even virtuous deeds are sinful if they do not arise from true faith.
	• Prosper, a disciple of Augustine, agreed that without faith, even virtuous actions are pleasing only to oneself and Satan.

â€¢ ••The Call of All Nations••
	• Prosper wrote that without worshiping the true God, even virtuous actions are sinful.
	• He emphasized that pleasing God requires faith in God.

â€¢ ••The Seed of True Faith••
	• Prosper argued that virtuous deeds become sinful if they do not arise from the seed of true faith.
	• He believed that faith is necessary for salvation and that virtuous actions without faith are mere pretenses.

â€¢ ••The State of Sin••
	• The nature of free will in a state of sin is characterized by a tendency to sin and a lack of ability to achieve righteousness.
	• This state is the result of the fall of humanity.

â€¢ ••The Moment of Calling••
	• The moment of calling and the progress of sanctification will be discussed in a later section.
	• The author expresses a desire to learn to depend entirely on God and to ascribe all salvation to His grace.

â€¢ ••The Glory of God••
	• The author quotes Psalm 115:1, "Not unto us, O Lord, but unto thy name be all the glory."
	• He expresses a desire to acknowledge God's mercy and to give Him all the glory.

â€¢ ••The Institutes of Elenctic Theology••
	• The Institutes of Elenctic Theology is a work by Francis Turretin, a pastor and professor of theology.
	• The book is a comprehensive treatment of theology, covering various topics and arguments.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

• ••The Law of God••
	• The doctrine of the law of God is a fundamental aspect of theology
	• It has multiple uses in theology, including:
		- Direction of life
		- Knowledge of sin
		- Preparation for grace
• ••Etymology of the Word "Law"••
	• The Hebrew word for law is "tvrh", meaning "to teach"
	• The Greek word for law is "nomos", meaning "to rule" and "to distribute"
	• The Latin word for law is derived from "legendo", "leger", or "ligando"
• ••Definition of Law••
	• Law is a rule of conduct prescribed by God
	• It is used in different ways in Scripture, including:
		- Broadly, for the whole word of God
		- Strictly, for the Mosaic dispensation
		- For the covenant of works
		- For the rule of things to be done and avoided
• ••Types of Law••
	• Natural law: founded on the perfectly just and holy nature of God
	• Positive law: built on the free and positive right of God
• ••Natural Law••
	• Is a law that is inherent in the nature of God
	• Is a law that is known through reason
• ••Positive Law••
	• Is a law that is built on the free and positive right of God
	• Is a law that is based on God's will
• ••The Law of God in Scripture••
	• Is used to describe the whole word of God
	• Is used to describe the Mosaic dispensation
	• Is used to describe the covenant of works
• ••The Purpose of the Law••
	• Is to direct our lives
	• Is to reveal our sin
	• Is to prepare us for grace
• ••The Relationship between Law and Grace••
	• The law is a schoolmaster that leads us to Christ
	• The law reveals our sin and our need for salvation
	• The law prepares us for the reception of grace

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••Definition of Natural Law••
	• Natural law is a concept that refers to the moral principles that are inherent in human nature
	• It is not just a command of God, but a principle that is just and good in itself

â€¢ ••Two Ways to Understand Natural Law••
	• ••Broadly••: includes the wise government of God over all creatures and the direction of their ends
	• ••Strictly••: refers to the practical rule of moral duties to which men are bound by nature

â€¢ ••Orthodox vs. Libertine Views••
	• ••Orthodox••: affirm that there is a natural law of God that is the rule of justice and injustice
	• ••Libertine••: believe that justice and virtue depend on human will alone and are measured by individual utility

â€¢ ••Historical Examples••
	• ••Carneades and the Cyrenaics••: denied all natural justice, saying that justice is determined by law and custom
	• ••Epicurus••: also believed that justice is determined by human convention, not by nature

â€¢ ••Modern Examples••
	• ••Calvin••: testifies that the libertine view is an impious error
	• ••Hobbes••: approaches the libertine view in his work "Elementa philosophica de cive"

â€¢ ••Orthodox View of Natural Law••
	• ••Divine Origin••: natural law arises from a divine obligation impressed on the conscience of man
	• ••Practical Principles••: contains the principles of immovable truth, such as worshiping God and living virtuously

â€¢ ••Remains of Natural Law in Human Nature••
	• ••Corrupted and Obscured••: natural law has been corrupted and obscured by sin
	• ••Still Felt••: no mortal can escape the force of natural law, even if it is felt more or less strongly

â€¢ ••Knowledge of Natural Law••
	• ••From Creatures••: natural law becomes known from the aspect of creatures and their nature
	• ••Not from Bare Nature••: natural law depends on God, the supreme lawgiver

â€¢ ••Purpose of Natural Law••
	• ••To Guide Human Behavior••: natural law is meant to guide human behavior and provide a standard of right and wrong
	• ••To Promote Virtue••: natural law promotes virtue and the common good

â€¢ ••Implications of Natural Law••
	• ••Universal Application••: natural law applies to all humans, regardless of their cultural or social background
	• ••Objective Standard••: natural law provides an objective standard of right and wrong, independent of human opinion or convention

• ••The origin of natural law••
	• Not to be sought in the Noahic precepts
	• Not to be acquired by tradition or instruction, but impressed upon the mind by nature
• ••The seven precepts of the Jews••
	• Not a reliable source for natural law
	• Founded on tradition alone, not on natural right
	• Not all moral and of perpetual observance, but some ceremonial and positive
• ••The right of nature••
	• Founded on the nature of God, the Creator
	• Founded on the condition of rational creatures themselves
	• Bound to perform or avoid things that sound reason and conscience enjoin
• ••The scope of the right of nature••
	• Used broadly and improperly by lawyers to refer to the law of nations and civil law
	• Used strictly and properly to refer to that which has reference only to rational creatures
• ••The distinction between primary and secondary notions••
	• Primary notions are principles, known of themselves and immovable
	• Secondary notions are conclusions, deduced from the principles
• ••The corruption of natural law••
	• Corrupted by natural corruption, wrong education, and vicious custom
	• Still remains the same among all, as to its first principles and immediate conclusions
• ••The proof of natural law••
	• To be proven from Scripture
	• Many arguments prove the existence of natural law
• ••The nature of natural law••
	• Engraven by God upon every individual
	• Distinguishes between virtue and vice, and knows what to avoid and what to do
• ••The relationship between natural law and conscience••
	• Natural law is the light and dictation of conscience
	• Conscience is the guide to distinguish between right and wrong
• ••The importance of natural law••
	• A universal and eternal law, applicable to all rational creatures
	• A source of moral guidance and direction for human beings

â€¢ ••The Gentiles and the Law••
	• The Gentiles, who do not have the written law of Moses, still do the things contained in the law by nature.

â€¢ ••The Consent of Nations••
	• Even savage nations have a law that obtains, from which they have learned to worship God, honor parents, and lead a virtuous life.
	• Many laws concerning equity and virtue have been enacted by heathen legislators, drawn from nature itself.

â€¢ ••The Conscience of Each One••
	• Each person's conscience dictates the good to be done and the evil to be shunned.
	• Conscience exhibits practical principles as universal rules of things to be avoided and omitted.

â€¢ ••The Conscience as a Law••
	• Conscience makes an application and test of itself to the rule of right and wrong.
	• Distresses of conscience arise from the sight of sin and the sense of divine judgment.

â€¢ ••The Natural Law••
	• The natural law is impressed upon man and knows that certain actions are worthy of death.
	• It is called "the law not written, but born" and "the unwritten law of God".

â€¢ ••God's Government over Man••
	• As a creature, man must depend on the Creator and be governed by him physically.
	• It is absurd that a rational creature should not be subject to the Creator in matters of morality.

â€¢ ••The Absurdities of the Opposite Opinion••
	• If nothing is just by nature, but only what ministers to human advantage, then men are born for the purpose of serving their own interests.

â€¢ ••The Implications of the Opposite Opinion••
	• If nothing is just by nature, then all laws and moral principles are arbitrary and based on human convenience.

â€¢ ••The Necessity of a Natural Law••
	• The existence of a natural law is necessary to explain the universal principles of right and wrong that are observed in all nations and individuals.

â€¢ ••The Source of the Natural Law••

â€¢ ••The Natural Law••
	• The natural law is a universal principle that guides human behavior
	• It is not established by opinion, but by nature
	• It is the basis of justice, piety, and all virtues

â€¢ ••Consequences of Rejecting the Natural Law••
	• If the natural law is rejected, all things would be equally lawful
	• Hate and love, honor and kill, would be equally acceptable

â€¢ ••The Testimonies of Heathen Philosophers••
	• Plato, Aristotle, and the Stoics opposed the idea that morality is relative
	• Cicero argued that we are born to justice and that right is established by nature
	• Socrates believed that the distinction between utility and nature was the source of all human vices

â€¢ ••The Definition of True Law••
	• True law is right reason conformable to nature
	• It is universal, unchangeable, eternal, and applies to all people
	• It is not liable to derogation or abrogation

â€¢ ••The Sovereignty of the Natural Law••
	• The natural law is the sovereign master and emperor of all beings
	• It is the author, promulgator, and enforcer of the law
	• God himself is the author of the natural law

â€¢ ••The Cauterization of Conscience••
	• The wicked can suppress the natural law in their actions
	• However, this does not mean that the natural law is extinct or destroyed
	• Insensibility of conscience is not the same as the extinction of the natural law

â€¢ ••Wicked Laws among the Heathen••
	• Various wicked laws obtained among the heathen, repugnant to the natural law
	• These laws do not prove that no light of reason was granted to men by nature
	• They only show that men can suppress the natural law in their actions

â€¢ ••The Role of Reason••
	• Reason is granted to men by nature
	• It is the light that guides human behavior and informs the natural law

â€¢ ••The Importance of the Natural Law••
	• The natural law is essential for human society and order
	• It is the foundation of right and the basis of justice and piety

â€¢ ••The Consequences of Rejecting the Natural Law••
	• If the natural law is rejected, all foundations of right will be removed
	• Government, honesty, and order in human society will perish
	• The world will be turned into mere confusion and villainy

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••Dispute about the Moral Law••
	• Concerns its immutability and perfection
	• Dispute about its parts (division of precepts and their genuine sense)
	• Dispute about its use (absolute or relative to various states of man)

â€¢ ••Statement of the Question••
	• Whether the moral law is of natural and indispensable right

â€¢ ••Distinction of Terms••
	• Obligation: the right of the law over man
	• Dispensation: when the obligation of the law is taken away from some man
	• Declaration/interpretation: when the law does not bind in a particular case
	• Irritation: when a law is abolished before it can perfectly bind
	• Abrogation: when a law is simply abolished and taken away
	• Derogation: when a law is partly taken away and partly remains

â€¢ ••Simple and Mixed Precepts••
	• Simple precepts: merely moral, belonging to natural right
	• Mixed precepts: moral and ceremonial, partly of natural and partly of positive right

â€¢ ••Right of God••
	• Right of God is either of dominion or of government
	• Dominion: right to possess, dispose, and use creatures as a lord or proprietor
	• Government: right to govern rational creatures as ruler and legislator

â€¢ ••Natural and Positive Right••
	• Natural right: based on the perfection, eminence, holiness, and rectitude of God's nature
	• Positive right: based on God's free will and good pleasure

â€¢ ••Prior Reasonables••
	• Things that involve a contradiction as commanded and belong to natural right
	• Examples: God cannot command the hatred of himself, blasphemy, and lying

â€¢ ••Connection to God's Nature••
	• Things that have a close connection with God's nature, perfection, and holiness belong to natural right

â€¢ ••Implications of God's Right••
	• God cannot deny himself or do anything contrary to his own holiness and perfection
	• God's right is not based on his will, but on his nature and perfection

â€¢ ••Bradwardine's Concept••
	• Prior reasonables: things that are naturally antecedent to the divine will and involve a contradiction as commanded

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••Natural vs. Positive Right••
	• Natural right is based on the nature and holiness of God
	• Positive right is based on the free will of God and the constitution of things

â€¢ ••Types of Divine Right••
	• Primary (uncreated, natural) based on God's nature
	• Secondary (created, positive) based on the nature of things

â€¢ ••Characteristics of Primary Right••
	• Immutable and absolute
	• Cannot be changed by God without denying his nature
	• Includes duties such as reverence for God and hatred of sin

â€¢ ••Characteristics of Secondary Right••
	• Can be changed by God in certain cases
	• Based on the order of things and created nature
	• Includes duties such as murder and stealing, which can become lawful under certain circumstances

â€¢ ••Distinction between Precepts••
	• Those connected to God's nature belong to natural right
	• Those based on God's free will belong to positive right

â€¢ ••Agreement on Distinction••
	• Almost all agree on the distinction between natural and positive right
	• Disagreement on the specific enumeration of precepts

â€¢ ••Immutability and Indispensability••
	• Can be understood absolutely or comparatively
	• Some precepts are absolutely indispensable, while others are relatively so

â€¢ ••God's Ability to Dispense with Laws••
	• As supreme Lord and lawgiver, God can dispense with some laws without sin
	• This is not the case for humans, who are subjects and accused

â€¢ ••Moral Law vs. Ceremonial Law••
	• The moral law is not of mutable positive right
	• The question remains whether the precepts of the moral law are of natural or positive right

â€¢ ••Importance of Dispensability••
	• Understanding dispensability is crucial for understanding the nature of divine right and the distinction between natural and positive right.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••Three opinions on the nature of law••
	• Opinion 1: Moral law is dispensable, founded on positive right alone
	• Opinion 2: Moral law is partly dispensable and partly not
	• Opinion 3: Moral law is simply indispensable, based on the intrinsic reason of justice and duty

â€¢ ••Opinion 1: Dispensability of moral law••
	• Held by many Scholastics (e.g. Occam, Gerson, Peter of Ailly)
	• Also held by Socinians, who want to prove the imperfection of the Mosaic Law
	• Some of our party also hold this opinion, saying that moral goodness and wickedness flow from God's free will

â€¢ ••Opinion 2: Partial dispensability of moral law••
	• Held by Scotus and Gabriel (Biel)
	• They say that three precepts of the first table are indispensable, but the fourth is partly dispensable
	• Others of our party approach this opinion, saying that certain precepts are absolutely indispensable, but others are dispensable as to God

â€¢ ••Opinion 3: Indispensability of moral law••
	• Held by Thomas Aquinas and his followers
	• They say that the moral law is simply indispensable because it contains the intrinsic reason of justice and duty
	• This is the more common opinion of the orthodox

â€¢ ••Limitations of the indispensable moral law••
	• Not all precepts are equally based on the primary right of nature
	• Some precepts flow absolutely from the nature of God, while others depend on the constitution of the nature of things

â€¢ ••Dispensability and interpretation••
	• A dispensation properly so called does not have place in the precepts that depend on the constitution of the nature of things
	• However, a declaration or interpretation may be given concerning these precepts, taking into account the changed circumstances of the things or persons

â€¢ ••God's role in the moral law••
	• God's free will comes into play in the constitution of the nature of things
	• However, God cannot will the contrary without a contradiction in the precepts that flow absolutely from the nature of God

â€¢ ••The relationship between God's will and the moral law••
	• Things are good and just only because they are commanded by God
	• However, God cannot command the contrary without a contradiction

â€¢ ••The role of human reason in the moral law••
	• Human reason can understand the intrinsic reason of justice and duty
	• However, human reason is not the ultimate source of the moral law

â€¢ ••The importance of the moral law••
	• The moral law is necessary and incapable of being dispensed with, not only by men but also by God
	• The moral law contains the intrinsic reason of justice and duty, and is simply indispensable.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••Necessary dependence on God••
	• The rational creature is dependent on God in the genus of morals and reason.
	• This dependence is necessary and indispensable.

â€¢ ••God's right to subject the creature••
	• God has the right to subject the rational creature to himself and bind it to obedience.
	• This right is evident from God's independence, preeminence, perfection, and supreme dominion.

â€¢ ••Equality of dependence••
	• The creature's dependence on God is similar to its dependence on God as its second cause.
	• This dependence is necessary and essential.

â€¢ ••Moral dependence on God••
	• The moral dependence of the rational creature on God is no less necessary and immutable than its natural dependence.
	• This dependence is rooted in God's perfection and holiness.

â€¢ ••God's liberty and necessity••
	• God's will is free, but he is necessitated to act in certain ways once he has willed something.
	• This is evident from Cajetan's quote on the exercise of free acts.

â€¢ ••God's conservation and concurrence••
	• Once God has created the creature, he must necessarily conserve and concur with it.
	• This is because God's will is bound to fulfill his promises and govern justly.

â€¢ ••Establishment of law••
	• It was necessary for God to establish a law for the creature to obey.
	• This is because the creature's existence under God implies a need for law and governance.

â€¢ ••Nature of things commanded••
	• If all precepts of the law are dispensable, God was free to make or not make them.
	• This would imply that God could command the opposite of what is morally right.

â€¢ ••Consequences of dispensable precepts••
	• If precepts are dispensable, God could command the creature to hate and blaspheme him.
	• This would imply that the most horrible sins would become praiseworthy.

â€¢ ••Absurdity of dispensable precepts••
	• The proposition of such monstrous absurdities is their own refutation.
	• It is clear that God cannot do such things without denying himself and doing violence to his own nature.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••1. God's Nature and the Moral Law••

• The moral law is a reflection of God's nature, which is true and holy.
• God cannot command falsehoods or base actions, as they contradict his nature.

••2. The Will of God and the Moral Law••

• The will of God is not the sole rule of justice, but rather one aspect of it.
• The moral law is not subject to the will of God, but rather is a reflection of God's nature.

••3. The Difference between Moral and Ceremonial Law••

• The moral law is not the same as the ceremonial law, which is subject to change.
• The moral law is immutable and perpetual, while the ceremonial law is not.

••4. The Conformity of the Moral Law with the Eternal Law••

• The moral law corresponds with the eternal law of God, which is immutable and perpetual.
• The moral law is a copy and shadow of the eternal law, and is therefore also immutable.

••5. The Identity of the Moral Law with the Natural Law••

• The moral law is the same as the natural law, which is immutable and founded on reason.
• The moral law is derived from the light of nature and is therefore perpetual.

••6. The Sources of the Moral Law••

• The moral law is not derived from human convention or custom.
• The moral law is based on reason and is therefore universal and eternal.

••7. The Immutability of the Moral Law••

• The moral law is immutable and perpetual, as it is based on reason and the nature of God.
• The moral law cannot be changed by human actions or circumstances.

••8. The Relationship between the Moral Law and Human Nature••

• The moral law is based on human nature and is therefore universal and eternal.
• The moral law is necessary for human nature to attain its end.

••9. The Sources of Human Society••

• Human society is based on the distinction and ownership of goods.
• The natural law does not command a community of goods, but rather allows for private ownership.

••10. The Authority of the Moral Law••

• The moral law is based on the authority of God and is therefore immutable and perpetual.
• The moral law is a reflection of God's nature and is therefore universal and eternal.

	• Refers to the genuineness and substance of the oath, not the form expressed by Matthew

â€¢ ••Christ's words on communication••
	• Do not speak absolutely and universally of all conversation
	• Refer to ordinary habit and practice in lighter cases

â€¢ ••The three things commended••
	• Simplicity of speech, as opposed to the habit of swearing
	• Truthfulness, as opposed to falsehood and equivocation
	• Constancy and fidelity, as opposed to fickleness and inconstancy

â€¢ ••The meaning of "whatsoever is more than these"••
	• Refers to superfluous, unnecessary additions in light and rash oaths
	• Does not extend to necessary and just additions in weightier oaths

â€¢ ••Christ's teaching on the sixth commandment••
	• Christ extends the sixth commandment to include not only physical harm but also insult and thought
	• This is in contrast to the Pharisaic school, which only considered actual slaughter as capital punishment

â€¢ ••Retaliation and vengeance••
	• Christ quotes the law of retaliation (Ex. 21:24) but opposes it with his own teaching ("resist not evil," Mt. 5:39)
	• He does not abolish vengeance entirely, but rather refutes the Pharisees' interpretation of the law

â€¢ ••Private revenge vs. public vengeance••
	• Christ teaches his followers to prefer to suffer injuries rather than avenging them themselves
	• This is in line with Moses' teaching to love one's neighbor as oneself (Lev. 19:18)

â€¢ ••The law of retaliation••
	• The law of retaliation can still have a place in its own sense, but not precisely and formally
	• It is used in a moral estimation, rather than as a literal command

â€¢ ••Turning the other cheek••
	• Christ's words about turning the other cheek (Mt. 5:39) are not to be taken literally
	• They are meant to convey the importance of patience and forbearance in the face of injury

â€¢ ••Culpable resistance••
	• Culpable resistance, arising from revenge, is forbidden by Christ's teaching
	• However, lawful defense and unblamable protection are not forbidden

â€¢ ••The seventh commandment••
	• Christ extends the seventh commandment to include not only external actions but also internal motions
	• This is in line with the law's spiritual sense, which regards not only external but also internal motions

â€¢ ••Adultery and desire••
	• Christ's teaching on adultery (Mt. 5:28) unfolds the true sense of the law
	• The law regards not only external actions but also internal motions, such as desire and looks

â€¢ ••Divorce and remarriage••
	• Christ's teaching on divorce and remarriage (Mt. 19:4-5) agrees with the law of Moses
	• The Pharisees' interpretation of the law is not the same as Christ's teaching

â€¢ ••The Pharisees' interpretation••
	• The Pharisees usually spoke categorically and imperatively, "give her a writing of divorcement"
	• Christ's words are not to be taken in the same sense as the Pharisees' interpretation

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Jesus' Teaching on Divorce••

• The Pharisees allowed divorce without any limitation, whereas Moses had restrictions.
	• Moses allowed divorce "on account of some uncleanness" (Dt. 24:1).
	• The Pharisees allowed divorce without any reason, as long as a formula was followed.

••II. Jesus' Correction of the Pharisees••

• Jesus corrected the Pharisees' understanding of Moses' teaching on divorce.
	• Jesus added the word "he permitted" to indicate that divorce was only allowed by a civil and forensic dispensation.
	• Jesus did not intend to allow divorce by a moral dispensation or as a relaxation of right.

••III. The Command to Love Our Neighbor••

• The command to love our neighbor is not restricted to the Old Testament.
	• The object of love is the same in both the Old and New Testaments.
	• The command to love our neighbor is extended to all men, including enemies.

••IV. Who is Our Neighbor?••

• Our neighbor is not limited to a Jew or fellow countryman.
	• The term "neighbor" includes any stranger, including an enemy.
	• Examples of loving an enemy include giving bread to a hungry enemy (Prov. 25:21) and helping an enemy's beast of burden (Ex. 23:4-5).

••V. The Law of Retaliation••

• The law of retaliation does not restrict the command to love our neighbor.
	• The law of retaliation concerns the right of the magistrate, not private revenge.
	• The law of retaliation does not restrict the command to love our neighbor, which concerns private duties of love.

••VI. Intermarriage with the Canaanite Nations••

• The Israelites are forbidden to intermarry with the Canaanite nations.
	• This does not mean they are commanded to hate them.
	• There is a medium between friendship and hatred, and mercy towards the Canaanite nations is not prohibited absolutely.

••VII. The Command Concerns Destruction••

• The command to destroy the Canaanite nations concerns their destruction as enemies of God.
	• The command does not concern hatred, but rather the destruction of God's enemies.
	• The command is not a restriction on loving our neighbor, but rather a command to destroy God's enemies.

••VIII. God's Command to Love Our Enemy••

• God commands us to love our enemy, including giving bread to a hungry enemy (Prov. 25:21).
	• This command is not a restriction on loving our neighbor, but rather a command to love our enemy.

••IX. The Pharisaical Gloss••

• The Pharisaical gloss that we should love our neighbor and hate our enemy is not a restriction on the law.
	• This gloss is not an imperfection of the law, but rather an addition that is not part of the original law.

••X. The Same Command in Both Testaments••

• The command to love our neighbor is the same in both the Old and New Testaments.
	• The object of love is the same, and the command is extended to all men, including enemies.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••The Commandment of Love••
	• The commandment of love was not corrected by Christ in terms of mode and intensity.
	• The command to love God and our neighbor is not susceptible of degree.

â€¢ ••Love for God••
	• The greatest love for God is to love him as the highest good, not just for blessings, but for his excellency.
	• This love is not greater than the love for our neighbor.

â€¢ ••Love for Our Neighbor••
	• We are commanded to love our neighbor as ourselves, but this does not mean we love them more than ourselves.
	• The command to lay down life for a brother is an example, not a measure of comparison.

â€¢ ••Examples of Self-Sacrifice••
	• Moses, David, and others in the Old Testament showed self-sacrifice for others.
	• The heathen also showed self-sacrifice for their country and friends.

â€¢ ••The Mark of Comparison••
	• The phrase "as ourselves" is not to be understood canonically, but exemplarily.
	• It shows an example of love, not a measure or rule.

â€¢ ••Love as an Example••
	• He who lays down his life for a brother does not love that brother more than himself, but as himself.
	• He loves his own life less than the other's safety, especially for the glory of God.

â€¢ ••The Commandment of Love is Not New••
	• The commandment of love was not corrected by Christ in terms of substance.
	• It is called new relatively and comparatively, renovated by Christ and restored to its former splendor.

â€¢ ••The Commandment of Love is Eternal••
	• The commandment of love is perpetual and eternal.
	• It is new with regard to duration, not substance.

â€¢ ••No Addition to the Moral Law••
	• Christ did not add anything to the precepts of the moral law as to essentials.
	• The Lord's prayer and worship of Christ and the Father are not new, but renovated and illustrated by Christ.

â€¢ ••The Lord's Prayer••
	• The Lord's prayer as to form was instituted by Christ, but it has nothing new in terms of matter and things to be sought.
	• The prayers of the saints in the Old Testament express the same things as the Lord's prayer.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. The Relationship Between the Law and Love••

• The law contains the love of God and neighbor, but also implies self-denial, bearing the cross, and imitating Christ.
	• Self-denial is necessary to love God with all one's heart.
	• Bearing the cross and imitating Christ are implied in the law.

••II. The Duties of the Law••

• The law treats explicitly of duties towards God and neighbor.
• Under these duties, the law necessarily contains duties towards oneself.
	• One cannot love God without every kind of holiness.
	• One cannot love neighbor as oneself without regulating one's love of oneself by the law of God.

••III. Christ and Moses••

• Christ is compared to Moses, not as a new lawgiver, but in doctrine, dignity, and glory.
	• Christ's doctrine is evangelical, while Moses' is legal.
	• Christ infinitely surpasses Moses in dignity and glory.

••IV. Repentance and the Law••

• The law does not directly and formally enjoin repentance.
• However, the law is related to repentance materially and indirectly.
	• The law prescribes the rule of right living and what is pleasing to God.
	• Repentance is the design of the law.

••V. The Question of Adding to the Moral Law••

• The question is whether anything can be added to the moral law in the way of counsel.
• The papists argue that counsels are good works not enjoined upon, but demonstrated by Christ.

••VI. Papist Definition of Counsels••

• Counsels are defined as good works not commanded, but commended by Christ.
• These are called "evangelical" and "of perfection" because they lead to a greater perfection of holiness.
	• Counsels are said to be more difficult and perfect than precepts.
	• Counsels pertain only to a certain order of men, while precepts are universal.

••VII. Papist View of Counsels••

• The papists argue that counsels obtain a greater and more excellent reward than precepts.
• The three principal counsels are continence, obedience, and poverty.
	• These counsels are built up into the monastic life.
	• The three vows of monks correspond to these counsels.

••VIII. Orthodox View of Counsels••

• The orthodox do not deny that there are certain indifferent works left to each one's own will.
• Counsels may be given in the word of God, but are not necessarily to be obeyed.
	• Examples of counsels include Paul's counsel on marriage and the use of wine.

••IX. Nature of Counsels••

• Counsels are not necessarily to be obeyed, but are rather recommendations.
• Counsels are not necessarily universal, but rather pertain to a certain order of men.

••X. Conclusion••

• The question of adding to the moral law in the way of counsel is a matter of dispute between the papists and the orthodox.
• The papists argue that counsels are good works demonstrated by Christ, while the orthodox argue that counsels are recommendations rather than necessities.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••The Nature of Counsels••
	• The author argues that counsels are not pleasing to God and deserve no punishment or reward when neglected or observed.
	• Counsels are distinguished from commands, which are binding on all men.

â€¢ ••Types of Precepts••
	• There are universal precepts (binding on all men, e.g. loving God and neighbor).
	• There are special precepts (suitable for certain persons in a particular state and manner of life, e.g. duties of magistrates).
	• There are private precepts (imposed on particular individuals, e.g. Noah's command to build an ark).

â€¢ ••The Question at Hand••
	• The question is whether the gospel has added anything by way of counsel, not precept, regarding moral things.
	• The adversaries affirm that the gospel has added counsels, while the author denies this.

â€¢ ••Reasons for the Non-Existence of Evangelical Counsels••
	• (1) All morally good works are contained in the moral law and therefore fall under precept.
	• (2) Counsel and command are used interchangeably in Scripture (e.g. Prov. 1:30, Lk. 7:30).
	• (3) Whatever conduces to the perfection of the Christian is commanded by Christ (Mt. 5:48).
	• (4) So-called evangelical counsels are either commanded in the word or invented by men without authority.

â€¢ ••Examples of Counsels••
	• The love of enemies (Mt. 5:44, Rom. 12:20).
	• Suffering injuries (Mt. 5:39).
	• Chastity or celibacy (1 Cor. 9:5).
	• Voluntary poverty (Lk. 14:33, Mt. 16:24).

â€¢ ••Counter-Examples••
	• Regular obedience is repugnant to the liberty in Christ (Gal. 5:1).
	• Perpetual continence is not a gift belonging to everyone (Mt. 19:11).
	• Voluntary poverty is not recommended without a special call or necessity (Mt. 19:21, 27).

â€¢ ••The Mandate to the Proud Young Man••
	• The mandate to sell all and give to the poor (Mt. 19:21) was not a counsel of perfection, but a rebuke of pride.
	• The perfection proposed was not a perfection of glory, but a perfection of righteousness.

â€¢ ••Sources of Solution••
	• The author argues that the gospel has not added any counsels, but rather has emphasized the importance of obedience to the moral law.

â€¢ ••Implications of the Non-Existence of Evangelical Counsels••
	• The author argues that the non-existence of evangelical counsels has significant implications for the practice of Christianity.

	• This is because it is better to marry than to burn (1 Cor. 7:9).

••III. Apostles and Marriage••

• Some apostles were unmarried, but not due to a vow.

• Others remained married even after their call.
	• 1 Cor. 9:5 and Lk. 4:38 are cited as evidence.

••IV. Property and Ministry••

• Apostles did not give up their ownership of property, but abstained from using it for their own benefit.

••V. Preaching the Gospel••

• The gratuitous preaching of the gospel was not enjoined by a common command.

••VI. The Glory of Preaching••

• Paul claims glory for himself in preaching the gospel.
	• 1 Cor. 9:15 is cited as evidence.
• This is not because he did an undue and supererogatory work, but because he faithfully executed the office entrusted to him.

••VII. Following Christ••

• Christ's command to follow Him is not a counsel, but a command to all.
	• Mt. 19:21 and 1 Pet. 2:21 are cited as evidence.
• No one can have a hope of salvation unless they follow Christ.

••VIII. The Decalogue••

• The question is not whether the precepts are more or fewer than ten, but how they are to be distributed between the two tables.
• The number of precepts in each table is disputed.

••IX. The First Table••

• Four precepts are commonly assigned to the first table.
	• The exact precepts are not specified.

••X. The Second Table••

• Six precepts are commonly assigned to the second table.
	• The exact precepts are not specified.

• The duties of religion towards God (1st table) should not be confused with duties of justice and love towards our neighbor (2nd table)
• The 1st and 2nd precepts differ in meaning, so they should differ in order
• The 10th precept should not be divided into two, as it is a single prohibition against covetousness

• The papists join the 2nd commandment to the 1st, but this is not the traditional division

••V. Conclusion••

• The division of precepts is a matter of controversy, but the teaching of the whole Decalogue should be preserved
• The number of precepts should not be mutilated, and the traditional division should be respected.

• ••The prohibition of image worship••

	• The immediate worship of God is contained in the first table.
	• The internal worship of God includes retaining the true object of worship and worshipping in a lawful manner.

• ••The mediate worship of God••
	• The mediate worship of God includes duties towards our neighbor.
	• The external duties towards our neighbor include the duties of superiors towards inferiors and of neighbors towards neighbors.

• ••Rules of explanation and obedience••
	• The rules of explanation and obedience of the decalogue are necessary to understand the genuine sense of the precepts.
	• The rules of explanation include holding against perverse judgments and interpreting the law spiritually.
• ••The spiritual nature of the law••
	• The law is spiritual and should be interpreted as such.
	• The law demands obedience from us, and we must know what it demands in order to obey.
• ••The importance of obedience••
	• Obedience to the law is necessary to avoid sin and to please God.
	• The rules of obedience are essential to understand what the law demands of us.

Here are the 10 bullets and sub-bullets summarizing the text:

• ••Rule 1: The Lawgiver's Perspective••
	• The lawgiver is divine and heavenly, not human and earthly.
	• He sees the internal motions of the mind, not just external acts.
	• He demands internal obedience, not just external compliance.
• ••Rule 1: Christ's Teaching••
	• Christ extends the meaning of certain sins to include internal motivations.
	• For example, murder includes hatred of a brother, and adultery includes lust.
• ••Rule 2: Affirmative and Negative Precepts••
	• Affirmative precepts imply negative ones, and negative precepts imply affirmative ones.
	• Virtues are commended when vices are forbidden.
	• For example, "thou shalt not kill" implies that we must love and cherish our neighbor's life.
• ••Rule 2: Virtues and Vices••
	• Virtues are not just the absence of vices, but also the presence of positive actions.
	• For example, benevolence is implied when theft is prohibited.
• ••Rule 3: Synechdoche in Precepts••
	• Synechdoche is used in precepts to include all under the same genus.
	• For example, "thou shalt not commit adultery" includes all affections for another's wife.
• ••Rule 3: Prohibited Vices••
	• Prohibited vices include not only the base and capital sins, but also all others that flow from or lead to them.
	• For example, all angry feelings are included under the prohibition of homicide.
• ••Rule 4: The Purpose of Synechdoche••
	• Synechdoche is used to impress a greater detestation of sin upon our minds.
	• It helps us to see the gravity of sin and to avoid it.
• ••Rule 4: The Flesh's Tendency••
	• The flesh tends to dilute the foulness of sin and to cover it under specious pretexts.
	• Synechdoche helps us to see through these pretexts and to understand the true nature of sin.
• ••Rule 5: The Lawgiver's Judgment••
	• The lawgiver's judgment is not based on human standards, but on divine wisdom.
	• He rates sins more severely than we do, and we must learn to see them in the same light.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••Rule 1: The Cause and Effect of Precepts••
	• The law prohibits not only the effect, but also the cause of the effect.
	• For example, prohibiting adultery also prohibits illicit desires and their springs (intemperance and incitements).

â€¢ ••Rule 2: The Scope of Precepts••
	• The law requires not only the action, but also the necessary conditions for the action.
	• For example, commanding children to honor their parents also requires parents to cherish their children and bring them up in the nurture of the Lord.

â€¢ ••Rule 3: The Priority of Precepts••
	• The precepts of the first table (love of God) take precedence over those of the second table (love of neighbor).
	• When the two cannot coexist, the love of God must be prioritized.

â€¢ ••Rule 4: The Relationship between Ceremonial and Moral Law••
	• The ceremonial law (first table) yields to the moral law (second table) because God desires mercy, not sacrifice.
	• Moral worship is primary and necessary, while ceremonial law is secondary and only necessary because of the moral law.

â€¢ ••Rule 5: The Nature of Affirmative and Negative Precepts••
	• Affirmative precepts (ordering things to be done) bind always, but not to always.
	• Negative precepts (prohibiting things to be avoided) bind always to always.

â€¢ ••Rule 6: The Exception to Affirmative Precepts••
	• The general affirmative command to love God obliges always and to always, with no exception.

â€¢ ••Rule 7: The Beginning and End of All Precepts••
	• Love is the beginning and end of all precepts.
	• Love discharges all claims of God's beneficence and man's obedience, and includes all man's duties.

â€¢ ••The Two Loves Commanded••
	• A twofold love is commanded: love of God (first table) and love of neighbor (second table).
	• The love of God is the fullness of the gospel, while the love of man is the fullness of the law.

â€¢ ••The Great Commandment••
	• The love of God is called the "first and great commandment" because it demands all the powers and faculties of man.
	• It is great with regard to the object (God), the subject (man), and amplitude and extension.

â€¢ ••The Relationship between the Two Loves••
	• The love of God is the foundation and source of the love of neighbor.
	• The love of neighbor is a consequence and application of the love of God.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••First Rule of Observation of the Law••

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. The Question at Hand••

• The question is whether saints should be revered with a sacred worship of piety, rather than with a respect of love and fellowship.
	• This is a point of contention between the author and the papists.

••II. The Role of Saints••

• The question is not whether saints are mediators and intercessors with God, but whether they should be invoked as such.
	• The papists believe that saints can bestow blessings, while the author disagrees.

••III. The Nature of Worship••

• The question is whether worship and invocation should be due to God alone, or whether it can also be rendered to angels and saints.
	• The papists believe that worship can be rendered to saints, while the author asserts that it should only be rendered to God.

••IV. Papist Opinion••

• The papist opinion is based on their practice and the sanction of the Council of Trent.
	• The Council of Trent decreed that the invocation of saints and the veneration of relics are essential parts of the Catholic faith.

••V. Papist Authorities••

• Various papist authorities support the invocation of saints, including:
	• Bellarmine, who says that holy beings can be invoked piously and usefully.
	• The Roman Catechism, which argues that saints labor in prayers for the salvation of men and that God bestows blessings on account of their merit.
	• Perronius, who claims that the invocation of saints is not only useful but also necessary.

••VI. Erasures from Indexes••

• The Expurgational Indexes have erased passages from various authors that contradict the papist view on the worship of God alone.
	• Examples include:
		- "Who believe in God will be saved, but who do not will perish" (from the books of Vatablus).
		- "God alone is to be adored and no creature" (from the Index of Athanasius).
		- "The saints are to be honored by imitation, not by adoration" (from Augustine).

••VII. Papist Practice••

• The papists practice the worship of saints in various ways, including:
	• Honoring saints with temples, chapels, altars, images, and rayed heads.
	• Offering gifts and sacrifices to saints.
	• Addressing prayers to saints.
	• Taking oaths and making vows to saints.
	• Placing hope of salvation and confidence in saints.

••VIII. Invocation of Saints••

• The papists invoke all saints, not just specific ones, and believe that they can bestow blessings and protection.
	• This is evident in the practice of invoking saints in various contexts.

••IX. Implications of Papist View••

• The papist view on the invocation of saints has significant implications for the nature of worship and the role of God in salvation.
	• The author argues that this view is contrary to the Bible and the teachings of the early Church Fathers.

••X. Conclusion••

• The author concludes that the papist view on the invocation of saints is contrary to the Bible and the teachings of the early Church Fathers.
	• The author argues that worship and invocation should only be due to God alone.

••I. Invocation of Saints••

• The Catholic Church invokes saints in prayer, asking for their intercession and help.
	• Examples of prayers to saints include:
		- "O happy apostles, deliver me from sin."
		- "O Shepherd Peter, mild and good, receive my prayers."
		- "O James, hasten to blot out my wickedness."

••II. Role of Saints••

• Saints are not only invoked as intercessors, but also as bestowers of good.
	• Catholics believe that saints can provide hope and confidence.
	• They are often invoked in times of need, such as at death.

••III. Worship of Saints••

• Catholics worship saints, not just invoking them.
	• Examples of worship include:
		- Calling the Virgin Mary "Goddess, Mistress, Queen of Heaven."
		- Transferring psalmist's ascriptions to God to the Virgin Mary.

••IV. Types of Worship••

• Catholics distinguish between three types of worship:
	• Latria (divine worship)
	• Cultus civilis (human worship)
	• Dulia (intermediate worship)

••V. Dulia••

• Dulia is worship given to saints and angels.
	• It can be simple or "hyperdulia" (given to the humanity of Christ or the Virgin Mary).

••VI. Worship of the Virgin Mary••

• Catholics worship the Virgin Mary as a superior being.
	• They attribute divine names and articles to her.
	• Examples include the Psalterium Marianum, which transfers psalmist's ascriptions to God to the Virgin Mary.

••VII. Honor Due to Superiors••

• Catholics believe that worship is the honor due from an inferior to a superior.
	• Three things are required for worship: an act of the intellect, an act of the will, and an external act.

••VIII. Three Kinds of Adoration••

• Catholics distinguish between three kinds of adoration:
	• Latria (divine worship)
	• Cultus civilis (human worship)
	• Dulia (intermediate worship)

••IX. Diversity of Worship••

• Catholics believe that a diversity of worship is proper according to the diversity of excellence in objects.
	• They distinguish between two types of worship: religious (due to God alone) and civil (given to creatures).

••X. Worship of Christ and the Virgin Mary••

• Catholics worship the humanity of Christ and the Virgin Mary as superior beings.
	• They attribute "hyperdulia" to these beings, which is a type of worship that is greater than simple dulia.

••II. The Formula of a Vow and Oath••

• The formula is described as: "I swear that I will not show you any kindness, no more than it is not lawful to use things sacred to God."
• The formula is used to devote to God whatever help the child might give to their parent, making it not right to touch anymore.

••III. The Meaning of the Passage••

• The passage is about the Pharisees forbidding the child to assist their parent, so they may have a share with the son.
• This is intimated in Mark 7:12, where it says "And ye suffer him no more to do ought for his father or his mother."

••IV. The Rites of the Jews••

• The formula of oaths and vows was frequent among the Jews, and similar phrases can be found in the Talmud.

• This opinion takes children away from duties they are bound to perform by nature.

••VI. The Obedience Due to God••

• The obedience due to God is not involved in this matter, as it forbids us to be the servants of men (1 Corinthians 7:23).
• The obedience due to God is not repugnant to it, but rather is involved in a different way.

••VII. Children's Independence••

• Children are not independent and cannot decide for themselves, especially when their parents are unwilling.
• The law considers a vow void which a virgin has vowed in her father's house.

••VIII. The Pharisees' Tradition••

• The Pharisees' tradition of withholding children from the power of parents is severely rebuked by Christ and his followers.
• This tradition makes the commandment of God of none effect.

••IX. The Consequences of the Pharisees' Opinion••

• The Pharisees' opinion leads to children being withdrawn from the reverence due to them and from duties they are bound to perform.
• This opinion is contrary to the law and the commandment to honor parents.

••X. The Importance of Obedience••

• Obedience to parents is of great importance, and the law considers it a duty that children are bound to perform by nature.
• The obedience due to God is not involved in this matter, but rather is involved in a different way.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••Objection to children leaving home••
	• The objection is that children are not bound to obey their parents if they leave home.
	• However, the law does not limit this to girls who have not reached puberty, but rather to all virgins in the house of their father.

â€¢ ••Consequences of children leaving home••
	• If children are allowed to leave home without obeying their parents, it would destroy human society.
	• Parents would labor to nourish and bring up children, only to have them torn away and become strangers.

â€¢ ••Canon 16 of the Council of Gangra••
	• The canon opposes the idea of children leaving home without due reverence to their parents.
	• The canon speaks absolutely and without limitation, and it is not lawful to restrict the obedience due to parents to extreme necessity.

â€¢ ••Abraham's example••
	• Abraham's example is often cited as a precedent for children leaving home, but it is not applicable.
	• Abraham was already married and no longer under his father's guardianship, and he had a special divine command.

â€¢ ••Levites' example••
	• The Levites' example is also cited as a precedent, but it is not relevant to children leaving home.
	• The Levites were commanded to obey God and disregard their family relationships, but this is not the same as children leaving home without due reverence.

â€¢ ••Psalm 45:10••
	• The psalm is often cited as a precedent for children leaving home, but it is not applicable.
	• The psalm is referring to a wife leaving her family to cleave to her husband, not to children leaving home without due reverence.

â€¢ ••Christ's command to hate parents••
	• Christ's command to hate parents for his sake does not mean that children should deny their parents' due reverence.
	• The command must be understood comparatively, so that the love of parents yields to divine love.

â€¢ ••Christ's permission to leave home••
	• Christ does not permit children to leave home without due reverence to their parents.
	• Children should only leave home if they are called to a special divine purpose, and even then, they should do so with the consent and blessing of their parents.

â€¢ ••Importance of obedience to parents••
	• Obedience to parents is a natural and indispensable duty.
	• Children should honor and obey their parents, even if they are called to a special divine purpose.

â€¢ ••Consequences of rejecting parental authority••
	• Rejecting parental authority would lead to chaos and destruction of human society.
	• Children should respect and obey their parents, even if they disagree with them, and only leave home if they are called to a special divine purpose.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••Divine Call vs. Parental Obligations••
	• A divine call to follow Christ is to be preferred to the obligations of burying a parent.
	• However, this does not mean a child can take a vow to leave their parents without a call from Christ.

â€¢ ••Leaving Parents vs. Embracing a Monastic Life••
	• Leaving dead parents to be buried is different from throwing off living parents to devote oneself to a monastic life.
	• A monastic life requires a call from Christ, not just a desire to leave one's parents.

â€¢ ••Question 1: Consent of Parents for Marriage••
	• The question is whether children have the right to contract marriage without their parents' consent.

â€¢ ••Papists' Opinion on Clandestine Marriages••
	• Papists believe that clandestine marriages made with free consent are legal and true marriages.
	• However, the holy synod condemns such marriages as accursed.

â€¢ ••Bellarmine's View on Parental Consent••
	• Bellarmine holds that the consent of parents is of honesty, but not of necessity.

â€¢ ••Orthodox View on Parental Consent••
	• The orthodox maintain that the consent of parents is not only of honesty, but also of necessity.
	• Without parental consent, marriages are not legitimate and may be broken.

â€¢ ••Scope of Parental Authority••
	• The question does not concern insane or maniacal parents, or captive parents in a distant region.
	• It concerns sane and free parents who can use their rightful power.

â€¢ ••Minors and Parental Authority••
	• The question especially concerns minors who are still under parental authority.
	• Children who are freed and in their majority are not subject to parental authority.

â€¢ ••Dissent of Parents and Marriage••
	• Dissent of parents cannot hinder or render void a marriage.
	• However, children are not absolutely bound to their parents' will if they have a valid reason for dissent.

â€¢ ••Necessity of Parental Consent••
	• The necessity of parental consent is proven from the law (Ephesians 6:1-3).

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••Reason 1: Obedience to parents••
	• Children are required to obey their parents in all things (Eph. 6:1)
	• Marriage is a significant decision that requires parental involvement
	• Children cannot be said to obey their parents if they make important decisions without their consent

â€¢ ••Reason 2: Scriptural passages••
	• Specific passages in the Bible provide guidance on parental involvement in marriage (Ex. 34:16, Dt. 7:3, Jer. 29:6, 1 Cor. 7:38)
	• These passages imply that children are under parental authority, especially in matters of marriage

â€¢ ••Reason 3: Law regarding defiled daughters••
	• There is a law that requires the father's consent for a daughter to be married after being defiled (Ex. 22:16, Dt. 22:29)
	• This law implies that the father has authority over his daughter's marriage

â€¢ ••Reason 4: Parental authority over vows••
	• A father can void a daughter's vow, which implies that he has authority over her promises
	• If a father has authority over a promise made to God, he certainly has authority over a promise made to men

â€¢ ••Reason 5: Practice under the Old and New Testaments••
	• Examples from the Bible show that parents were involved in their children's marriages (Gen. 24, 21:21, 29:21, Jdg. 1:12, 14:3, 21:7, 2 S. 13:13)
	• These examples demonstrate the importance of parental involvement in marriage

â€¢ ••Reason 6: Children are not independent••
	• Children are not their own masters and are under parental authority
	• This is evident from the fact that parents can sell their children into servitude (Ex. 21:7)

â€¢ ••Reason 7: Parental authority over daughters••
	• A father's consent is required for his daughter to be married (Ex. 22:16, Dt. 22:29)
	• This implies that the father has authority over his daughter's marriage

â€¢ ••Reason 8: Parental authority is not limited to daughters••
	• A father's authority extends to his sons as well (Ex. 21:7)

â€¢ ••Reason 9: Parental authority is not limited to specific circumstances••
	• The law regarding defiled daughters implies that parental authority is not limited to specific circumstances (Ex. 22:16, Dt. 22:29)

â€¢ ••Reason 10: Parental authority is a biblical principle••
	• The Bible teaches that children are under parental authority (Eph. 6:1, Job 1:2, 10, 12)
	• This principle is not limited to specific circumstances, but is a general biblical principle.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••The Problem of Self-Disposal••
	• The text argues that it is not lawful for a person to dispose of themselves without the consent of their parents.
	• This is because parents have authority over their children (Num. 30:5).

â€¢ ••The Consequences of Self-Disposal••
	• The text lists several consequences of self-disposal, including:
		- Violation of the divine law concerning honor to parents
		- Weakening of the authority of fathers
		- Trampling of public morality
		- Introduction of an heir against the will of the father
		- Disturbance of domestic peace
		- Placing children in imminent danger

â€¢ ••The Civil Laws••
	• The text cites various civil laws that support the idea that the consent of parents is necessary for marriage.
	• Examples include:
		- Justinian's Institutes (1.10)
		- Paulus's Corpus Iuris Civilis (I: Digesta 23.2.2)
		- Ulpianus's Corpus Iuris Civilis (23.2.9)

â€¢ ••Reasons for Parental Consent••
	• The text lists several reasons why parental consent is necessary, including:
		- The paternal power of parents over their children
		- The succession of inheritance
		- The affection of parents for their children
		- The judgment of infirm children

â€¢ ••Popish Canonists' Opinion••
	• The text notes that most popish canonists do not disagree with the idea that parental consent is necessary for marriage.
	• Examples include:
		- Euaristus
		- Leo I
		- Pelagius
		- Urban V
		- Nicholas of Cusa

â€¢ ••Sources of Explanation••
	• The text mentions several sources that can be consulted to understand the idea that parental consent is necessary for marriage, including:
		- Espensaeus's "De clandestinis matrimoniis"
		- Zanchius and Gherardus's "De conjugio, coelibatu et similibus argumentis"

â€¢ ••Esau's Marriage••
	• The text notes that Esau's marriage without consulting his parents is an example of the invalidity of such marriages.
	• The text argues that Esau's marriage had a bitter and dreadful end.

â€¢ ••Isaac's Indulgence••
	• The text notes that Isaac did not declare Esau's marriage void, which is attributed to parental indulgence.

â€¢ ••The Importance of Parental Consent••
	• The text emphasizes the importance of parental consent for marriage, citing various civil laws and canonists' opinions.

â€¢ ••The Consequences of Ignoring Parental Consent••
	• The text warns of the consequences of ignoring parental consent, including the violation of divine law and the weakening of paternal authority.

â€¢ ••The Need for Explanation••
	• The text notes that the idea that parental consent is necessary for marriage requires explanation and justification, citing various sources that can be consulted.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••Marriage and Consent••
	• The argument from fact to right is not valid in determining the validity of a marriage.
	• Laws, not examples, should guide our understanding of marriage.
	• An ecclesiastical blessing cannot ratify a marriage that violates God's laws.

â€¢ ••God's Role in Marriage••
	• God cannot be considered the author of a union that violates his laws.
	• An unlawful marriage cannot be justified by citing God's role in it.

â€¢ ••Leaving Parents and Cleave to Wife••
	• The expression "leave and cleave" only applies to true and lawful marriages.
	• In a wicked connection, it is better to cleave to the wife, even if it means leaving parents.

â€¢ ••Clandestine Marriages••
	• Marriages without parental consent are unlawful, even if the church blesses them.
	• The church's blessing does not make an unlawful marriage valid.

â€¢ ••Parental Power••
	• Parents have the right to make their children's marriages void, even if the children have already copulated.
	• This right is not taken away by the fact that the children have already engaged in illicit intercourse.

â€¢ ••Slaves and Children••
	• The obligation between a slave and his master is civil, but between parents and children it is natural.
	• Children belong to parents by generation, not just by possession.

â€¢ ••Marriage of Slaves••
	• Slaves can marry without their master's consent, as they are property.
	• The master has the power to give a wife to his slave.

â€¢ ••Consent and Authority••
	• The lawful consent of parents is required for a child's marriage.
	• A child is not absolutely independent and master of themselves, even if they are free.

â€¢ ••War and Punishment••
	• The rights of war and punishment are not contained under the Sixth Commandment.
	• Suicide is not prohibited under the Sixth Commandment.

â€¢ ••Dueling and Suicide••
	• Dueling is prohibited under the Sixth Commandment.
	• Suicide is not prohibited under the Sixth Commandment.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••Judicial Homicide is Not Prohibited••
	• Committed by public magistrates against private persons
	• Magistrates are armed with the sword to avenge evil (Rom. 13:4; 1 Pet. 2:14)
	• Applies to all magistrates, whether believers or not

â€¢ ••Duty of the Magistrate••
	• Requires punishment of the guilty to maintain public tranquility and peace
	• Could not be preserved if the sword could not be unsheathed against the guilty

â€¢ ••Not Opposed by God's Command••
	• Respects private persons, not magistrates and ministers of God
	• Christian charity can love the persons and punish the crimes

â€¢ ••Not Opposed by Christian Charity••
	• Leaving the desperately wicked unpunished would be a violation of the law of charity
	• Would be injurious to the good and pernicious to the republic

â€¢ ••Not Opposed by Prophecy••
	• Isaiah 11:6 refers to believers, not magistrates
	• Believers should grow mild and live peacefully together after putting on the yoke of Christ

â€¢ ••Not Opposed by Christ's Words••
	• "Resist not evil" (Mt. 5:39, 40) refers to private vengeance, not public punishment
	• Paul's words "Recompense to no man evil for evil" (Rom. 12:17) do not apply to public punishment

â€¢ ••Not Opposed by Scripture••
	• Mt. 26:52 refers to taking the sword without it being given, not lawful use
	• Christ did not condemn the adulteress (Jn. 8:11) because he did not act as a magistrate or judge

â€¢ ••Right of War••
	• Belongs to the magistrate and can be lawfully exercised in a just and necessary war
	• Unjust and hasty wars are condemned

â€¢ ••Against Anabaptists and Socinians••
	• They think the right of war is abolished under the New Testament
	• We maintain that the right of war is still valid and can be lawfully exercised

â€¢ ••Against Unjust Wars••
	• Unjust and hasty wars are condemned, undertaken without just and necessary cause
	• Magistrates should exercise the right of war in a just and necessary manner

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

• ••The Old Testament••
	• The Old Testament allows for war and violence
	• God's approval of war in the Old Testament should also be valid in the New Testament
	• Socinus' objection that God did not disapprove of war in the Old Testament is not relevant under the New Testament
• ••The New Testament••
	• The New Testament also approves of war and violence
	• John the Baptist sanctioned military discipline and did not order soldiers to give up their profession
	• The faith of the centurion, the piety of Cornelius, and the testimony of an angel all demonstrate the acceptability of military service
• ••The Office of the Magistrate••
	• The office of the magistrate demands the right to carry out war and violence
	• The magistrate has been given the sword as the avenger of crimes (Rom. 13:4; 1 Pet. 2:14)
	• The magistrate is bound to defend his subjects and maintain public tranquility and safety
• ••Revelation••
	• The Apocalypse records and approves various wars of the pious under the New Testament
	• These wars are not just spiritual, but also external and involving real bloodshed
• ••Sources of Explanation••
	• The right to war is not invalidated by New Testament passages about peace and disarmament
	• Passages such as Isaiah 2:4 and Zechariah 9:10 refer to spiritual and internal peace, not the abolition of war
• ••Just War••
	• Defensive wars are just, even if offensive wars are not
	• The right to war is necessary for the magistrate to defend his subjects and maintain public safety
• ••The Nature of War••
	• War is not inherently wicked or unlawful
	• War can be a necessary means of defending against unjust violence and maintaining public order
• ••The Role of the Magistrate••
	• The magistrate has a duty to defend his subjects and maintain public safety
	• This duty includes the right to carry out war and violence when necessary
• ••The Relationship between War and Morality••
	• War is not inherently immoral, but can be a necessary means of upholding morality and justice
	• The right to war is not invalidated by moral and natural law, but is rather a necessary aspect of it.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••The Kingdom of Christ is not achieved through carnal weapons••

â€¢ ••The magistrate's right to wage war is not abolished by the gospel••

â€¢ ••The private duty of believers is different from the public duty of the magistrate••

â€¢ ••Objections from Matthew 5:39 do not prove that every war is unlawful••

	• The hatred of enmity and revenge is prohibited, not the care of justice

â€¢ ••James' teaching on the origin of wars does not imply that every war is evil••
