	• The magistrate may be justified in repelling and avenging offensive injury

â€¢ ••Defensive homicide is not forbidden••
	• Defensive homicide is justified when someone kills another in self-defense against a violent and unjust aggressor
	• Four conditions must be met for defensive homicide to be considered lawful

â€¢ ••The conditions for lawful defensive homicide••
	• The aggressor must unjustly assail and fall upon the defender
	• The defender must be blameless and have no other way to escape
	• The defense must be made during the attack, not after it is over
	• The defender must act with the sole intention of defending themselves, not with anger or revenge

â€¢ ••The reason for defensive homicide••
	• It is a natural and perpetual right to repel force with force and defend oneself
	• This right is especially justified when the aggression is violent and lacks public authority

â€¢ ••Civil laws also approve of defensive homicide••
	• The Codex to the Cornelian law and the Aquilian law support the idea of defensive homicide
	• These laws recognize the right to defend oneself against unjust aggression.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••Right to Self-Defense••
	• The right to repel force with force is allowed by law (Digesta 48.8, Ad legem Corneliam de sicariis)
	• God himself has intimated this right in the law (Exodus 22:2)

â€¢ ••Defense of Life••
	• Defense of one's own life or the life of a loved one is a justifiable reason for self-defense
	• Examples include defending parents, wives, children, friends, and others with a close tie

â€¢ ••Defense of Chastity••
	• Defense of one's own chastity or the chastity of another is also a justifiable reason for self-defense
	• Examples include brave virgins who killed those attempting to violate their chastity

â€¢ ••Private Revenge vs. Blameless Protection••
	• Private revenge is prohibited (Romans 12:19)
	• Blameless protection, however, is not prohibited and is a necessary defense of life

â€¢ ••Public Authority of the Law of Nature••
	• Just self-defense is done through the public authority of the law of nature, not private undertaking

â€¢ ••Love of Enemies••
	• The injunctions to love enemies do not take away the necessary defense of life
	• The foundation of the love of neighbors is the love of oneself

â€¢ ••Just Self-Defense••
	• Just self-defense is not the same as revenge (Matthew 26:52)
	• The passage in Matthew 26:52 does not take away just self-defense

â€¢ ••Casual Homicide••
	• Casual homicide is not prohibited, provided it is not intended and treachery is absent
	• Asylums and cities of refuge were appointed for such cases

â€¢ ••Private Homicide••
	• All private homicide is forbidden
	• This includes private manslaughter committed by private authority and wicked treachery

â€¢ ••Prohibited Motives••
	• Private homicide is prohibited when committed with motives such as hatred, studied vengeance, or evil intent
	• Examples include killing someone with poison or through cunning.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••Sanction of Homicide••
	• Divine: man is the image of God and cannot be destroyed without injury to God
	• Natural: all things seek self-preservation, and those who deprive men of life are enemies of the human race
	• Civil: homicide disturbs and overthrows civil society

â€¢ ••Inclusion of Suicide••

â€¢ ••Reasons for Prohibiting Suicide••

	• Violates the natural inclination to love and preserve one's own life

â€¢ ••Opposition to Natural Law••
	• Binds each one to self-preservation
	• Opposed to confidence and piety in God
	• Wisdom is also opposed, as the crime is often committed in a state of fury and wild impulse

â€¢ ••Opposition to Justice••
	• Man is not lord of his own life, but a servant to a higher authority
	• Should not be irregular or leave his station at his own pleasure

â€¢ ••Opposition to Fortitude••
	• Arises from impatience of evil or fear of it
	• Does not belong to magnanimity, but rather to cowardice

â€¢ ••Consent of the Wiser••
	• Pythagoras, Plato, Aristotle, Seneca, Cicero, and others consider suicide to be wicked

â€¢ ••Examples of Wise Men••

â€¢ ••Consequences of Suicide••
	• Causes grief to family and community
	• Brings shame and scandal to the Christian system
	• Occasions scoffing to enemies of the faith

â€¢ ••Conclusion••
	• Suicide is a most heinous sin, opposed to God, nature, justice, wisdom, and fortitude.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••The Divine Authority••
	• No laws, whether of war or the state, can stand opposed to divine sanction.
	• Public authority cannot bind us in opposition to divine authority.

â€¢ ••Conscience and Morality••
	• No disadvantage to the enemy or advantage to the country can excuse us from our conscience.
	• The intention to injure the enemy cannot be abstracted from the knowledge of destroying oneself and others.

â€¢ ••Rendering to God••
	• We should render to God what has been given by him, but only when it is demanded and restored in due manner.
	• Death can be lawfully wished for, but not sought.

â€¢ ••Death and Bravery••
	• Despising death is brave, but voluntarily rushing upon it is rash and insane.
	• The love of country, safety of others, and desire of immortality should not impel us to invite death when it is unsent.

â€¢ ••Suffering Death vs. Killing Oneself••
	• Suffering death is lawful in some circumstances, but killing oneself is not.
	• The former is exemplified by Christ, martyrs, and heroes.

â€¢ ••The "Giving of the Body to be Burned"••
	• This phrase refers to meeting martyrdom at the call of God, not a rash and useless act.
	• It involves meeting death at the call of God, not refusing it by lying or denying the truth.

â€¢ ••Unlawful Duels••
	• Duelling is prohibited, except in cases of necessary defense of life against an unjust aggressor.
	• Public authority duels for the common good are also allowed.

â€¢ ••Condemnation of Duelling••
	• Duelling directly assails the precept "Thou shall not kill".
	• No reason can make duelling honorable and lawful.

â€¢ ••Defense of Duelling••
	• Defenses of worldly honor and the avoidance of disgrace are not valid reasons for duelling.
	• The defense of goods and the manifestation of truth are also not valid reasons.

â€¢ ••Prioritizing Divine Honor••
	• Wounded honor can be better and more easily healed than the death of the injurer.
	• No loss of honor is to be compared to the danger of the soul.

	• Natural reason: the conjunction of male and female is directed by right reason

	• This includes adultery, fornication, and other forms of lewdness

	• Fornication is condemned as a heinous sin in both the Old and New Testaments
• ••The Consequences of Illicit Interourse••

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. The Nature of Evil••

• Evil is inherent in itself and cannot be made good or lawful.
	• A lie is evil in itself and cannot be justified by its end.
	• A lie is a disorder both in the liar's mind and in their relationship with others.

••II. The Definition of a Lie••

• A lie is a statement that signifies something that is not in the mind of the speaker.
	• This is contrary to the natural order of speech, which is to convey one's thoughts.
	• The Philosopher (Aristotle) concludes that a lie is inherently wicked and to be avoided.

••III. The Illegality of a Lie••

• A lie is inherently unlawful (anomia) due to its deformity and disorder (ataxia).
	• This is not just because of its end, but because of its inherent nature.
	• No circumstances can change a thing that is inherently evil.

••IV. The Justification of a Lie••

• A lie cannot be justified by its end, even if it is intended to benefit others.
	• This is because evil must not be done, even if good may come from it.
	• Augustine and other theologians agree that all lying is sinful.

••V. The Severity of Lying••

• Lying is more sinful when done with the intention of injuring others.
	• This is because it involves a greater degree of malice and harm.
	• Augustine says that saying any lie is just is to say that there are just sins and unjust things.

••VI. The Sources of Explanation••

• The Bible provides examples of lying, but these are not to be taken as justifications.
	• The Egyptian midwives lied to Pharaoh, but their good intentions and kindness were rewarded, not their lie.
	• Augustine distinguishes between the act of lying and the motivations behind it.

••VII. The Teaching of Augustine••

• Augustine frequently teaches that all lying is sinful.
	• He distinguishes between lying with the intention of benefiting others and lying with the intention of injuring others.
	• He argues that saying any lie is just is to say that there are just sins and unjust things.

	• The consequences of lying can be far-reaching and devastating.

• The Tenth Commandment prohibits coveting, but the concept of concupiscence is complex and multifaceted
	• The author has discussed the nature of concupiscence, its types, and the importance of honesty in all aspects of life.

â€¢ ••Two relations of the ceremonial law••
	• The legal relation: the law as a covenant of works, referring to the guilt and curse of sin
	• The evangelical relation: the law as a type of good things to come, referring to the covenant of grace and Christ

â€¢ ••The legal relation••
	• The ceremonial law discovered sin, sealed its guilt, and threatened God's wrath
	• It was a reminder of the "handwriting" against us, a remembrance of sins

â€¢ ••The evangelical relation••
	• The ceremonial law was a symbol and seal of the grace of God in Christ
	• It supported believers in the hope of good things to come and confirmed them against the sense of sin and God's anger

â€¢ ••Connecting the relations••
	• The two relations are connected and must be considered together
	• Separating them can lead to a distortion of the truth

â€¢ ••Understanding the Old Testament economy••
	• The ceremonial law must be understood in its dual relation to the covenant of works and the covenant of grace
	• Neglecting one relation can obscure the other

â€¢ ••The middle way••
	• The safest way to understand the ceremonial law is to consider both relations together
	• This approach avoids distorting the truth and preserves the balance between law and gospel

â€¢ ••Implications for our day••
	• The question of whether the ceremonial law was given from wrath to wrath or as a type of good things to come remains a topic of debate
	• A careful consideration of both relations is necessary to arrive at a correct understanding.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

• ••The relationship between the legal and evangelical relations••
	• The legal relation is inferior to the evangelical relation
	• The evangelical relation is the primary and ultimate end of God's economy
• ••The nature of the ceremonial law••
	• It cannot be said that the ceremonial law was given from wrath to wrath
	• Sacrifices were not a remedy for sin, but a handwriting (chirographum)
• ••The purpose of the ceremonial law••
	• It was given to adumbrate and seal gospel mysteries and the saving grace of Christ
	• It was not given to seal guilt and bondage, but to point to Christ's future expiation

	• This refers to the law considered in opposition to the gospel
	• It is a ministry of death and condemnation, not a legitimate use of the law

	• It was a schoolmaster unto Christ, leading people to Christ
	• It was not a legitimate use of the law, but a temporary means to an end

	• It is described as weak and beggarly elements of the world
	• This refers to the law considered in itself, apart from Christ the Mediator

	• It had only the shadow of good things to come, not the very image
	• This does not mean it was not referred to Christ to shadow forth his grace

	• This refers to the legal relation, not the evangelical relation
	• It is not meant to blot out the evangelical relation, but to point to Christ's future expiation

	• Circumcision is a seal of the righteousness of faith, not a seal of guilt

	• It was given to point to Christ's future expiation and to seal gospel mysteries
	• It was not given to seal guilt and bondage, but to lead people to Christ.

â€¢ ••Sacred persons••

â€¢ ••Sacred persons initiated by circumcision••

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. The Twofold Altar••

• Represented the two parts of Christ's priestly office:
	• Satisfaction (humiliation): offering of body and blood
	• Intercession (exaltation): living and continual representation of sacrifice

••II. The Golden Censer••

• Symbolized Christ's intercession in heaven
• Incense burned on the altar represented the prayers of the faithful

••III. The Brazen Altar••

• Represented the sacrifice of Christ on the cross
• Must be preceded by satisfaction (humiliation) for prayers to be effective

••IV. The Table, Candlestick, and Altar of Incense••

• Correspond to:
	• Light of the word (candlestick)
	• Bread of life (table)
	• Sacred worship (altar of incense)

••V. The Brazen Laver••

• Represented the purification required for those who draw near to God
• Must be washed of guilt and pollution through faith in Christ

••VI. Sacred Times••

• Represent the blessings of God, past or future
• Include:
	• Continual sacrifice (daily prayers and worship)
	• Festivals and celebrations

••VII. Festivals••

• Threefold kind:
	• Weekly (Sabbath): creation and redemption
	• Monthly (new moons): sanctification of months and changes
	• Annual (anniversary festivals): commemoration of past blessings and promise of spiritual benefits

••VIII. Anniversary Festivals••

• Most solemn were:
	• Passover: deliverance from Egypt
	• Pentecost: blessing of the law
	• Feast of Tabernacles: divine protection in the desert

••IX. Significance of Festivals••

• Recollection of past blessings
• Conjoined adumbration and promise of spiritual benefits to be conferred by Christ

••X. Conclusion••

• Sacred times and festivals represent the blessings of God and the spiritual benefits of Christ's sacrifice and intercession.

â€¢ ••Abrogation of Jewish law••

â€¢ ••Distinguishing between common and particular right••
	• Laws that were of particular right (e.g. laws concerning a husband's brother, divorce) are abrogated.
	• Laws that were of common and universal right (e.g. laws concerning trials, punishment of crimes) remain in force.

â€¢ ••Criteria for distinguishing between common and particular right••
	• (1) Laws that prevail among both Jews and Gentiles are of common right.
	• (2) Laws that conform to the precepts of the Decalogue are of common right.
	• (3) Laws that are repeated in the New Testament are of common right.

â€¢ ••Sources of explanation••
	• The substance of a precept must be distinguished from its circumstances.
	• Some laws are of common right as to substance and circumstances, while others are of common right as to substance but particular right as to circumstances.

â€¢ ••Perpetual vs. mutable laws••
	• Laws that are of perpetual right are not subject to change.
	• Laws that are of particular right and mutable are subject to change.

â€¢ ••Laws that are mixed with types••
	• Laws that are mixed with types are changeable and have been abrogated.
	• Examples include laws concerning primogeniture, asylums, and the Jubilee.

â€¢ ••Forensic laws accommodated to the Jewish polity••
	• Laws that were accommodated to the Jewish polity are no longer binding.
	• Examples include the Levirate law, the law of jealousy, and the law concerning the rest of the field.

â€¢ ••Reasons for abrogation••
	• The Jewish polity has been taken away, so laws that were peculiar to it are no longer binding.
	• Laws that were temporary and had a political end are no longer binding.

â€¢ ••Nature of the moral and perpetual law••
	• The moral and perpetual law remains in force.
	• This law is common to all and is not subject to change.

â€¢ ••Importance of distinguishing between common and particular right••
	• Distinguishing between common and particular right is essential for understanding the law.
	• This distinction helps to identify which laws are still binding and which have been abrogated.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••Distinctions in the Covenant of Grace••
	• Condition can be used antecedently and a priori (meritorious cause) or concomitantly and a posteriori (means and disposition)
	• Condition can be natural or supernatural and divine
	• Federal promise can be concerning the end (salvation) or the means (faith and repentance)

â€¢ ••The Covenant of Grace••
	• If condition is taken antecedently and a priori, the covenant is unconditionally gracious
	• If condition is taken consequently and a posteriori, the covenant is conditional

â€¢ ••Conditional vs. Unconditional Covenant••
	• Conditional covenant is proposed with an express condition (e.g. John 3:16, Romans 10:9)
	• Unconditional covenant would imply God is bound to man, not man to God

â€¢ ••Promises of the Covenant••
	• If promises are concerning the end, they are conditional (faith and repentance)
	• If promises are concerning the means, they are simple and absolute

â€¢ ••Covenant in Relation to Christ••
	• In relation to Christ's first sanction, the covenant has no previous condition
	• In relation to its acceptance and application to the believer, faith is a condition
	• In relation to its consummation, the covenant has the relation of condition and means

â€¢ ••Differences between the Covenant of Grace and the Law••
	• Legal condition is an entire and perfect obedience to the law
	• Evangelical condition is faith (Romans 10:9, John 3:16)

â€¢ ••Threatenings in the Gospel••
	• Threatenings imply a conditional covenant, where neglect of faith and obedience is culpable

â€¢ ••Reciprocal Obligation in the Covenant••
	• In a covenant, there is always a mutual agreement and reciprocal obligation
	• God is not bound to man in the covenant, but man is bound to God

â€¢ ••Infinite Progression••
	• If the condition of the condition is always demanded, there would be an infinite progression

â€¢ ••Consummation of the Covenant••
	• The covenant has the relation of condition and means in relation to its consummation with faith, obedience, and the desire of holiness.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Distinction between Legal and Evangelical Conditions••

• The legal condition is:
	• Commanded, but not given or promised
	• Meritorious, with life granted due to obedience
• The evangelical condition is:
	• Commanded and promised, and also given
	• Supernatural, depending on God's grace

••II. Nature of the Evangelical Condition••

• It is a pure gift (charisma) of God
• It is not a cause of salvation, but rather an instrument to apprehend the promised thing
• It is necessary for obtaining salvation

••III. Covenant of Grace••

• The covenant of grace is not dependent on a human condition
• Its efficacy and immutability are not weakened by a supernatural condition
• It is based on God's grace, faithfulness, and the infinite merit of Christ

••IV. Christ's Answer to the Young Man••

• Christ's answer to the young man was based on the Mosaic Law, not the covenant of grace
• He was convicting the young man of his inability to keep the law

••V. Covenant of Grace as a Testament••

• The covenant of grace is set forth under the notion of a testament
• It is suspended on no condition, and all human duties are blessings of God

••VI. Federal Relation of the Covenant of Grace••

• The covenant of grace has a federal relation, with conditions on the part of man
• It is called "a covenant by a testament"

••VII. Conditions in the Covenant of Grace••

• The question is: What are the conditions in the covenant of grace?
• Is faith alone the condition, or is it accompanied by repentance and obedience?

••VIII. Relation of Faith in the Covenant of Grace••

• Faith is a condition of the covenant, but not absolutely and according to its nature
• It is contained under obedience and cannot be contradistinguished from it

••IX. Instrumental Role of Faith••

• Faith is considered relatively and instrumentally, embracing Christ and applying to him for righteousness
• It obtains the right to eternal life through Christ

••X. Distinguishing Faith from Works of the Law••

• Faith is distinguished from the works of the law, which could not be done if faith were taken absolutely
• Faith is necessary for obtaining salvation, but it is not the only condition.

••I. The Consolation of the Holy Spirit••

	• This consolation is a gift that helps us understand our relationship with God

••II. Mutual Consent of Love••

• Our love for Christ is a response to His love for us, and we give ourselves entirely to Him (Gal. 2:20; 2 Cor. 5:15)
	• This mutual consent is a key aspect of our relationship with Christ

••III. The Nature of Consent••

• Our consent should be present, not future, and should not distinguish between Christ's benefits and duties (Rom. 8:9; 1 Cor. 6:17)
	• We should receive Christ as both Savior and Lord, and be willing to obey Him in all things

••IV. The Benefits of Communion with Christ••

• Our communion with Christ brings us fellowship in the same Spirit, life, righteousness, glory, and inheritance (Rom. 8:9; 1 Cor. 6:17; Gal. 2:20)
	• This communion is a key aspect of our relationship with Christ

••V. Christ's Expectations••

• Christ expects from us love and submission, which should be sincere, full, and constant (Jn. 21:17; 1 Pet. 1:8; Eph. 5:24)
	• We should be willing to obey Christ in all things

••VI. Faith as a Condition••

• Faith is the sole condition of the covenant because it is the only condition that is receptive of Christ and capable of applying His righteousness (Jn. 3:16, 36; Rom. 10:9)
	• Faith is the key to receiving Christ and His benefits

••VII. Other Virtues as Conditions••

• Repentance and obedience of the new life can be considered conditions in a broader sense, but not in a strict and proper sense (Jn. 13:17; 2 Cor. 5:17; Rom. 8:13)
	• These virtues are important aspects of our relationship with Christ, but they are not the sole condition of the covenant

••VIII. Antecedent and Subsequent Conditions••

• A condition can be either antecedent (a cause why we are received into the covenant) or subsequent (a means by which we go forward in the covenant)
	• Understanding the difference between these two types of conditions is important for understanding the covenant

••IX. The Role of Faith••

• Faith is the sole condition of the covenant because it is the only condition that is receptive of Christ and capable of applying His righteousness
	• Faith is the key to receiving Christ and His benefits

••X. The Importance of Obedience••

• Obedience to Christ is an important aspect of our relationship with Him, and we should be willing to obey Him in all things
	• Obedience is a key aspect of our communion with Christ

â€¢ ••Faith and the Covenant••
	• Faith is the sole condition of the covenant in one sense
	• In another sense, holiness and obedience are conditions because they are the means to arrive at the full possession of the covenant's blessings
	• Faith is effective through love (Gal. 5:6)

â€¢ ••Justification and the Covenant••
	• Justification is not related to faith in the sense that it is not a condition for justification
	• However, faith is related to the covenant as an inseparable attendant of true and sincere faith
	• Faith is a fruit of the Spirit in Christ (Rom. 8:2, 9, 10)

â€¢ ••Holiness and Obedience••
	• Holiness and obedience are required for the observance of the covenant
	• They are not the same as justification, but rather a means to possess the covenant's blessings
	• They are duties owed to God (Lk. 17:10)

â€¢ ••Acceptance and Keeping of the Covenant••
	• Acceptance of the covenant is through faith, while keeping it is through obedience
	• The two are connected, with acceptance preceding keeping
	• The covenant is not just about accepting it, but also about keeping it

â€¢ ••Legal and Evangelical Obedience••
	• Legal obedience is prescribed for the meriting of life
	• Evangelical obedience follows as a fruit of life, not as a means to obtain it
	• The former is perfect and absolute, while the latter is sincere and imperfect

â€¢ ••Covenants of Works and of Grace••
	• The covenants of works and of grace agree in various particulars
	• They agree in their author (God), contracting parties (God and man), general end (glory of God), and extrinsic form (restipulation)

â€¢ ••Differences between Covenants••
	• The covenants differ in their author (God's relation to man)
	• In the covenant of works, God is viewed as Creator and Lord, while in the covenant of grace, he is viewed as Redeemer and Father
	• In the covenant of works, God's love and benevolence are towards an innocent creature, while in the covenant of grace, his mercy and grace are towards a miserable creature

â€¢ ••Contracting Parties••
	• In the covenant of works, there were only two parties (God and man)
	• In the covenant of grace, a mediator was necessary to make peace and reconcile men to God and God to men

â€¢ ••Foundation of the Covenants••
	• The covenant of works rested upon man's own obedience and the strength of nature or free will
	• The covenant of grace, on the other hand, is based on God's mercy and grace towards a miserable creature

â€¢ ••Agreement and Difference between Covenants••
	• The covenants agree in their general end (glory of God) and promise (life and happiness)
	• They differ in their author, contracting parties, foundation, and mediator

â€¢ ••The First Covenant••
	• Promised life as a reward for perfect righteousness
	• Required works as a condition for life

	• The second covenant's end is the manifestation of God's mercy and love

â€¢ ••The Manifestation of Each Covenant••

â€¢ ••The Nature of the Second Covenant••
	• The second covenant is a covenant of the people, based on God's power and protection
	• The second covenant is a covenant of salvation, bringing deliverance from sin and death

â€¢ ••The Significance of the Second Covenant••

	• The second covenant is a mystery that can only be known through supernatural revelation

	• The covenant of grace is one and the same as to substance under each dispensation

	• The Socinians assert that the law of Christ contains two promises not contained in the law of Moses: eternal life and the Holy Spirit
	• The Socinians believe that the new covenant is superior to the old covenant in terms of promises and benefits

â€¢ ••The Opinion of Volkelius and Smaltzius••

	• They do not deny that the fathers of the Old Testament were saved or would be saved in eternal happiness

â€¢ ••The Unity of the Covenant of Grace••
	• The covenant of grace is one and the same as to substance under each dispensation
	• The Socinians, Anabaptists, and Remonstrants deny the unity of the covenant of grace

â€¢ ••The Covenant of Works and the Covenant of Grace••
	• The covenant of works is a basis for appeal to the covenant of mercy
	• The covenant of grace is a remedy for those who have violated the covenant of nature

â€¢ ••The Sin Against the Holy Ghost••
	• The sin against the Holy Ghost is unpardonable because it is committed against the covenant of grace
	• There is no other covenant by which one can be reconciled to God after violating the covenant of grace

â€¢ ••The Relationship Between the Covenants••
	• The covenant of works is a basis for the covenant of mercy

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

• ••Socinians' views on the Old Testament••
	• They agree that God pardoned sins in the Old Testament, although it was not promised or signified
	• They believe the fathers had some knowledge and hope of eternal life, but not promised to them
	• They distinguish between the faith of the ancients and ours, with ours being a faith in Christ
• ••Socinians on Christ in the Old Testament••
	• They believe Christ was predicted by the prophets, but not that the ancients looked to Christ or were saved in his coming
	• They hold that the faith of the ancients was in God simply, not in Christ
• ••Smaltzius' views on the Old Testament••
	• He believes the faith of the ancients and ours differs in three things, including the command to believe in Christ
	• He holds that Christ was not manifested in the Old Testament, so faith in him was not exercised
• ••Volkelius' views on the Old Testament••
	• He believes the faith of the ancients and ours differs in that we are commanded to believe in Christ as much as in God
	• He holds that faith in Christ was not exercised in the Old Testament
• ••Remonstrants' views on the Old Testament••
	• They do not differ from the Socinians, but rather agree with them on the main points
	• They believe the agreement of both testaments is in the obedience of faith required in both
• ••Remonstrants on faith in Jesus Christ••
	• They call the question of faith in Jesus Christ under the Old Testament "absurd, ambiguous, and useless"
	• They distinguish the manner of revelation (clear or obscure) and say faith in Jesus Christ was taught indirectly and obscurely
• ••Remonstrants on the promise of eternal life••
	• They believe the promise of eternal life was not clearly promised in the Old Testament
	• They hold that if there were general promises, they should be believed to include the promise of eternal life
• ••Remonstrants on the covenant••
	• They believe the promise of eternal life was comprehended in the covenant itself
	• They hold that special promises in the Old Testament do not include a clear promise of eternal life
• ••Remonstrants on the object of faith••
	• They believe the one object of faith is Christ
	• They hold that the difference between the Socinians and themselves is in some accidental matters that do not detract from the substantial unity
• ••Remonstrants on the manner of revelation••
	• They distinguish the manner of revelation (clear or obscure) and say faith in Jesus Christ was taught indirectly and obscurely in the Old Testament

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••The Anabaptist Error••
	• Many Anabaptists believed that the Israelite people were only granted temporal goods and earthly promises, with no hope of heavenly immortality.
	• This view was also held by Servetus, who was disputed by Calvin.

â€¢ ••The State of the Question••
	• The question is not about the differences in the covenant of grace between the Old and New Testaments in terms of accidentals and dispensations.
	• The question is whether the covenant of grace was the same in terms of substance and essential parts, including the mediator, faith, promises, and way of reconciliation.

â€¢ ••The Covenant of Grace••
	• The question is whether the covenant of grace was the same for both the Old and New Testaments.
	• The opponents deny this, while the author affirms it.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Introduction••

• The covenant of grace was visibly begun on the day of Pentecost (Acts 2:17, 18) and should be continued invisibly under the kingdom of Christ.
• The extent of the covenant of grace is being questioned.

••II. The Question••

• Was the covenant of grace ever universal, either as to presentation or acceptance?
• The question is related to the object of the covenant of grace, which is being agitated by the patrons of universal grace.

••III. The Opinion of the Remonstrants••

• The Remonstrants (a group of Dutch theologians) held that Christ's death reconciled God to the whole human race, making it possible for God to enter into a new covenant of grace with sinners.
• They believed that this new covenant was made with the whole human race, and that no nation or individual was excluded from it.

••IV. The Opinion of the Remonstrants (continued)••

• The Remonstrants believed that the spiritual gifts of the covenant were available to all nations, even if they did not have the ordinary preaching of the gospel.
• They also believed that no one was born absolutely a stranger to the covenant.

••V. The Opinion of the Universalists••

• Some Lutherans and universalists (such as Testard and Amyrald) agreed with the Remonstrants on this point.
• They believed that the covenant of grace was universal, and that God had made it with the whole human race from the beginning.

••VI. Testard's Opinion••

• Testard believed that God made a covenant with Adam after his fall, and that this covenant was renewed with Noah and Abraham.
• He believed that God concealed the grace of the new covenant neither from any nation nor from any individual.

••VII. Amyrald's Opinion••

• Amyrald believed that the degree of love and mercy by which God was induced to make the covenant with the whole human race was a matter of debate.

••VIII. The Implications of Universalism••

• If the covenant of grace is universal, then it implies that all people are under the same terms and conditions.
• This raises questions about the nature of God's justice and truth.

••IX. The Reformed Position••

• The Reformed position (represented by the Synod of Dort) denies the universality of the covenant of grace.
• They believe that the covenant of grace is not universal, and that it is only available to those who are elect.

••X. Conclusion••

• The question of the extent of the covenant of grace is a matter of ongoing debate among theologians.
• The Reformed position denies the universality of the covenant of grace, while the Remonstrants and universalists believe that it is universal.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

• ••The Covenant of Grace••
	• Can be viewed in two ways: objective (external presentation) and subjective (internal reception)
	• Some argue it is universal in both respects, while others argue it is only universal in its objective presentation
• ••Reformed Opinion••
	• The Reformed hold to a particularity of the covenant, not universal with each and all
	• The covenant is particular only with the true elect members of Christ
• ••Two Ways to Regard the Covenant••
	• Internally: as to internal essence, answering to the internal calling and invisible church of the elect
	• Externally: as to external dispensation, answering to the external calling and visible church of the called
• ••External Presentation of the Covenant••
	• Regarded as to promulgation and presentation by the external call
	• Includes external benefits, such as preaching, sacraments, and participation in sacred things
• ••Internal Reception of the Covenant••
	• Regarded as to acceptation and conferring and reception of all federal benefits and internal communion with Christ by faith
	• Pertain only to the elect, who are really partakers of the covenant according to God's intention
• ••Universality of the Covenant••
	• The Reformed deny the covenant is universal, not only as to acceptation and bestowal, but as to promulgation or presentation
• ••Statement of the Question••
	• The question concerns the purpose and intention of God in sanctioning the covenant of grace
	• The question is not about the event and saving fruit of the covenant, but about God's intention
• ••Real Call to Faith••
	• The question is whether there is a real call through the works of nature by which all are summoned to the covenant of grace
	• The Reformed deny this, while their opponents assert it
• ••Salvation without Christ••
	• The question is not whether men can be saved without Christ, but whether there is a real call to the covenant of grace without Christ
• ••Implications of the Question••
	• The question has implications for the nature of the covenant, the call to faith, and the purpose of God in sanctioning the covenant

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

• ••The Question at Hand••
	• The question is whether God's blessings are saving and flow from the covenant of grace and the merit of Christ.
	• The opposing view affirms this, while the writer denies it.
• ••The Covenant of Grace••
	• The covenant of grace is particular, not universal.
	• This is established from its destination, procurement, and promises.
• ••Destination of the Covenant••
	• God's purpose is not to pity the whole human race, but to select and appoint a certain number for salvation.
	• This is not a universal will, but a particular will.
• ••Procurement of the Covenant••
	• The satisfaction of Christ, which procures the covenant, is particular and made only for those in whose place he was bound to substitute himself as surety.
	• These individuals were given by the Father to be redeemed as his seed, people, and body.
• ••Promises of the Covenant••
	• The promises of the covenant belong only to the elect and believers.
	• These promises are absolute, not conditional, and spring from the mere grace of God.
• ••Nature of the Promises••
	• The promises concern the end, means, and conditions themselves, excluding every condition.
	• The promise is not dependent on man's will, but is a gift of God.
• ••Conditional vs. Absolute Promise••
	• The promise is conditionally proposed and applied to individuals, but it does not depend on man's will.
	• The conditional promise is a consequence of an absolute promise.
• ••Objection to the Covenant••
	• The objection that the covenant of grace is either absolute or conditional is rejected.
	• The covenant of grace differs from the legal covenant, which promises life under a condition that it exacts from man, but does not effect in him.
• ••Nature of the Covenant of Grace••
	• The covenant of grace is not a legal covenant, but a testament given to the elect.
	• It is a gift of God, not dependent on man's will.
• ••Implications of the Covenant••
	• The covenant of grace is not entered into with those from whom God only wishes to demand a condition, but not to effect it in them.
	• This would be repugnant to the nature of the covenant of grace.

â€¢ ••The Decalogue and its Purpose••

	• The covenant of grace promises salvation and remission of sins, while the decalogue demands obedience and threatens death

â€¢ ••The Matter and Form of the External Economy••

â€¢ ••The End of the Economy••

â€¢ ••The Purpose of the Economy••
	• The purpose of the economy was to lead people to reject their own righteousness and embrace another's

â€¢ ••The Relationship to Christ••
	• The law was a schoolmaster to Christ, containing the shadow of things to come

â€¢ ••Two views on the old and new covenants••
	• Some theologians (e.g. Rollock, Piscator) distinguish between two covenants with different substances.
	• Others (e.g. Calvin, Martyr, Ursinus) take a broader view, seeing the covenant as embracing both the promise of grace and the law.

â€¢ ••Distinguishing between the old and new covenants••
	• The first view sees the old covenant as a covenant of works and the new as a covenant of faith.
	• The second view sees the old and new covenants as two aspects of the same covenant, distinguished by the way the promise of grace is dispensed.

â€¢ ••Lutheran view on the old and new covenants••
	• Lutherans distinguish between the old and new covenants in substance, excluding the promise of grace from the old covenant.
	• They accuse other theologians of error in describing the nature of the old covenant.

â€¢ ••Brochmann's view on the old covenant••
	• Brochmann defines the old covenant as a legal covenant made with the Israelites under Moses.
	• He argues that the question is whether the old covenant is the same in substance as the new covenant.

â€¢ ••Granting a difference between the old and new covenants••
	• The old covenant and the Mosaic covenant are distinct in substance from the new covenant.
	• However, this difference is only in the manner of dispensation, not in the substance of the covenant.

â€¢ ••The old covenant as a covenant of grace••
	• The old covenant was made with the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who acted out of gratuitous adoption and love.
	• This suggests that the old covenant was not just a legal covenant, but also an evangelical one.

â€¢ ••The threefold matter of the old covenant••
	• The old covenant had a threefold matter: doctrine, worship, and polity.
	• This matter was both legal and evangelical, containing promises of Christ and his grace.

â€¢ ••The twofold form of the old covenant••
	• The old covenant had an external form, which was a legal obligation to keep the law.
	• This form was subordinate to the doctrine, worship, and polity of the covenant.

â€¢ ••The relationship between the old and new covenants••
	• The old covenant is opposed to the new covenant in terms of law and Moses vs. grace and Christ.
	• However, the old covenant is not entirely distinct from the new covenant, but rather is a precursor to it.

â€¢ ••The controversy over the old and new covenants••
	• The controversy centers on the nature of the old covenant and whether it is the same in substance as the new covenant.
	• The Lutherans take a stricter view, excluding the promise of grace from the old covenant, while other theologians take a broader view.

	• In civil law, a distinction is made between a fidejussor (one who gives security) and an expromissor (one who takes on another's obligation)

• ••The nature of Christ's suretyship••
	• Christ's suretyship is a perfectly absolute and immutable will to substitute himself for the elect and make satisfaction for their sins.
	• This implies a real transference of debts to Christ and the full deliverance and immunity of those for whom he agreed.
• ••Fidejussio vs. Expromissio••
	• Fidejussio is a promise to pay a debt, but the principal debtor remains obligated and can still be applied to before the surety.
	• Expromissio is a true transference of debt, where the surety takes on the obligation and the original debtor is no longer bound.
• ••Christ's role as expromissor••
	• Christ took on the obligation of the elect's sins and became the one from whom payment was demanded.
	• The elect were freed from personal obligation and no longer bound to pay for themselves.
• ••The crime of the Jews••
	• The Jews were guilty of trying to establish their own righteousness in addition to the acquired righteousness of God.
	• This was a crime of despising the Messiah and trying to add to God's righteousness.

	• Scripture testifies that God laid the iniquity of us all on Christ and that his stripes healed us (Is. 53:5, 6).
	• This implies a true transference of debt and liberation of the guilty.
• ••The difference between demanding a debt and laying iniquities on Christ••
	• Demanding a debt from Christ is different from laying iniquities on him and imputing them to him.
	• A debt can be imputed to the surety long before it is demanded for present payment.
• ••Isaiah's testimony••

	• Rather, sins were exacted of Christ because they had already been imputed to him as surety in the counsel of God.

••VII. The Nature of the Covenant of Grace as Proof••

• The text argues that the nature of the covenant of grace is proof that the fathers were not under guilt.
	• The covenant implies the communion of the covenanted with God and the communication of all spiritual goods required for full felicity.

••VIII. The Implications of the Covenant of Grace••

• The text discusses the implications of the covenant of grace for the fathers.
	• The covenant implies that the fathers were received into it and therefore freed from the curse of the law and the guilt of sin.

••IX. The Relationship between Guilt and Justification••

• The text discusses the relationship between guilt and justification.
	• The authors argue that reconciliation cannot consist with wrath, blessing with cursing, and a state of justification with the guilt of sin.

••X. The Conclusion••

• The text concludes that the fathers were not under guilt and that the suretyship of Christ and the nature of the covenant of grace are proof of this.

••I. Three Covenants••

• The Reformed tradition holds that there are three covenants:
	• The first natural covenant with Adam in the earthly paradise
	• The second covenant of grace with fallen men in the gospel
	• The third, the legal covenant, confirmed through Moses with the Israelites on Mount Sinai

••II. Nature of the Legal Covenant••

• The legal covenant is considered "ancient" or "subservient" because it was made to prepare the Israelites for the covenant of grace
• It was made to restrain them from wickedness and to inflame them with a desire for the promise and the gospel covenant

••III. Comparison with the Covenant of Nature••

• The legal covenant agrees with the covenant of nature in:
	• Contracting parties (God and man)
	• Stipulation (obedience to the law)
	• Promise (a happy life in Canaan)
• The legal covenant differs from the covenant of nature in:
	• Object (the Israelites alone, not all men)
	• Promise (a happy life in Canaan, not life in the earthly paradise)
	• Stipulation (including ceremonies, not just obedience to the law of nature)
	• Foundation (based on the election of the Israelite people and their deliverance from Egypt, not creation and general conservation)
	• End (preparation for Christ, not the exaction of duty from man)
	• Mediator (Moses, not none)

••IV. Comparison with the Covenant of Grace••

• The legal covenant agrees with the covenant of grace in:
	• Author (God)
	• Object (man, a sinner)
	• Mediator (Moses, not Christ)
	• End (to show sin and lead to Christ)
• The legal covenant differs from the covenant of grace in:
	• Relation (God is considered simply as rebuking sin and approving righteousness alone)
	• Stipulation (do this and live, not believe and thou shalt be saved)
	• Mediator (Moses, not Christ)
	• Object (man stupefied by sin, not the conscience terrified by sin)
	• Effects (bondage, not liberty)

••V. Common Opinion of the Orthodox Concerning the Three Fold Covenant••

• The Reformed tradition recognizes only two covenants:
	• The covenant of works, which promises life to the doer
	• The covenant of grace, which promises salvation to believers
• The Sinaitic covenant is considered a new economy of the covenant of grace, not a third covenant.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. The Mystery of the Incarnation••

• The mystery of the incarnation is described in Scripture and among the ancients using various words, including:
	• PhanerÅsis en sarki ("manifestation in the flesh")
	• SÅmatos kasartismos ("adaptation" or "preparation of a body")
	• KenÅsis ("emptying" and assumption of the form of a servant)
	• EpilÄ“psis ("taking on" of the seed of Abraham)
	• Epiphaneia ("appearing")

••II. The Necessity of the Incarnation••

• The necessity of the incarnation is a topic of debate and can be broken down into three questions:
	• Would it have been necessary for the Son of God to become incarnate even if man had not sinned?
	• Was it necessary for the Son of God to become incarnate for us, and was there no other mode of salvation possible with God?
	• Was it necessary for our own mediator to be God-man (theanthrÅpon)?

••III. First Proposition: The Incarnation was not Necessary except on Account of Sin••

• The first proposition is that the incarnation was not necessary except on account of sin.
• This is opposed to the views of some Scholastics, such as Alexander of Hales, Occam, and Bonaventure, who asserted that the incarnation was necessary regardless of sin.
• Osiander, a Lutheran, also held this view, and it has been revived by the Socinians in recent times.

••IV. Proof from Scripture••

• The necessity of the incarnation is proven from Scripture, which consistently presents the end of Christ's advent and incarnation as the salvation of his people from sin.
• This is seen in:
	• The promise of salvation after the fall (Gen. 3:15)
	• The shadowing forth of salvation through sacrifices for the expiation of sins (Old Testament)
	• The angel's confirmation in the New Testament (Mt. 1:21)
	• The statements of Zachariah (Lk. 1:67ff), Simeon (Lk. 2:30, 34), John the Baptist (Jn. 1:29), Christ himself (Mt. 9:13; 20:28), the apostles, Paul (Gal. 4:4, 5; 1 Tim. 1:15; Heb. 2:14), and John (1 Jn. 2:1, 2; 3:8)

••V. Proof from Christ's Office••

• Christ's office is occupied only with sinners, and his work is focused on saving them from sin.
• This is seen in:
	• His prophetic office, where he teaches sinners and calls them to faith and repentance (Is. 61:1, 2; Mt. 9:13)
	• His priestly office, where he gives himself as a ransom for sins (1 Tim. 2:6; Is. 53:10; 1 Jn. 2:2) and prays for transgressors (Is. 53:12; Jn. 17)
	• His kingly office, where he governs his people and defends them against the Devil, the world, and the flesh (Mt. 9:13)

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••The Incarnation of the Trinity••
	• The question is not whether the Trinity can be incarnate, but which person of the Trinity took on human form.
	• The text asserts that the second person of the Trinity, the Son, took on human form.

â€¢ ••Scriptural Evidence••
	• The Bible ascribes the incarnation to the Son alone, not to the Father or the Holy Spirit.
	• The Son is said to have been made flesh (John 1:14), taken on the form of a servant (Philippians 2:6-7), and participated in flesh and blood (Hebrews 2:14-15).

â€¢ ••The Father's Incapability••
	• The Father could not be incarnate, as he is the first person of the Trinity and could not be sent by anyone or act as mediator.
	• The Father's incarnation would also create a problem of two sons, one by eternal generation and one by incarnation in time.

â€¢ ••The Holy Spirit's Incapability••
	• The Holy Spirit could not be incarnate, as he is to be sent by the Mediator to the church (John 16:7).
	• The Holy Spirit could not send himself, creating a paradox.

â€¢ ••The Son's Fitness for Incarnation••
	• The Son alone could rightly undertake the function of incarnation.
	• The Son is the mediator between God and men, and it was fitting that he who was the Son by nature should make us adoptive sons by grace.

â€¢ ••The Son's Role in Reconciliation••
	• The Son was the well-beloved Son of the Father, in whom he was well pleased (Matthew 3:17).
	• The Son was the one who recreated and reformed us after his image in the second creation.

â€¢ ••The Incarnation of the Divine Nature••
	• Although the divine nature may be said to have been incarnate in the Son, it does not follow that the whole Trinity became incarnate.
	• The incarnation is a work terminating on the person, not on the nature.

â€¢ ••The Distinction between Persons••
	• The incarnation of one person does not hinder the relation between the persons themselves.
	• The distinction between persons is not abolished, and one person can be distinguished from the others.

â€¢ ••The Incarnation in Relation to the Essence••
	• The incarnation of one person does not hinder the relation between the person and the essence.
	• The distinction between persons is not abolished, and one person can be incarnate without the others.

â€¢ ••Interpretation of Scripture••
	• When Scripture ascribes incarnation to God, it must be understood of the divine nature relative to the characteristic of the Son.
	• The fathers hold that the divine nature is incarnate in one of the hypostases, specifically in the hypostasis of the Word.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••The Essence of God••
	• The essence of God is simple and cannot be divided into parts.
	• However, it is one way in the Father, another way in the Son, and another way in the Holy Spirit.

â€¢ ••The Human Nature of Christ••
	• The human nature of Christ was assumed according to the one mode of subsisting that constitutes the one person of the Trinity.
	• It could not be assumed according to the other modes that constitute the remaining persons of the Trinity.

â€¢ ••The Intuitive Vision and Hypostatical Union••
	• There is a difference between the intuitive vision in the blessed and the hypostatical union in Christ.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. The Nature of Christ's Incarnation••

• The Son of God took on human nature to perform the necessary work of redemption.
	• This was not a conversion or transmutation, but an assumption and sustentation of human nature.

••II. The Composition of the God-Man••

• The term "theanthrÅpou" (God-man) refers to the composition of the divine and human natures in one person.
	• This is not a physical or accidental composition, but a hyperphysical and extraordinary one.
	• The divine nature assumes and perfects the human nature, rather than the other way around.

••III. The Two Unions in Christ••

• There are two unions in Christ: a personal union of the divine and human natures, and a natural union of the soul and body.
	• The personal union is hyperphysical and inseparable, while the natural union is physical and separable.

••IV. The Charge of Nestorianism••

• Some Lutherans falsely charge that the author holds a twofold hypostatical union in Christ, which is a form of Nestorianism.
	• However, the author argues that the two unions are distinct and differ in kind, terminus, subject, and adjuncts.

••V. The Question of Incarnation••

• The question remains whether the Son of God truly joined with himself in unity of person, not just a human nature.
	• The Socinians deny this, but the author affirms it.

••VI. The Hypostatical Union••

• The hypostatical union is proved from John 1:14, which says "the word was made flesh".
	• This passage shows a distinct union of two extremes: the Word (divine person) and flesh (human nature).

••VII. The Nature of the Union••

• The union is not a conversion or change, but an assumption and sustentation of human nature.
	• The Son of God remains the same in himself, true and eternal God, while taking on human nature.

••VIII. The Impious Gloss of Socinus••

• Socinus corrupts the passage in John 1:14 by suggesting that the verb "egeneto" means "was" rather than "was made".
	• This gloss is impious and contradicts the common interpretation of the passage.

••IX. The Importance of the Hypostatical Union••

• The hypostatical union is essential to understanding the nature of Christ's incarnation.
	• It shows that the Son of God truly joined with himself in unity of person, not just a human nature.

••X. The Affirmation of the Hypostatical Union••

• The author affirms the hypostatical union, which is proved from John 1:14.
	• This union is essential to understanding the nature of Christ's incarnation and his role as Mediator.

â€¢ ••Understanding the Hypostatic Union••
	• The hypostatic union is a unique and singular relationship between two natures (divine and human) in Christ.
	• It is not a disparate relationship, but rather an identical one, where the subject and predicate designate the same person in different respects.

â€¢ ••Synonymical and Tropical Predication••
	• The hypostatic union can be described as synonymical because the subject and predicate are taken concretely for the unity of person.
	• It is also tropical because the subject and predicate designate the same person in different respects (deity and humanity).

â€¢ ••Communication of the Hypostasis••
	• The communication of the hypostasis of the Logos (Logos made flesh) can be understood in three ways:
		- Effectively: forming another hypostasis (heretical)
		- Transitively: formally transferring the hypostasis into the flesh (heretical)
		- Assumptively: assuming flesh into the same hypostasis and uniting it to himself (true and orthodox)

â€¢ ••Personal Properties••
	• A personal property is incommunicable and cannot be formally transferred from one person to another.

â€¢ ••Contradictions and Respect••
	• Contradictions cannot agree in the same subject, manner, and respect.
	• However, Christ can be described as both dependent and independent, finite and infinite, in different respects.

â€¢ ••Infinite Distance••
	• A local infinite distance can hinder the union of two natures, but not an infinite distance of perfection (such as exists between human and divine natures).

â€¢ ••Assumption of Human Nature••
	• If the Son of God assumed our nature, nothing was added to him intrinsically to perfect his nature.
	• Only something was added extrinsically for the work of redemption.

â€¢ ••Transmutation and Assumption••
	• Someone who is made what they were not before is changed transmutatively.
	• However, someone who is only made what they were not before is changed assumptively.

â€¢ ••Hypostatical Union••
	• The hypostatical union of the two natures in Christ is such that neither the person is divided nor the natures are confounded.

â€¢ ••Avoiding Heresies••
	• Two rocks are to be shunned about the hypostatical union: Nestorianism and Eutychianism.

••IV. Mary as Mother of God••

• Mary is rightly called the Mother of God in the concrete and specific sense
• She brought forth the person of Christ, who is also God
• This title was perverted by superstitious men into an occasion of idolatry

••V. Eutychianism••

• Eutychianism is a heresy that confounds the two natures of Christ into one
• It is opposed to Nestorianism, which divides the person of Christ into two

••VI. Reasons against Eutychianism••

• The opposition of the two natures in Christ is frequent in Scripture
• Two wills are ascribed to Christ, which could not be if there were not two natures
• Contraries are ascribed to Christ, which could not be if there were not two natures

••VII. Distinction of Natures••

• The distinction of natures is well denoted, but not the division of the person
• The humanity of Christ is in the temple of the divinity, but not in the same sense as a physical temple

••VIII. Hypostatical Union••

• The hypostatical union is the union of the two natures in Christ
• It is a union without change or confusion

••IX. Properties and Conditions••

• Each nature retains its own properties and conditions
• The natures are not confounded or mixed with each other

••X. Scripture and Tradition••

• The opposition of the two natures in Christ is frequent in Scripture
• The title Mother of God was perverted by superstitious men, but the lawful use of the name remains

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Introduction••

• The Catholic Church believes in the communication of attributes between God and man in Christ.
• This means that properties of God can be attributed to Christ, and properties of Christ can be attributed to God.

••II. Luther's Disagreement••

• Luther disagreed with the Catholic Church's view on the communication of attributes.
• He believed that properties should only be attributed to Christ in the concrete, not in the abstract.

••III. Definition of Communication of Attributes••

• The communication of attributes refers to the idea that properties of one nature can be attributed to another nature.
• This can be seen in phrases such as "This man created the world" and "This God suffered".

••IV. Paul Eberus' Agreement••

• Paul Eberus, a Wittenberg divine, agreed with Luther's view on the communication of attributes.
• He believed that properties of one nature cannot be attributed to another nature in the abstract.

••V. The Question at Hand••

• The question is not whether the properties of the human nature were communicated to the divine nature.
• The question is whether only certain properties of the divine nature were communicated to the human nature.

••VI. Denial of Communication of Attributes••

• The author denies that only certain properties of the divine nature were communicated to the human nature.
• They argue that there is no communication of attributes in the abstract.

••VII. Reasons for Denial••

• The divine essence cannot be communicated to a creature.
• If the divine essence were communicated, it would be contradictory for a created thing to be both created and uncreated.

••VIII. Further Reasons••

• Properties are not communicated.
• If properties were communicated, they would cease to be proper and become common to the nature to which they are communicated.

••IX. Conclusion••

• The communication of attributes in the abstract is not possible.
• The properties of one nature cannot be attributed to another nature in the abstract.

••X. Implications••

• The diversity of the human nature of Christ from other created things does not favor the communication of attributes.
• The communication of attributes cannot have a place in the nature of Christ.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Christ's Nature and Attributes••

• The nature of Christ's majesty is a topic of debate:
	• Some argue that it refers to the excellence of the flesh, but not a communication of divine properties.
	• Others argue that it refers to the deity itself, which would imply a communication of divine properties to the flesh.

••II. Christ's Being••

• Some argue that Christ has a twofold being:
	• Local, in a certain space, and illocal, everywhere from the beginning of the incarnation.
	• However, this is absurd because it implies a temporal and not-temporal (or eternal) being, which is not maintained.
	• Locality and illocality are contradictories that cannot belong to the same thing.

••III. Christ's Omnipresence••

• Some argue that Christ's deity is omnipresent by itself, while his humanity is only present in a limited sense:
	• However, this distinction is false because it takes away the subject itself (Christ) and implies that omnipresence belongs to the body of Christ.
	• In divine things, possession or proprietorship cannot be distinguished from use.

••IV. Examples of Communication of Properties••

• The examples of the soul and fire communicating properties to the body or iron do not favor the communication of properties:
	• The life produced in the body by the soul is not a property of the soul, but an effect.
	• The power of shining and burning in the heated iron is not in the iron, but in the fire.

••V. The Two-Fold State of Christ••

• Christ's office as Mediator is bound to a twofold state:
	• A state of humiliation and a state of exaltation.
	• This is demonstrated by the oracles of the Old Testament, which foretell both the suffering and glory of Christ.

••VI. The State of Humiliation••

• The state of humiliation refers to Christ's suffering and death:
	• This is demonstrated by the Old Testament oracles, which foretell Christ's suffering and death.

••VII. The State of Exaltation••

• The state of exaltation refers to Christ's glory and triumph:
	• This is demonstrated by the Old Testament oracles, which foretell Christ's glory and triumph.

••VIII. The Relationship between the Two States••

• The two states are not mutually exclusive, but rather complementary:
	• Christ's humiliation is necessary for his exaltation.
	• Christ's exaltation is the goal of his humiliation.

••IX. The Implications of the Two-Fold State••

• The two-fold state of Christ has implications for our understanding of his person and office:
	• It emphasizes the importance of Christ's suffering and death for our salvation.
	• It highlights the glory and triumph of Christ, which is the goal of his humiliation.

••X. Conclusion••

• The two-fold state of Christ is a fundamental aspect of his person and office:
	• It is demonstrated by the Old Testament oracles and is essential for our understanding of Christ's mission and purpose.

••I. The Nature of Christ's Sufferings and Glory••

• The Messiah was made lower than the angels through suffering, but was also crowned with glory and honor.
	• This is depicted in Psalm 110:7, where Christ is said to drink from the brook of suffering and lift up his head in glory.
	• The brook represents the multitude, weight, and short continuance of Christ's sufferings.

••II. The Communion of Sufferings••

• Christ's sufferings were a communion of sufferings, borne by him in his journey through life.
	• This is denoted by the idea of drinking from the brook, which represents the communion of sufferings.

••III. The Glory that Followed Sufferings••

• The glory that followed Christ's sufferings was ordained by God and necessary for our salvation.
	• This is depicted in Luke 24:26 and Philippians 2:9, where Christ's glory is said to follow his sufferings.

••IV. Christ as the Cornerstone••

• Christ is compared to a stone and a foundation, rejected by the scribes and priests, but constituted by God as the head of the church and a cornerstone.
	• This is depicted in Psalm 118:22, Isaiah 28:16, and 1 Corinthians 3:10.

••V. The Necessity of Christ's Sufferings and Glory••

• The necessity of Christ's sufferings and glory is evinced on the part of God, Christ, and humanity.
	• On the part of God, satisfaction was to be made to offended justice, and the gifts of grace were to be poured out upon men.

••VI. The Necessity on the Part of Christ••

• Christ's necessity is evinced on the part of his twofold relation as surety and head.
	• As surety, he must act for us with God by doing and suffering all that we owed.
	• As head, he must act in the name of God towards us, imparting the benefits of the covenant and drawing us into communion with him.

••VII. The Necessity on the Part of Humanity••

• Humanity is pressed by two evils brought upon us by sin: guilt in the sight of God and pollution in ourselves.
	• Guilt could not be taken away except by the blood of Christ, which was a ransom for our souls.
	• Pollution could not be washed away except by the grace of the Spirit, who was the fruit of Christ's exaltation.

••VIII. The Necessity on the Part of Salvation••

• Two things were required for the fruition of salvation: acquisition and application.
	• Acquisition refers to the satisfaction of justice and the pouring out of the gifts of grace.
	• Application refers to the imparting of the benefits of the covenant and the drawing of humanity into communion with Christ.

••IX. The Role of the Prophets••

• The prophets diligently inquired of the sufferings and glory that should follow.
	• This is depicted in 1 Peter 1:10-11, where the prophets are said to have inquired of the sufferings and glory.

••X. The Fulfillment of the Oracles••

• The New Testament sets forth the fulfillment of the oracles in various passages.
	• This includes Philippians 2:7-9, 2 Corinthians 13:4, 1 Corinthians 15:3-4, Hebrews 2:9, 1 Peter 3:18, and 1 Timothy 3:16.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Humiliation and Exaltation••

• The humiliation of Christ was necessary for his acquisition, as it could not be acquired except through death.
	• He merited for us a right to life through his righteousness.
	• He actually conferred life upon us through his power.
• The exaltation of Christ was necessary for his application, as it could not be applied except through the efficacy of life.
	• He accomplished the work given to him by the Father in both humiliation and exaltation.

••II. Nature of Humiliation and Exaltation••

• Humiliation and exaltation are ascribed to Christ's person, but with a great difference.
	• To the human nature, humiliation and exaltation are real depression and exaltation.
	• To the divine nature, humiliation and exaltation are concealment and manifestation, relative to the flesh as a veil.

••III. Emptying and Exaltation••

• Emptying belongs to the human nature, as Christ took up our weaknesses and suffered and died.
	• Exaltation belongs to the human nature, as Christ rose and laid aside all weaknesses and assumed a glory it had not before.
• Emptying is ascribed to the divine nature as concealment and restraining of glory and majesty under the form of a servant.
	• Exaltation is ascribed to the divine nature as manifestation and unfolding of its glory.

••IV. Concealment and Manifestation••

• The Son of God emptied himself by a concealment of his deity under the servile form.
	• He became poor, not by a loss of heavenly riches, but by a hiding of them under the weak and needy flesh.
• The divine nature was not lessened in humiliation, nor increased in exaltation.

••V. Dignity of the Christian Era••

• The nativity of Christ is the chief of all epochs and the origin of the Christian people.
	• All preceding times look to it as their happy and prosperous center, and all posterior times flow from it.

••VI. Beginning of the Christian Era••

• The Christian era began with the nativity of Christ.
	• The dignity of the Christian era is so great that it is the origin of the Christian people and the birthday of the head is the birthday of the body.

••VII. Use of the Christian Era••

• Although the excellence and utility of the Christian era are great, Christians have only lately thought of settling and using it.
	• Before the seventh century, we do not read of the Lord's birthday being applied to the designation of any business either civil or ecclesiastical.

••VIII. Justinian's Use of the Christian Era••

• Justinian, who reigned 500 years after Christ, was the first to use the Lord's birthday in a civil context.
	• He applied it to the designation of a business, but it was not widely used until later.

••IX. Significance of the Christian Era••

• The Christian era is significant because it marks the beginning of a new era in human history.
	• It is a time of great change and transformation, as the world is redeemed through Christ.

••X. Celebration of the Christian Era••

• The Christian era is celebrated through the feast of the nativity, which is a time of great joy and celebration.
	• It is a time to reflect on the significance of Christ's birth and its impact on human history.

••I. Faith in Christ••

	• It's not a fiducial apprehension of God's mercy, which is unique to sinners.

• Hope is also ascribed to Christ, but with limitations.
	• The perfection of hope as certainty is attributed to Christ.
	• However, the imperfection of hope as a still obscure expectation is not attributed to Christ.

••III. Christ's Knowledge and Hope••

• Although Christ's soul rejoiced in happiness and enjoyed God from the beginning, he didn't have fullness of happiness.
	• He obtained fullness of happiness after his resurrection and ascension.
	• This allowed him to believe in God and hope for the promised glory.

••IV. The Nature of Christ's Knowledge••

• The Scholastics divide Christ's knowledge into three types: blessed, infused, and acquired.
	• Blessed knowledge is seeing God according to essence.
	• Infused knowledge is knowing heavenly things through a supernatural habit.
	• Acquired knowledge is understanding things through reason and nature.

••V. Christ's Knowledge on Earth••

• Christ's knowledge on earth is twofold: infused and acquired.
	• Infused knowledge is received through the Holy Spirit's sanctifying gifts.
	• Acquired knowledge is gained through ratiocination and experience.

• The question is not about Christ's knowledge in glory, but about his knowledge on earth.

• The question is whether Christ's soul was imputed with knowledge from the beginning.

••VIII. Christ's Knowledge and Experience••

• Christ gained acquired knowledge through ratiocination and experience.

••IX. Christ's Knowledge and Sin••

• Christ did not labor under gross ignorance or sin.

• The dispute is about the nature and extent of Christ's knowledge on earth.

â€¢ ••Dignity and Efficacy of Christ's Sacrifice••

â€¢ ••Communion of Attributes in Christ••

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Christ as Mediator••

• Christ is the Mediator between God and men
	• He is the God-man, with both divine and human natures
	• He is the only one who can unite God and men in a mystical union of will and operations

••II. Requirements for a Mediator••

• A mediator must be equally distant and proximate to both parties
• Christ meets this requirement as the God-man, approaching God and receding from men, and approaching men and receding from God

••III. Christ's Mediation••

• Christ's mediation is not just as God, but as God manifest in the flesh
• He is a true peacemaker, who can reconcile us to God by an infinite price

••IV. Moses as Mediator••

• Moses was only a mere man, and not a true peacemaker
• Christ's mediation is not just a repetition of Moses' office, but a new and higher level of mediation

••V. Christ's Divinity and Mediation••

• Christ's divinity does not make him inferior to the Father
• His consubstantiality with the Father is not denied, but rather distinguished from the Father's essence

••VI. Christ and Angels••

• Theologians vary in their opinions on whether Christ is the Mediator of angels
• Some think Christ can be called the Mediator of angels, but only of their conservation and confirmation, not of their redemption

••VII. Christ as Creator and Conservator••

• Christ is the Creator and Conservator of all things, including angels
• Angels were confirmed through a new grace of God, not as Mediator, but as Creator and Conservator

••VIII. Reasons for Denying Christ as Mediator of Angels••

• The Scriptures call Christ the Mediator between God and men, but never between angels
• There is no need of a Mediator where there is no discord

••IX. Christ's Role as Mediator••

• Christ's role as Mediator is not just to reconcile men to God, but to reconcile God to men
• He is the only one who can unite God and men in a mystical union of will and operations

••X. Conclusion••

• Christ is not the Mediator of angels, but rather the Creator and Conservator of all things, including angels.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Christ's Relationship with Angels••

• Christ is not joined with angels, but with men
	• Reason: Christ took on the seed of Abraham, not angels
	• Purpose: to save men, not angels

••II. Christ as Mediator••

• Christ is the Mediator of those for whom he is the propitiation
	• This does not pertain to angels

	• Not of angels, who are distinguished from the church

	• Angels are under him as their Lord, whom they worship

	• This is diffused by the regenerating Spirit of Christ upon men alone, redeemed by the blood of Christ

	• God covenanted to reward them irrespective of their desert

••VII. Grace and Redemption••

• All medicinal and liberating grace flows from the Mediator in the order of redemption
	• There is not the same will for confirming and conserving grace, which belongs to the order of creation

••IX. The Papist View of Mediation••

	• They conflate to us the favor of God by their prayers and merits

••X. The Question of Mediation••

• The question is whether besides Christ, the saints can properly be called our mediators with God
	• This involves mediation properly so called, by which one intercedes by their own virtue and merits.

	• 3. Calling: Christ was consecrated to enter into his office, involving unction and inauguration.

	• God selected Christ as a Mediator to reconcile the elect.
	• Referred to in 1 Pet. 1:20, Acts 2:23, and Rev. 13:8.

â€¢ ••Mission••
	• Christ was promised under the Old Testament and predicted in various prophecies.
	• He was sent into the world to take on human nature and accomplish the work of salvation.

â€¢ ••Calling••
	• Involves unction and inauguration.
	• Christ was consecrated to enter into his office, as referred to in Is. 42:6 and Ps. 110:4.

â€¢ ••Vocation••
	• Embraces two parts: unction and inauguration.
	• unction: the name "Messiah" and "Christ" were given to Christ.

â€¢ ••The Names of Christ••
	• Derived from unction.
	• "Messiah" and "Christ" were peculiar to our Redeemer.

â€¢ ••Consecration to Office••
	• Belongs to the person of Christ, even according to his divine nature

â€¢ ••Bestowal of Graces and Gifts••

â€¢ ••Kingly Function••

â€¢ ••Manner of Christ's Threefold Office••
	• Christ sustained the three functions conjointly, not separately
	• Christ's three functions were united in him due to his supreme perfection

â€¢ ••Christ's Unique Office••
	• Christ alone perfectly fulfilled the three functions of the mediatorial office
	• Christ's office is superior and eternal, as demonstrated by his oath (Ps. 110:4)
