Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Introduction to the Gospel••

• The Gospel is called the "word of the cross" and the "troph y of the king"
	• It is the mystery of salvation
	• It is the law of the prophet, the scepter of the king, and the sword of the priest

••II. The Spirit and the Gospel••

• The Spirit is the effect of prophecy
• The Spirit is a fruit of the priesthood
• The Spirit is a gift of the king

••III. The Question of Christ's Ascension••

• The question is: Was Christ caught up into heaven before beginning his public ministry?
• The Socinians (a group of theologians) answer yes, but the orthodox reject this view

••IV. The Socinian View••

• The Socinians believe Christ was uninstructed in his doctrine until he was 30 years old
• They believe Christ was caught up into heaven to be taught by God
• They think this event occurred during Christ's 40-day fast in the desert

••V. The Orthodox View••

• The orthodox reject the Socinian view as purely fictitious and not found in Scripture
• They recognize no other descent from heaven in Christ's days of flesh than his incarnation

••VI. Reasons for the Orthodox View••

• The silence of Scripture, which mentions no such event
• The passages adduced by the Socinians have a different reference
• The evangelists would have mentioned such an event if it occurred

••VII. Christ's Knowledge of Mysteries••

• Christ did not need a translation to gain knowledge of mysteries
• He was the Word of the Father and beheld all his secrets
• He had knowledge of mysteries according to his human nature as well

••VIII. The Incarnation••

• The orthodox view recognizes no other descent from heaven in Christ's days of flesh than his incarnation
• The incarnation is a metaphorical descent from heaven

••IX. The Resurrection and Transfiguration••

• The resurrection and transfiguration are events that occurred when no one was present
• The evangelists would have mentioned such events if they occurred

••X. Conclusion••

• The orthodox view is that Christ did not need a translation to heaven to gain knowledge of mysteries
• The Socinian view is rejected as purely fictitious and not found in Scripture.

Here are 10 concise bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Christ's Ascension and Descent••

• Christ's ascension and descent are not to be understood literally
	• He is not said to have ascended to heaven in the sense of his humanity
	• His descent refers to his manifestation in the flesh

••II. Mystical Ascent••

• Christ's mystical ascent refers to his sublime knowledge of heavenly mysteries
	• He penetrates the secret of heaven and understands divine counsels
	• This is not to be understood as a physical ascent, but rather a spiritual one

••III. No One Knows Heavenly Things••

• Only Christ knows heavenly things and is acquainted with divine counsel
	• This is because he is the one who has revealed mysteries to humanity

••IV. Christ's Descent from Heaven••

• Christ's descent from heaven refers to his manifestation in the flesh
	• It is not a physical descent, but rather a spiritual one
	• He comes forth from the Father to work among humanity

••V. Christ's Ascension after Resurrection••

• Christ's ascension after resurrection refers to his divinity, not his humanity
	• He ascends to where the Word (Logos) was before, with God

••VI. Christ's Knowledge of the Father••

• Christ's knowledge of the Father is not due to being caught up into heaven
	• He has intimate communion with the Father and speaks what he heard

••VII. Christ's Teaching and Revelation••

• Christ's teaching and revelation are not due to being carried up into heaven
	• He is taught of God in a far more excellent manner due to his hypostatical union

••VIII. Christ's Superiority••

• Christ is not inferior to Moses and Paul, who were carried up into heaven
	• He is superior because of his hypostatical union and intimate communion with the Father

••IX. Christ's Teaching and Wisdom••

• Christ's teaching and wisdom are not due to being carried up into heaven
	• He is sufficient for his office and has treasures of wisdom and knowledge laid up in him

••X. Christ's Preeminence••

• Christ is preeminent over all, including Moses and Paul
	• He is the one who has revealed mysteries to humanity and has intimate knowledge of the Father

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Introduction••

• The priestly dignity of Christ is the basis of all the benefits he purchased by his death.
• The text will discuss the priesthood of Christ and its double grade (satisfaction and intercession).

••II. The Priesthood of Christ••

• The priesthood of Christ is the function of the mediatorial office.
• He performs two things with God: offering himself as a victim for sinners and interceding for them always with the Father.
• The excellence of this function is evident from the fact that no mystery was predicted by clearer prophecies or adumbrated by more frequent types.

••III. Controversy with Socinians••

• The Socinians deny that Christ's priesthood is proper, but rather figurative and analogical.
• They argue that Christ's death was not a sacrifice, but a preparation for a sacrifice to be offered in heaven.
• They also argue that no expiation of sin was made by any sacrifice on earth, but rather in heaven.

••IV. Orthodox View••

• The orthodox view affirms that Christ is a real Priest and his priesthood is properly so called.
• The priesthood is formally distinguished from the kingship, with the former consisting in the offering of sacrifice and intercession, and the latter in government and defense of the people.

••V. Proof that Christ was a True Priest••

• Christ is frequently called a Priest in Scripture (e.g. Ps. 110:4; Heb. 5:5).
• He is reckoned among priests properly so called (Heb. 5:1) and appointed to offer gifts and do what ought to be done with God.
• His priesthood is distinguished from the Levitical priesthood, but this does not imply that it is improper or figurative.

••VI. Priestly Acts Ascribed to Christ••

• All priestly acts are ascribed to Christ, including oblation and intercession (Heb. 7:27; 9:24; 10:7).
• He was adumbrated by various types, both common and peculiar to the Levitical priesthood.

••VII. Christ's Priesthood is Proper and Perfect••

• Christ's priesthood is not inferior to the Levitical priesthood, but rather superior and more excellent.
• It is therefore proper and perfect, just as the priesthood of Melchizedek was not inferior to the Levitical priesthood.

••VIII. Christ's Sacrifice was a True Sacrifice••

• Christ's death was a true sacrifice, offered on earth for the expiation of sin.
• It was not a preparation for a sacrifice to be offered in heaven, but rather the actual sacrifice that accomplished our redemption.

••IX. Christ's Intercession is Ongoing••

• Christ's intercession is not limited to his death, but is an ongoing function of his priesthood.
• He continues to intercede for us with the Father, offering himself as a victim for our sins.

••X. Conclusion••

• The priesthood of Christ is a central aspect of his mediatorial office.
• It is a proper and perfect priesthood, distinguished from the Levitical priesthood and superior to it.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Introduction to Satisfaction••

• The doctrine of satisfaction is essential to understanding the atonement of Christ
• God's justice requires a satisfaction for sin, which cannot be remitted without it

••II. Principles for Understanding Satisfaction••

• The doctrine of satisfaction can be understood by considering:
	• Sin, for which a satisfaction is required
	• The satisfaction itself that is to be made
	• God, to whom the satisfaction is to be rendered
	• Christ, by whom satisfaction is made

••III. Sin and Satisfaction••

• Sin can be viewed in three ways:
	• As a debt to be paid to divine justice
	• As an enmity that makes God hate us
	• As a crime that makes us worthy of punishment
• Three things are required for redemption:
	• Payment of the debt contracted by sin
	• Appeasement of divine hatred and wrath
	• Expiation of guilt

••IV. Nature of Satisfaction••

• Satisfaction involves:
	• Payment of the debt
	• Appeasement of divine wrath
	• Expiation of guilt
• The principal relation of satisfaction is to the punishment imposed by the supreme Judge

••V. Types of Payment••

• There are two types of payment:
	• One that sets the debtor free by paying the exact amount owed
	• One that is not sufficient to liberate the debtor, but is accepted as a satisfaction

••VI. Pecuniary and Penal Debt••

• In a pecuniary debt, payment frees the debtor
• In a penal debt, the case is different because the obligation regards not only what is paid, but also the person who pays

••VII. Vicarious Satisfaction••

• Vicarious satisfaction involves the act of a judge or ruler to relax the law and accept a substitute punishment
• This is called "relaxation" or "pardon" when the personal punishment of the guilty person is dispensed with

••VIII. Relaxation and Pardon••

• Relaxation involves the act of the judge or ruler to accept a substitute punishment
• Pardon involves the dispensing with the personal punishment of the guilty person

••IX. Importance of Understanding Satisfaction••

• Understanding satisfaction is essential to understanding the atonement of Christ
• It helps to clarify the nature of sin and the requirements for redemption

••X. Conclusion••

• The doctrine of satisfaction is a complex and nuanced topic that requires careful consideration of various principles and concepts.

		- On the part of men, the guilt of whose sin must be removed.

â€¢ ••Conclusion••

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. The Sufficiency of Christ's Satisfaction••

• The Bible teaches that Christ's death is sufficient to make a full satisfaction for all the elect (Is. 53:6, 2 Cor. 5:14, Heb. 10:14)
• This is in contrast to the idea that one person cannot satisfy for many others of the same rank, but a superior person can satisfy for those of a lower rank

••II. The Imputation of Sin••

• The rule laid down by Ezekiel (18:20) that the soul that sins shall die cannot be understood absolutely and simply
• It must be understood relatively in the ordinary way of providence, not in the extraordinary way of grace
• This rule is not applicable in God's common government of men, where he visits the iniquities of the fathers upon the children (Ex. 20:5)

••III. The Effect of Christ's Satisfaction••

• Christ's satisfaction is the most efficacious means of holiness and the death of sin itself (Rom. 6, Tit. 2:14, 1 Pet. 2:24)
• It is not a means of impiety or security, but rather a means of living unto righteousness

••IV. The Perfection of Christ's Satisfaction••

• The Romanists claim that Christ's satisfaction is not perfect and that something was lacking to make it full and complete
• However, this is not a correct understanding of the perfection of Christ's satisfaction

••V. The Nature of Satisfaction••

• A satisfaction made to God differs from one made to man
• A satisfaction made to man is either private (a reparation) or public (canonical)

••VI. The Romanist View of Satisfaction••

• The Romanists restrict Christ's satisfaction to sins committed before baptism and to the guilt of fault, not punishment
• They also restrict it to eternal punishment, not temporal punishment

••VII. The Implications of the Romanist View••

• The Romanist view weakens and overturns the perfection of Christ's satisfaction
• It implies that Christ's satisfaction is not sufficient to cover all sins, but only those committed before baptism

••VIII. The Importance of Understanding Satisfaction••

• Understanding the perfection of Christ's satisfaction is crucial for understanding the nature of sin and salvation
• It is also important for understanding the relationship between God and humanity

••IX. The Sufficiency of Christ's Satisfaction for All Sins••

• Christ's satisfaction is sufficient to cover all sins, not just those committed before baptism
• It is sufficient to cover both eternal and temporal punishment

••X. The Implications of Christ's Satisfaction••

• Christ's satisfaction is the means by which we are justified and reconciled to God
• It is the foundation of our hope of salvation and our confidence in God's mercy and forgiveness.

â€¢ ••The Obedience of Christ••

â€¢ ••The Benefits of Christ's Obedience••
	• Redemption must procure two opposite benefits: deliverance from death and a right to life.

		- Liberation from the curse of the law and the bestowment of blessing (Gal. 3:13)
		- Freedom from the law, and the adoption of sons (Gal. 4:5)

		- Forgiveness of sins, and inheritance among them which are sanctified (Acts 26:18)

â€¢ ••The Indissoluble Connection between Benefits••

â€¢ ••Distinguishing between Benefits••
	• The two benefits are not to be confounded as if they were one and the same thing.
	• They are to be distinguished because it is one thing to free from death, and another to introduce a right to life.

â€¢ ••The Law and Its Relation to Man••
	• The law has two aspects: precepts (duties) and sanctions (rewards and punishments)
	• Man is bound to both obedience and punishment under the law, but in different capacities (as a creature and as a sinful creature)

â€¢ ••The Nature of Debt Under the Law••
	• A penal debt is one thing, arising from past transgression
	• An obediential debt is another thing, arising from the creature's indispensable obligation to God, which cannot be exempted even in suffering punishment

â€¢ ••Threefold Subjection to the Law••
	• Natural subjection: the creature is bound to obey God as a rule of holiness, eternal and indispensable
	• Federal subjection: the creature is bound to obey God as a condition for acquiring happiness, mutable and dependent on the creature's state
	• Penal subjection: the sinful creature is bound to suffer punishment, necessary and inevitable

â€¢ ••Characteristics of Each Subjection••
	• Natural subjection: absolute and immutable, founded in God's essential right and natural authority
	• Federal subjection: economical and mutable, founded in God's free right and voluntary dispensation
	• Penal subjection: necessary and inevitable, founded in God's judicial right and vindicatory justice

â€¢ ••Who is Subject to Each Subjection••
	• All rational creatures (angels and men) are subject to natural subjection
	• Adam, in a state of innocence, was subject to federal subjection
	• Devils and reprobate men are subject to penal subjection

â€¢ ••Christ's Relation to the Law••
	• Christ was made under the law (hypo nomon) and subject to the law
	• He was subject to the law for himself as a rule of holiness by a common and natural subjection

â€¢ ••Christ's Subjection to the Law••
	• He was not subject to the law as commanding the condition of happiness by an economical and federal subjection
	• He was not subject to the law as a penal subjection, since he was holy and free from sin

â€¢ ••Christ's Undertaking of the Twofold Office••
	• He undertook the twofold office of fulfilling the law and redeeming man from sin

â€¢ ••Implications of Christ's Relation to the Law••
	• Christ's relation to the law has implications for our understanding of his role as mediator and redeemer

â€¢ ••Conclusion••
	• The threefold subjection to the law provides a framework for understanding Christ's relation to the law and his role as mediator and redeemer.

	• The universal particle "pantos" (all) must be referred to kinds of men, not to persons.
	• Calvin explains that the apostle means that not only Jews, but also Gentiles, are redeemed by the death of Christ.

â€¢ ••The world for which Christ was sent••
	• The world for which Christ was sent and died cannot be extended universally to the whole human race.
	• Innumerable persons of that world perish, so it must denote either the universality of the elect or all peoples, Jews and Gentiles.

â€¢ ••Allusion to the promise to Abraham••
	• The promise made to Abraham that in his seed (Christ) all families of the earth should be blessed is alluded to in John 3:16.
	• This promise belongs to all the promised seed without distinction of nation.

â€¢ ••Justification and salvation by faith••
	• Not all men are justified and saved by faith, as explained in Galatians 3:8 and 16.
	• Paul explains that the seed of Abraham is "of faith" and "called in Isaac" (Romans 4:16 and 9:7).

â€¢ ••The world for whose life Christ gave his flesh••
	• The world for whose life Christ gave his flesh to death is none other than the world to which he is said to give life.
	• This cannot be extended to all men universally and severally, since the giving of life imports its actual application and communication.

â€¢ ••Christ as the Lamb of God••
	• Christ is said to be "the Lamb of God that taketh away the sin of the world" (John 1:29).
	• The word "air ein" signifies not only taking, but also taking away, so the sins of the reprobate cannot be said to be removed entirely.

â€¢ ••The world of the elect••
	• The world of the elect, made up of Jews and Gentiles indiscriminately, is the only world that can be meant.
	• These are said to be blessed because their transgression has been taken away (Psalm 32:1).

â€¢ ••Christ as propitiation for sins••
	• When John says that Christ is a propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only, but for the sins of the whole world (1 John 2:2), he does not wish to extend this to each and every one.
	• Christ can only be an expiation and propitiation for those who can console themselves by the intercession of Christ and the remission obtained through him (the elect).

â€¢ ••Christ as Advocate••
	• Christ is not an Advocate for all, as those learned divines confess on John 17:9.
	• Christ is an Advocate only for those who are joined together with him by the apostle as equal and inseparable.

â€¢ ••Interpretation of 1 John 2:2••

â€¢ ••The nature of Christ's mission••

â€¢ ••Perishing and actual perdition••

â€¢ ••The universality of Christ's sacrifice••
	• Christ's sacrifice is universal in its scope, but not all people will be saved.
	• The phrase "whole world" refers to the universal offer of salvation, but not the universal acceptance of it.

â€¢ ••The distinction between the elect and the reprobate••
	• The elect alone receive special grace and are reconciled to God through Christ.
	• The reprobate are not included in the scope of Christ's sacrifice, but are rather excluded from the covenant.

â€¢ ••The purpose of John's message••
	• John's message is to console believers against the remains of sin.
	• The message is intended to make the blessing of Christ's sacrifice common to the whole Church.

Here are 10 concise bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Perishing of a Brother••

• A brother can perish by our knowledge (Rom. 14:15)
	• Not a permanent destruction, but a temporary lapse
	• Caused by our failure to preserve them through our actions
• This is not a reference to eternal perdition, but rather a warning against causing harm to a weak brother

••II. False Prophets••

• False prophets can "deny the Lord that redeemed them" (2 Pet. 2:1)
	• Not a reference to redemption from eternal death, but rather a liberation from error and idolatry
	• A call to Christianity and a setting apart to the work of the ministry

••III. Redemption••

• Redemption properly so called refers to a permanent and eternal salvation
	• Given by the Father to Christ to be redeemed and kept forever
• External redemption refers to a liberation from error and idolatry through an external call to Christianity

••IV. Sanctification••

• There are two types of sanctification:
	• Internal, spiritual, and real, belonging to those who are actually redeemed and regenerated by Christ
	• External and apparent, referring to a profession of faith without true regeneration

••V. Hypocrites••

• Hypocrites can obtain sanctification through an external calling or reception of sacraments
	• But they are not truly sanctified, as they lack faith
	• Christ does not belong to them, as they are destitute of faith

••VI. Profaning the Blood of the Covenant••

• Paul speaks of those who profane the blood of the covenant (Heb. 10:29)
	• Refers to an external sanctification, not an internal one
	• Those who profane the covenant are those who have renounced Christ and apostatized from the gospel

••VII. Hypothetical Expression••

• Paul's expression is hypothetical, not absolute
	• Points out the connection between external sanctification and apostasy

••VIII. Unworthy Reception of the Eucharist••

• Those who receive the Eucharist unworthily are guilty of the body and blood of Christ (1 Cor. 11:27, 29)
	• Similar to those who profane the blood of the covenant

••IX. Liberation from Error••

• Liberation from error and idolatry is a key aspect of external redemption
	• A call to Christianity and a setting apart to the work of the ministry

••X. Importance of Understanding••

• Understanding the nuances of redemption and sanctification is crucial for avoiding error and hypocrisy
	• Requires careful consideration of the biblical text and its context

â€¢ ••The distinction between true and false faith••

	• False faith is a dead faith that does not respond to the gospel and does not trust in Christ

â€¢ ••The importance of understanding faith••
	• Faith is not a simple or straightforward concept

• ••I. The Necessity of Christ's Intercession••

• ••V. The Nature of Christ's Intercession••
	• Christ's intercession is not just figurative, but a real and essential part of his priestly office
	• It is not just a part of his kingly office, but a distinct aspect of his priestly office

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Christ's Intercession as a Priest••

• Christ's intercession is a part of his priestly office, distinct from his kingly office.
• The orthodox view is that Christ's intercession is a real and essential part of his priestly office.

••II. Reasons for Christ's Intercession as a Priest••

• ••1. Scripture••: Christ is introduced as performing the office of intercession, not as a King, but as a Priest (Heb. 9:24-25).
• ••2. Christ as Advocate••: Christ is called our Advocate (paraklÄ“tos) with God (1 Jn. 2:1) to plead for the pardon of our sins and defend us against Satan's accusations.
• ••3. The Angel with the Golden Censer••: The intercession of Christ is represented by the angel with the golden censer in Rev. 8:3, which is a sacerdotal, not kingly act.
• ••4. Distinction between Priestly and Royal Offices••: If Christ's intercession is nothing else than an employment of his kingly power, the two offices would be confused, and Christ would not be compared with priests, but with kings only.

••III. Sources of Explanation••

• ••1. Scripture••: The intercession ascribed to Christ does not derogate from his glory because it is not supplicatory, but an efficacious address after the manner of jurisdiction.
• ••2. Paul's Teaching••: Paul claims both Christ's sitting at the right hand and his intercession for us (Rom. 8:34) to indicate that both properly belong to him: the former belongs to him as a King, and the latter to him as a Priest.

••IV. Conclusion••

• Christ's intercession as a Priest does not lessen his glory, but is an essential part of his priestly office.
• His divinity and regal power do not prevent him from interceding for us as a Priest.

••I. The Subjectation of All Things to Christ••

• The subjectation of all things to Christ is a theme in Scripture (Ps. 8:4-6, Heb. 2:5-8)
	• This subjectation is to be understood in the context of Christ's headship over the church
	• It may also refer to the humanity of Christ, which should be subject to God forever
	• Alternatively, it may refer to Christ's office and mediation, which should be subject to the Father

••II. God Will Be All in All••

• God will be all in all, excluding external means of communication (1 Cor. 15:28)
	• This will be a direct and unmediated communication between God and the saints
	• The saints will see God face to face, but not to the exclusion of Christ, the head and Bridegroom of the church
• God will be all in all, not absolutely and simply, but with regard to believers and saints
	• God will make the saints fully partake of his own happiness
	• This will be a full and complete communication of God's blessings and glory to the saints

••III. The Work of Salvation••

• The work of salvation has been finished and consummated
	• There is no further need for the economical mediation of salvation
	• The truth of our union with Christ, the head, remains forever

••IV. Christ's Kingdom••

• Christ will exercise an essential kingdom over the saints as Logos (1 Cor. 15:28)
	• This will not prevent him from reigning over them as God-man (theanthrÅpos) and as Mediator
	• The kingdom of nature does not take away the kingdom of grace in the church

••V. The Kingdom of Christ••

• The kingdom of Christ can be called both temporal and eternal
	• Temporal with respect to the mode of government in this life among enemies
	• Eternal properly and by itself, because it will never have an end

••VI. Adoration and Worship of Christ as Mediator••

• A controversy has arisen regarding the adoration and worship of Christ as Mediator
	• The Socinians deny that Christ should be adored or that his divinity can be proved from such adoration and worship
	• The orthodox have also debated this issue

••VII. Occasion of the Question••

• The Romanists have inquired about the adoration of the human nature of Christ
	• Thomas Aquinas has written on this topic (ST, III, Q. 25, Art. 1-3, pp. 2153-56)
• The Lutheran Ubiquitarians have disputed about the adoration of the body of Christ

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••The question of Christ's adoration••
	• Concerns the nature of Christ's adoration as Mediator
	• Arises from the Socinian controversy, which distinguishes between worship of God and worship of Christ as Mediator

â€¢ ••The Socinian argument••
	• Adoration given to Christ as Mediator does not prove his deity or consubstantiality
	• Adoration is given to Christ as Mediator, not as God

â€¢ ••The orthodox response••
	• Denies the minor premise of the Socinian argument
	• Affirms that Christ as Mediator is worthy of adoration

â€¢ ••The importance of the question••
	• Although not principal, it is still important to dispute against the Socinians
	• Allows for a stronger and more successful defense against Socinianism

â€¢ ••Statement of the question••
	• Concerns the formal object or relation under which Christ is to be adored
	• Specifically, whether Christ is to be adored as God only or also as Mediator

â€¢ ••The formal object of adoration••
	• Not the material object (Christ himself), but the relation under which he is adored
	• Can be taken in a wide or strict sense, depending on the context

â€¢ ••The relation of adoration••
	• Can be "as," "inasmuch as," or "because" Christ is Mediator
	• Is taken in a strict and reduplicative sense, not a wide and specificative sense

â€¢ ••The motives for adoration••
	• Not the only reason for adoring Christ, but one of several
	• Includes the preeminence of his divine majesty and the benefits he bestows upon us

â€¢ ••The scope of the question••
	• Does not concern the adoration of Christ itself, but the relation under which he is adored
	• Is a matter of dispute among the orthodox, with some affirming and others denying the adoration of Christ as Mediator

â€¢ ••The significance of the question••
	• Allows for a stronger and more successful defense against Socinianism
	• Is a matter of importance, despite not being principal.

â€¢ ••The Object of Adoration••
	• The person of the Mediator (Christ) is the object of adoration
	• Not as God or man simply, but as God-man (theanthrÅpos)

â€¢ ••The Foundation of Adoration••
	• The deity alone is the foundation of adoration

â€¢ ••The Motive of Adoration••
	• The motive is not the excellency of the divinity alone

â€¢ ••The Adjunct of Adoration••
	• The body or human nature of Christ is the adjunct of adoration
	• Without which the person is not adored

â€¢ ••Adoration Due to Christ••
	• Adoration is due to Christ, the Mediator
	• Properly belongs to the person of the Mediator and pertains to it

â€¢ ••Scriptural Basis for Adoration••
	• Adoration of Christ is defended by the orthodox from Scripture
	• Examples include Psalms 2:11, 12; Hebrews 1:6; Matthew 2:2, 11; etc.

â€¢ ••The Foundation of Adoration is Divinity••
	• The foundation and formal relation of adoration is not human nature or mediatorial office
	• But the divinity only

â€¢ ••Why Divinity is the Foundation of Adoration••
	• Only the divine essence is adorable due to its infinite, omniscient, omnipotent, and eternal nature
	• This is a confession and celebration of omniscience, omnipresence, and omnipotence

â€¢ ••Human Nature is Not Adorable••
	• Human nature is created and finite, and therefore not adorable in itself
	• The Nestorians were condemned for adoring Christ as the Son of the blessed virgin, separate from the eternal Son of God

â€¢ ••Mediation is Not the Foundation of Adoration••
	• The mediatorial office is a work of God among creatures and a contingent and temporary adjunct
	• Therefore, it cannot lay the foundation for legitimate adoration
	• Adoration of the Mediator terminates in the deity, not the mediation.

â€¢ ••Why is Jesus adored?••

â€¢ ••Christ as Mediator••
	• Christ is to be adored as Mediator because of his role in mediating between God and humanity.
	• This adoration is based on the person of Christ, who is both divine and human.

â€¢ ••Socinian Objections••
	• The Socinians argue that if Christ is adored as Mediator, he should also be adored as man.
	• However, this is not the case, as the adoration of Christ as Mediator does not imply that humanity is a formal object of worship.

â€¢ ••Christ's Divinity••
	• Christ's divinity is implied by his role as Mediator.
	• The name and concept of Mediator involve Christ's deity, and therefore, his divinity is a necessary aspect of his mediation.

â€¢ ••Christ's Inferiority to the Father••
	• Christ is inferior to the Father in terms of office and assumption of a human body.
	• However, this inferiority does not detract from his divinity or essential adorability.

â€¢ ••Formal Object of Adoration••
	• The formal object of adoration is the person of Christ, who is both divine and human.
	• Divinity is the primary object of adoration, while humanity is a secondary object.

â€¢ ••Natures of Christ••
	• The natures of Christ (divine and human) are not confounded or made equal by the adoration of Christ as Mediator.
	• The adoration of Christ as Mediator ascribes to him what belongs to him according to both natures.

â€¢ ••Adoration of Christ's Humanity••
	• Christ's humanity is not adored "by itself" or "on account of itself" because it is a creature and not adorable in its own nature.
	• However, Christ's humanity is adored in the Logos (Christ's divine nature), with whom it is personally united.

â€¢ ••Ultimate Term of Adoration••
	• The ultimate term of adoration is not the flesh (humanity) but the deity (divine nature).
	• The deity is the proper object of adoration and its true and proper cause.

â€¢ ••Orthodox View of Christ's Humanity••
	• Some orthodox theologians have said that Christ's humanity is adorable, but this does not mean that humanity is the proper object of adoration.
	• Rather, it means that the worship paid to Christ is not to be separated into various species.

â€¢ ••Nestorian and Romanist Errors••
	• The Nestorians and Romanists have erred in separating the adoration of Christ into different species (e.g., adoring Christ as God and as man separately).
	• This error is corrected by recognizing that the worship paid to Christ is not to be separated into various species.

â€¢ ••Calling and Faith••
	• Calling is a general call to salvation, not a special call to a particular office.

â€¢ ••The Nature of Calling••
	• Calling is an act of God's grace in Christ, by which he calls men to union with Christ and salvation.
	• It involves a transition from a state of sin and condemnation to a state of union with Christ and holiness.

â€¢ ••The Terms of Calling••
	• The term "from which" refers to the state of sin and condemnation in which we lie.
	• The term "to which" refers to the state of union with Christ and holiness to which we are called.

â€¢ ••The Benefits of Calling••

	• It involves a transition from darkness and the world to union with Christ and eternal glory.

â€¢ ••The Importance of Faith••
	• Faith is essential to the calling process, as it involves a response to God's call and a trust in Christ's salvation.
	• Faith is not just a mental assent, but a deep and abiding trust in Christ and his work.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••The Concept of Calling••
	• The "heavenly calling" or "high calling" is from heaven and calls to heaven
	• It is a call to return to God, like Adam's call in Genesis 3:9
	• It is a call to conversion, using the voice of the gospel and preaching of the word

â€¢ ••Why the Holy Spirit Used This Nomenclature••
	• To designate the misery of man and recall him to God
	• To point out the means God uses in conversion (the voice of the gospel and preaching of the word)
	• To exhibit the various relations under which calling can be viewed (new creation, resurrection, dignity of sons of God, etc.)

â€¢ ••The Various Relations of Calling••
	• Calling as a new creation, bringing us out of nothingness to life
	• Calling as a resurrection, arising from sins
	• Calling as the supreme dignity of sons of God and a glorious office
	• Calling as a stadium and race course, set before us

â€¢ ••Distinguishing Calling••
	• Some make calling threefold: real by works, verbal by the gospel, spiritual by the Spirit
	• However, this assumes a calling to salvation by the works of nature, which is disputed

â€¢ ••The Twofold Calling••
	• A twofold calling is acknowledged, corresponding to the twofold state of the church (visible and invisible)
	• The external calling takes place through the ministry of the word and sacraments
	• The internal calling takes place with the additional power of the Holy Spirit

â€¢ ••The Differences Between External and Internal Calling••
	• External calling only knocks at the ears of the body, while internal calling knocks at the heart
	• External calling only persuades morally, while internal calling persuades and draws efficaciously

â€¢ ••Agreement and Difference in Calling••
	• Both external and internal calling agree in various particulars (God as author, men as dead and lost in sin, word as instrument, etc.)
	• However, they differ in their effects and means (external calling only persuades morally, while internal calling persuades and draws efficaciously)

â€¢ ••The Author of Calling••
	• God is the author of calling, who calls men to his kingdom

â€¢ ••The Men Called••
	• Men are dead and lost in sin as to internal qualities, and weak, unwise, and ignoble as to external qualities

â€¢ ••The Instrument of Calling••
	• The word is the ordinary instrument of calling in both external and internal calling

â€¢ ••The End of Calling••
	• The glory of God and the salvation of the called are the ends of calling in both external and internal calling

••I. External and Internal Calling••

	• Amplitude: broad, extending to many, including the reprobate
	• Event: always ineffective
	• Duration: temporal and revocable
• ••Internal Calling••
	• God acts operatively, supplying strength and working within what he enjoins
	• Done by the Spirit also
	• Amplitude: limited to few, the elect
	• Event: efficacious and attains its end
	• Duration: immutable and not to be repented of

••II. Distinction between External and Internal Calling••

• ••Lutheran View••
	• Internal and external calling are one and the same
	• External calling is efficacious in one and not in another due to human will
• ••Arminian View••
	• Calling is ineffective in some but not in others due to human will
	• Good will of man superadds efficacy and freely receives the word
• ••Orthodox View••
	• Difference between external and internal calling is due to God's decree and nature of calling
	• Subjective grace operates more efficaciously in some than in others

••III. Reasons for Orthodox View••

• ••Internal Calling is According to Purpose••
	• Depends on God's decree
	• Eternal and without repentance
• ••Event Depends on God's Decree••
	• God powerfully directs calling to accomplish its end in the elect
• ••Human Will is Not the Cause••
	• Man does not make himself different
	• God works in us to will and to do

••IV. Objections and Examination••

• ••Objections from Opponents••
	• Will be examined when treating of the efficacy of calling
• ••Importance of Understanding Calling••
	• Understanding calling is crucial for understanding God's sovereignty and human responsibility

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••Ordinary and Mediate vs. Extraordinary and Immediate••
	• God's ordinary dispensation of grace involves external means (ministry of men)
	• Extraordinary and immediate calling is reserved for certain individuals (e.g. the thief, Paul)

â€¢ ••The Calling of the Reprobate••
	• Question: Are reprobates called with the intention of salvation?
	• Answer: No, they are not called with the intention of salvation, but rather as a means to an end (III)

â€¢ ••Differences between Elect and Reprobate••
	• External call is extended to both elect and reprobate, but in different manners
	• Elect are called primarily and directly, while reprobate are called secondarily and indirectly (III)

â€¢ ••The End of Calling••
	• Can be considered from two perspectives: God's end or the end of the thing (IV)
	• God's end is not always the same as the end of the thing (e.g. the end of the law is conviction, not happiness)

â€¢ ••God's End vs. the End of the Thing••
	• God's end is special with respect to the elect or reprobate (V)
	• Common end of calling is the demonstration of the mode and way of salvation (V)

â€¢ ••God's Seriousness and Sincerity••
	• God always acts seriously and sincerely, even if his end is not the same as the end of the thing (II)

â€¢ ••Hypocrisy and Dissimulation••
	• God cannot be accused of hypocrisy or dissimulation, even if his intentions are not the same as the reprobate's (II)

â€¢ ••The Ministry of the Gospel••
	• The ministry of the gospel was instituted to collect the church and increase the mystical body of Christ (III)

â€¢ ••The Word of God••
	• The word of God cannot return unto him void (Is. 55:11), but is still extended to the reprobate (III)

â€¢ ••The Separation of God's End and the End of the Thing••
	• This separation is seen in the legal proclamation, where the end of the thing is life by the law, but God's end is conviction and leading to Christ (IV)

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. The Nature of God's Calling••

• The calling of God has a special purpose for the elect, which is to bestow salvation upon them.
	• This involves not only prescribing duty, but also performing that duty through the Spirit.
• The calling of God also has a different purpose for the reprobate, which is to convict them and make them inexcusable.

••II. The Threefold Principle of God's Calling••

• The calling of God springs from three principles:
	1. The authority of a legislator who has the right to prescribe duty.
	2. The goodness and grace of a Lord who shows the way of salvation and blesses the creature.
	3. The justice of a Judge who convicts the stubborn and rebellious.
• These principles result in a threefold end:
	1. The prescription of duty, so that the individual knows what God demands.
	2. The promise of blessing on the condition of faith and repentance.
	3. The detection of the wickedness of the heart and its inexcusability.

••III. The Question of God's Intention••

• The question is not whether God wills to bestow any grace on the reprobate, but whether he intends to give saving grace or salvation to them.
• Our opponents maintain that God's intention is to give saving grace to all, while we deny this.

••IV. The Disparity of the Event••

• The event of external calling is not the same for all, and those who spurn the heavenly call are made inexcusable.
• The question is whether the disparity of the event proves a disparity of intention in the caller.

••V. Proof that God Acts Seriously in Calling Reprobates••

• God cannot intend the salvation of those whom he reprobated from eternity and from whom he decreed to withhold faith and other means leading to salvation.
• This would be contrary to God's wisdom, goodness, and power.

••VI. God's Intention and Faith••

• God does not intend faith in the reprobate, therefore neither does he intend salvation (which cannot be attained without faith).
• This is gathered from the fact that God.

••VII. God's Decree and the Reprobate••

• God decreed to withhold faith and other means leading to salvation from the reprobate.
• This decree is based on God's wisdom, goodness, and power.

••VIII. The Implications of God's Decree••

• If God decreed to withhold faith and other means leading to salvation from the reprobate, then he cannot intend their salvation.
• This is because salvation requires faith, which God does not intend for the reprobate.

••IX. The Nature of God's Calling••

• God's calling is not the same for all, and the disparity of the event proves a disparity of intention in the caller.
• This is because God's intention is to give saving grace to the elect, not to the reprobate.

••X. Conclusion••

• God acts seriously in calling reprobates, although he does not intend their salvation.
• This is based on the principles of God's authority, goodness, and justice.

â€¢ ••Sufficient vs. Efficacious Grace••
	• The distinction between sufficient and efficacious grace is a common point of debate
	• Sufficient grace is that which enables man to will to believe, but does not guarantee it
	• Efficacious grace, on the other hand, is that which guarantees man's conversion and good works

â€¢ ••Bellarmine's Definition••
	• Bellarmine defines sufficient grace as that which enables man to will to believe, but does not guarantee it
	• He defines efficacious grace as that which guarantees man's conversion and good works

â€¢ ••Critique of Bellarmine's Definition••

	• This is a form of Pelagianism, which holds that man's will is the primary factor in his salvation

â€¢ ••Pelagianism••
	• Pelagianism is the idea that man's will is the primary factor in his salvation
	• This is a form of heresy that denies the sovereignty of God in salvation

â€¢ ••The Problem with Sufficient Grace••
	• If sufficient grace is not efficacious, then it is insufficient to produce the desired effect
	• This means that additional grace is needed to make sufficient grace effective

	• Efficacious grace is necessary to guarantee man's conversion and good works

â€¢ ••The Reformed View••
	• The Reformed view holds that sufficient and efficacious grace are not distinct, but rather are two sides of the same coin
	• Efficacious grace is not a separate entity from sufficient grace, but rather is the guarantee of God's sovereignty in salvation.

â€¢ ••The Romanist Position••

â€¢ ••The Arminian Position••

	• They argue that God's universal will is the basis for their position on sufficient grace.

â€¢ ••The Issue of Universal Salvation••
	• The question at hand concerns whether God's gratuitous favor regards individuals so kindly as to communicate to all.

	• Sufficient grace is not just any kind of help or assistance, but rather a saving and efficacious grace.

â€¢ ••The Implications of Sufficient Grace••
	• If sufficient grace is given to all, then it would imply that all are saved.

••III. The New Covenant••

• The new covenant does not require God to supply sufficient strength to man
	• The equality of credit and debt is not based on the state of sin, but on the state of creation
	• Man's inability to pay is due to his own fault, not God's lack of provision

••IV. The Examples of the Eunuch and Cornelius••

• The examples of the eunuch and Cornelius are not pertinent to the discussion of unregenerate infidels
	• They were already imbued with a knowledge of the Jewish religion and were granted a further knowledge of the gospel
	• They were not simply unregenerate infidels who received the light of grace

••V. Effective Calling••

• Effective calling is not denominated from the event or congruity, but from the supernatural operation of grace
	• The Romanists and Arminians are incorrect in their views on effective calling

••VI. Romanist Opinions on Effective Calling••

• There are three opinions held by Romanists on effective calling
	• 1. Molina, Lessius, Becanus, and most Jesuits: effective calling is from the event
	• 2. Bellarmine, Suarez, and others: effective calling is from its congruity
	• 3. Thomists and Dominicans: effective calling is from physical predetermination

••VII. The First Opinion (Molina, etc.)••

• This opinion makes effective calling consist in the assent and cooperation of man
	• It brings back the error of Pelagius, who transferred the principal cause of conversion to the free will

••VIII. The Second Opinion (Bellarmine, etc.)••

• This opinion deduces effective calling from its congruity
	• It is incorrect because it does not take into account the supernatural operation of grace

••IX. The Third Opinion (Thomists, etc.)••

• This opinion draws effective calling from physical predetermination
	• It is incorrect because it does not take into account the role of human cooperation

••X. Conclusion••

• Effective calling is a supernatural operation of grace, not simply an event or congruity
	• The Romanists and Arminians are incorrect in their views on effective calling.

â€¢ ••Rejection of the first opinion••

••1. The Orthodox View of Predestination••

• The orthodox view of predestination is expressed in five propositions.
• The propositions aim to clarify the nature of God's grace and its relationship to human free will.

••2. The Inefficacy of Human Effort••

• The orthodox view holds that human effort is not the primary cause of salvation.
• Instead, salvation is the result of God's supernatural power and divine motion.

••3. The Nature of God's Grace••

• God's grace is not a physical or natural phenomenon, but rather a supernatural and divine one.
• It perfects nature and does not injure the will, but rather makes it more free and active.

••4. The Five Propositions••

• The five propositions aim to clarify the nature of God's grace and its relationship to human free will.
• The propositions are:
	• Proposition 1: The ways of the Lord in grace are inscrutable, but the fact of God's grace is revealed to us.
	• Proposition 2: The movement of efficacious grace in man is not after the manner of an act or simultaneous concourse, but also after the manner of a principal and previous concourse or predetermination.
	• Proposition 3: The movement of efficacious grace in man is not a physical or natural phenomenon, but rather a supernatural and divine one.
	• Proposition 4: The movement of efficacious grace in man is not a result of human effort or merit, but rather a result of God's sovereign will.
	• Proposition 5: The movement of efficacious grace in man is not a result of a change in God's will, but rather a result of God's eternal and unchanging will.

••5. The Inscrutability of God's Ways••

• The orthodox view holds that the ways of God are inscrutable and incomprehensible to us.
• This means that we cannot fully understand the reasons behind God's actions or the mode of his operation.

••6. The Mode of God's Operation••

• The orthodox view holds that the mode of God's operation is not something that can be accurately described or explained.
• Instead, it is something that is felt by experience and is a mystery that is beyond human comprehension.

••7. The Relationship Between God's Grace and Human Free Will••

• The orthodox view holds that God's grace and human free will are not mutually exclusive, but rather complementary.
• God's grace perfects nature and makes it more free and active, rather than injuring the will or limiting its freedom.

••8. The Opposition to Pelagianism••

• The orthodox view opposes the Pelagian view, which holds that God concurs in good only by way of act, and not by way of previous concourse or predetermination.
• The orthodox view holds that God's concourse is not just a simultaneous act, but also a previous concourse or predetermination.

••9. The Importance of Experience••

• The orthodox view holds that experience is a more reliable guide to understanding God's operation than reason or speculation.
• This means that we should rely on our experience of God's grace and its effects, rather than trying to understand the mode of its operation.

••10. The Relationship Between Faith and Reason••

• The orthodox view holds that faith and reason are not mutually exclusive, but rather complementary.
• Faith is necessary for understanding the mysteries of God's operation, and reason is necessary for understanding the implications of those mysteries.

â€¢ ••Regeneration and Free Will••
	• The Catholic Church views regeneration as a process where the Spirit infuses new qualities in man, making him a passive subject.
	• The Spirit's action is followed by man's free will, which becomes the active instrument of his actions.

â€¢ ••Socinian View of Regeneration••
	• Socinians, like Pelagius, deny original sin and attribute depravity to frequent acts of sin.
	• They recognize no other regeneration than a change of custom and life, reforming according to Christ's doctrine.
	• According to this view, man cooperates with God from the first moment.

â€¢ ••Romanist View of Regeneration••
	• The Council of Trent affirms that man's free will cooperates with God's grace.
	• The will is not passive, but rather free to consent or dissent to God's excitation and drawing.

â€¢ ••Distinction between Prevenient and Subsequent Grace••
	• Adversaries (e.g., Bellarmine) distinguish between prevenient (exciting, operating) and subsequent (cooperating) grace.
	• Prevenient grace refers to the first movement of efficacious grace, which converts man before any cooperation.
	• Subsequent grace refers to the second movement, which assists the converted and is cooperated with by the will.

â€¢ ••Augustine's View on Grace••
	• Augustine employs the distinction between prevenient and subsequent grace.
	• He affirms that God's mercy goes before man, preparing a good will, and assists it when prepared.

â€¢ ••Augustine's View on Human Cooperation••
	• Augustine states that God operates without man, but cooperates with man when he wills.
	• Man has no ability to do good works without God's operation or cooperation.

â€¢ ••Bellarmine's View on Prevenient Grace••
	• Bellarmine implies that prevenient grace is sufficient, acting by illumination and moral suasion.
	• This type of grace does not subject the free will to itself, but rather is subject to the will's power to receive or reject.

â€¢ ••Cooperating Grace••
	• Cooperating grace refers to the action of God with the yet unconverted will.
	• The will not yet converted cooperates with this grace, which is distinct from prevenient grace.

â€¢ ••Implications of the Distinction••
	• The distinction between prevenient and subsequent grace has implications for the role of human cooperation in salvation.
	• The Catholic Church affirms that God's grace is the primary cause of salvation, while human cooperation is a necessary condition.

â€¢ ••Augustine's View on the Source of Good Works••
	• Augustine affirms that good works are due to God's operation or cooperation, rather than human ability alone.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Introduction••

• The Synergists acknowledge that God's grace is not just "given to the grateful" but also "making grateful"
• The author disagrees with this distinction and proposes a different understanding of God's grace

••II. Distinguishing God's Grace••

• The author distinguishes God's grace into two types:
	• "Given to the grateful" (gratuitous love of God that flows into us)
	• "Given by the grateful" (saving benefits that flow from God's gratuitous love)

••III. Cooperation of Man••

• The cooperation of man is impugned (rejected) by the author
• The reasons for this rejection are:
	• Corruption of man (man is by nature a sinner and cannot cooperate with God)
	• Nature of regeneration (regeneration is a change of nature that only God can accomplish)
	• Infinity of power required (regeneration requires divine omnipotence, which cannot be ascribed to human will)
	• Absurdities attending it (if man cooperates with God, the glory of conversion is divided between God and man)

••IV. Argument 1: Corruption of Man••

• Man is by nature a sinner and cannot cooperate with God
• Man is dead in sins and laboring under a total impotence to good

••V. Argument 2: Nature of Regeneration••

• Regeneration is a change of nature that only God can accomplish
• Man cannot regenerate himself, but is merely passive in the process

••VI. Argument 3: Infinity of Power Required••

• Regeneration requires divine omnipotence, which cannot be ascribed to human will
• It is a work of creation and resurrection, which cannot admit of cooperation

••VII. Argument 4: Absurdities Attending It••

• If man cooperates with God, the glory of conversion is divided between God and man
• Man would have matter for glorying because he had made himself to differ

••VIII. Sources of Explanation••

• 1 Corinthians 15:10 does not help the Synergists (it refers to Paul's ministry, not conversion)
• The apostle Paul often and expressly testifies to the falsity of the Synergist's view (e.g. 1 Corinthians 4:7, Ephesians 2:8-9)

	• This statement is meant to emphasize the greatness of the sin of the Jews, not to imply that the Tyrians and Sidonians would actually be converted.

â€¢ ••The Foundation of the Curse••
	• The foundation of the curse is not necessarily in grace sufficient for conversion.
	• The curse is based on the appearances (ek tÅn phainomenÅn) and the probability of the thing, as well as Christ's knowledge of the disposition of the subjects.

â€¢ ••The Nature of Repentance••
	• The repentance being referred to is external repentance, not internal conversion.
	• External repentance is expressed by signs such as sackcloth and ashes.

â€¢ ••The Insufficiency of Miracles for Conversion••
	• Miracles are only an external means and are not sufficient for conversion unless an internal and heart-turning power accompanies them.
	• The Jews' failure to respond to the miracles is sufficient for their condemnation.

â€¢ ••The Nature of Obedience••
	• The act of obedience produced by efficacious grace is free and a true act of obedience.
	• Efficacious grace does not introduce violence or brute necessity, but leaves the individual's spontaneity and purpose intact.

â€¢ ••The Relationship between Grace and Freedom••
	• Man does not cease to will most freely what he wills, although he wills it necessarily.
	• The grace that accompanies efficaciousness does not negate human freedom, but rather leaves it intact.

	• Faith is essential for salvation and good works
	• Faith is the means by which we receive Christ and his benefits.

	• Abraham's faith was a result of divine faith, but it didn't mean he had to believe in the specific outcome of his actions

â€¢ ••II. Obedience to God's Command••
	• Abraham was obedient to God's command, even when it seemed impossible
	• His faith was evident in his willingness to obey, not in the specific outcome

â€¢ ••III. Conditions of Faith••
	• The Israelites were not bound to believe that every individual would enter the land of Canaan without condition
	• Faith was always implied, and many were excluded from the blessing due to a lack of faith

â€¢ ••IV. God's Will vs. Human Action••
	• We are bound to believe that God willed something, even if it doesn't happen due to human obstinacy
	• We are not bound to believe a falsehood, but rather that God willed something to be done

â€¢ ••V. Deception and Error••
	• God is not said to have deceived the people effectively, but rather permissively
	• The people were seduced and deceived by false prophets or judicially given up to a spirit of error

â€¢ ••VI. Object of Faith••
	• The object of faith is not the event or outcome, but rather the written word of God
	• Faith is distinct from knowledge, which can be gained from nature and works

â€¢ ••VII. Revelation and Faith••
	• Faith is gained from supernatural grace and revelation through the hearing of the word
	• The written word is the object of faith, not the unwritten word of the church

â€¢ ••VIII. The Written Word••
	• The written word is the only God-inspired word that establishes our faith
	• We are strictly prohibited from adding to or taking away from the written word

â€¢ ••IX. Degrees of Revelation••
	• The word of God is revealed at sundry times and in diverse manners
	• The object of faith is not simply the word, but the word revealed in its various forms

â€¢ ••X. The Nature of Faith••
	• Faith is distinct from knowledge and is gained through supernatural revelation
	• The written word is the object of faith, and we are bound to believe it as revealed by God.

	• Special mercy can be viewed in three ways: as promised, as actually conferred, or as having already been bestowed

â€¢ ••The Dispositive Act of Faith••
	• This act disposes us to receive the special mercy of God on account of Christ

â€¢ ••The Justificatory Act of Faith••
	• This act involves believing that remission of sins is actually bestowed in the present upon oneself
	• It is the absoving sentence of our justification that attends this act

â€¢ ••The Consolatory Act of Faith••
	• This act involves beholding the special mercy as having been bestowed already in the past
	• It involves believing that one's sins have been forgiven on account of Christ

â€¢ ••The Relationship Between Faith and the Gospel Promise••
	• The gospel promise is not given to men simply as such, but to men believing and repenting
	• Faith is the condition and instrument by which believers become partakers of the promises

â€¢ ••The Importance of Understanding the Proper Object of Faith••
	• The question of the proper object of faith is not a trivial matter, but rather a crucial aspect of understanding the nature of faith and salvation
	• The Romanists' view of faith as a simple assent is rejected in favor of a more nuanced understanding of faith as a complex and multifaceted concept.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Faith and Salvation••

• The faith that justifies is not a mere intellectual assent, but a fiducial apprehension of special mercy.
	• This faith is not a one-time event, but a continuous trust in God's mercy.
	• It is the foundation of our salvation and consolation.

••II. The Apostles' Creed and Special Mercy••

• The Apostles' Creed implies the fiducial apprehension of special mercy.
	• This is evident in the article about the remission of sins and eternal life.
	• Faith in God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit necessarily implies special mercy.

••III. The Object of Justifying Faith••

• The faith that justifies regards the whole word of God, including historical and dogmatic truths.
	• However, its proper object is special mercy, which is the mercy of God in Christ.
	• This faith cannot justify except as it regards the mercy of God in Christ.

••IV. Faith and Preaching, Sacraments, and Good Works••

• Faith in special mercy does not do away with preaching, sacraments, and good works.
	• Instead, it supposes their necessity as means of sealing, confirming, and increasing faith.
	• The grace of God is not a cause of licentiousness, but an incentive to holiness.

••V. The Measure of Revelation••

• The faith of believers has been according to the measure of revelation in the Old and New Testaments.
	• In the Old Testament, faith was more obscure, but still had for its object God's special mercy in Christ.
	• In the New Testament, Christ clearly proclaimed himself as the Messiah and Savior of the world.

••VI. The Form of Justifying Faith••

• The form of justifying faith is not love or obedience to God's commands.
	• This is denied against the Romanists and Socinians.
	• The two-fold question concerns the form of faith: (1) against the Romanists, and (2) against the Socinians.

••VII. Against the Romanists••

• The Romanists hold that love is the form of faith.
	• They distinguish faith into formed and unformed, with unformed faith being separated from love.
	• They term formed faith as perfected by love as the form.

••VIII. Against the Socinians••

• The Socinians hold that the form of faith consists in obedience to God's commands.
	• This is also denied, as faith is not merely a matter of obedience, but a fiducial apprehension of special mercy.

••IX. The Nature of Faith••

• Faith is not a mere intellectual assent, but a fiducial apprehension of special mercy.
	• It is a continuous trust in God's mercy, which is the foundation of our salvation and consolation.

••X. The Importance of Faith••

• Faith is essential for salvation and is the means by which we are justified.
	• It is not a one-time event, but a continuous process of trusting in God's mercy.

Here are 11 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Faith and Obedience••

• Faith cannot be obedience to commands because it would confuse two distinct virtues: faith and love
	• Faith is concerned with the promises of the gospel
	• Love is concerned with the precepts of the law

••II. Faith and Works••

• Faith and works are opposed as opposites and contraries in the matter of justification
	• Works are the effect of faith, not its cause
	• Faith is the instrument of justification, while works are its consequent fruit

••III. Works in Justification••

• No kind of works can be opposed to faith in justification
	• All works, whether perfect or not, are opposed to faith in justification
	• Faith does not justify as a work, which is the fundamental error of opponents

••IV. Faith as Obedience••

• To believe is to obey the command to believe prescribed in the gospel
	• Faith is not obedience to God's commands in the sense of our opponents
	• Our opponents confuse the commands of the gospel with the precepts of the law

••V. Faith as the "Work of God"••

• Faith is called the "work of God" in John 6:29
	• This was done imitatively, in response to the petition of the crowd
	• Faith gives what the crowd vainly sought in the works of the law

••VI. Abraham's Faith••

• The faith by which Abraham was justified cannot be called obedience to commands
	• Abraham's faith was in the promise, not in obedience to commands
	• His walking before God was the effect of his faith, not a condition of justification

••VII. Love and Faith••

• Love is not separable from faith
	• Love is the proper and immediate effect of faith
	• Faith cannot be separated from its cause, which is love

• Faith is dead without works (Jam. 2:20)
• John asserts that the knowledge of God without worship is false and deceitful (1 Jn. 2:4)

• The gospel commandment is to faith and love as two marks of true believers
	• Faith and love are mutually inseparable
	• The gospel commandment is not a conclusion arising from the preceding discussion, but a new argument

••X. The Faith of Miracles••

• The faith of miracles in 1 Cor. 13:2 is not justifying faith
	• The subject is the faith of miracles, not justifying faith
	• This is not an objection to the inseparability of faith and love

••XI. Conclusion••

• The contrary cannot be proved from 1 Cor. 13:2
	• The subject is the faith of miracles, not justifying faith
	• This is not a conclusion arising from the preceding discussion, but a new argument.

••Faith and Love••

	• Faith is a cognitive act, while love is an affective act
	• Faith can cease in heaven, but love remains (1 Cor 13:8)

	• The knowledge acquired through faith will be consummated by sight in heaven

••The Subject of Faith••

• A question is raised about the faith of infants
	• Two extremes: Anabaptists deny faith to infants, while Lutherans attribute actual faith to them

••Orthodox View••

• The orthodox occupy the middle ground between these two extremes
	• They deny actual faith to infants, but attribute a seminal or radical faith to them
• This view is limited to the infants of believers, not infidels or heathens
	• The faith attributed to infants is not a certainty, but a possibility

••Proof Against Lutherans••

• Infants do not have actual faith
	• They do not possess actual knowledge of anything
	• They are unable to discern good from evil (Dt 1:39, Is 7:16, Jon 4:11)
• The objection that knowledge is born with us is not relevant
	• This is a different kind of knowledge from actual faith

••Additional Points••

• The predestination of God makes a difference between children (Rom 9:11)
	• The promise of the covenant was ratified in the children of the promise, not the children of the flesh
• The orthodox view is not a certainty, but a possibility
	• It is left to the secret counsel and supreme liberty of God to determine the salvation of infants.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Faith and Infants••

• Faith is elicited from a renewed mind, and reason is necessary for faith.
	• Without reason, there can be no actual faith.
• Pedobaptism is not based on the actual faith of infants, but on the general command to baptize and the promise of the covenant.

••II. Covenant and Baptism••

• The covenant promise pertains to infants as well as adults.
	• God promises to be the God of Abraham and his seed (Gen. 17:7).
	• The promise is made with the fathers and their children (Acts 2:39).

••III. Effectiveness of Baptism••

• The sacrament of baptism is efficacious and ratified by God, even if not received by faith.
	• This is because the sacrament is a promise of God, not a mutual stipulation between God and man.

••IV. Fruit of Baptism••

• There are two types of fruit of baptism: active sealing by God and passive sealing by man.
	• Infants receive the former, but not the latter.

••V. Examples of Jeremiah and John••

• Jeremiah and John the Baptist are examples of infants receiving the Holy Spirit.
	• However, this does not imply that they actually believed.
	• Their examples are singular and extraordinary, and do not establish a universal rule.

••VI. Praise of God••

• Infants praise God objectively and materially, not subjectively and formally.
	• They praise God through the wonderful manifestation of his glory in their care and preservation.

••VII. Seminal Faith••

• Seminal faith is granted to infants.
	• This is the seed or root of faith, which is ingenerated in them from an early age.

••VIII. Habitual Faith••

• Habitual faith is not well ascribed to infants, but it is rightly predicated of them broadly.
	• It denotes potential or seminal faith, which is the Holy Spirit working in infants.

••IX. Development of Faith••

• The seed of faith in infants proceeds into act in more mature age.
	• Human instruction and the grace of the Holy Spirit promote the development of faith.

••X. Covenant Blessings••

• The blessings of the covenant, such as remission of sins and sanctification, ought to pertain to infants.
	• These blessings are promised to the fathers and their children (Acts 2:39).

â€¢ ••Infants have common notions••
	• Infants draw from natural generation common notions and principles of the natural law
	• These principles are not necessarily sinful, but rather neutral
	• Infants are capable of receiving supernatural regeneration and seeds of faith

â€¢ ••Solution to difficulties••
	• There may seem to be no marks of the Holy Spirit in infants, but this does not mean they are excluded
	• The reason of their salvation demands that they be included
	• Examples of sanctified infants demonstrate that this is possible

â€¢ ••Believers before actual faith••
	• Men are properly called rational before they use reason
	• Infants can be termed believers before actual faith because they have the seed of faith
	• This seed is the principle of faith, which is given to them

â€¢ ••Denial of faith in infants••
	• Some theologians (e.g. Peter Martyr, Beza, Piscator) deny that infants have faith
	• This is meant of actual faith, not the seed of faith or the Spirit of regeneration
	• These theologians argue that infants are saved by election and the Holy Spirit

â€¢ ••Calvin's response••
	• Calvin responds to the question of how infants are regenerated without knowledge of good or evil
	• He argues that the work of God is not limited by human understanding or experience

â€¢ ••The Holy Spirit in infants••
	• The Holy Spirit is the root of faith, hope, and love in infants
	• He works in them, giving them motions and inclinations suited to their age
	• This is not necessarily an internal experience, but rather a supernatural work

â€¢ ••Conclusion••
	• Infants are included in the promise of salvation and regeneration
	• They are capable of receiving the seed of faith and the Spirit of regeneration
	• This is demonstrated by examples of sanctified infants and the work of the Holy Spirit in them.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••Temporary faith vs. Justifying faith••
	• Temporary faith is not the same as justifying faith
	• The Remonstrants argued that the difference is only in degree and duration, not in kind

â€¢ ••Differences between temporary and justifying faith••
	• ••Origin••
		- Justifying faith comes from the special grace of election
		- Temporary faith depends on common grace

â€¢ ••Subject receiving faith••
	• In justifying faith, the subject is an elect person
	• In temporary faith, the subject is a reprobate

â€¢ ••Nature of the heart••
	• Temporary faith is received into a "stony heart"
	• Justifying faith is received into a "good and honest heart"

â€¢ ••Internal principle and rooting••
	• The principle of saving faith is the Spirit of regeneration and adoption
	• Temporary faith lacks this internal principle and rooting

â€¢ ••Foundation of faith••
	• Justifying faith is built on the immovable foundation of God's election
	• Temporary faith is not built on this foundation

â€¢ ••Duration and continuance••
	• Temporary faith differs from justifying faith in duration and continuance
	• Justifying faith continues to the end, while temporary faith does not

â€¢ ••Nature of temporary faith••
	• Temporary faith is not true justifying faith, but rather a different species of faith
	• It is not pleasing to God in the same way as justifying faith

â€¢ ••Implications of temporary faith••
	• Temporary faith is not a sign of salvation, but rather a test of God's patience
	• It is a means of increasing guilt in those who reject God's offer of salvation

â€¢ ••Conclusion••
	• The difference between temporary and justifying faith is specific and essential
	• Justifying faith is a unique and saving faith that comes from the special grace of election.

â€¢ ••Temporary Faith vs. Justifying Faith••

â€¢ ••Reasons for Temporary Faith's Weakness••
	• People imagine salvation belongs to them without a true foundation

	• They seek salvation from false conceptions or external means

â€¢ ••Consequences of Temporary Faith••
	• Leads to a vain sleep and a lack of inquiry into the foundation of one's imagination
	• Can result from a false conception of God's mercy or external means of salvation

â€¢ ••Desertion of Christ••

â€¢ ••Consequences of Temporary Faith••

â€¢ ••Conditional Threatenings••

â€¢ ••Difference between Temporary and True Faith••

â€¢ ••Perseverance of Faith••
	• The question of whether the true believer can ever totally or finally fall from faith is denied by the Romanists, Socinians, Remonstrants, and others

â€¢ ••Two Questions Concerning Faith••
	• Two questions arise concerning justifying faith: perseverance and certainty
	• The question concerning perseverance is agitated by the old and new Pelagians and Semipelagians

â€¢ ••Opposition to Perseverance••
	• The Romanists, Socinians, Anabaptists, and Remonstrants oppose and deny perseverance
	• They depart from the orthodox doctrine and were condemned by the Synod of Dort

â€¢ ••Statement of the Question••
	• The question concerning perseverance is stated as whether the true believer can ever totally or finally fall from faith

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••Who is the question about?••
	• Not about believers and saints who are equivocally called
	• Not about those who are univocally and properly believers, planted in Christ by true faith

â€¢ ••What is the question not about?••
	• Not about the possibility of failing on man's part
	• Not about the act or exercise of faith (e.g. interruptions, diminishment)
	• Not about demeritorious loss of faith (i.e. loss due to human failure)

â€¢ ••What is the question about?••
	• The possibility of failing on God's part (hypothetically and relatively)
	• The essence of spiritual life and the state and habit of faith
	• Whether a true believer can lose faith effectively and totally

â€¢ ••What is the question not asking?••
	• Whether a believer can lose faith due to enormous sins (although this is a related issue)
	• Whether a believer can incur God's paternal indignation or lose fitness for the kingdom of heaven

â€¢ ••What is the question really asking?••
	• Whether a true believer can fall into the hostile hatred of God, losing their right to the kingdom of heaven
	• Whether a believer can lose faith entirely, objectively and subjectively, and remain in unbelief and impenitency

â€¢ ••Who holds this view?••
	• The Pelagians, Romanists, Socinians, Remonstrants, and others who follow them

â€¢ ••What is the opposing view?••
	• That a true believer cannot lose faith effectively and totally, due to the intervening grace of God

â€¢ ••What is the scope of the question?••
	• Not just about the act of faith, but about the essence of spiritual life and the state and habit of faith
	• Not just about the believer's own failure, but about God's purpose and the event itself

â€¢ ••What is the outcome of losing faith?••
	• Eternal condemnation and separation from God and the kingdom of heaven

â€¢ ••What is the underlying issue?••
	• The nature of faith and its relationship to God's grace and purpose

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Orthodox View of Faith••

• The orthodox view holds that faith is a habit that can be strained or remitted, but never wholly and finally destroyed.
	• Faith can be weakened by sin, but not lost.
	• The grace of regeneration is not taken from man.

••II. Opponents' Views••

• Opponents are divided into two groups:
	• Some argue for a temporary cutting off of faith and justification.
		- Faith may fail, but is restored before death by God's special grace.
	• Others argue for a total and final apostasy of the saints and excision of faith.

••III. Proof of Perseverance of Faith••

• The orthodox view is supported by:
	• The election of God (immutable and unchangeable).
	• The nature of the covenant of grace (firm and immutable).

••IV. Election of God••

• The election of God is:
	• Eternal and unchangeable (Heb. 6:17; Rom. 9:11).
	• Firm and efficacious (2 Tim. 2:19).
	• Implies that faith, as a fruit of election, is firm and immutable.

••V. Nature of the Covenant of Grace••

• The covenant of grace is:
	• Firm and immutable.
	• Founded on God's grace alone, not on man's obedience.
	• Implies that the blessings dependent on it, including faith, justification, and regeneration, are perpetual and immutable.

••VI. Jeremiah's Prophecy••

• Jeremiah's prophecy (Jer. 31:32-33; 32) testifies to the covenant of grace:
	• God will make a new covenant with the church, bestowing all saving gifts.
	• The covenant will be perpetual and eternal, with God's constant love and fear in the hearts of the people.

••VII. God's Promises••

• God promises:
	• To bestow both the constancy of his love and the perpetuity of our fear.
	• To fulfill both his part and ours in the covenant.

••VIII. Augustine's View••

• Augustine says:
	• God wills it to belong only to his grace that man should come to him.
	• God wills it to belong only to his grace that man should not depart from him.

••IX. Implications••

• The orthodox view implies that:
	• Faith is firm and immutable.
	• The covenant of grace is perpetual and eternal.
	• God's love and fear are constant and perpetual in the hearts of the people.

••X. Conclusion••

• The orthodox view is supported by the election of God and the nature of the covenant of grace.
• The covenant of grace implies that faith, justification, and regeneration are perpetual and immutable.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••God's promises of guardianship and preservation••

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••Conditional vs. Absolute Promises••
	• Conditional promises are not granted because they lead to an infinite regress
	• Absolute promises can be understood in two ways: excluding means or excluding conditions

â€¢ ••Meaning of Absolute Promises••
	• In one sense, absolute promises exclude means, but in another sense, they exclude conditions
	• The promise of perseverance is not conditional because there is no condition that does not fall under the promise itself

â€¢ ••Means of Fulfilling Promises••
	• Perseverance is not physical, but moral, and can be perfected by man through the aid of grace
	• The means of fulfilling promises are included in the promise itself, so they can be fulfilled by man

â€¢ ••God's Role in Fulfilling Promises••
	• The defect is not on God's part, but on man's, who withdraws himself from what is offered
	• God fortifies us from external enemies, but not from ourselves and domestic perfidy

â€¢ ••Scripture's View of Promises••
	• Scripture makes no mention of a condition as the cause of fulfillment of the promise
	• Instead, it intimates that God promises and affords the very conditions he requires

â€¢ ••Faith and Repentance••
	• Faith and repentance are required in the subject because the promise is given only to the believer
	• However, perseverance which is promised ought not to be supposed at once

â€¢ ••Promises to the Church••
	• The promises made to the church regard also its individual true members who share in the nature of the body

â€¢ ••Jeremiah 31 and 32••
