Here are 10 concise bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. The Nature of Righteousness••

• The righteousness of the righteous is not enough to save them if it is not constant and perpetual.
	• If the righteous turns away, all their previous works are in vain.
	• They will die in their iniquity because they have not persevered in righteousness.

••II. The Case of Judas••

• Judas is not considered one of the elect who were given to Christ to be saved.
	• He is referred to as the "son of perdition" (John 17:12).
	• He was destined for perdition and destruction by God's eternal judgment.

••III. Falling from Grace••

• There are two ways to fall from grace: positively and negatively.
	• Positively: a real privation of grace already received.
	• Negatively: not obtaining grace in the first place.

••IV. The Incompatibility of Grace and Merit••

• Seeking righteousness in the law is incompatible with receiving grace.
	• Those who seek their righteousness in the law will fall from grace.

••V. Deliverance to Satan••

• There are two ways to be delivered to Satan: for eternal torment and for destruction of the flesh.
	• The believer can be delivered in the latter way, not the former.

••VI. Excommunication••

• Excommunication does not exclude the fallen from the kingdom of heaven.
	• It is a healthful medicine that works in true believers through the grace of God.
	• The excommunicated person does not cease to be a member of Christ, although they may be cut off from the external body of the church.

••VII. The Mercy of God••

• Although saints deserve exclusion from the kingdom of heaven due to grievous sins, God's mercy intervenes.
	• Their right to the kingdom of heaven is not taken away.
	• Justification and adoption are not recalled.
	• Their state of regeneration is not lost.

••VIII. The Purpose of Excommunication••

• Excommunication is a means of correction and reform.
	• It is a rod of a pious mother over a bad son.
	• The goal is to reform the individual and not cease to be a member of Christ.

••IX. The Relationship between Excommunication and Salvation••

• Excommunication does not affect a person's salvation.
	• It is a temporary measure to correct and reform the individual.

••X. The Importance of Perseverance••

• Perseverance in righteousness is necessary for salvation.
	• The righteous must persevere in their righteousness to receive eternal life.

â€¢ ••Objective vs. Subjective Certainty of Faith••
	• The text distinguishes between objective certainty (the doctrine delivered in the word) and subjective certainty (the habit of believing).
	• Objective certainty should be evident from Scripture, while subjective certainty arises from the believer's heart and experience.

â€¢ ••Certainty of Faith••
	• The text notes that the certainty of faith is not lessened by the fact that it is not explicitly stated in Scripture.
	• Rather, it is deduced from and founded upon the doctrine delivered in the word.

â€¢ ••Two Kinds of Certainty••
	• The text notes that there are two kinds of certainty: revealed and experimental.
	• Both kinds of certainty are of divine faith, resting on a divine and infallible testimony.

â€¢ ••Fear and Certainty••
	• The text notes that not every fear is incompatible with the certainty of grace.
	• Servile fear (fear of punishment) is incompatible with certainty, while filial fear (fear of sin) is not.

â€¢ ••Filial Fear and Certainty••
	• Filial fear is actually a means of producing and confirming certainty in believers.
	• This fear is directed towards avoiding sin and promoting holiness.

â€¢ ••Certainty and Means••
	• The text notes that certainty does not exclude the means of achieving it, but rather supposes the necessity of the means.
	• Therefore, filial fear, which is a means of achieving holiness, does not take away certainty, but rather posits it.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Definition of Faith••

• Faith is not just a feeling, but a sincere and contrite heart (Ps. 51:17)
	• Not hypocritical, but genuine and prayerful (Ps. 32:5)
	• Based on Christian liberty and gratuitous justification (Rom. 6:2; 1 Pet. 2:15, 16)

••II. Object and Mode of Faith••

• Faith is directed towards God and Christ (the fountain of all good and the fullness of grace)
	• Not based on novelty or license to sin, but on Christian liberty
	• Involves contrition, grief for sin, and a desire for righteousness

••III. Acts of Faith••

• Faith involves a permanent sense of grace, a good conscience, and carefulness to avoid sin
	• A desire to approve oneself to God through the practice of holiness
	• Not a momentary or superficial commitment, but a serious and constant one

••IV. Perfection of Faith••

• Absolute perfection is not expected, but sincerity is
	• Christ does not break the bruised reed or extinguish the smoking flax
	• The quality of faith is more important than its quantity

••V. Belief and Certainty••

• What we are bound to believe with divine faith should be believed as undoubted
	• Articles of faith are immediately revealed and independent of us
	• But the certainty of remission of sins is not immediately revealed, but arises from inner experience and sense of the heart

••VI. Conditional Certainty••

• Conditional certainty depends on some condition, such as the use of means
	• This is the kind of certainty the believer has concerning the remission of sins
	• It is not absolute, but depends on the believer's use of means to confirm it

••VII. Fear and Certainty••

• Fear of a future evil is incompatible with certainty
	• But fear of an evil that could happen unless we guard against it can produce certainty and induce solicitude and watchfulness

••VIII. Means and Certainty••

• The certainty we urge should always be connected with the use of means
	• We search for it in vain in the impenitent sinner
	• The believer cannot exercise true certainty while indulging in sin or committing grievous sin

••IX. Perseverance in Sin••

• Perseverance in sin is inconsistent with certainty
	• The believer should not be ignorant of this and should not say, "I was once certain of the grace of God, I ought therefore to be certain hereafter, whatever I may do."

••X. Conclusion••

• The believer should always be aware of the need to use means to confirm their certainty
	• This involves a serious and constant commitment to the practice of holiness.

â€¢ ••Proper and improper uses of the verb "justify"••
	• Properly, the verb means to absolve or declare someone just in a trial
	• Improperly, it can mean to bring to righteousness, free, or compare someone's justice to another's

â€¢ ••Question with Romanists••
	• The question with Romanists is whether the word "justify" should be taken precisely in a forensic sense or also in a physical and moral sense
	• Romanists do not deny that the word can be used in a forensic sense, but they argue that it often signifies a true production, acquisition, or increase of righteousness

â€¢ ••Definition of Justification••
	• Justification is a movement from sin to righteousness

â€¢ ••Proof that Justification is Forensic••
	• The word "justification" is used in a forensic sense in various passages (e.g. Job 9:3, Ps. 143:2, Rom. 3:28)

â€¢ ••Opposition to Condemnation••
	• Justification is opposed to condemnation (Rom. 8:33-34)
	• Condemnation implies a trial, and therefore justification must also imply a trial
	• To condemn or justify implies a judicial decision, either to punish or absolve

â€¢ ••Equivalent Phrases••
	• Equivalent phrases for justification are judicial in nature (e.g. "not to come into judgment", "not to be condemned")
	• These phrases imply a forensic sense of justification

â€¢ ••Paul's Use of the Word••
	• Paul used the word "justification" in a forensic sense in his dispute with the Jews
	• He did not speak of an infusion of righteousness, but rather of how the sinner could stand before God's judgment seat

â€¢ ••Fear of Divine Judgment••
	• The thought of justification arose from a fear of divine judgment and wrath
	• Therefore, the word "justification" must be used in a forensic sense

â€¢ ••Distinction from Sanctification••
	• Justification and sanctification are distinct concepts
	• The nature of the thing and Scripture frequently prove this distinction

â€¢ ••Consequences of a Non-Forensic Sense••
	• If the word "justification" is not used in a forensic sense, it would be confounded with sanctification
	• This would lead to confusion and misinterpretation of Scripture

â€¢ ••Agreement with Other Theologians••
	• Even theologians like Tolemus and Cornelius a Lapide agree that justification implies a forensic sense

â€¢ ••Conclusion••
	• The word "justification" must be used in a forensic sense, implying a judicial decision to absolve or condemn.

	• Ablution is a specific benefit that is adumbrated in baptism
	• Justification is a more general term that includes both justification and sanctification

â€¢ ••Sources of Explanation••
	• The apostle's intention is to disclose the foundation of the connection between being exposed to death and the right to life
	• This connection is based on our union with the first and second Adam

â€¢ ••Abundance of Grace••
	• The "abundance of grace and of righteousness" (Rom. 5:17) does not denote habitual grace or inherent righteousness
	• This abundance of divine mercy and righteousness is obtained through the obedience of the Mediator

â€¢ ••Imputation of Righteousness••
	• The gift of righteousness is said to be greater than the sin of Adam
	• This is because the grace of God gives us the righteousness of Christ, which takes away the guilt of all actual sins

â€¢ ••Faith and Imputation••
	• We receive the abundance of grace by the hand of faith
	• This is not by way of infusion or inhesion, but by way of imputation

â€¢ ••Christ's Name••
	• To be justified in the name of Christ is nothing else than to be justified by and on account of Christ
	• There is no other name by which we can obtain salvation

â€¢ ••Regeneration and Justification••
	• Paul does not say that we are justified by regeneration
	• Justification is ascribed to the grace of God, not to righteousness inhering by regeneration

â€¢ ••Two Benefits••
	• God bestows two benefits upon us: regeneration and justification
	• Regeneration is the fruit of justification, not the cause

â€¢ ••The Design of the Apostle••
	• The apostle's intention is to point out how God will have us saved by two benefits
	• This is based on our union with the first and second Adam

â€¢ ••Justification is through faith, not inherent righteousness••

â€¢ ••The accusation of sin cannot be removed by our own righteousness••
	• Our own righteousness, even if infused, cannot remove the accusation of sin
	• It cannot make the accusation false, nor can it expunge it through suffering

â€¢ ••Justification is through the satisfaction of Christ, not our own efforts••

	• This is the fundamental basis of justification, not our own righteousness or good works.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Introduction••

• The question of justification is crucial for Christians
• The text aims to affirm the righteousness and obedience of Christ as the meritorious cause of justification

••II. The Nature of Justification••

• Justification is a forensic act of God, not a private transaction
	• It is a ruling of a supreme magistrate, not a subordinate judge
	• God acts according to his autocratic right, showing favor to the guilty
• God's justice requires satisfaction for sin, which cannot be ignored

••III. The Need for a Perfect Righteousness••

• God cannot justify anyone without a perfect righteousness
• No mortal has such righteousness after sin, so it must be sought in another
• Human courts often justify the guilty through ignorance, injury, or iniquity, but God's court cannot

••IV. The Role of Christ••

• The gospel teaches that Christ, the God-man, is the one who satisfies God's justice
• Christ's perfect obedience and sacrifice bring an eternal righteousness to us
• This righteousness is the only means by which we can be justified before God

••V. The Implication of Christ's Righteousness••

• Christ's righteousness is imputed to us, making us just before God
• This imputation is the foundation of our justification, not our own inherent righteousness

••VI. The Rejection of Romanist and Socinian Views••

• The Romanists and Socinians place justification in inherent righteousness, which is rejected
• The true cause of justification is the righteousness and obedience of Christ, imputed to us by God

••VII. The Importance of Understanding Justification••

• The truth and mode of justification must be clearly seen and strongly retained
• The text aims to provide a clear understanding of justification against the cavils of opponents

••VIII. The Role of Mercy in Justification••

• God's mercy is not in conflict with his justice, but rather is an expression of it
• God's justice requires satisfaction for sin, which is provided by Christ's sacrifice

••IX. The Satisfaction of God's Justice••

• Christ's sacrifice satisfies God's justice, making it possible for God to show favor to the guilty
• This satisfaction is the foundation of our justification, not our own inherent righteousness

••X. The Conclusion••

• The righteousness and obedience of Christ are the meritorious cause of our justification
• This is the only means by which we can be justified before God, and it is the foundation of our salvation.

••IV. Adoption and Inheritance••

• Adoption and inheritance are a greater blessing than being freed from punishment
• To be pronounced children and heirs is the climax and crowning blessing of mercy

••V. Connection between Remission and Imputation••

• Paul argues from remission of sins to imputation of righteousness (Rom. 4:5-7)
• Remission of sins is given to no one without imputation of righteousness, and vice versa

••VI. Remission of Sins••

• Remission of sins does not consist in an absolute removal of them
• Rather, it consists in the pardon of them

••VII. Punishment after Remission••

• After guilt is remitted, a certain punishment is retained
• This punishment is not wholly remitted

••VIII. Romanist View••

• The Romanists deny that remission of sins consists in the pardon of them
• They affirm that remission of sins consists in an absolute removal of them

••IX. Three Propositions••

• The remission of sins is not the abolition of them (against Romanists)
• The remission of sins does not consist in an absolute removal of them
• The remission of sins consists in the pardon of them

••X. Conclusion••

• Remission of sins is a complex concept that involves pardon and imputation of righteousness
• It is not the same as absolute removal of sins or abolition of them.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Definition of Remission••

• Remission of sin is the pardon of the criminality and guilt arising from sin, not the removal of the corruption itself.
	• This is opposed to the Romanist view that remission involves the real taking away of sin, both corruption and guilt.

••II. Arguments Against the Romanist View••

• The mode of speaking and signification of remission among men implies pardon, not extinction of sin.
	• A prince remitting a crime does not take it away, but pardons it and frees it from punishment.
• Scripture uses synonymous phrases to teach that remission involves pardon, not removal of sin.
	• Examples: "covering" (Ps. 32:1), "not imputing" (Ps. 31:2), "not remembering" (Jer. 31:34), "blotting out" (Pss. 51:1; 103:12; Acts 3:19; Col. 2:14), "casting behind his back" (Mic. 7:19), "purging" (Heb. 1:3; 9:14), "turning away" (Ps. 51:9), "putting away" (2 S. 12:13).

••III. Implications of the Romanist View••

• If remission of sin involved the taking away of inherent corruption, it would be perfect, but Scripture testifies that sin remains in us.
	• Saints always struggle with the flesh and the Spirit.
• If not imputing sin is to expel it and infuse righteousness, then imputing sin would be to infuse sin.
	• This is false, as seen in the case of Christ, to whom sin was imputed but not infused.

••IV. Nature of Remission••

• Remission consists in freeing the guilty person from actual punishment, not from all vitiosity.
	• Potential guilt and the intrinsic merit of sin remain, even after remission.
• Paul says there is no condemnation to those in Christ (Rom. 8:1), but this does not mean there is nothing condemnable or worthy of condemnation.
	• Sin remains in us as long as we live, and there is always something condemnable, although God does not actually condemn us due to interceding grace.

••V. Theoretical Covering of Sinners••

• There is a theoretical covering of sinners that belongs to omniscience, according to which it is certain that nothing can be hidden from God.
	• This covering is not the same as the actual pardon of sin through remission.

	• It does not mean sin is absolutely taken away

	• Remission of sins is expressed by various phrases, but does not imply total abolition of sin

â€¢ ••Remission vs. abolition of sin••

â€¢ ••Pardon vs. expulsion••

â€¢ ••Second proposition: remission of sin••

â€¢ ••Implications of partial remission••
	• If guilt is remitted while punishment is not, it would introduce great disturbance into the Scriptures
	• It would also pour great darkness over the divine promises and threatenings

â€¢ ••Ancient Indulgences••

â€¢ ••Modification of Indulgences••

â€¢ ••Difference between Ancient and Modern Indulgences••

	• Modern indulgences are held to be relaxations of the satisfactory punishments of divine justice

â€¢ ••Extension of Remission to All Sins••

â€¢ ••Distinction between Past and Future Sins••

	• Remission of sin requires confession and repentance, which cannot be made until the sin is committed

â€¢ ••Justification and Remission••
	• Justification leaves no room for condemnation
	• Remission of sins is applied to sins committed, not anticipated

â€¢ ••Daily Remission of Sins••
	• Sinners are ordered to seek remission of sins every day
	• Remission is applied to sins committed, not to anticipate their perpetration

â€¢ ••What is Adoption?••
	• A juridical act of God by which he adopts individuals into his family through faith in Christ
	• Based on his mercy, not merit
	• Bestows the name and right of sons as to inheritance

â€¢ ••Types of Adoption••
	• Not an external calling and reception into the covenant (as with the Jews)
	• Not emancipation (as with believers in the New Testament)
	• Not the full manifestation of adoption (which will occur in the resurrection)

â€¢ ••Definition of Adoption••
	• A lawful act imitating nature introduced for the consolation of those who have no children
	• Requires an adopter, a person adopted, and a change in the person's state and name

â€¢ ••Key Elements of Adoption••
	• The adopter is God, who exercises his gracious will towards us
	• The person adopted is a stranger and foreigner, transferred from the family of the old Adam to God's family
	• The adopter gives the person adopted the dignity of sons and a right to all his goods of grace and glory

â€¢ ••How Adoption Differs from Human Adoption••
	• A work of mere good will (eudokias), not a legal or contractual arrangement
	• Not based on human merit or effort, but on God's mercy and election

â€¢ ••The Purpose of Adoption••
	• To transfer us from the family of the old Adam and the power of darkness to God's family and the kingdom of light
	• To give us the dignity of sons and a right to all God's goods of grace and glory

â€¢ ••The Result of Adoption••
	• We are given the glorious name of dearly beloved sons
	• We are given a right to all God's goods of grace and glory
	• We are bound to filial worship and obedience to God

â€¢ ••The Basis of Adoption••
	• Not based on human merit or effort, but on God's mercy and election
	• Based on our faith in Christ and our election to salvation from eternity

â€¢ ••The Analogy with Civil Adoption••
	• While there are similarities, there are also significant differences
	• Human adoption is a legal and contractual arrangement, whereas God's adoption is a work of mere good will

â€¢ ••The Significance of Adoption••
	• It is a fundamental aspect of our relationship with God
	• It gives us a new identity and a new status as sons of God
	• It is a source of great joy and comfort for believers

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Adoption as a Divine Act••

• God adopts believers as sons, not because they are good, but to make them good.
	• This adoption is a work of mere grace, not based on human merit.
	• It supposes nothing good in us, but rather transforms us into good children.

••II. The Testamentary Disposition••

• The Father's testamentary disposition is the final and immutable will sealed in Scripture.
	• It is confirmed by the blood and death of Christ.
	• It pronounces elect believers as heirs of God's kingdom.

••III. The Inheritance••

• The goods left by the testament pertain to the inheritance of heaven or the kingdom of heaven.
	• This inheritance is especially the inheritance of God himself.
	• Believers are the portion and inheritance of God.

••IV. Common Privilege••

• The privilege of being sons of God and heirs of the heavenly inheritance is common to all believers.
	• Both Old and New Testament believers share this privilege.

••V. Condition of New Testament Believers••

• New Testament believers are no longer in an infantile age, but are adults and emancipated by Christ.
	• They have a full sense and fruit of their right, thanks to the Spirit of adoption.
	• They can confidently cry out, "Abba, Father."

••VI. Adoption as a Benefit••

• Adoption is a benefit by which God makes us good children.
	• It is not a benefit that we earn, but rather one that is given to us by God's grace.

••VII. Justification and Adoption••

• Justification and adoption are not separate benefits, but rather different aspects of God's gracious work in us.
	• Adoption is not prior to justification, but rather a consequence of it.

••VIII. Adoption as a Work of Grace••

• Adoption is a work of mere grace, not based on human merit.
	• It supposes nothing good in us, but rather transforms us into good children.

••IX. The Spirit of Adoption••

• The Spirit of adoption is received by believers, allowing them to confidently cry out, "Abba, Father."
	• This Spirit gives us a full sense and fruit of our right as sons of God.

••X. Conclusion••

• The privilege of being sons of God and heirs of the heavenly inheritance is a common privilege shared by all believers.
	• New Testament believers have a better condition than Old Testament believers, thanks to the Spirit of adoption.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Adoption and Justification••

• Adoption is included in justification as a part that constitutes the whole benefit of justification.
	• Adoption includes the remission of sins and the acceptance to life.
	• It is not distinguished from justification except in its formal conception.

••II. Adoption and Union with Christ••

• Adoption cannot be confounded with union with Christ.
	• Union with Christ is the cause and foundation of adoption.
	• Adoption is an effect of union with Christ.

••III. Christian Liberty••

• Christian liberty flows from adoption.
	• It is not an immunity from all laws and a license to live according to pleasure.
	• It is a spiritual and mystical manumission obtained by the blood of Christ.

••IV. Christian Liberty (continued)••

• Christian liberty is obtained through the communion of all Christ's benefits.
	• It includes the communion of justification, sanctification, and glory.
	• It brings dominion over creatures and heirship to the kingdom of Heaven.

••V. Justification of Faith••

• The question is whether faith justifies properly and by itself or only relatively and instrumentally.
	• The Socinians, Remonstrants, and Romanists maintain that faith justifies properly and by itself.

••VI. Justification (continued)••

• Justification can be viewed actively (on the part of God) or passively (on the part of man).
	• A twofold handling of justification can be adopted: with respect to the benefit conferred by God or with respect to its reception and application by faith.

••VII. Faith and Justification••

• Faith justifies, but the manner in which it justifies is disputed.
	• The Socinians maintain that faith justifies properly and by itself.

••VIII. Active and Passive Justification••

• Justification can be viewed actively (on the part of God) or passively (on the part of man).
	• The benefit of justification is conferred by God, and its reception and application are made by faith.

••IX. Christian Liberty and Adoption••

• Christian liberty flows from adoption.
	• It is a spiritual and mystical manumission obtained by the blood of Christ.

••X. Conclusion••

• The question of whether faith justifies properly and by itself or only relatively and instrumentally is disputed.
	• The Socinians, Remonstrants, and Romanists maintain that faith justifies properly and by itself.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Justification and its Declaration••

• Justification should be declared immediately after death and publicly on the last day
	• This declaration is a solemn declaration of the justification once made and an adjudication of the reward
	• It is not a justification in itself, but rather a declaration of the justification that has already taken place

••II. Justification as an Undivided Act••

• Justification is an undivided act on the part of God
	• It is not a series of successive acts, but rather a single act
	• This act is based on God's decree, merit, and application of the absolving sentence

••III. Unity, Perfection, and Certainty of Justification••

• The unity, perfection, and certainty of justification are the three principal adjuncts of justification
	• These will be discussed briefly, as they have been discussed partially elsewhere

••IV. Unity of Justification among Believers••

• Unity can be regarded in two ways: relative to believers among themselves and absolutely with respect to him who is justified
	• In the former sense, justification is "one in species" or "equal in all believers" of all times and places
	• This is because God justifies all believers in the same manner, by his grace and the merit of Christ through faith

••V. Examples of Justification••

• The apostle Paul proves that justification is by faith in Romans 3:30 and Romans 4
	• He cites examples of David and Abraham, who were justified by faith
	• He also cites examples of all the saints of the Old Testament, who were justified by faith

••VI. No Dissimilar Examples••

• There are no dissimilar examples of a person justified in another way in the Old or New Testament
	• Peter says that all the prophets witness that through Christ's name, whoever believes will receive remission of sins

••VII. Christ as the Same Yesterday, Today, and Forever••

• Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever
	• He is the Way, the Truth, and the Life, and no one can come to the Father except by him

••VIII. Objections to the Identity of Justification••

• The Socinians brought forward objections against the identity of justification of the believers of the Old and New Testaments
	• These objections are discussed in Topic XII, Question 5 concerning the unity of the covenant of grace

••IX. Difference in Degree and Sense••

• Although the same benefit as to substance was common to the believers of the Old Testament no less than to those of the New, there was a multiple difference as to degree and sense
	• This difference is more clearly revealed and more fully and efficaciously felt by us now

••X. Numerical Unity of Justification••

• The same justification is one numerically in individuals
	• It is not promoted successively after the manner of sanctification by repeated acts, but is finished in one judicial act

Here are the 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••I. Romanist Error on Justification••
	• Romanists believe in a twofold justification: one by infusion of righteousness and another by increase of righteousness
	• This is based on a false hypothesis and contradicts the biblical concept of justification

â€¢ ••II. Justification is a Single Event••
	• Justification is a single event that occurs when a person is justified by faith
	• It is not a process or a series of events

â€¢ ••III. Justification is not Infused••
	• Justification is not an infusion of righteousness, but rather a declaration of righteousness
	• It is not a physical change, but rather a spiritual one

â€¢ ••IV. Justification is not a Feeling••
	• The blessing of justification is a gift that is not dependent on feelings or emotions
	• It is a gift that is received through faith

â€¢ ••V. Justification is not Renewed••
	• Justification is not renewed or repeated, but rather it is a one-time event
	• The blessing of justification remains the same, even if the believer's feelings or knowledge of it change

â€¢ ••VI. Active and Passive Justification••
	• Active justification refers to God's declaration of righteousness
	• Passive justification refers to the believer's reception of that declaration through faith

â€¢ ••VII. Justification and Sanctification••
	• Justification and sanctification are related, but distinct concepts
	• Sanctification is the process of growing in righteousness, while justification is the declaration of righteousness

â€¢ ••VIII. Justification is not Declared on the Last Day••
	• Justification is not declared on the last day, but rather it is a gift that is received through faith
	• The sentence pronounced by the supreme Judge on the last day is a declaration of the possession of the kingdom of heaven, not a new justification

â€¢ ••IX. Justification is not Repeated••
	• Justification is not repeated or renewed, but rather it is a one-time event
	• The believer's justification is sufficient to cover all sins, even if they fall into new sin

â€¢ ••X. Remission of Sins is not Revival of Sin••
	• Remission of sins is not the revival of sin, but rather it is a gift that is received through faith
	• The parable of the ungrateful servant does not teach that sins once discharged revive and return again.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••1. The Parable of the Unmerciful Servant••
• The parable in Matthew 18:23-35 is used to illustrate that God's mercy is not exercised towards the unmerciful.
• The parable shows that sins are not pardoned by God unless the person forgives the offenses of others.

••2. Perfection in Justification••
• Perfection belongs to justification, which is a complete and absolute state.
• Justification is free from increase and decrease, but our faith in it can advance gradually.
• Justification is not intermittent, even if our faith is active and remitted.

••3. Certainty of Justification••
• The certainty of justification is twofold:
	• One aspect is the object of justification, which is the immutability and perseverance of God's pardon.
	• The other aspect is the subject of justification, which refers to the sense of justification in the believer's heart.

••4. Immutability of God's Pardon••
• God's pardon is immutable and never recalled.
• The gifts of God bestowed upon the elect are without repentance.

••5. Certainty of the Subject••
• The certainty of the subject refers to the sense of justification in the believer's heart.
• This sense of justification can vary in degree, depending on the proportion of faith.

••6. Doubts Concerning Grace••
• Even believers, including Abraham and David, have struggled with doubts concerning God's grace.

••7. Sanctification and Justification••
• Sanctification is a real and internal renovation of man, which is distinct from justification.
• Sanctification is the benefit of sanctification that immediately follows justification.

••8. Homonyms of Sanctification••
• The word "sanctification" is used in different ways in Scripture, including:
	• Separation from common use and consecration to a sacred use.
	• Federal sanctity by external calling.
	• Internal renovation of man.

••9. Definition of Sanctification••
• Sanctification is a real and internal renovation of man, which delivers the believer from native depravity and transforms him into God's image.

••10. Relationship between Sanctification and Justification••
• Sanctification is inseparable from justification, but yet really distinct from it.
• The benefit of sanctification immediately follows justification as an inseparable connection.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Distinguishing Justification and Sanctification••

• ••Justification and Sanctification are distinct••
	• They have different objects, forms, recipients, degrees, and orders
• ••Justification is concerned with guilt, while sanctification is concerned with pollution••
	• Justification deals with the remission of sin and imputation of righteousness
	• Sanctification deals with the infusion of righteousness and internal renovation

••II. Key Differences••

• ••Object••: Justification deals with guilt, while sanctification deals with pollution
• ••Form••: Justification is a judicial and forensic act, while sanctification is a physical and moral act
• ••Recipient••: Justification is received objectively, while sanctification is received subjectively
• ••Degrees••: Justification is given fully in this life, while sanctification is begun in this life but perfected in the next
• ••Order••: Justification is prior to sanctification in the order of nature

••III. Relationship between Justification and Sanctification••

• ••Justification is a prerequisite for sanctification••
	• God sanctifies those who are reconciled and justified by faith
• ••Sanctification is not included in justification••
	• Sanctification is a separate benefit that is distinct from justification

••IV. Sanctification and Glory••

• ••Sanctification is often referred to as "glory"••
	• This is because sanctification is the beginning of glory
• ••Sanctification is a complement to glorification••
	• Glorification is the consummation of sanctification

••V. Sanctification and Righteousness••

• ••Sanctification makes us righteous habitually••
	• However, it does not make us righteous imputatively or justified
• ••The etymology of sanctification does not prove that it is the same as justification••

••VI. Sanctification and Sin••

• ••Sanctification purges us from all sin••
	• However, this must be understood as the removal of pollution, not guilt
• ••Guilt remains until justification••

••VII. Cause of Justification and Sanctification••

• ••Justification and sanctification have the same cause (the blood and death of Christ)••
	• However, they are not the same because the cause produces them in different ways
• ••Justification is related to sanctification materially, while sanctification is related to the cause efficiently and mediately••

••VIII. Baptism and Justification/Sanctification••

• ••Baptism seals both justification and sanctification••
	• However, each benefit is sealed according to its own fashion
• ••Justification takes away guilt, while sanctification removes pollution••

••IX. Power of the Blood of Christ••

• ••The blood of Christ has a twofold power••
	• It takes away guilt and covers sin, and it removes and washes away pollution.

••I. The Council of Trent's Position••

• The Council of Trent affirms that the commands of God are possible to be observed by the justified man.
• However, it also acknowledges that a perfect observance of the law is not possible for the believer, except by a special privilege from God.

••II. The Imperfection of Sanctification••

• The imperfection of sanctification and the impossibility of fulfilling the law are proven:
	• From the remains of sin
	• From the struggle between the flesh and the Spirit

••III. The Remains of Sin••

• Sin always dwells in believers, as stated in 1 John 1:8, James 3:2, 1 Kings 8:46, and Proverbs 20:9.
• To say that these sins are only venial is to suppose what is to be decided, as all sin is mortal and against the law.

••IV. Augustine's Position••

• Augustine distinguishes between two questions:
	• Can the commands be kept?
	• Can man live without sin?
• However, he does not find these questions to be distinct, as one cannot obey the commands without living without sin.

••V. The Struggle between Flesh and Spirit••

• The struggle between the flesh and the Spirit is a source of imperfection in sanctification.
• This struggle is a result of the remains of sin in believers.

••VI. The Impossibility of Fulfilling the Law••

• The impossibility of fulfilling the law is proven from the remains of sin.
• No one can obey the commands without living without sin, and no one can live without sin unless they keep the commandments.

••VII. The Council of Trent's Canon 23••

• Canon 23 of the Council of Trent pronounces an anathema on those who teach that a person once justified can avoid even venial sins, except by a special privilege from God.

••VIII. The Hypocrisy of Bellarmine••

• Bellarmine argues that the sins of believers are only venial, but this is to suppose what is to be decided.
• He also distinguishes between two questions, but this is a false distinction.

••IX. The Necessity of a Special Privilege••

• The necessity of a special privilege from God for perfect observance of the law is acknowledged by the Council of Trent.

••X. The Imperfection of Sanctification••

• The imperfection of sanctification and the impossibility of fulfilling the law are proven from the remains of sin and the struggle between the flesh and the Spirit.

	• ••2. Excessive Affirmation••: Others (e.g. Pharisees, false apostles, Romanists, Socinians) affirm the necessity of good works
		- They believe good works are necessary for justification and merit
	• ••3. Orthodox View••: The orthodox view holds that good works are necessary, but not for merit or causality

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Romanist Definition of Merit••

• The Romanists define "merit" as an action to which a reward is due.
	• They distinguish between three types of merit: congruity, worth, and condignity.

••II. Types of Merit••

• ••Congruity••: a work morally good, done from free will unassisted by grace.
	• Suitable to the divine goodness to infuse the grace of justification.
• ••Worth••: the suitableness or aptitude of the worker to obtain what they deserve.
	• Based on the person working rather than the work itself.
• ••Condignity••: a good work done from free will assisted by grace.
	• Worthy of a reward due to the intrinsic value of the work and the equality between the work and the reward.

••III. Reduction of Merit Types••

• Some modern Romanists (e.g. Bellarmine) reduce the three types to two:
	• Merit of congruity is reduced to merit of worth.
	• Merit of condignity remains the same.

••IV. Critique of Romanist Merit••

• Many Romanists (e.g. Thomas Waldensis, Paul Burgensis) reject the concept of merit of congruity.
• Others (e.g. Stapleton, Becanus) acknowledge its emptiness and lack of relation to merit.

••V. Definition of Merit••

• Biel defines merit as "a work imputable to praise" (worthy of praise).
• Bellarmine enumerates seven conditions of a meritorious work:
	• 1. Good work
	• 2. Free work
	• 3. Done in obedience to God
	• 4. Done by a justified person and a friend of God
	• 5. Proceeds from love
	• 6. Has the promise of God annexed
	• 7. Has intrinsic worth and value

••VI. Conditions of Merit••

• The conditions listed by Bellarmine are not sufficient to render a work meritorious.
• True merit requires something additional, such as intrinsic worth and value.

••VII. Romanist View of Merit••

• The Romanists believe that merit is a means of obtaining eternal life.
• They see merit as a way of earning God's favor and reward.

••VIII. Protestant Critique of Romanist Merit••

• Protestants reject the Romanist view of merit as earning God's favor.
• They see merit as a work of the law, rather than a work of faith.

••IX. Implications of Merit••

• The concept of merit has implications for the nature of salvation and the relationship between God and humanity.
• It raises questions about the role of works and faith in obtaining eternal life.

••X. Conclusion••

• The Romanist view of merit is complex and nuanced, with different types and conditions.
• The Protestant critique of Romanist merit highlights the differences between the two traditions.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••Understanding Merit of Condignity••
	• Merit of condignity refers to the idea that good works deserve a reward from God due to their inherent worth.
	• This concept is distinct from merit of congruity, which refers to the idea that good works are pleasing to God and deserving of a reward due to His gracious nature.

â€¢ ••Romanist Opinions on Merit of Condignity••
	• There are three main opinions among Romanists on merit of condignity:
		- Opinion 1: Good works are meritorious from condignity by reason of the work itself.
		- Opinion 2: Good works are not meritorious from condignity by reason of the work, but only by reason of the divine covenant and acceptance.
		- Opinion 3: Good works are meritorious neither simply in themselves, nor only from the covenant, but with respect to the covenant and the work at the same time.

â€¢ ••Council of Trent's Stance on Merit••
	• The Council of Trent explicitly asserted the existence of merits, but did not clarify the reason or mode of merit.
	• The Council's statement was intentionally ambiguous to avoid taking a stance on the Scholastic debates surrounding merit.

â€¢ ••Bellarmine's Opinion on Merit••
	• Bellarmine follows Opinion 3, which holds that good works are meritorious with respect to both the covenant and the work.
	• Bellarmine's opinion is that of the Council of Trent, although nothing certain can be drawn from the Council's statement.

â€¢ ••Scotus' Opinion on Merit••
	• Scotus and his followers hold that good works proceeding from grace are not meritorious from condignity by reason of the work, but only by reason of the divine covenant and acceptance.

â€¢ ••Criticisms of Romanist Opinions••
	• The Romanist opinions on merit of condignity are criticized for being unclear and ambiguous.
	• The opinions are also criticized for being overly focused on the work itself, rather than the divine covenant and acceptance.

â€¢ ••The Problem with Merit of Condignity••
	• The concept of merit of condignity is problematic because it implies that good works deserve a reward from God due to their inherent worth.
	• This concept can lead to Pharisaical pride and a diminished view of divine mercy.

â€¢ ••The State of the Question••
	• The question at hand is not whether good works are pleasing and acceptable to God, but rather whether they deserve a reward from God due to their inherent worth.
	• The question is also not whether it is lawful to work with a view to the reward, but rather what is the nature of the reward and how it is obtained.

â€¢ ••The Need for Clarity••
	• The Romanist opinions on merit of condignity are in need of clarification and definition.
	• A clear understanding of the concept of merit of condignity is necessary to avoid confusion and ambiguity.

â€¢ ••The Importance of Divine Mercy••
	• The concept of merit of condignity can lead to a diminished view of divine mercy and an overemphasis on human works.
	• A correct understanding of merit of condignity must take into account the role of divine mercy and the gracious nature of God.

••I. Caution in Regard to Rewards••

• The reward of eternal life should not be seen as a due price, but rather as a gratuitous boon.
	• This is to avoid a Pharisaical attitude that sees rewards as earned rather than given.
• The glory of God should be regarded above all things, and the reward of eternal life should be seen as secondary to this.

••II. The Relationship Between Works and Eternal Life••

• The question is not whether works have any relation to eternal life, but rather whether they have a causal relationship.
	• The answer is no, works do not have a causal relationship with eternal life.
• There is a fitness and proportion between good works and eternal life, but this is not a causal relationship.

••III. The Question of Merit••

• The question is not whether God is obligated to pay a reward to good works, but rather whether works merit and obtain the reward promised by God.
	• The answer is no, works do not merit and obtain the reward promised by God.

••IV. The Catholic Doctrine••

• The Catholic doctrine holds that the value and dignity of eternal life should be ascribed to the works of the just without any agreement or favor.
	• This is in contrast to the Protestant view that eternal life is a gratuitous gift.

••V. The Merits of Christ••

• The Catholic doctrine holds that the works of the just derive no accession of worth from the merits of Christ or from his person.
	• This is in contrast to the Protestant view that the merits of Christ are essential to salvation.

••VI. The Debt of God••

• The Catholic doctrine holds that God is a debtor and under obligation to man, not just from the promise but also from our work.
	• This is in contrast to the Protestant view that God's debt is only to himself and his own faithfulness.

••VII. The Gift of God••

• The Scriptures frequently and severely condemn the proud and Pharisaical doctrine that sees eternal life as a reward for good works.
	• Instead, eternal life is seen as a gratuitous gift from God.

••VIII. The Wages of Sin and Righteousness••

• The apostle Paul says that the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life.
	• This shows that eternal life is not acquired by merit, but is a gratuitous gift.

••IX. The Condition of Life and Death••

• The condition of life and death are not equal, and eternal life is not acquired by righteousness in the same way that death is acquired by sin.
	• Instead, eternal life is given to no merit, but is a gratuitous gift.

••X. The Protestant View••

• The Protestant view holds that eternal life is a gratuitous gift, conferred from pure liberality, and not acquired by merit.
	• This is in contrast to the Catholic doctrine that sees eternal life as a reward for good works.

••I. Christ's Merit••

• Christ's merit is unique and cannot be replicated by others.
	• Christ did not produce other christs secondarily.
	• Christ's merit did not produce other secondary merits.

	• Christ's merit has fully acquired the right we seek, making room for new merits unnecessary.

••II. The Simile of the Sun••

• The simile of the sun is not applicable to meritorious causes.
	• Meritorious causes cannot suffer subordination.
	• The order of nature is different from the order of grace.
	• God willed for Christ to be the unique and singular cause of our salvation.

••III. Believers' Merit••

• Believers, as servants of God, cannot merit anything.
	• Christ's words in Luke 17:10 are clear: "When ye shall have done all those things which are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do."
	• Christ speaks hypothetically and by way of concession.
	• Christ does not mean that believers speak only through humility and modesty.
	• Christ refers to believers as slaves who belong wholly to their master.

••IV. The Nature of Servants••

• Believers are called "unprofitable servants" not only because of their own nature, but also because of their state of grace.
	• The apostle addresses those who are supposed to do things which no one can do of himself.
	• Believers are useless to God and to themselves.
	• Since believers owe nothing to God, and can merit nothing from their master, it is incontestably proved that there can be no merit with God.

••V. Bellarmine's Response••

• Bellarmine tries to escape the force of these arguments, but ultimately takes refuge in Augustine's explication of the words of our Lord.
	• Augustine agrees that believers can be called unprofitable servants when they have kept all divine commands.
	• Augustine's explanation does not remove the difficulty, but rather highlights the unique relationship between God and believers.

	• The definition is faulty because it is not distinguished according to the various significations it has from Scripture, which are highly necessary to set forth its nature.
	• The definition is also faulty because it does not include, but excludes, the form and proper adjuncts of the thing defined (i.e., the church, by which it is itself constituted and distinguished from other assemblies of men).

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. The Church and Faith••

• The church is composed of members in whom faith ceases as to act and habit.
• However, a member can be in whom faith ceases only as to the second and exercised act (as in the excommunicated).
• Still not as to the first act and habit.

••II. The Excocommunicated••

• The excommunicated is one thing to hold as a heaten and a publican (i.e., to consider him an alien from religion and the communion of the church).
• Another for him to be such in the truth of the thing.
• Concerning the excommunicated, the former can be said, but not the latter.
• If they are not cut off from the body of Christ, they do not forthwith suffer loss, since it is a great harm to be cast forth from the visible church and to be deprived of the communion of sacred things.

••III. The Invisible Church••

• Bellarmine says, "The excommunicated is in the church in mind, or desire, which suffices him for salvation, still he is not in body, or by external communion, which properly makes a man belong to that visible church which is on earth."
• He plainly agrees with us because he holds that since there is no salvation out of the church, a certain invisible church must be acknowledged beside the visible.
• In it men can be saved in spirit, if not in body.
• He clearly confirms this when he says, "Excommunication makes the unjust friends of God and of the spirit of the church."

••IV. Schismatics••

• To touch briefly upon schismatics, we readily grant that those who rashly and unjustly secede from the true church, by lacerating its unity, do not belong to the church.
• But we reject those who spitefully traduce us with this false name (because "[we] are unwilling to be in subject to the Roman pontiff," as Bellarmine has it) as being excluded from it.

• A. Dissension among Christians is not a sign of disunity, but rather a sign of the truth being unimpaired.
• B. Dissension is a property of a well-constituted church.

••V. The Nature of Church Unity••

• A. Church unity is not a sign of true unity, but rather a sign of disunity.

• C. An agreement as to the foundation remains, even if there are differences in other matters.

••VI. Examples of Disunity in the Early Church••

• A. There were differences between the apostles about primacy, between Paul and Peter, Paul and Barnabas.
• B. There was a fierce contention between the Eastern and Western churches in the ancient church.

• ••Question 14: Can the Church of Rome today be called a true Church of Christ?••
	• The question is not about every church in Rome, but about the papal church of today under the power of the Pope.
	• The Romanists claim it is the only true church, but we deny this.
• ••Marks of the Church••
	• The question can be answered by considering the marks of the church, either concerning the Roman church or the Reformed and evangelical church.
	• We will treat this separately and first of the Roman church.
• ••The Church of Rome can be regarded in two ways••
	• Either as Christian, with regard to the profession of Christianity and the gospel truth it retains.
	• Or as papal, with regard to submission to the Pope and corruption and capital errors (in faith as well as morals) it has mingled with and built upon those truths beside and contrary to the word of God.
• ••Two aspects of the Church of Rome••
	• In the former respect, we do not deny that there is some truth in it.
	• In the latter (under which it is regarded here), we deny that it can be called Christian and apostolic, but Antichristian and apostate.
• ••Threefold respect in which the Church of Rome can be called Christian••
	• First, with respect to the people of God or the elect still remaining in it, who are ordered to come out of her, even at the time of the destruction of Babylon (Rev. 18:4).
	• Second, with respect to external form or certain ruins of a scattered church, in which its traces are seen to this day, both with respect to the word of God and the preaching of the gospel.
	• Third, with respect to a certain relative and improper sense, in which it can still be called a Christian church.

	• The Church is not built solely on the foundation of the prophets and apostles.

	• The Church adds to the foundation by joining the canonical Scriptures with unwritten human traditions.
	• These traditions are rejected by Christ himself (Matthew 15:9).
	• The Church lays another foundation than that which is laid (1 Corinthians 3:11).
	• The Church invents another head of the Church than Christ, with other merits besides his obedience alone.
• ••Consequences of Adding to the Foundation••
	• Adding things that are homogeneous with the foundation does not overthrow the foundation.
	• Adding things that are contrary and incompatible with the foundation does overthrow the foundation.
	• The Church that adds unwritten traditions to be received with equal affection and reverence as the Scriptures denies that the Scriptures are a rule to which nothing is to be added and from which nothing is to be taken.
• ••The Nature of the Foundation••
	• The unity and perfection of Christ's sacrifice are denied by adding another propitiatory sacrifice.
	• Sewing on other merits to the merit of Christ denies that his righteousness is sufficient for us.
• ••The Importance of the Foundation••
	• Since the unity belongs to the nature of the foundation, no other can be laid beside that which is laid (1 Corinthians 3:11).
	• There is no salvation in any other than Christ (Acts 4:12).
	• No one can add anything to the foundation without overthrowing it.

••II. The Roman Bishop's Authority••

• The Roman bishop held the first place among the patriarchs for various reasons.

••III. The First Place and First Rank••

• The first place (tÃ  protÄ“ia) and first rank (tÃ  presbeia) were assigned to the Roman bishop.

••V. The Council of Nicaea••

• In the Council of Nicaea, it was decreed that the order of ecclesiastical provinces should follow the civil and political arrangements.
• This meant that the Roman bishop obtained the first place (tÃ  presbeia) or primacy of order because he was the bishop of the city that held dominion over the world.

••VI. The Council of Chalcedon••

• In the Council of Chalcedon, it was decreed that the order of ecclesiastical provinces should follow the civil and political arrangements.
• This reinforced the Roman bishop's position as the first among the patriarchs.

••VII. The Roman Bishop's Succession••

• The Roman bishop did not obtain the first place because he was the successor of Peter.

••VIII. The Meaning of the Words••

• The words themselves do not indicate that the authority of the bishop of Alexandria should be found in the power of the Roman bishop.

• Bellarmine's gloss is absurd because it contradicts the testimony of all manuscripts and the meaning of the words themselves.
• The gloss implies that the authority of the bishop of Alexandria should be found in the power of the Roman bishop, rather than in custom.

••X. Conclusion••

• The Roman bishop's position as the first among the patriarchs was derived from the dignity of the city of Rome, rather than from his succession to Peter.
• The absurdity of Bellarmine's gloss lies in its contradiction of the testimony of all manuscripts and the meaning of the words themselves.

	• This is evident in various passages, including Acts 20:28 and 1 Timothy 3:2

	• In Acts 20:28, Paul addresses the Ephesian presbyters as "bishops"
	• In Philippians 1:1, the apostle Paul salutes all the saints in Philippi, together with the bishops and deacons

	• There is no indication in Scripture that bishops and presbyters are distinct offices
	• The apostle Paul would not have omitted mentioning presbyters if they were a distinct office

	• The qualities of a presbyter are the same as those of a bishop
	• This is evident in 1 Timothy 3:2, where the apostle Paul teaches that a bishop must be blameless

	• The passage in Titus 1:5-7 confirms that the apostle Paul left Titus in Crete to ordain elders (presbyterous katapolin) in every city
	• The apostle Paul teaches what those presbyters ought to be in Titus 1:7
• ••No distinction in virtue••
	• The apostle Paul teaches that a bishop must be blameless, but does not mention presbyters
	• This suggests that the apostle Paul did not consider presbyters to be a distinct office

	• Greek scholars interpret the presbyters as being the same as bishops (presbyterous toous episkopous kalei)
	• This interpretation is supported by other scholars, such as Jerome
• ••Conclusion••
	• The evidence from Scripture suggests that the terms "bishop" and "presbyter" are interchangeable
	• There is no indication in Scripture that bishops and presbyters are distinct offices.

	• The first is common to all Christians, since there is no one who is not called lawfully by his baptism (both for the glory of God and for his salvation) to reject the errors opposed to the nature and purity of true faith and to stir up his brethren to that very thing
• ••Distinguishing the Call••
	• The call to reform is not common to all, but peculiar to those only who are specially called to it
	• No one ought to obtrude himself into it
• ••Reason for the Distinction••
	• A reform consists in acts of faith and love which belong to all and from which no one can be excused because no one can say that he is not bound to exercise faith and love
• ••Public Authority••
	• The preaching of the word, the administration of the sacraments, and the exercise of discipline are acts of public authority, which no one ought to perform in his own name (but in another's) and which therefore demand a peculiar call (which may confer such a power)
• ••Ministry with Respect to its Essence and Accidents••
	• The sacred ministry can be considered either with respect to its essence and those things which are necessarily required to constitute it; or with respect to its accidents, which pertain to its good or bad state and condition
• ••Essential and Non-Essential Aspects••
	• What is essential to the ministry cannot be changed without making another ministry
	• But the essence remaining untouched, it does not cease to be the same ministry, although a varied and manifold change may have taken place in the accidents
• ••Purpose of the Ministry••
	• The purpose of the ministry is placed in this â€“ that all saving truth pertaining to the conservation of faith and piety be retained and taught

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. The Right to Call Bishops••

• The right to call bishops is not only reserved for the church or assembly of believers, but also for presbyters themselves.
• This right is transferred to bishops alone, descending in an uninterrupted succession, especially to the Roman Pope or ecumenical bishop of the whole church.

••II. Council of Trent Decrees••

• The Council of Trent decrees that:
	• Neither the consent nor call of the people, nor of any secular power and magistrate, is required for the ordination of bishops, priests, and other orders.
	• The ordination is invalid without it.
	• Those who enter this ministry, being called and instituted only by the people or a secular power and magistrate, are not to be regarded as ministers of the church, but as thieves and robbers.

••III. Bellarmine's Opinion••

• Bellarmine says that all Catholics teach with entire unanimity that the right to ordain and call bishops cannot belong to the people.
• However, the right to elect was sometimes and in some measure with the people, but by the concession and condescension of the popes, not by divine law.

••IV. The Fountain of Error••

• The Romanists' fountain of error is the false idea of the call, conceiving it to be a sacrament, which they call the sacrament of order.
• Hence, at one time, the opinion arises that the people cannot confer a sacrament.
• They hold that this sacrament impresses an indelible mark, which is a physical quality inhering in the mind of the pastor.
• They contend that Christ and the apostles deposited this sacrament in the hands of the bishops so that it could be dispensed by no one except themselves.

••V. Our Opinion••

• Our opinion is that the right to call belongs originally and radically to the church, with whom Christ deposited it to be exercised.
• However, by the rulers in the name of the church, as the royal official, this right is usurped.

••VI. The Sacrament of Order••

• The Romanists consider the call to be a sacrament, which they call the sacrament of order.
• They believe that this sacrament is a physical quality inhering in the mind of the pastor.

••VII. The Indelible Mark••

• The Romanists believe that this sacrament impresses an indelible mark, which cannot be erased.

••VIII. The Deposit of Christ and the Apostles••

• The Romanists believe that Christ and the apostles deposited this sacrament in the hands of the bishops.

••IX. The Right to Dispense••

• The Romanists believe that only the bishops have the right to dispense this sacrament.

••X. Our Rebuttal••

• Our opinion is that the right to call belongs originally and radically to the church, and not to the bishops or secular powers.

Here are 10 concise bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••1. Polygamy and Marriage••

• The Romans and other Gentiles practiced polygamy, but it was not a just or fitting cause for the apostle to disapprove of it.
• Although polygamy might be tolerated in some measure, it was not to be corrected, even if it was vicious.

••2. Marriage as a Primeval Institution••

• The power to marry was given to all without exception, both by divine right and by the right of nature.
• This is evident from the desire implanted in all to have a helper worthy of himself and to see children and propagate the race in them.

••3. Natural Law and Marriage••

• No law can be shown that can abrogate this right so solemnly given.
• As no one can hinder the natural inclination of conservation by meat and drink, so no one can be bound not to take a wife, especially under a necessity so urgent as a remedy of incontinence.

••4. Christ's Confirmation of Marriage••

• Christ repeated, confirmed, and vindicated that primeval institution which was common to all (Matthew 19:4, 5; 5:27).
• The apostle prescribed rules of living for husbands and wives without distinction of political and ecclesiastical order among Christians (Ephesians 5, 6; 1 Peter 3).

••5. Marriage as a Necessary Institution••

• Although the concept concerning marriage is affirmative, it does not follow that it can be abrogated with respect to some and a contrary law imposed upon them.
• Especially in an urgent case of necessity, not only for the good of propagation, that the human race may not perish, but also to prevent fornication in those who do not have the gift of continence.

••6. The Two-Fold Right of Nature••

• There is a two-fold right of nature: one, which all must use; the other, from which no one is to be kept, of which kind is matrimony.

••7. Celibacy and Marriage••

• The evil attending celibacy is not to be considered as a reason for forbidding marriage.
• The apostle's prescription of rules for living for husbands and wives does not imply that marriage is to be forbidden.

••8. The Right of Nature and Marriage••

• The right of nature must be used by all, but no one should be prevented from using it.
• The two-fold right of nature is one, which all must use; the other, from which no one is to be kept, of which kind is matrimony.

••9. Marriage and Propagation••

• Marriage is necessary for the propagation of the human race.
• The apostle's prescription of rules for living for husbands and wives implies that marriage is necessary for the good of propagation.

••10. The Importance of Marriage••

• Marriage is a primeval institution that is necessary for the propagation of the human race.
• The apostle's prescription of rules for living for husbands and wives implies that marriage is necessary for the good of propagation and to prevent fornication in those who do not have the gift of continence.

••I. Definition of a Sacrament••

• A sacrament is constituted intrinsically and extrinsically, whether as essential parts or necessary conditions.
• There are four principal elements:
	• The external and visible element with the rite
	• The heavenly and spiritual thing contained in the promise of grace
	• The divine institution (and that immediate) that it may be a sacrament
	• The stated and ordinary use of it in the church

••II. Constituents of a Sacrament••

• A sacrament is constituted intrinsically from the element with the rite and the word of the promise of grace as essential parts.
• A sacrament is constituted extrinsically from the divine institution as the efficient and immediate cause, and from the stated and ordinary use of the testimony and sealing in the church as the proximate end.

••III. Examples of Sacraments••

• The sacraments of the Old and New Testaments are examples of the divine institution and the external sign with some rite annexed.

	• Circumcision (Genesis 17:9-14)
	• The Passover (Exodus 12:3-20)
	• Baptism (Matthew 28:19)
	• The Supper (Matthew 26:26-28)

	• The necessity of the sacraments of institution

	• The Catholic Church affirms the efficacy of sacraments as signs and seals of grace.
	• The sacraments are not external badges of profession, but rather instruments of God's grace.

••I. Nature of Signs and Seals••

• Signs and seals are expressions of the covenant of grace
	• Contain nothing in themselves
	• Do not confer anything by inherent virtue
	• Signify the grace already bestowed or to be bestowed
• There is a difference between significance and efficiency
	• Miraculous signs (e.g. rainbow, fleece of Gideon) signify and seal, but contain nothing in themselves

••II. Purpose of Sacraments••

• Sacraments presuppose grace
	• Cannot operate or confer by inherent power
	• Presuppose or demand something before hand in the subject (e.g. regeneration and justification)
• God does not will sacraments to be administered promiscuously to adults, but to those who believe and are partakers of grace by faith

••III. Word and Sacraments••

• The word does not confer grace by any power implanted in the sound or letters
	• But by the power of the Spirit who accompanies it
• The same relation exists between the word and sacraments, and they confer grace in the same way
	• As external means which God uses to bestow grace upon us

••IV. Baptism••

• Baptism is a sign and seal of the remission of sins
	• For those who have already believed and received remission of sins by faith
	• Not for infants of unbelievers, but for infants of believers

••V. Circumcision••

• Circumcision is a sign and seal of the righteousness of faith
	• For Abraham, who had not yet been circumcised
	• Signified the righteousness of faith which he had

••VI. Word and Spirit••

• The word does not confer grace by any power implanted in the sound or letters
	• But by the power of the Spirit who accompanies it
• The same relation exists between the word and sacraments, and they confer grace in the same way
	• As external means which God uses to bestow grace upon us

••VII. Sacraments and Faith••

• Sacraments presuppose faith
	• Not faith as a condition, but faith as a result
• The sacraments are not a means of obtaining faith, but a means of confirming and sealing faith

••VIII. Word and Sacraments••

• The word and sacraments are not two separate means of grace
	• But two external means which God uses to bestow grace upon us

	• The former have the promise of grace, but the latter contain the reality of grace.
• ••The Certainty of the Sacraments of the New Testament••
	• The certainty concerning the sacraments of the New Testament arises only from the institution of Christ.
	• If the sacraments are administered, it is certain that the thing itself in the legitimate use is sealed and conferred.

	• The nature of the sacraments is to seal and confer the thing itself in the legitimate use.
	• The sacraments are not just a picture or a symbol, but a real and effective means of conveying God's grace.

• ••The Question of the Sacraments••
	• The question of whether the sacraments of the Old and New Testaments are the same or different is complex.
	• The answer depends on the context and the perspective of the interpreter.
• ••The Romanist Perspective••
	• The Romanists (Catholics) emphasize the efficacy of the sacraments of the New Testament.
	• They downplay the significance of the sacraments of the Old Testament, making them only shadows and figures of the grace conferred by the sacraments of the New Testament.
• ••The Difference between the Old and New Testaments••
	• The difference between the sacraments of the Old and New Testaments is not abolished, unless the latter effect what the former signified.
	• The difference is not in the efficient cause and author (God), but in various particulars.
• ••Similarities between the Old and New Testaments••
	• The same thing is signified (Christ with his benefits).
	• The same instrument of application (faith).
	• The same word of command and promise, although not the same words in both.
	• The same end and effect, and mode of operation (signification and sealing).
• ••Differences between the Old and New Testaments••
	• In external signs and rites.
	• In number, the Old Testament had more, ordinary and extraordinary, while the New Testament has fewer, more restricted, and more excellent.
	• In the facility of using, the New Testament surpasses the Old, as appears from a comparison of baptism with circumcision.
	• In the mode of signifying, the Old Testament had respect to and shadowed forth Christ to come, while the New Testament regards Christ as having come.
	• In the amplitude of object, the Old Testament was bound to the posterity of Abraham alone, while the New Testament pertains to all the Gentiles.
	• In duration, the Old Testament was to continue until the time of reformation (diorthÅsÄ“) or the advent of Christ, while the New Testament is to continue until the end of the world.
	• In clearness and perspicuity, not so much from the matter of the signs, as from the institution of the added word, which is far clearer in the New Testament than in the Old.

••I. Baptistia and Baptism••

• The term "baptistia" was used by Justin Martyr to describe the Pharisees' practice of daily baptism.
	• This practice was seen as a way to be cleansed and purified from all sin.

••II. Metaphorical Meanings of Baptism••

• Two metaphorical meanings of baptism are derived from its traditional significance:
	• Baptism as affliction and calamity, compared to floods of water in Scripture.
	• Baptism as a transfer of gifts, similar to the effusion of the Holy Spirit.

••III. Vicarious Baptism••

• Some interpret baptism as vicarious, referring to the baptism of the dead:
	• This could refer to the suffering of martyrs or confessors.
	• Or, it could refer to the resurrection of the dead.

••IV. Baptism of the Sick••

• In ancient times, baptism was also practiced on the sick in bed:
	• This was seen as a way to cleanse and purify the soul.

••V. Homonymy••

• The term "baptism" has multiple meanings, leading to homonymy:
	• This can lead to confusion and different interpretations.

••VI. Transference of Gifts••

• Baptism can be seen as a transfer of gifts, similar to the effusion of the Holy Spirit:
	• This is based on the idea that the Holy Spirit is poured out on the soul.

••VII. Old Testament Precedents••

• The Old Testament uses water as a metaphor for the communication of the Spirit:
	• This is seen in passages such as Isaiah 44:3 and Joel 2:28.

••VIII. Distinction between Baptistia and Baptism••

• The distinction between baptistia and baptism is based on the different meanings of the term:
	• Baptistia refers to the traditional significance of baptism, while baptism refers to the specific practice of immersion.

••IX. Interpretations of 1 Corinthians 15:29••

• The passage in 1 Corinthians 15:29 is interpreted in different ways:
	• Some see it as referring to the baptism of the dead, while others see it as referring to vicarious baptism.

••X. Conclusion••

• The term "baptism" has multiple meanings and interpretations:
	• This can lead to confusion and different understandings of the practice.

• Baptism belongs to those who are to be taught (not just unbelievers)
• Christ joined instruction with baptism in consideration of the condition of the time
• Unbelievers alone are not taught that they may become believers, but believers, adults as well as the younger, in order to become proficient and persevering in faith and declare themselves more and more by their works to be disciples of Christ

• A great part of those recorded to have been baptized by the apostles were unbelievers (because the Christian church was still to be constituted)

••V. The Opinion of the Romanists••

• The Romanists contend for the absolute necessity of baptism, which they hold to be such and so great that they exclude from the kingdom of heaven all who are deprived of baptism, even if that has happened through no fault or contempt of the divine command

••VI. The Council of Trent••

• The Council of Trent sets forth its meaning in these words: "If anyone should say that baptism is free, that is, not necessary for salvation, let him be accursed" (Session 7)

• ••The Distinction between Origin and Validity••
	• The question of whether baptism administered by heretics is lawful is distinct from the question of its validity.
	• The validity of baptism is a matter of debate among the early church fathers.
• ••The Importance of Re-baptism••
	• Some believe that those who approach the Catholic faith after being baptized by heretics should be rebaptized.
	• This is seen as a way of ensuring that they are truly baptized into the Catholic Church.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

• ••I. Validity of Baptism••
	• The baptism administered by a heretic is valid if the essentials of baptism are retained.
	• The sacrament is the property of the church, which is administered in her name and faith.
• ••II. Hidden Error of the Minister••
	• The hidden error of the minister does not detract from the integrity of the baptism.
	• The essentials of baptism must be observed, and nothing can be changed or corrupted in the word or element.
• ••III. Validity of Baptism in an Orthodox Church••
	• Baptism administered in an orthodox church by a minister imbued with Antitrinitarian or Jewish errors (but not detected) is valid.
	• The public faith of the church is to be considered, into which he (who is baptized) is introduced and the promises made to him by Christ.
• ••IV. Reasons for Validity••
	• The essentials remain as much as to form as to matter (the word with the element and the formula prescribed by Christ).
	• Neither the prophets, nor Christ, nor the apostles ever reprehended circumcision as void which had been performed in the Jewish church by idolatrous and heretical priests.
• ••V. Examples and Precedents••
	• The example of Zipporah teaches that an invalid circumcision as to men is valid with God.
	• We do not read of anyone who were baptized by heretics having been rebaptized by the apostles.
• ••VI. Heretics and True Membership••
	• Although heretics are not true members of the invisible church, that does not hinder them from administering true baptism provided they retain its essentials.
	• They accommodate the tongue and hand only in this act to God.
• ••VII. God's Role in Baptism••
	• It is God who baptizes and who is efficacious through the minister.
	• As God through a corrupt ministry
• ••VIII. Validity of Baptism in Heretical Churches••
	• Baptism administered by heretics who retain the fundamentals of baptism is valid.
	• Although they may err on various articles of faith, and their baptism may be mixed up with various extraneous rites in accidents.
• ••IX. No Re-baptism••
	• We do not read of anyone who were baptized by heretics having been rebaptized by the apostles.
• ••X. Conclusion••
	• The validity of baptism is not dependent on the minister, but on the essentials of the sacrament being observed.

• ••Orthodox Opinion••
	• Some difference should be made between John's baptism and Christ's baptism
	• However, this difference should be accidental with respect to circumstances and degree, not substantial and specific with respect to essence
• ••Reasons for the Difference••
	• The mode of exhibition and measure of gifts, not the thing itself

	• The waters of John's baptism were not as rich in gifts as the baptism of the apostles, where there was a greater and often visible manifestation of the Holy Spirit

	• Remission of sins is not a new thing, but a repetition of the same thing.
	• It is not a new act, but a renewal of the same act.
• ••The Effect of Baptism••
	• Baptism has a perpetual effect, and its sealing power lasts forever.
	• It is not a momentary thing, but a lasting one.
• ••The Relationship Between Baptism and Repentance••
	• Baptism is the sacrament of repentance, and repentance is the fruit of baptism.
	• Repentance is not the cause of baptism, but the effect of it.
