Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. The Covenant Pertains to Infants••

• The covenant of God pertains to infants from the clause of the covenant.
	• The promise is unto you and to your children (Acts 2:39)
	• The covenant is primarily and principally to adults, but also to infants.

••II. Reasons Why the Covenant Pertains to Infants••

• From the order of God, because He wished His grace to be extended from parents to their children.
• From the nature of the thing, because children are a part of their parents and of the same condition with them.
• Among men, pacts embrace the children of the contracting parties; therefore also in God's covenant.
• Because to infants belongs the thing signified (remission of sins, regeneration, the kingdom of heaven); therefore also the sign.

••III. The Sign of the Covenant••

• The sign of the covenant is baptism, which is a washing of regeneration (John 3:5).
• The sign of the covenant is not limited to adults, but also to infants.

••IV. The Lord's Supper••

• The Lord's Supper should also be administered to infants because the thing signified belongs to them.
• Although the same thing is signified in both the Lord's Supper and baptism, there is a difference in the manner of signifying.
• In the Lord's Supper, the grace of Christ is sealed by way of solid food, which infants are not capable of receiving.
• In baptism, it is signified by way of the washing of regeneration, which they are.

••V. The Lord's Supper and Baptism••

• The Lord's Supper demands a two-fold condition: a preceding examination and a concurrent commemoration of the death of Christ, both of which presuppose the use of reason.
• Neither of these conditions is required in baptism; therefore, formerly the Passover was distinguished from circumcision, that the latter was administered to infants and the former to adults alone.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. The Creator and Creation••

• The Creator blesses creation when He presents it with good and affects it with blessing.
	• The blessing of God is operative and inculcates His benevolence.
	• When He blesses, He does what He says (Augustine, Psalm 103:1-3).

••II. The Creature Blessing the Creator••

• The creature blesses the Creator when he piously celebrates His blessings and Him.
	• This is seen in the formulas found everywhere in the Psalms: "Bless the Lord, O my soul" (Psalm 103:1, 104:1, 35).
	• The divine blessing always anticipates the human, and God is blessed because He has blessed us (Ephesians 1:3).

••III. The Creature Blessing a Creature••

• The creature blesses a creature when he desires good things for it and wishes it well.
	• This blessing is proposed in the words, now of one asking (when the speech is directed to God, as in Deuteronomy 33:11), now of one wishing (when it is directed to the creature, as in Numbers 6:24).
	• The blessing has reference either to persons, by wish (when we wish them well); or to things, by sanctification.

••IV. The Two-Fold Relation in Sacramental Blessing••

• In this sacramental blessing, a two-fold relation (schema) must be attended to:
	• The first to God, that thanks may be given to Him for the wonderful blessing of the whole work of redemption because He sent Christ into the world and delivered Him to death and because He gives Him to us for vivifying food.
	• The second to the symbols, that a blessing may be obtained upon the creatures spread before us (and soon to be extended to believers) in virtue of which they (otherwise of themselves incapable of it) may be rendered effective to the spiritual use and benefit of the recipients.

••I. The Problem of Predication••

• The subject (Christ) cannot be predicated in a proper way because it does not belong to any of the categories (genus, species, property, accident).
	• The body of Christ is neither genus, species, property, nor accident of the bread.

••II. Consequences of Predication••

• If the bread is said to be the body of Christ, it would imply:
	• All attributes of Christ's body belong to the bread (e.g. born, died, rose again).
	• All attributes of the bread belong to Christ's body (e.g. sown, reaped, ground, baked).
	• Christ took and broke his own body and poured out his blood before being crucified.
	• Breaking the body of Christ and pouring out his blood today would be meaningless since he has risen and is in a state of glory.

••III. The Sign of the Sacraments••

• The bread and wine are signs, not the things signified.
• The body and blood are the things signified, not the signs.
• Unless the enunciation is explained, it will not be sacramental and the nature of the sacraments will be overturned.

••IV. The Second Class of Arguments••

• The second class of arguments is drawn from the design of Christ, the state of the disciples, and the circumstances of the institution.
• The design of Christ was twofold:
	• General: to institute a sacrament of the New Testament.
	• Special: to substitute a new rite for the old, the holy Supper for the paschal lamb.

••V. The Two-Fold Argument••

• A two-fold argument arises from the twofold design:
	• The words are to be taken according to the mind and scope of the speaker.
	• The words are to be taken according to the literal and proper sense.

Here are 10 concise bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. The Lord's Supper••

• The Lord's Supper is a common food, not the Lord himself.
	• The bread and wine are symbols, not the actual body and blood of Christ.

••II. Dual Nature of the Lord's Supper••

• The Lord's Supper consists of two things: earthly and heavenly, corporal and spiritual.
	• It requires two distinct modes of perception.
	• The Scriptures often use one word with different significations.

••III. Union with Christ••

• Our bodies are united to Christ's body, but not necessarily orally.
	• The union is spiritual and mystical, not physical.
	• Faith and love are the means by which we participate in this union.

••IV. Faith and the Lord's Supper••

• Faith is necessary for the Lord's Supper to be effective.
	• Without faith, the Supper is useless to us.
	• The presence or absence of Christ does not depend on our faith or want of faith.

••V. Instrumentality of Faith••

• Faith is the instrument and means by which we receive Christ.
	• It is not a separate entity from Christ, but a subordinate one.
	• Faith is not a means of separating ourselves from Christ, but of uniting with him.

••VI. The Lord's Supper as a Mystery••

• The union with Christ is a great mystery.
	• It is not something that can be fully understood or explained.
	• It is a reality that is experienced through faith and love.

••VII. The Lord's Supper and Profanity••

• The Lord's Supper can be profaned by an unworthy approach.
	• This is not because of the Supper itself, but because of the attitude of the person approaching it.
	• The Supper is not a means of profaning itself, but of being profaned by human actions.

••VIII. The Lord's Supper and the Church••

• The Lord's Supper is not a separate entity from the Church.
	• It is an institution of Christ, and is to be celebrated according to his word.
	• The Church is the body of Christ, and the Lord's Supper is a means of participating in this body.

••IX. The Lord's Supper and the Individual••

• The Lord's Supper is not just a communal celebration, but also an individual experience.
	• Each person must approach the Supper with faith and love.
	• The Supper is not just a ritual, but a means of experiencing the presence of Christ.

••X. The Lord's Supper and Worship••

• The Lord's Supper is a means of worshiping Christ.
	• It is a way of expressing our love and gratitude to him.
	• It is a means of participating in the life of Christ, and experiencing his presence and power.

••5. Priesthood••

••I. The Concept of the "Last Things"••

• The "last things" refer to the ultimate events that will occur at the end of time
	• The end of the world
	• The consumption of time
	• The trumpet of God (1 Corinthians 15:52)

••II. The Four Comprehended Things••

• The four things that are commonly referred to as the "last things"
	• Death
	• The last judgment
	• The glory of heaven
	• The pain of hell

••III. The Resurrection of the Dead••

• The resurrection of the dead is one of the "last things"
	• There are two types of resurrection:
		- Metaphorical (regeneration and conversion to God)
		- Proper (bodily resurrection)

••IV. The Proper Resurrection••

• The proper resurrection refers to the bodily resurrection of all men
	• Good and bad alike
	• Will occur on the last day
	• Will be distinguished into two types:
		- Resurrection unto life and happiness
		- Resurrection unto death and condemnation

••V. The Resurrection of the Dead (continued)••

• The resurrection of the dead is not just a metaphorical or spiritual event
	• But a real and bodily event that will occur on the last day
	• Will involve the resurrection of all men, both good and bad

••VI. The Last Judgment••

• The last judgment is one of the "last things"
	• Will occur on the last day
	• Will involve the resurrection of the dead
	• Will be a time of judgment and reward or punishment

••VII. Eternal Life and Death••

• Eternal life and death are two of the "last things"
	• Will occur on the last day
	• Will involve the resurrection of the dead
	• Will be a time of eternal reward or punishment

••VIII. The End of the World••

• The end of the world is one of the "last things"
	• Will occur at the end of time
	• Will involve the consumption of time
	• Will be a time of judgment and reward or punishment

••IX. The Trumpet of God••

• The trumpet of God is a symbol of the last day
	• Will sound at the end of the world
	• Will signal the resurrection of the dead
	• Will be a time of judgment and reward or punishment

••X. The Importance of Meditating on the Last Things••

• The last things are important to meditate on
	• Will help us prepare for the end of the world
	• Will help us understand the nature of eternal life and death
	• Will help us live a life of faith and obedience to God.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••Interpretation of "deliverances"••
	• Refers to the renewal of the world (anakainismos)
	• Not an annihilation of the former world, but a change
	• Supported by Peter's interpretation (2 Peter 3:13) and comparison (purification from filthiness and renovation)

â€¢ ••Objection 1: "New heavens and new earth"••
	• The verb "to create" often implies restoration (e.g., Eph. 2:10, 2 Cor. 5:17, Ps. 51:10)
	• Things are often said to be "new" which are renewed (e.g., "new commandment", "new creation")
	• Therefore, "new heavens and new earth" means relatively and comparatively new, not absolutely and simply

â€¢ ••Objection 2: "The former shall not be remembered"••
	• According to Scripture style, the collection of old things will fade away
	• Greater and better things will succeed or joyful and prosperous things will take the place of sad ones
	• All memory of the former things is said to be absorbed, nay, extinguished

â€¢ ••Objection 3: "The heaven and earth will pass away"••
	• Not said that they will pass away as to substance and matter, but as to form and state
	• A change of form or state does not imply absolute destruction, but relatively and comparatively
	• A passing away which puts on another form, a different appearance; thus the world is rightly said to pass away because its form (schema) and figure pass away

â€¢ ••Change of qualities or state does not imply destruction••
	• A change of qualities or state does not imply absolute destruction, but relatively and comparatively
	• Aretas observes: "This does not prove the non-existence of the creation, but a change for the better"

â€¢ ••Scripture style and interpretation••
	• Scripture often uses phrases that imply a change or renewal, rather than absolute destruction
	• The phrase "new heavens and new earth" is an example of this

â€¢ ••Anakainismos and its meaning••
	• Anakainismos refers to the renewal of the world
	• Not an annihilation of the former world, but a change

â€¢ ••Peter's interpretation and comparison••
	• Peter quotes the phrase in 2 Peter 3:13
	• The comparison made is one of purification from filthiness and renovation

â€¢ ••Scripture examples of restoration and renewal••
	• Eph. 2:10: "created in Christ Jesus for good works"
	• 2 Cor. 5:17: "if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation"
	• Ps. 51:10: "Create in me a clean heart, O God"

â€¢ ••Conclusion••
	• The objections raised do not have force
	• The interpretation of "deliverances" and "new heavens and new earth" is supported by Scripture style and interpretation

â€¢ ••The Invisibility of God••
	• God neither has been seen nor can be seen by the bodily eyes.
	• The Scriptures enumerate invisibility among the essential and immutable properties of God.
	• The passages are: Col. 1:15, 1 Tim. 1:17, 6:16, Heb. 11:27, Ex. 33:20.

â€¢ ••The Incapacity of Human Sight••
	• Sight in the other life will succeed to faith (2 Cor. 5:7).
	• This is mental and intellectual, not sensual.
	• Neither the whole essence can be seen (because there is no proportion between the faculty and the object).

â€¢ ••The Limitations of Human Knowledge••
	• Human knowledge is limited and imperfect.
	• Human sight is limited to the natural and external, not the supernatural and spiritual.

â€¢ ••The Nature of God's Knowledge••
	• God's knowledge is intuitive and comprehensive.
	• God's knowledge is not limited by the proportion between the faculty and the object.
	• God's knowledge is not subject to the limitations of human sight.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••The nature of God's sight••
	• God's sight is not essential, but rather hypothetical (i.e., considered in relation to the incarnate Son of God with respect to his human nature)
	• This is also the meaning of the passage in 1 John 3:2

â€¢ ••The error of assuming God can be seen••
	• This error is not opposed by Job 19:25, where Job says he will see God with his eyes
	• However, Job is speaking of God considered not essentially, but hypothetically (i.e., in relation to the incarnate Son of God with respect to his human nature)

â€¢ ••The meaning of passages that speak of seeing God••
	• Passages that speak of seeing God, such as Psalm 16:11, 17:15, and 1 Corinthians 13:12, refer to a mental vision metaphorically
	• Or to a symbolic vision in God's works (Romans 1:20) or in assumed bodies (Genesis 32:24-32, Exodus 33:19-23, Isaiah 6:5)

â€¢ ••The resurrection and the eyes••
	• Although the resurrection will change the eyes, they will not become spirits, but remain corporeal
	• The body itself, although it becomes spiritual, is always a body

â€¢ ••The distance between God and created intellect••
	• God is not less distant infinitely from a created intellect than from bodily sight
	• If the created intellect is raised by supernatural light to know God intuitively, it does not follow that the bodily sight can also be raised to know God as to his essence

â€¢ ••The reason for this••
	• The reason is widely different
	• (a) The Scriptures teach that God is seen mentally, not ocularly
	• (b) God is by nature knowable, not visible
	• (c) A faculty can be elevated above its own natural grade by supernatural grace, but not above its own species and the object analogous to it

â€¢ ••God is not seen with a comprehensive vision••
	• God cannot be seen by the creature with an adequate and comprehensive vision
	• But only with an inadequate and apprehensive vision because the finite is not capable of the infinite

â€¢ ••The incomprehensibility of God••
	• The deity is incomprehensible (akatalÄ“ptos to theion)
	• This is said by John of Damascus (Exposition of the Orthodox Faith 1.4)

â€¢ ••The saints as apprehenders••

â€¢ ••The race having been finished••

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Introduction••

• The text discusses the concept of transformation and its relation to the gifts and qualities of the blessed
• The transformation is not a change of substance, but a change in reference to qualities

••II. Transformation••

• The verb "metaschematize" (used by Paul in Phil. 3:21) is often taken for a change of accidents merely
• Just as schema also properly signifies an external appearance and habit (1 Cor. 7:31; Phil. 2:8)
• Christ is said to have been "transformed" (metamorphÅthÄ“is) before his disciples (Mt. 17:2), when his face shone as the sun
• The transformation is not a destruction of the substance of his body, but "because the fashion of his content was altered" (Lk. 9:29)

••III. Gifts and Qualities••

• Some enumerate more, others fewer gifts and qualities belonging to the blessed
• The Scholastics commonly reduce them to four, which are so many properties of the light which will shine in the bodies of the blessed (viz., splendor, impassibility, subtlety, and agility)

••IV. Incorruptibility••

• The first quality ascribed to them is incorruptibility (aphtharsia)
• This consists of:
	• Immortality, inasmuch as they cannot be corrupted as to parts, nor dissolved as to the whole body because mortality will be swallowed up by life (2 Cor. 5:4)
	• The corruptible must put on incorruptibility, and the mortal must put on immortality (1 Cor. 15:42-44)

••V. Impassibility••

• Impassibility answers to incorruption
• It is the quality that corresponds to glory
• We must say something of each of these according to the order of the apostle

••VI. Splendor••

• Splendor answers to glory
• It is the quality that corresponds to impassibility
• We must say something of each of these according to the order of the apostle

••VII. Agility••

• Agility answers to power
• It is the quality that corresponds to subtlety
• We must say something of each of these according to the order of the apostle

••VIII. Subtlety••

• Subtlety answers to spiritual
• It is the quality that corresponds to agility
• We must say something of each of these according to the order of the apostle

••IX. Conclusion••

• The text discusses the concept of transformation and its relation to the gifts and qualities of the blessed
• The transformation is not a change of substance, but a change in reference to qualities

••X. Final Thoughts••

• The blessed will be transformed into the likeness of Christ's glorious body
• The gifts and qualities of the blessed will shine in their bodies
• The text concludes with a discussion of the qualities of the blessed, including incorruptibility, impassibility, splendor, agility, and subtlety.

• ••Distinguishing immortality••
	• From the immortality of God, who is essentially and absolutely immortal
	• From the immortality of Adam, which was the power not to die
	• From the immortality of angels and souls, which is by the grace of creation and on account of their immaterial and spiritual essence
	• From the immortality of the damned, by which they live forever and may die forever
• ••The nature of immortality••
	• The former immortality takes away the act of dying, but does not exclude all power of dying (at least remotely)
	• The latter abolishes both

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Immortality and Punishment••

• The immortality of the wicked is not a blessing, but a punishment and a form of death itself.
• They will be tormented in soul, just as they were in body, but this will be joined with an inability to suffer.

••II. Impassibility••

• The immortality of the wicked is also characterized by impassibility, meaning they will be subject to no passions at all.
• This is because they will no longer have the tinder of concupiscence, the defilement of sin, or inordinate desire.

••III. Perfection and Health••

• The immortality of the saints, on the other hand, will be characterized by perfection and health.
• They will be free from all disease and misery, and will possess all good.

••IV. Brightness and Glory••

• The second quality attributed to glorified bodies is brightness and glory, opposed to ignominy.
• This will consist of a splendor and beauty of the body, by which they will shine and glitter like the stars and the sun.

••V. No Suffering••

• Neither from within nor from without will they suffer anything.
• Perfect health and a good state (eusebeia) of body will keep them free from all disease.

••VI. No Evil••

• An entire removal of all evils and the possession of all good will deliver them from all misery and danger.

••VII. No Hunger or Thirst••

• They will no longer hunger or thirst.
• Neither the sun nor any heat will shine on them.

••VIII. No Death or Sorrow••

• There will be no more death, nor sorrow, nor crying, nor pain.
• This is because they will be free from all evil and possess all good.

••IX. No Danger••

• They will be kept safe from all danger by divine irradiation.
• They will be free from all necessity and evil.

••X. Splendor and Beauty••

• Their bodies will shine with a splendor and beauty, like the stars and the sun.
• This will be a glory that is worthy of their Father.

Here are 10 bullets and sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. The Resurrection Body••

• The resurrection body is capable of being looked at by mortal eyes.
• A specimen of this was exhibited under the Old Testament in the case of Moses, whose face shone with great light and brightness after his interview with God.
• The same specimen, but more illustrious, was given under the New Testament in the transfiguration of Christ.

••II. Glory••

• The glory of God will flow from the blessed vision of God, whom we will see face to face.
• The glory will also flow from the glorious view of Christ exalted in his kingdom.
• The glory will be nothing else than the irradiation of God's glory, from which the bodies will be made to shine.

••III. Power••

• The third quality is power and strength.
• "It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power" (1 Cor 15:43).
• "As Christ was crucified through weakness, yet he lived by the power of God. So we also are weak in him, but we shall live with him by the power of God towards you" (2 Cor 13:4).

••IV. Strength and Vigor••

• The power will be placed in the strength of the bodies, which will be strong and vigorous.
• The bodies will be able to effect anything (which can be effected by a creature).
• The bodies will be able to move themselves most readily from place to place, to ascend or descend (as is clear from the example of Christ).

••V. Agility and Velocity••

• The power will also be placed in the agility and velocity by which the bodies will be able to move themselves.
• The bodies will be able to ascend or descend, as is clear from the example of Christ.

••VI. Removal of Weakness••

• Both depend on the removal of the causes of weakness.
• There will be nothing whatever, either within or without, which will be able to interfere with the soundness, strength, and firmness of the glorious bodies.

••VII. Integrity••

• The glorious bodies will grow into that state which is exactly becoming to the glorious bodies and the most perfect operations of the happy souls in them.
• In that best and most perfect state, no imperfection ought to remain.

••VIII. Perfection of Health••

• The glorious bodies will not only be perfect in health, but also in absolute integrity.

••IX. Perfection of Operations••

• The glorious bodies will be perfect in the most perfect operations of the happy souls in them.

••X. No Imperfection••

• In that best and most perfect state, no imperfection ought to remain.

• There are different degrees and kinds of glory, not just a single level of glory

• The purpose of distinct mansions is not to create a sense of competition or rivalry, but rather to highlight the diversity and complexity of the kingdom of heaven
• The distinct mansions are meant to reflect the different levels and kinds of glory that exist in the kingdom of heaven.

• ••Definition of Scholasticism••
	• Scholasticism is a method of approaching and thinking about theological thoughts in a "school" fashion.
	• It involves arranging theological thoughts in terms of questions, propositions, and sources of solution.
• ••Francis Turretin's Work••
	• Turretin's work is a basic instruction in theology.
	• He entitled his work an "Institutio" (Institution), suggesting foundational or basic instruction.
• ••Elenctic Theology••
	• Elenctic theology is derived from the Greek word for that which exposes error.
	• It is polemical theology, devoted to refutation of errors.
	• However, Turretin is not only concerned with refutation of error, but also with the statement of truth.
• ••Turretin's Twenty Loci••
	• The first two of Turretin's twenty loci deal with the formal principle of the Reformation: the object and nature of theology and the doctrine of Scripture.
	• The material element of the Reformation is dealt with in topics 3-20.
• ••Content of Turretin's Work••
	• Turretin's work covers topics such as theology, God's decrees, creation, providence, angels, man, sin, free will, the law, the covenant of grace, the person of Christ, the mediatorial office of Christ, calling and faith, justification, sanctification and good works, the church, sacraments, and eschatology.
• ••Organization of Turretin's Work••
	• Each of the twenty loci is subdivided into various questions.
	• Turretin usually begins and ends with God.
• ••Turretin's Method••
	• Turretin's method involves the dialectic of introducing opposing points of view.
	• This is intended to focus discussion on the question.
• ••Calvinism and Scholasticism••
	• Calvinism and scholasticism are synonymous with precision.
	• Francis Turretin was a Calvinistic scholastic theologian in an age of Protestant, Catholic, Lutheran, and Socinian scholastics.

• ••Early Life••
	• Born on June 6, 1822, in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania
	• Moved to Baltimore, Maryland, at an early age
	• Lived with his maternal uncle, Dr. George W. Musgrave
• ••Education••
	• Attended the Baltimore Academy under Mr. John Prentiss
	• Enrolled in the College of New Jersey at Princeton in 1838
	• Graduated with a Bachelor of Arts in 1841
	• Matriculated at the Princeton Theological Seminary in 1841
	• Graduated in 1844
• ••Career••
	• Found employment as a tutor at the College of New Jersey (Princeton University) from 1844 to 1846
	• Served as Assistant Professor of Mathematics from 1846 to 1847
	• Appointed Adjunct Professor of Greek in 1847
	• Served in this capacity until 1854
	• Appointed Professor of Latin Language and Literature in 1854
	• Held this position until 1865
• ••Additional Responsibilities••
	• Also lectured in architecture for several years before his retirement
	• Named Professor Emeritus of Latin and Lecturer Extraordinary in Architecture at the College in 1865
• ••Personal Life••
	• Described as a "small, delicate, dark man" with piercing eyes and long flowing hair
	• Kept a personal receipt book that contains receipts for fine hats and coats, as well as periodic payments for laundry service
• ••Religious Life••
	• Professed his faith in March 1841 at Third Presbyterian Church, Baltimore, Maryland
	• Received as a candidate for the ministry on September 9, 1841, by the Presbyterian Church of Baltimore (PCUSA)
	• Licensed to preach the "everlasting gospel" on June 13, 1843, by the same PCUSA
• ••Later Life••
	• Retired due to ill health
	• Died of consumption on October 11, 1865, at the home of his uncle, Dr. Musgrave, in Philadelphia
• ••Legacy••
	• Described as a man of sartorial polish by Thomas Wertenbaker
	• Attended Second Presbyterian Church, Princeton, for his pew rent payments in 1855 and 1856

		- Ambrose, Ambrosius, and others

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

• ••Augustine's Works••
	• Wrote against various heresies and sects, including the Donatists, Pelagians, and Manichaeans
	• Defended the Catholic faith against various opponents
• ••Against the Donatists••
	• Wrote several works against the Donatists, including "Against the Donatists" and "On the Grace of God"
	• Argued that the Donatists were heretics who rejected the authority of the Catholic Church
• ••Against the Pelagians••
	• Wrote several works against the Pelagians, including "Against the Two Letters of the Pelagians" and "On the Grace of God"
	• Argued that the Pelagians were heretics who rejected the doctrine of original sin and the necessity of divine grace
• ••Against the Manichaeans••
	• Wrote several works against the Manichaeans, including "Against the Epistle of Manichaeus Called Fundamental" and "On the Nature of the Soul"
	• Argued that the Manichaeans were heretics who rejected the doctrine of the Trinity and the divinity of Christ
• ••The City of God••
	• Wrote a comprehensive work on the nature of the Church and the City of God
	• Argued that the Church is the true City of God, and that it is the source of all true wisdom and knowledge
• ••The Christian Instruction••
	• Wrote a work on the nature of Christian instruction and the importance of faith and reason
	• Argued that faith and reason are both necessary for a complete understanding of the Christian faith
• ••Against the Arians••
	• Wrote several works against the Arians, including "Against the Arians" and "On the Trinity"
	• Argued that the Arians were heretics who rejected the divinity of Christ and the doctrine of the Trinity
• ••Against the Eunomians••
	• Wrote several works against the Eunomians, including "Against the Eunomians" and "On the Trinity"
	• Argued that the Eunomians were heretics who rejected the doctrine of the Trinity and the divinity of Christ
• ••Against the Priscillianists••
	• Wrote several works against the Priscillianists, including "Against the Priscillianists" and "On the Nature of the Soul"
	• Argued that the Priscillianists were heretics who rejected the doctrine of the Trinity and the divinity of Christ
• ••Other Works••
	• Wrote several other works on various topics, including the nature of the Church, the importance of faith and reason, and the nature of the soul.
